title: [codex] add worktree cleanup command
body:
## Summary

Adds a workspace-configurable worktree cleanup command that runs during task archive before ctx removes a managed task worktree. The command shares the worktree lifecycle execution path used by bootstrap, receives the worktree environment plus `CTX_TASK_ID`, and fails closed: if cleanup exits nonzero, times out, or cannot spawn, ctx marks archive cleanup failed and preserves the managed worktree root for recovery.

The existing worktree bootstrap config endpoint is extended with `cleanup_command` and `cleanup_timeout_sec`, and Settings now presents the section as Worktree Lifecycle with setup and cleanup controls.

title: Add Homebrew cask for the macOS desktop app
body:
## Summary

- Adds a Homebrew cask (`packaging/homebrew/Casks/ctx.rb`) so macOS users can install ctx with `brew install --cask`.
- Resolves the Apple Silicon and Intel DMGs from the stable release channel with their published SHA256 checksums, and selects the right architecture automatically.
- Adds a `livecheck` block that reads `latest_version` from the release manifest so new versions are detected, plus a `zap` stanza that removes `~/.ctx` and app caches on uninstall.
- Adds `packaging/homebrew/README.md` documenting direct installation and how to publish the cask to a `ctxrs/homebrew-tap`.

## Why

Closes #3. Today the only install path is `curl https://ctx.rs/install | sh`; a cask gives macOS users a first-class `brew` install/upgrade/uninstall flow.

## Validation

- [x] `brew style packaging/homebrew/Casks/ctx.rb` — no offenses
- [x] `brew audit --cask` — passes
- [x] `brew audit --cask --online` — downloads both DMGs and verifies the checksums

## Notes

Homebrew discovers casks through taps, not application repos, so this file is the source of truth that a maintainer copies into a `ctxrs/homebrew-tap` (steps in the README). `version` and the two `sha256` values track the current stable release and need bumping per release; `brew livecheck ctx` reports when a newer version is available. macOS only — Linux ships as an AppImage via the existing install script.

title: Add side-by-side diff view to the diff review pane
body:
## Summary

- Adds a "Split" toggle to the diff review toolbar that switches expanded file diffs from the inline view to a side-by-side (original vs modified) view using Monaco's diff editor.
- Extends the unified-diff parser to reconstruct old/new file text from each file's hunks (context + deletions for old, context + additions for new), exposed as `oldText`/`newText` on `DiffFile`.
- De-duplicates the parser: the diff worker carried its own copy that had drifted from the shared implementation, so it now imports the single parser in `diffReviewDiffParser.ts`. This keeps the worker and the main-thread fallback in sync and is what populates the split view off the worker path.
- Applies to both the inventory-driven and plain-diff render paths; binary files fall back to the existing inline placeholder.

## Why

Closes #1. The review pane previously only rendered unified inline diffs; a side-by-side view makes larger changes easier to read.

## Validation

- [x] `pnpm test` (web) — 1890 tests pass, including new unit tests for the parser reconstruction and a component test for the Inline/Split toggle
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — clean
- [x] `pnpm lint` — clean
- [x] Manual run via the `/__cursor_diff_demo` route: confirmed the Split toggle renders a populated Monaco side-by-side editor (verified the original/modified models contain the reconstructed text) for a modified JSON file, with inline word-level highlighting.

## Notes

The split view reconstructs the changed regions from the diff hunks rather than the full file (full file contents aren't available client-side), so Monaco re-diffs the two reconstructed sides. New tests live in `diffReviewDiffParser.test.ts` and `DiffReviewPane.test.tsx`.

title: [Bug]: Official macOS installer fails: TLS handshake error on api.ade.ctx.rs redirect
body:
### What happened?

The official install script fails on macOS when downloading the stable DMG. The manifest resolves correctly from api.ctx.rs, but the download step redirects to api.ade.ctx.rs, where TLS handshake fails.


### What did you expect?

Suggested fix
Serve installer downloads from api.ctx.rs directly (same host as manifest/storage), or
Fix TLS configuration on api.ade.ctx.rs so redirects work from standard macOS curl/LibreSSL clients.


### Reproduction steps

Steps to reproduce
On macOS (arm64), run:
curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install | sh
The script resolves the manifest successfully, then fails while downloading the DMG.
Expected behavior
The installer downloads ctx_0.69.6_macos-arm64.dmg and installs the app to /Applications.

### Environment

OS: macOS (darwin, arm64)
curl: 8.7.1 (LibreSSL/3.3.6)
Install channel: stable
Release: 0.69.6
Expected DMG SHA-256: 2f5de0f46c25dea5560e0eef087d8932b46296e6f1f0f3900aa4c42a1ed61a40

This updates those fields to reset to `NULL` when the file changes, avoiding stale indexing metadata and bringing the behavior in line with the existing `source_import_files` UPSERT and `invalidate_provider_import_indexes()`.

title: Fix catalog import checkpoint semantics for changed transcripts
body:
## Problem

When a cataloged transcript file changes after import, `catalog_sessions.indexed_status` becomes `pending`, but the old `indexed_*` metadata can remain on the row. That makes the row look partially indexed for the current file version even though the current file is pending reimport.

External PR #15 correctly identified this stale completion-metadata bug, but clearing all old `indexed_*` metadata also removes the byte-size value that Codex append-only tail refresh currently uses as its import checkpoint. Without a separate checkpoint, ctx can reprocess old Codex JSONL events instead of importing only appended tail events.

## Desired fix

Separate the model concepts:

- `indexed_*`: completion metadata for the current cataloged file version.
- explicit import checkpoint metadata: the last successfully imported byte size/mtime/event count/timestamp, plus enough validation data to avoid trusting stale checkpoints after rewrites.

Append-only Codex session growth should keep using the prior checkpoint for tail import. Shrink, same-size changed content, and rewrite cases should not blindly reuse the old checkpoint.

## Acceptance criteria

- File changes clear stale current-version `indexed_*` completion metadata.
- Append-only Codex JSONL growth remains efficient and imports only the appended tail.
- Truncate/rewrite/same-size change cases avoid advancing from an unsafe checkpoint.
- Existing databases migrate old indexed metadata into checkpoint fields where sensible.
- Store, capture/import, and CLI tail-refresh tests cover the behavior.

title: Fix catalog import checkpoint state
body:
## Summary

Fixes #16.

This separates catalog completion metadata from incremental import checkpoint metadata for cataloged Codex transcript files.

## Problem

When a cataloged transcript changes, `catalog_sessions.indexed_status` correctly becomes `pending`, but old `indexed_*` fields could remain populated. That is misleading because those fields describe the previous file version, not the current cataloged file.

External PR #15 identified the real stale-metadata bug. Its approach of clearing all old `indexed_*` values on any file change is not sufficient for ctx, because Codex append-only session JSONL refresh was using `indexed_file_size_bytes` as the tail-import checkpoint. Clearing that value makes append refresh reprocess old events instead of importing only the appended tail.

## Data model change

- Keeps `indexed_*` fields as current-file completion metadata only.
- Adds explicit checkpoint columns on `catalog_sessions`:
  - `last_imported_at_ms`
  - `last_imported_file_size_bytes`
  - `last_imported_file_modified_at_ms`
  - `last_imported_file_sha256`
  - `last_imported_event_count`
- Bumps the history store schema to v14.
- Backfills existing databases from old `indexed_*` metadata where possible.

## Behavior

- Unchanged files preserve completion and checkpoint state.
- Changed files clear stale current-version `indexed_*` completion metadata.
- Append-only growth preserves a checkpoint only when the previous row was fully indexed to the prior EOF.
- Codex tail refresh reads the explicit checkpoint fields, validates the checkpoint prefix hash when available, and then imports only appended bytes.
- Migrated legacy checkpoints without hashes remain usable for compatibility; the next successful import writes a hash-backed checkpoint.
- Shrink and same-size changed metadata clear the checkpoint so old offsets are not trusted.

## Migration notes

The v14 migration adds nullable checkpoint columns and backfills `last_imported_*` from existing indexed metadata. New successful imports store `last_imported_file_sha256` so future tail refreshes can reject rewritten prefixes before using a checkpoint.

## Tests

- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store`
- `cargo test -p ctx --test cli search_refresh_auto_tail_imports_appended_codex_session_event`
- `cargo test -p ctx catalog_import_checkpoint_requires_matching_hash`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture`

title: [codex] Add history source plugin imports
body:
## Summary

Adds local history-source plugin support for custom agent histories on top of the `ctx-history-jsonl-v1` import format.

This PR now includes both halves of the intended product shape:

- explicit plugin imports via `ctx import --history-source`, `--plugin`, `--history-source-manifest`, and `ctx import --all`;
- search-time incremental refresh for installed plugin sources that are both `enabled: true` and `refresh: auto`.

A plugin is a local manifest plus a command-line exporter. ctx passes the previous cursor through the runtime environment, reads `ctx-history-jsonl-v1` JSONL from stdout, validates source identity/machine identity/schema, imports/indexes the records, and stores the updated cursor.

## Search Refresh Behavior

`ctx search` keeps the existing refresh contract:

- `--refresh auto` best-effort refreshes native sources and enabled auto plugin sources, then serves existing results if refresh fails;
- `--refresh strict` fails if native/plugin refresh fails;
- `--refresh off` never runs provider imports or plugin commands;
- provider-filtered native searches such as `--provider codex` do not execute custom plugin commands;
- `--provider custom` can refresh enabled auto plugin sources.

Plugin execution remains local-command based, not a plugin store or in-process ABI. Third parties can ship their own bridge CLI/script, and users can install it into ctx's plugin discovery paths.

## Guardrails

- Plugin commands are argv arrays, not shell strings.
- Plugin execution uses a limited inherited environment plus ctx-specific variables.
- Cursor files are private temporary files and are removed after execution.
- stdout is capped at 64 MiB and stderr at 256 KiB per run.
- Timeout now covers child execution plus stdout/stderr pipe draining, including helpers that inherit plugin pipes.
- `ctx setup` and `ctx sources` do not execute plugin commands.

## Docs

Updated docs describe the custom history source model, the manifest + exporter contract, search-time refresh behavior, and adapter shapes for DorkOS, OpenClaw, Hermes, and NanoClaw.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `cargo check -p ctx`

title: Add OMP (~/.omp/agent/sessions) to Pi provider default locations
body:
## Motivation

[OMP (Oh My Pi)](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi) is a Pi fork that renames the config root from `.pi` to `.omp`. Session history lives at `~/.omp/agent/sessions` in the identical per-session JSONL format Pi already uses.

Source (upstream OMP): `packages/utils/src/dirs.ts` — `CONFIG_DIR_NAME = ".omp"`, and `getSessionsDir()` resolves to `~/.omp/agent/sessions`.

Without this change, `ctx sources` / `ctx import --all` never discover OMP history natively; only an explicit `ctx import --provider pi --path ~/.omp/agent/sessions` works.

## Approach

Adds a second `ProviderDefaultLocation` entry to `PI_DEFAULTS` (`crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider_sources.rs`) for `~/.omp/agent/sessions`, reusing the existing `pi_session_jsonl` format — no new provider or source format needed since the on-disk schema is identical to `~/.pi/agent/sessions`.

This mirrors the `OPENCLAW_DEFAULTS` precedent, which already lists three default locations (`.openclaw`, `.clawdbot`, `.moltbot`) under a single provider. `discover_provider_sources_for_spec` and `default_location_import_probe` key off the provider (not the individual location), so both Pi default locations are probed/discovered/deduped automatically with no other code changes.

Follows up #40/#41 (0.19 Pi tree discovery support). No overlap with draft #43 (env-var-based custom directory discovery) — verified against its diff; it adds a new match arm elsewhere in `discover_provider_sources_for_spec` and never touches the `PI_DEFAULTS` constant.

## Validation

- Real-world OMP install: 326 sessions / 40k+ events previously importable only via explicit `--path`; discovery now finds the source natively.
- Added a regression test in `provider_sources.rs` mirroring the existing `.pi/agent/sessions` assertions (empty → available transitions, correct `source_format`) for the new `.omp/agent/sessions` location.
- Updated `docs/providers.md`, `docs/provider-support.md`, and `docs/provider-support-matrix.json` per the "Required Evidence For Promotion" checklist.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture`: 86 passed, 1 ignored.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-core provider_support`: 2 passed (matrix JSON still parses/matches schema).
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-capture --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo fmt`: clean.

title: Clarify PATH setup after Unix installer places ctx in ~/.local/bin
body:
After running the Unix installer, `ctx` may not be available as a bare command if `~/.local/bin` is not on the user's `PATH`.

Observed locally:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install | sh
command -v ctx
# no result

~/.local/bin/ctx --version
# ctx 0.19.0
```

The installer successfully installs the binary to `~/.local/bin/ctx`, but users can reasonably interpret `ctx: command not found` as an install failure.

Suggested improvement:

- Call out the default install directory in README/getting-started docs.
- Ensure the installer prints a clear note when the install directory is not on `PATH`.

I searched existing issues and PRs for `PATH`, `.local/bin`, and installer-related terms and did not find an existing report for this specific problem.

title: docs: clarify Windows C++ compiler requirements for local builds
body:
Hi maintainers

I was setting up the project locally on Windows and ran into the infamous `link.exe not found` / `gcc.exe missing` errors when running `cargo build`. 

It took me a minute to realize that because `ctx` relies on `rusqlite`, a C-compiler is strictly required on the machine to compile the bundled SQLite C code. 

To save future Windows contributors from hitting this same roadblock, I've added a small "Building from source" section to the README. It explicitly lists the Microsoft C++ Build Tools requirement and includes a quick Mermaid flowchart to visually explain why the compiler is needed.

Hope this is a helpful addition! Let me know if you'd like me to tweak any of the wording.

---

Implemented with updated Windows/MSVC wording in #988.

title: ctx import aborts on Cursor aborted-only agent transcript stubs
body:
## Problem

`ctx import --provider cursor` aborts when a transcript JSONL has no importable turns — e.g. only:

```json
{"type":"turn_ended","status":"aborted","error":"User aborted/interrupted manually."}
```

The entire Cursor import can fail even with allow_partial_failures. This same normalization path potentially affects other native JSONL providers (Gemini, Copilot CLI, Factory AI Droid).

## Repro

```bash
work=$(mktemp -d)
stub=$work/projects/demo/agent-transcripts/uuid/uuid.jsonl
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$stub")"
echo '{"type":"turn_ended","status":"aborted","error":"User aborted/interrupted manually."}' > "$stub"
ctx setup --data-root "$work/ctx" --progress none
ctx import --data-root "$work/ctx" --provider cursor --path "$work/projects" --progress none
```

**Got:** `invalid provider transcript path ... no Cursor agent transcript JSONL files found`

**Want:** skip the stub, continue import.

## Env

ctx 0.19.0 · macOS · `projects/*/agent-transcripts/*/*.jsonl`

title: Skip native JSONL files with no importable session header
body:
Fixes #56

## Motivation

`ctx import --provider cursor` aborts when a transcript JSONL contains parseable rows but no importable session header, such as Cursor `turn_ended` / aborted-only stubs. The failure is reported as `InvalidProviderTranscriptPath`, so it aborts the provider import before partial-failure handling can keep processing the rest of the tree.

## Approach

Treat non-empty headerless native JSONL files as per-file normalization failures and return a summary instead of raising `InvalidProviderTranscriptPath`. That lets tree imports keep valid transcripts while still surfacing the bad file in `summary.failures`.

- Cover Cursor aborted-only stubs in both tree import and explicit single-path import tests
- Update the Gemini headerless native JSONL regression to the new behavior

## Validation

- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --test cursor_native --locked`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --locked`
- `cargo test -p ctx --test cli native_provider_cli`

title: Does past-session search improve agent security review? (early feedback)
body:
You asked whether ctx / past-session search helps agents produce better security review work. Here is an early answer from actually testing it.

Yes, but at a specific layer. It does not improve raw detection (that is the scanner's job). What it improves is the agent's memory of prior findings and decisions:

- which issues were already found in this area,
- which were reviewed and accepted as deliberate exceptions (so the agent does not re-flag them or "fix" working code), and
- which fixes previously regressed.

Best used by querying history only when a scanner flags something, not by loading history at every agent start. That keeps token cost proportional to real findings instead of to history size. Concretely, this pairs well with a stateless scanner: run something like codesure on the changed code first, and only call ctx when the scan flags a problem, to pull the prior context for that specific finding.

One caveat specific to security: recalled transcript text re-enters a live agent's context, so it is a prompt-injection surface. In a security workflow especially, the agent should treat recalled history as data, not as instructions.

title: Add linux-aarch64 (ARM64) support
body:
## What

Add linux-aarch64 support to `install.sh`, the public-CLI build script, and the Buildkite pipeline.

## Why

Currently `ctx` only ships linux-x64 binaries. On ARM64 Linux hosts (AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon Linux VMs, Raspberry Pi, etc.) the installer fails with:

```
error: cannot detect this host platform; set CTX_PLATFORM
curl: (23) Failure writing output to destination
```

with no release artifact to download.

## Changes

1. **`scripts/install.sh`** — detect `Linux:aarch64` and `Linux:arm64`, allow `linux-aarch64` in the platform allow-list, and document it in `--platform` help text.
2. **`scripts/build-public-cli-artifact.sh`** — add `linux-aarch64` case (target `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu`, artifact name `ctx-linux-aarch64`) and reuse the existing `cargo build` path (no zig/cross needed on a native aarch64 host).
3. **`.buildkite/pipeline.yml`** — add a public-CLI build step gated on `CTX_PUBLIC_CLI_ARTIFACT_MATRIX`, targeting the existing `release-linux-managed` queue with `arch: arm64`.

## Testing

- Built locally on an aarch64 Linux host: `scripts/build-public-cli-artifact.sh linux-aarch64` produces a working `ctx-linux-aarch64` binary.
- That binary runs `ctx setup` successfully, indexing Pi / Codex / OpenCode / Hermes / Gemini sessions (19 sessions, 1,408 events).
- `ctx search` and `ctx show event` confirmed against the same data.
- `install.sh` now auto-detects `aarch64` instead of erroring.

## Notes for maintainers

- The pipeline step is gated by `CTX_PUBLIC_CLI_ARTIFACT_MATRIX`, same as the other public-CLI targets.
- `arch: arm64` will require either a native arm64 Buildkite agent in the `release-linux-managed` queue, or cross-tooling on existing x86_64 agents (gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu + libc6-dev-arm64-cross). Happy to wire up zig-based cross-compilation like the macOS targets if that is preferred.

---

*Tested and pushed from an aarch64 Linux host.*

title: fix(capture): skip oversized SQLite rows instead of aborting source
body:
## Summary

Provider SQLite databases can contain `data` values larger than ctx's 16 MiB per-value import cap. Before this PR, materializing one oversized value could abort the entire source import with `SQLITE_TOOBIG`, leaving otherwise readable rows unindexed.

This keeps the cap and makes the OpenCode-family SQLite adapter omit oversized values at the SQL layer instead of aborting the source:

- pre-scan relevant tables with a read-only, query-only connection that returns row ids only;
- exclude oversized ids from the bounded import query before SQLite materializes `data`;
- keep a per-row `SQLITE_TOOBIG` safety net for rows that slip past the prescan;
- count omitted rows as `skipped` / `skipped_events`, not failures;
- continue importing every other readable row.

No synthetic text, fake previews, truncated diffs, or summary events are generated. Oversized payload content is omitted.

Affected scope: OpenCode-family SQLite rows currently read by `normalize_opencode_sqlite`, including OpenCode/Kilo dialects. JSONL adapters are unchanged.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --check`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --lib tests::native_sqlite`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture`

Regression coverage includes mixed readable + oversized rows, all-oversized rows, and legacy `message` table rows.

title: feat(capture): emit synthetic events for oversized SQLite rows
body:
## Summary

Builds on #88. Phase 1 made oversized SQLite rows **not abort** the source import by skipping them at the SQL layer. The skipped rows themselves were invisible — no event landed in the store, no search hit referenced them, `ctx show session` silently omitted them. For providers like the Kilo Code VSCode extension that occasionally carry a single multi-hundred-MB message (e.g. a giant multi-file diff captured by the extension), that meant an entire legitimate session could be silently dropped from history.

This change re-imports each oversized row as a **synthetic event** carrying a truncated preview of the original payload plus a `_ctx_oversized` marker that records the original byte count and source table. The session stays searchable end-to-end, and downstream consumers can detect truncation explicitly.

- Add `truncated_oversized_message_rows` that opens an unbounded read-only connection (the bounded connection refuses to materialize the value, so truncation must run against an uncapped connection — same reasoning as `oversized_message_row_ids` in #88) and emits one `OpenCodeMessageRow` per oversized row, with `data` set to a synthetic JSON payload containing the truncated preview (`PROVIDER_MAX_TEXT_CHARS` chars) and a `_ctx_oversized` marker.
- Extend all three row fetchers (`opencode_session_message_rows`, `opencode_session_entry_rows`, `opencode_message_rows`) to append the synthetic rows before returning so they flow through the existing per-row import path unchanged.
- Drop the Phase 1 `summary.skipped` increment in `normalize_opencode_sqlite`: oversized rows are no longer skipped, they are imported as synthetic events and counted as `imported_events`.
- Surface the `_ctx_oversized` marker in `opencode_event.payload` as a top-level field alongside `body` for downstream visibility. The marker is also nested inside `body` but `provider_capped_json` would otherwise lose it for any oversized row whose synthetic preview also exceeds the body cap, so the top-level field is the canonical detection point.

Marker shape (at `event.payload.body.ctx_oversized`):

```json
{
  "original_bytes": <byte count of the oversized row>,
  "preview_chars": 16000,
  "source_table": "session_message",
  "source_format": "opencode_sqlite",
  "preview_truncated": false
}
```

Affected scope: only the OpenCode-family SQLite adapter (covers the Kilo Code extension via `KiloSqliteAdapter`). JSONL adapters are unaffected.

## Validation

- `cargo check -p ctx-history-capture` — clean
- `cargo build --workspace` — clean, only the 2 pre-existing warnings on the `ctx` bin (`ApplyResult::Applied` unused, `ProcessState::Running/NotRunning` never constructed) that exist on `main`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --lib tests::native_sqlite` — 29 passed, 0 failed
- Regression test `native_opencode_truncates_oversized_sqlite_text_value_and_preserves_other_rows` asserts:
  - `summary.failed == 0` (oversized rows must not be treated as failures)
  - `summary.imported_events >= 1` (other rows still import)
  - exactly one event in the session carries a non-null `payload.body.ctx_oversized`
  - `payload.body.ctx_oversized.original_bytes` matches the oversized row size
  - `payload.body.ctx_oversized.source_table` / `source_format` are set
  - `payload.body.message_id` preserves the original provider row id

## End-to-end verification

Built ctx from this branch and imported a synthetic `opencode.db` fixture (smoke-test schema) containing 2 normal rows + 1 oversized row (`MAX_PROVIDER_SQLITE_VALUE_BYTES + 1` bytes under `text`):

```
[ctx] imported: events=3, sessions=1, failed=0, skipped=0
[store] exactly one synthetic oversized event with _ctx_oversized marker
[store]   message_id preserved
[store]   original_bytes matches oversized row size
[store]   source_table=session_message, source_format=opencode_sqlite
[PASS] PR #88 + #89 verified end-to-end through ctx CLI
```

All three rows imported cleanly (Phase 1 effect: no `SQLITE_TOOBIG` abort), and exactly one synthetic event landed in the store with the `_ctx_oversized` marker at `payload_json.body.ctx_oversized` (Phase 2 effect).

## Depends on

- #88 (Phase 1: skip oversized SQLite rows instead of aborting source). This branch is based on top of `fix/search-refresh-oversized-skip` and should land after it.

## Related

- #90 tracks the separate Kilo Code dialect gap (schema lacks `text`/`content`/`message` keys, blocks all kilo imports regardless of oversized handling).

title: Kilo SQLite source fails to import: schema lacks text/content/message keys
body:
## Problem

`ctx search --refresh strict --provider kilo` and `ctx import --provider kilo` fail with:

```
import kilo source ~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db failed with 1 failure(s);
first failure: line 0: Kilo SQLite database contained no real conversational message rows
```

This blocks **every** Kilo session from being indexed, regardless of message size.

## Root cause

The Kilo Code VSCode extension stores its history in `~/.local/share/kilo/kilo.db`. ctx reads it through `KiloSqliteAdapter` → `normalize_opencode_sqlite` with `OPENCODE_KILO_DIALECT` (see `crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/adapter_impls/sqlite.rs:143` and `crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/opencode.rs:55`). The opencode adapter runs every fetched row through `opencode_data_has_real_message_content`, which requires the row's `data` JSON to have a top-level `text`, `content`, or `message` key (`crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/opencode.rs:708`):

```rust
data.get("text")
    .or_else(|| data.get("content"))
    .or_else(|| data.pointer("/message/role"))
```

Kilo's message schema does not use any of those keys. Representative message shapes from a real `kilo.db`:

- **user message**: `{"role":"user","time":{...},"summary":{"diffs":[...]},"agent":"code","model":{...},"editorContext":{...}}`
- **assistant message**: `{"role":"assistant","time":{...},"parentID":...,"modelID":...,"providerID":...,"mode":...,"agent":...,"path":...,"cost":...,"tokens":...,"finish":...}`

Top-level keys for both shapes are `role` / `time` / `agent` / `model` (or `modelID`) / `path` / `cost` / `tokens` / `finish` / `summary` / `editorContext`. No `text`, `content`, or `message`. As a result `opencode_data_has_real_message_content` returns `false` for every kilo row, the adapter concludes "no real conversational message rows", and the source import fails.

(Note: Kilo Code is the VSCode extension itself; z.ai is the coding-plan / model provider behind it, not the extension vendor. The `kilo.db` schema is owned by the extension.)

This is independent of the oversized-row handling that #88 / #89 recently fixed — kilo was already failing on schema grounds before the oversized path could matter.

## Reproduction

1. Install the Kilo Code VSCode extension locally and have at least one conversation.
2. Run `ctx sources --provider kilo` → source is detected and reported as available.
3. Run `ctx search "anything" --refresh strict --provider kilo` → fails with the error above.
4. Run `ctx import --provider kilo --json` → `failed=1`, `failures[0].error` contains "no real conversational message rows".

## Expected behaviour

Kilo messages should import analogously to opencode messages: each message becomes an event keyed by role (`user`/`assistant`/...), with payload body assembled from the fields kilo actually uses (`summary.diffs` for user turns, `path`/`mode`/`agent` for assistant turns, etc.). At minimum the role / time / agent / model fields that exist on every kilo row are enough to produce a searchable event.

## Proposed direction

Two reasonable options, both contained to `crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/opencode.rs`:

1. **Extend `opencode_data_has_real_message_content` / `opencode_event_text`** to recognize kilo's field set when `dialect.provider == CaptureProvider::Kilo` (or via a dialect flag). Smallest change, keeps the shared opencode pipeline intact.
2. **Add a dedicated `normalize_kilo_sqlite`** mirroring the pattern of the 13 existing per-provider adapters (`crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/{crush,firebender,goose,...}.rs`). Cleaner separation but more code.

The `KiloSqliteAdapter` is already plumbed (provider, source_format, dialect struct all exist), so either option is mostly local work — no schema migration, no SDK changes.

## Validation

A regression test along the lines of `native_opencode_imports_read_only_sqlite` (`crates/ctx-history-capture/src/tests/native_sqlite.rs:5`) but using a kilo-shaped fixture (rows with `role` / `time.created` / `summary.diffs` instead of opencode's `text` / `content`) would lock the fix in. The existing `write_opencode_smoke_db` fixture helper can serve as the template.

## Related

- #88 (oversized-row skip) — unblocks the `SQLITE_TOOBIG` abort for kilo's giant diff messages but does not address this schema gap.
- #89 (oversized-row truncation marker) — same; only meaningful once this issue lands and kilo rows actually flow through the import path.

title: Make usage analytics opt-in with install-time disclosure
body:
## Make usage analytics opt-in and disclose data collection up front

ctx indexes users' full agent conversation history — some of the most sensitive data on a developer's machine. The engineering already respects that (local-only indexing, no transcript egress, honest `docs/storage.md`), but the consent model doesn't match: analytics are default-on, the only disclosure lives in `docs/storage.md`, and `scripts/check-docs.sh` actively fails CI if the word "analytics" appears in the README. A user who runs `curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install | sh` starts transmitting install/device identifiers before they've had any chance to learn the behavior exists.

This PR aligns the consent model with the engineering:

### Changes

- **Analytics are now opt-in (default off).** `AppConfig::default()` sets `analytics.enabled = false`. A fresh install sends no events and creates no device identity.
- **New `ctx analytics enable | disable | status` subcommand**, mirroring `ctx upgrade enable/disable`. `enable` writes `[analytics] enabled = true` to `config.toml`; the command itself never emits an analytics event.
- **Installers disclose before acting and make opting in easy.** `scripts/install.sh` and `scripts/install.ps1` print a three-line `Privacy:` block (local index, opt-in analytics, daily auto-upgrade) before doing anything. Interactive `install.sh` runs ask once — `Share anonymous usage analytics to help improve ctx? [y/N]` via `/dev/tty`, defaulting to No; non-interactive runs stay off unless `--enable-analytics` / `CTX_INSTALL_ENABLE_ANALYTICS=1` (PowerShell: `-EnableAnalytics`).
- **README gains a "Private by default" section** stating the contract in plain language, with a pointer to `docs/storage.md` for the full payload details.
- **`docs/storage.md` and `docs/cli-reference.md` updated** from "default-on, here's the opt-out" to "off by default, here's how to opt in."
- **`scripts/check-docs.sh`** now permits analytics copy in `README.md` and `docs/cli-reference.md` (still banned everywhere else).
- **Tests:** all analytics integration tests now opt in explicitly (`CTX_ANALYTICS_ENABLED=true`); two new regression tests pin the contract — a default invocation sends nothing and creates no device identity, and the settings command round-trips `config.toml`.

### Not covered here (needs hosted-side changes)

The production hosted installer at `https://ctx.rs/install` is not in this repository. It currently POSTs stage-by-stage install diagnostics tagged with a per-download `install_attempt_id` before the user has seen any disclosure. Suggest porting the same pattern there: print the `Privacy:` block first, make the stage diagnostics opt-in (or at minimum gate them on the same prompt), and forward the analytics answer to the CLI.

### Why default-off matters for this tool in particular

For a general dev tool, default-on coarse analytics is a defensible norm. ctx is different: its entire value proposition is "point me at every secret-laden transcript on your machine, trust me that nothing leaves." The docs make exactly that promise ("local and private by default"). Default-on identifier transmission — however coarse — undercuts the trust the product depends on, and the users most likely to adopt ctx are precisely the ones most likely to notice. Opt-in costs some analytics volume, but an explicit install-time prompt should recover much of it while making every remaining data point consensual.

---

title: Fix Factory AI Droid import failures, support old and new session formats w/ nested message content/role
body:
# Fix Factory AI Droid Session Import (new format) + support both formats

## Summary
Fixes the "no importable native JSONL session header" error when importing Factory AI Droid sessions. The adapter now handles both the legacy session format (`sessionId` at root, `role`/`content` at message root) and the new session format (`id` instead of `sessionId`, nested `message.content`/`message.role`).

After investigating trade-offs, this PR focuses on fixing Factory AI Droid session import for users on newer Factory AI Droid versions, while keeping backward compatibility. Discovered, tested and solved for v0.168.2.

Solves https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/106 and implements backwards compatibility (although I couldn't verify e2e as I don't have the old format, so relying for that in current impl + tests).


## Problem

The Factory AI Droid native JSONL importer only recognized the legacy format:
```json
{"type":"session_start","sessionId":"abc","timestamp":"...","cwd":"/workspace","model":"factory/droid"}
{"type":"message","id":"msg-1","timestamp":"...","role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"prompt"}]}
```

But Factory AI Droid now writes sessions in a new format:
```json
{"type":"session_start","id":"abc","timestamp":"...","cwd":"/workspace","model":"factory/droid"}
{"type":"message","id":"msg-1","timestamp":"...","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"prompt"}]}}
```

This caused imports to fail with "no importable native JSONL session header".

## Changes

**crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/native_jsonl.rs**
- `native_jsonl_header_session_id`: Accept both `sessionId` and `id`
- `native_jsonl_role`: Check both `role` and `/message/role`
- `native_jsonl_event_text`: Check both `content` and `/message/content`
- `native_jsonl_model`: Check both `model` and `/message/model`
- `droid_content_has`: Check both `content` and `/message/content`

**crates/ctx-history-capture/src/tests/native_json.rs**
- Added `native_factory_ai_droid_supports_new_session_format` test
- Added `native_factory_ai_droid_supports_legacy_session_format` test

## Testing

All new tests pass:
- `native_factory_ai_droid_supports_new_session_format` 
- `native_factory_ai_droid_supports_legacy_session_format` 

Checks:
- All 12 existing provider fixture replay tests (important for back compat)

Before:
```

```

title: Bound Hermes import and FTS merge WAL growth
body:
## What changed

- persistently suppress FTS5 automatic/crisis merges during Hermes bulk ingest

## Why

The original transaction-batching draft did not fully solve the reported failure. On the contributor's 206–260 MB Hermes corpus, FTS5 could still perform a crisis/incremental merge inside a single INSERT and grow the WAL by multiple GiB, even with one capture per transaction. A checkpoint cannot bound work performed inside that statement.

This replacement prevents those automatic merges during ingest and performs the merge work explicitly in bounded, recoverable transactions.

title: `search --refresh wait` fails entirely when any source has a single malformed JSONL row
body:
`ctx search --refresh wait "<query>"` errors out and returns nothing when a provider source contains even one unparseable JSONL row:

```
Error: search refresh failed

Caused by:
    import claude source ~/.claude/projects failed with 6 failure(s);
    first failure: line 264: malformed JSONL: expected value at line 1 column 1
```

The same query with `--refresh background` succeeds: it serves the existing index and only warns:

```
warning: search refresh failed; serving existing index;
use --refresh wait to fail instead: ... malformed JSONL ...
```

In practice, long-lived `~/.claude/projects` and `~/.codex/sessions` directories almost always contain a few malformed rows (partial writes, truncated sessions), so `--refresh wait` is effectively unusable on any real machine, even though the malformed rows are a tiny fraction (~0.07% here).

`ctx import` already has the tolerant path: `import --partial` ("Allow valid rows in a source to commit when malformed rows are encountered") commits the good rows, skips the bad ones, and exits 0. Search-refresh doesn't offer that tolerance.

**Request:** apply the `--partial` tolerance to search-refresh. Either make `--refresh wait` skip-and-warn on malformed rows by default (like `import --partial`), or add a flag so a single bad transcript row can't abort the whole query. That makes `--refresh wait` (the only mode that guarantees fresh results before searching, without writing the index mid-query like `background`) actually usable.

**Repro:** ensure a source dir has at least one malformed JSONL line, then `ctx search --refresh wait "anything"` gives a hard error, while `ctx search --refresh background "anything"` warns and returns hits.

**Environment:** ctx 0.24.0 (built from source), Linux.

title: Bound FTS merge recovery steps on large indexes
body:
## What changed

Reduce the explicit FTS5 merge page budget from 1,024 to 16 pages per committed/checkpointed step.

## Why

The FTS5 merge page parameter is a work budget, not a hard bound on physical WAL pages. On a real 2.3 GiB ctx database populated from a 206 MiB Hermes source, one 1,024-page recovery step grew the WAL to 7.0 GiB before the process was stopped for disk safety. This also made ordinary `ctx search` appear hung because writable store open synchronously resumes the recovery marker.

The smaller step keeps the existing crash-safe marker, serialization, merge semantics, and strict checkpoint loop unchanged while reducing the amount of FTS work that can occur inside one statement.

## Real-corpus validation

Reused the exact interrupted database and `event_search_bulk_mode_v1` marker that reproduced the failure:

- before: 1,024-page step, WAL reached 7.0 GiB and did not finish safely
- after: 16-page step, recovery completed in 1m52s
- measured peak WAL: 14,959,752 bytes (~14.3 MiB)
- final WAL: 0 bytes
- recovery marker: cleared
- `ctx search Hermes --limit 3`: returned results, including a Hermes event
- exit status: 0

## Checks

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store connection_tests -- --nocapture` (7 passed)
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-store -p ctx --tests -- -D warnings`
- `cargo build -p ctx --release`

## Search latency follow-up

The same recovery marker also made ordinary search look hung because lexical event ranking re-joined the FTS5 virtual table after materializing its matches. This branch now keeps the match rows in a materialized CTE and ranks them without that second FTS scan. Scriptgram queries retain the existing path.

Live validation on the existing 2.3 GiB database after installing the release binary:

- `ctx search Hermes --refresh off`: 0.70–1.03s over repeated runs
- `ctx search Hermes --provider hermes --refresh off`: 0.69–0.72s
- WAL remained absent/0 bytes and no recovery marker remained

Additional checks: `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo test -p ctx-history-store search -- --nocapture` (38 passed), clippy, and release build.

## Idempotent refresh follow-up

Background search was also re-normalizing unchanged non-manifest native roots after inventory had already marked them indexed. This was especially expensive for live SQLite sources: Hermes (about 216 MiB), OpenCode (about 675 MiB), and OpenClaw (about 350 MiB). The import path now checks the persisted root inventory and skips provider normalization when the source metadata is unchanged and there is no pending import file. Full rescans and changed/pending sources still run normally.

Validation:

- regression test: `unchanged_root_source_skips_provider_normalization`
- unchanged Hermes source: plain `ctx search Hermes --provider hermes --limit 1` returned in 1.11s
- generic plain search completed in 20.95s while reporting six pre-existing malformed Codex records; it did not hang and final WAL was absent
- release binary installed locally from commit `31a4dfdf`

title: Bound FTS merge WAL on populated indexes

## What changed

- reduce each FTS5 merge step from 1,024 pages to 16 so physical WAL amplification remains safe on large indexes

- preserve explicit full optimization behavior, now using the safer 16-page steps
- cover pre-populated Hermes imports, full clean multi-source setup through final optimization, legacy interrupted merge recovery, WAL bounds, integrity, searchability, and replay

## Root cause

Two behaviors combined in the failing setup path. Hermes bulk finalization initiated a full FTS5 merge over the shared historical event index, and the logical page budget was not a hard physical WAL bound. On the contributor exact interrupted 2.3 GiB database, a 1,024-page step reached a 7.0 GiB WAL. The 16-page step recovered the same database with a measured 14.3 MiB peak and zero final WAL.

## Impact

New provider finalization no longer re-optimizes historical search segments. Legacy in-progress full merges and explicit final optimization use smaller checkpointed steps. Source atomicity, crash markers, serialization, and strict checkpoint handling remain unchanged.

title: Avoid rescanning FTS rows during lexical search
body:
## What changed

- materialize lexical FTS matches once and rank that relation without rejoining the FTS5 virtual table
- group ranking strictly by canonical event ID while preserving projected hit metadata
- keep mixed/scriptgram search on its existing path
- extract event search SQL construction into a focused module
- add regressions for query-plan scan count, deterministic pagination, event grouping, and metadata/cursor preservation

## Why

After the bounded FTS recovery work, ordinary lexical search could still appear hung on a populated index. The ranking query materialized matches and then joined them back through `event_search`, causing another expensive FTS5 virtual-table scan. The lexical-only path now carries the projection data through the materialized match relation and never rescans FTS for hydration.

The final query relies on the store's maintained one-row-per-event projection invariant and uses one event-ID aggregation. An independent review rejected a defensive window-function variant after a live benchmark showed roughly 2x regression on a common term.

## Impact

Search semantics, ordering, pagination, hit metadata, cursors, and mixed-script behavior remain unchanged. On the contributor's 2.3 GiB database, the original fast path reduced repeated `ctx search Hermes --refresh off` runs to 0.70–1.03s. Independent review on a 1.26M-row FTS index found the hardened event-ID grouping within about 4% of the contributor query for a common two-clause query and 14% for a pathological single common term.

title: Skip unchanged native search refreshes
body:
## What changed

- skip provider normalization during automatic search refresh when a non-manifest native root is already indexed and unchanged
- keep explicit imports, full rescans, and their existing summaries/semantics unchanged
- compute root statistics and a deterministic freshness token in one filesystem traversal
- include SQLite WAL and rollback-journal metadata while excluding reader-mutated shared memory
- invalidate indexed inventory when the root token or source format changes
- preserve event-search backfill even when provider normalization is skipped

## Why

Automatic search refresh was repeatedly normalizing unchanged native roots after inventory had already marked them indexed. For large live sources such as Hermes, OpenCode, and OpenClaw, that meant rereading hundreds of MiB before event deduplication could prove there was no work.

The contributor's initial root size/mtime fast path was too broad: full CLI testing showed that it changed explicit-import summary behavior and could miss rapid same-size SQLite updates. The final design limits the optimization to search refresh and uses a nanosecond-resolution metadata token over tree entries plus SQLite WAL/journal sidecars. Existing inventory rows perform one conservative reimport to acquire the new token.

## Impact

Unchanged search refreshes avoid provider parsing and return immediately after cheap inventory work. Changed roots, WAL-only commits, pending/failed inventory, source-format changes, explicit imports, and full rescans still run the adapter normally. Search projection repair remains automatic.

On the contributor's live host, the earlier fast path reduced repeated plain Hermes search to 1.11s with no WAL. This hardened version preserves that architecture while closing the stale-index and product-semantics gaps found in review.

## Validation

## Summary

The Safari-style `0081` quarantine marker deliberately triggers Finder/Gatekeeper first-open consent. On the physical Apple Silicon release host, `syspolicyd` completed its online scan successfully and then logged `Prompt shown ... waiting for response`; a headless SSH job therefore waited until any timeout. The hosted installer uses curl and does not simulate Finder. This change keeps the automated release claim narrow: exact signed bytes execute on native macOS, while signing/notarization are verified separately.

title: Preserve runtime-user provenance across deduplicated imports
body:
## Problem

ctx records the provider/runtime for imported history, but not the Unix user under which that runtime ran.

On a multi-user host, histories from the same provider in distinct user environments cannot be distinguished by downstream analysis. Deduplication can also observe one logical event from multiple user environments; retaining only one source loses that context.

## What this changes

Runtime remains the existing `provider`. This adds `ctx import --runtime-user` for the explicit Unix account under which the harness ran; it is neither the message author nor the user who runs `ctx import`.

Capture sources and sessions are scoped by that explicit user. Legacy rows remain `NULL`; migrations are additive and do not backfill.

## Design

An identical event observed for multiple runtime users remains one canonical event with per-source/session observations. For example, snapshots prepared for `alice` and `bob` can retain separate provenance without identity being inferred from paths.

Maintainer design question: is source-scoped `runtime_user` plus event observations the preferred shape, or would you prefer another integration point?

## Validation

Local verification: `cargo fmt --check`; workspace, capture, and store tests; the exact Codex fast-directory CLI test for `alice` + `bob`; and the Codex tail test.

title: `content_retention: "full_text"` is reported alongside `truncated: true` on the same message event
body:
**ctx version:** 0.24.0 (macos-arm64, unmanaged binary)
**Provider:** claude (`claude_projects_jsonl_tree`)

Thanks for ctx — the discovery-layer search over local agent history has been very
useful. This is a small correctness/documentation report about one indexed field
that can mislead a downstream consumer.

## Observed behavior

When a message body exceeds the message-text limit, the imported event stores the
text truncated to 16,000 characters **and** sets `body.truncated = true`, but the
sibling field `body.content_retention` is still `"full_text"` on the very same
event.

`content_retention` appears to name a *retention class* rather than a completeness
guarantee. Across event types I observed three values:

| event_type | role | `content_retention` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| message | user / assistant | `full_text` |
| tool_call | assistant | `metadata` |
| tool_output (successful) | user | `metadata_only` |

So `"full_text"` means "the text body was retained" (as opposed to metadata-only),
not "the text was retained in full / un-truncated". The problem is that the name
reads like the latter, and it sits directly next to a `truncated: true` flag that
says the opposite.

### Reproduction (synthetic data, isolated data root)

All input below is synthetic; the index is written to a throwaway `CTX_DATA_ROOT`
so nothing touches a real history index.

```bash
# 1. Isolated, throwaway data root and a synthetic Claude "projects" tree.
#    Use a non-symlinked path — ctx rejects symlinked provider-path components
#    (e.g. macOS /tmp -> /private/tmp), so resolve the real path first.
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"; WORK="$(python3 -c 'import os,sys;print(os.path.realpath(sys.argv[1]))' "$WORK")"
export CTX_DATA_ROOT="$WORK/data"
mkdir -p "$WORK/projects/demo-project"

# 2. One session with a single user message of 20,000 characters (> 16,000).
python3 - "$WORK" <<'PY'
import json, sys, uuid
work = sys.argv[1]
text = "[LONG BEGIN] " + ("x" * (20000 - len("[LONG BEGIN] ") - len(" [LONG END]"))) + " [LONG END]"
rec = {
    "parentUuid": None, "isSidechain": False, "userType": "external",
    "cwd": "/demo/workdir", "sessionId": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
    "version": "1.0.0", "type": "user",
    "message": {"role": "user", "content": text},
    "uuid": str(uuid.uuid4()), "timestamp": "2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
}
with open(f"{work}/projects/demo-project/session.jsonl", "w") as f:
    f.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")
print("input chars:", len(text))
PY

# 3. Import into the isolated index.
ctx import --provider claude --path "$WORK/projects" --no-daemon --quiet

# 4. Inspect the retention / truncation fields.
ctx sql --format json \
  "SELECT
     length(json_extract(payload_json,'\$.body.text'))          AS body_text_len,
     json_extract(payload_json,'\$.body.truncated')             AS truncated,
     json_extract(payload_json,'\$.body.content_retention')     AS content_retention
   FROM ctx_events
   WHERE event_type = 'message'"
```

Observed result:

```json
{ "body_text_len": 16000, "truncated": 1, "content_retention": "full_text" }
```

(`truncated` renders as `1` through `ctx sql`; in the stored JSON it is the boolean
`true`.)

The 16,000-character cut is exact: a 16,000-character message yields
`truncated = false`, and a 16,001-character message yields `truncated = true`
with `body.text` cut to 16,000. The cut is by character count, not bytes — a
20,000-character multi-byte message (60,000 UTF-8 bytes of one 3-byte character)
is retained as 16,000 characters / 48,000 bytes, still labelled `"full_text"`.

## Impact for a consumer

A consumer that reads `content_retention` as its truncation signal — a natural
reading given the value `"full_text"` — will treat a 16,000-character slice of a
much longer message as the complete text. In an audit / verbatim-quoting use case
this silently drops the tail (4,000 characters in the example above, more for
longer messages) while the label asserts the body is fully present. The only
reliable signal today is the separate `truncated` flag, which contradicts the
name of the retention field sitting next to it.

## Proposed direction

Any of these would remove the ambiguity (in rough order of preference):

1. **Rename / re-value the field** so completeness is not implied — e.g. keep it as
   a retention *class* under a clearer name (`retention_class`), or use a value
   like `"text"` instead of `"full_text"` so it no longer reads as "not truncated".
2. **Document** `content_retention` explicitly as a retention-class label (with the
   observed value set `full_text` / `metadata` / `metadata_only`) and state that
   `truncated` is the authoritative completeness signal, so `full_text` +
   `truncated: true` is a valid, expected combination.
3. Optionally, keep the field name but make `full_text` mutually exclusive with
   truncation (e.g. emit a distinct value such as `"text_truncated"` when the body
   was cut).

Happy to help test a change against the synthetic reproduction above. Thanks!

title: Feature request: make the 16,000-character message-text truncation length configurable
body:
**ctx version:** 0.24.0 (macos-arm64, unmanaged binary)
**Provider:** claude (`claude_projects_jsonl_tree`)

Thanks for ctx. This is a feature request to expose the message-text truncation
length as a configuration option, motivated by a long-message audit use case.

## Observed behavior

Imported message text is truncated to a fixed **16,000 characters**. A message
longer than that is stored as its first 16,000 characters with `body.truncated`
set. There does not appear to be any CLI flag, environment variable, or documented
option to raise (or lower) this limit — `ctx import --help` and `ctx setup --help`
expose only `--data-root`, `--provider`, `--path`, format/progress flags, etc., and
the `limitations` / `provider-import-policy` docs describe bounding provider text
but do not surface a length knob.

The cut is exact and by character count (not bytes):

- a 16,000-character message → `truncated = false`
- a 16,001-character message → `truncated = true`, `body.text` length 16,000
- a 20,000-character multi-byte message (60,000 UTF-8 bytes) → retained as 16,000
  characters (48,000 bytes), `truncated = true`

### Reproduction (synthetic data, isolated data root)

All input is synthetic and imported into a throwaway `CTX_DATA_ROOT`.

```bash
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"; WORK="$(python3 -c 'import os,sys;print(os.path.realpath(sys.argv[1]))' "$WORK")"
export CTX_DATA_ROOT="$WORK/data"
mkdir -p "$WORK/projects/demo-project"

# Three synthetic user messages: 16000 (exact), 16001, and 20000 characters.
python3 - "$WORK" <<'PY'
import json, sys, uuid
work = sys.argv[1]
def rec(n, i):
    body = f"[MSG{i} BEGIN] " + ("x" * (n - len(f"[MSG{i} BEGIN] ") - len(f" [MSG{i} END]"))) + f" [MSG{i} END]"
    assert len(body) == n
    return {
        "parentUuid": None, "isSidechain": False, "userType": "external",
        "cwd": "/demo/workdir", "sessionId": "00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
        "version": "1.0.0", "type": "user",
        "message": {"role": "user", "content": body},
        "uuid": str(uuid.uuid4()), "timestamp": "2025-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    }
with open(f"{work}/projects/demo-project/session.jsonl", "w") as f:
    for i, n in enumerate([16000, 16001, 20000]):
        f.write(json.dumps(rec(n, i)) + "\n")
PY

ctx import --provider claude --path "$WORK/projects" --no-daemon --quiet

ctx sql --format json \
  "SELECT
     length(json_extract(payload_json,'\$.body.text')) AS body_text_len,
     json_extract(payload_json,'\$.body.truncated')    AS truncated
   FROM ctx_events
   WHERE event_type = 'message'
   ORDER BY event_seq"
```

Observed result:

```
{ "body_text_len": 16000, "truncated": 0 }   // 16000-char input, not truncated
{ "body_text_len": 16000, "truncated": 1 }   // 16001-char input, truncated
{ "body_text_len": 16000, "truncated": 1 }   // 20000-char input, truncated
```

## Use case / impact for a consumer

We use ctx as the discovery layer over local agent-session history, and one class
of task is auditing / quoting long individual messages (large pasted context,
long tool-driven turns, long agent outputs). At the current fixed limit, for any
message over 16,000 characters ctx can serve only discovery; recovering the
full body always requires falling back to the raw provider file. For an
audit-heavy workflow this fallback is frequent enough that a higher, opt-in limit
would let more of the work stay inside ctx.

We fully understand the limit exists for good reasons — search quality, index
size, and keeping secret/blob exposure minimal — as stated in the import policy.
The request is not to change the default, only to make the ceiling adjustable for
users who knowingly accept a larger index.

## Proposed direction

Expose the message-text truncation length as configuration, defaulting to the
current 16,000 so existing behavior is unchanged. For example, any one of:

1. an `import` / `setup` flag (e.g. `--max-message-chars <N>`);
2. an environment variable (e.g. `CTX_MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS`), consistent with the
   existing `CTX_DATA_ROOT` / `CTX_QUIET` pattern;
3. a value in the local config/storage so it applies to subsequent imports.

Keeping `body.truncated` accurate relative to whatever limit is in effect would
preserve the completeness signal. If a hard upper bound is desirable to protect
the index, an enforced maximum with a clear error/diagnostic when exceeded would
be reasonable.

Happy to test a change against the synthetic reproduction above. Thanks for
considering it!

title: fix: nonce-tag recalled snippet delimiters to prevent boundary spoofing
body:
Related discussion: #60

## Summary

When the history-search feature recalls a past snippet and renders it back to an agent (CLI or MCP text output), the snippet is now wrapped in a delimiter carrying a random, single-use nonce. This makes it structurally impossible for the *content* of a recalled snippet to forge the delimiter that marks its own boundary.

## Why this matters

`ctx search` returns text that an agent reads and acts on. Some of that text — the recalled snippet itself — originates from data the system doesn't fully control (something said or stored earlier, possibly by another party). If there's nothing reliably marking "this part is recalled data, not a live instruction," a snippet could contain text that looks like the end of the recalled block, followed by what reads as a fresh instruction. An agent parsing the output has no reliable way to tell a real boundary from a fake one embedded in the data.

This is a boundary-spoofing / prompt-injection risk: the danger isn't that the recalled content is wrong, it's that the *structure* around it can be faked.

## How the fix works

Recalled snippets are now wrapped like this:

```
[[RECALLED_DATA nonce=3f9a2e7c-...]]
...snippet content, XML-escaped...
[[/RECALLED_DATA nonce=3f9a2e7c-...]]
```

- **Nonce is a random UUIDv4**, generated fresh per response. Because it's generated after the snippet content already exists in storage, nothing inside a snippet can pre-guess it and forge a matching delimiter.
- **One nonce per response, not per snippet.** All snippets in a single response share a nonce, so an agent can tell which ones came from the same recall call. This doesn't weaken the protection — an attacker can't predict a future random value whether it's scoped per-response or per-snippet — so sharing it is a readability win with no security cost.
- **The closing delimiter carries the nonce too, not just the opening one.** If only the opening tag were nonce-tagged, injected content could still forge a plain closing tag and escape the boundary early.
- **Content is clipped to the display length limit *before* wrapping, not after.** This guarantees the closing delimiter itself is never truncated — clipping after wrapping could cut a long snippet off mid-delimiter and leave the block unclosed in the rendered output.
- **Snippet content is XML-escaped** before wrapping, so special characters inside it can't be mistaken for markup.

## What this does *not* solve

This PR hardens the **boundary** only — it makes it structurally impossible for recalled content to impersonate a new instruction or forge a delimiter it didn't generate. It does **not** address the separate, deeper problem @hampsterx raised: an agent trusting a *claim* inside a recalled snippet (e.g. "this was already reviewed and approved") without checking that claim against something access-controlled. The nonce guarantees the box is real; it says nothing about whether the contents of the box are true. That's a distinct piece of work and a good candidate for a follow-up discussion.

## Scope / Compatibility

- Only touches **human/agent-facing text rendering** — CLI output and MCP text responses.
- The **`--json` path is untouched on purpose.** Scripted consumers (`ctx search --json | jq ...`) parse structured fields directly and don't face this ambiguity, so wrapping isn't needed there.
- **Note for reviewers:** this does change the visible shape of CLI/MCP text output (snippets are now wrapped). Anything downstream scraping the plain-text output with fixed assumptions — rather than using `--json` — should be checked against this change.
- `threat-model.md` is updated to document this mitigation and its boundaries.

## Testing

All of the following pass on this branch:

```bash
cargo build --workspace
cargo test -p ctx-history-search
cargo clippy -p ctx-history-search --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

## Files changed (8)

| File | Role |
|---|---|
| `snippets.rs` | Core wrapping/escaping logic for recalled snippets |
| `lib.rs` | Wires the new wrapping logic into the public API |
| `tests/snippets.rs` | Unit tests for delimiter/nonce wrapping |
| `tests/mod.rs` | Test module registration |
| `mcp/text.rs` | MCP text-rendering integration |
| `search_render.rs` | CLI render integration |
| `commands/search.rs` | `ctx search` command wiring |
| `threat-model.md` | Documents the mitigation and its scope |

## Follow-up

Happy to open a separate discussion on the content-trust problem (verifying claims inside recalled data against an access-controlled source) if useful — keeping this PR scoped to the tagging mitigation that was already flagged as worth trying.

cc @hampsterx

---
Suggested labels: `security`, `enhancement`

title: macOS: running the test suite can require manually canonicalizing temporary paths
body:
While running the test suite on macOS I ran into an issue that took a while to track down, so I wanted to document it in case others hit the same thing.

Some tests that exercise provider imports can fail with an error like:
```
invalid provider transcript path ...
symlinked provider transcript path components are rejected

```
I found this was caused by the temporary directory path on macOS. By default, temporary directories are often created under /var/..., which resolves through the /var -> /private/var symlink. The production symlink checks are working as intended, but the test environment ends up passing a non-canonical path.

Using the canonical /private/... path (or otherwise resolving the temp directory before running those tests) made the failures disappear.

I haven’t dug into what the best fix would be, and it may simply be something to document or handle in shared test helpers if @luca-ctx think it’s worthwhile. I mainly wanted to report the contributor experience in case others run into the same thing.

title: Make tolerant import the only import behavior
body:
## Summary

- remove `--partial`, strict/partial import modes, and all corresponding public/internal API options with no compatibility shim
- preserve independently valid records by default while isolating record, source, and ctx-owned systemic failures
- add import result schema v2 with explicit run/source outcomes, bounded rejection details, and coarse path-free analytics
- keep rejected sources retryable without advancing durable cursors; retain 64-unit/8 MiB transactions and coordinated FTS finalization from #154
- update public docs, fixtures, and provider/search/setup/plugin behavior across the board

## Failure contract

- malformed/invalid independent records are rejected and reported; valid content commits
- unreadable, corrupt, locked, or schema-incompatible provider sources fail independently
- ctx store/index/locking/worker/operational-I/O failures abort the run
- failures with zero useful accepted content never report success

This is an intentional breaking 0.x change. There is no deprecated flag, no no-op alias, and no legacy strict/partial API residue.

## Verification

- `cargo test --workspace --locked`
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`
- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets --locked`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- targeted CLI/provider/store regression suites
- exact import-mode residue scan and `git diff --check`

Follows the already-merged #154 transaction/FTS fix.

title: Make provider import state converge safely
body:
## Summary

- persist convergent provider import outcomes and parser revisions
- fence inventory, completion, and missing-path transitions with a durable per-source generation
- keep transient I/O failures retryable while deterministic record rejection converges
- repair legacy failed rows and completed rows whose materialized session is missing

## Why

Provider import state could previously remain ambiguous after mixed rejection, parser changes, or overlapping source scans. An older in-flight scan could also report against a newer observation. This change makes every durable result conditional on the exact current source observation without rewriting unchanged catalog rows.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store catalog::tests` (34 passed)
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store schema::tests` (29 passed)
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture codex` (44 passed, 1 ignored manual benchmark)
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture retained_existing_content`
- `cargo test -p ctx commands::import::native::tests` (8 passed)
- `cargo test -p ctx --test native_provider_rejections` (16 passed)
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-store -p ctx-history-capture -p ctx --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- two independent adversarial review passes; all findings resolved or assigned to the separate write-pressure PR as preexisting scope

This is the first PR in a stacked import-indexing resilience series. It is ready for CI and review, but will be held from merge until the combined stack passes cross-platform and real-corpus validation.

title: Clarify the intended semantics of body.content_retention when body.truncated is true
body:
While inspecting imported message payloads, I noticed a combination of fields that seems ambiguous from a consumer's perspective.

For a truncated message, the stored payload contains:

```json
{
  "content_retention": "full_text",
  "truncated": true
}
```
At first glance, content_retention: "full_text" reads as though the complete message body has been retained, while truncated: true indicates that the stored text is only a prefix of the original message.Is this the intended contract?

If content_retention is meant to describe the retention class (text vs. metadata) rather than whether the stored text is complete, then truncated would be the authoritative completeness signal. That interpretation makes sense, but it wasn’t immediately obvious when consuming the JSON.

title: Canonicalize test temp roots on macOS
body:
## Summary

- canonicalize the system temporary root before creating provider-import test directories
- route provider-source discovery tests through the same canonical test helper
- preserve production symlink rejection unchanged

## Root cause

On macOS, temporary directories are commonly returned under `/var/folders/...`, while `/var` resolves to `/private/var`. Tests either passed the lexical `/var/...` path into production validation or compared it with a canonical `/private/var/...` discovery result.

## Validation

Closes #161.

title: Observe logical provider import units
body:
## Summary

- inventory provider history as explicit logical import units instead of treating every source root as one opaque file
- observe SQLite databases with stable WAL/rollback-journal snapshots and companion dependencies
- persist source observations, unit outcomes, and inventory-generation completion behind concurrency fences
- retry superseded inventories without allowing stale work to report success

## Why

This gives incremental import a deterministic answer to “what changed?” across all provider adapters and prevents concurrent setup, search, or daemon work from committing observations for an obsolete source generation. It is the correctness layer required before append-only readers and bounded background scheduling can safely avoid full rescans.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p ctx -- --test-threads=1`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store -p ctx-history-capture`
- `cargo clippy -p ctx -p ctx-history-store -p ctx-history-capture --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings`
- `cargo check -p ctx -p ctx-history-store -p ctx-history-capture --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`
- `cross check -p ctx -p ctx-history-store -p ctx-history-capture --target x86_64-unknown-freebsd`

title: Provider-session lookup is ambiguous for duplicate same-source Claude imports
body:
Title: Provider-session lookup is ambiguous for duplicate same-source Claude imports

## Summary

`ctx show session --provider claude --provider-session <id>` can fail with an ambiguity error even when the indexed rows appear to represent one logical Claude transcript from the same source.

In the local index I checked, Claude has widespread duplicate physical `ctx_session_id` rows for the same `(provider_session_id, source_path)` pair. The documented provider-session lookup path then asks the user to switch to `ctx_session_id`, but there is no deterministic way to choose the right row from the provider-session lookup alone.

## Repro

Version:

```text
ctx 0.24.0
```

Command:

```sh
ctx show session --provider claude --provider-session 00396831-5087-49ad-a150-6ce5d0c6d08b --mode lite
```

Actual:

```text
Error: multiple claude sessions with provider_session_id "00396831-5087-49ad-a150-6ce5d0c6d08b" are indexed; use ctx_session_id
```

Expected:

If all matching rows are provably the same provider session from the same capture source identity/path/root, `ctx show session --provider ... --provider-session ...` should resolve deterministically, or the CLI should expose enough source metadata to disambiguate without requiring a prior SQL query.

## Local Evidence

Read-only query:

```sh
ctx sql --json "
SELECT provider, COUNT(*) rows, COUNT(DISTINCT provider_session_id) provider_ids,
       COUNT(DISTINCT source_path) source_paths
FROM ctx_sessions
WHERE provider IN ('claude','codex','opencode')
GROUP BY provider
ORDER BY provider"
```

Result:

| provider | rows | provider IDs | source paths |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| claude | 3,160 | 1,704 | 1,787 |
| codex | 16,684 | 15,796 | 15,789 |
| opencode | 406 | 406 | 1 |

Claude duplicate distribution:

```sh
ctx sql --json "
SELECT provider, n, COUNT(*) provider_ids
FROM (
  SELECT provider, provider_session_id, COUNT(*) n
  FROM ctx_sessions
  WHERE provider IN ('claude','codex','opencode')
  GROUP BY provider, provider_session_id
)
GROUP BY provider, n
ORDER BY provider, n"
```

Claude result:

| rows per provider_session_id | provider IDs |
| ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 331 |
| 2 | 1,371 |
| 26 | 1 |
| 61 | 1 |

Representative exact duplicate same-source group:

```sh
ctx sql --json "
SELECT provider_session_id, source_path, COUNT(*) rows,
       COUNT(DISTINCT ctx_session_id) ctx_ids,
       COUNT(DISTINCT source_identity) source_identities
FROM ctx_sessions
WHERE provider = 'claude'
GROUP BY provider_session_id, source_path
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY rows DESC
LIMIT 20"
```

For the repro session:

| provider_session_id | source_path | rows | ctx IDs | source identities |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `00396831-5087-49ad-a150-6ce5d0c6d08b` | `/home/.../.claude/projects/-home-...-NUI/00396831-5087-49ad-a150-6ce5d0c6d08b.jsonl` | 2 | 2 | 1 |

The first 20 duplicate `(provider_session_id, source_path)` groups all had 2 physical rows, 2 distinct ctx IDs, and 1 source identity.

There are also two high-duplication Claude outliers:

| provider_session_id | rows | source paths | source identities |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `6bce5269-b71e-4d20-84ce-b3cb80f6ac4e` | 61 | 60 | 1 |
| `fb116638-83b5-4ed4-856d-ddb51f43aae1` | 26 | 25 | 1 |

## Related Providers

Codex also has duplicate provider-session IDs, but sampled groups had multiple source paths and multiple source identities, which looks more like legitimate cross-source representation, such as overlap between history and session-tree sources.

OpenCode had no duplicate provider-session IDs in this index.

Because of that, Claude seems like the clean minimal repro for same-source duplicate physical rows.

## Possible Fixes

Any of these would make the provider-session lookup path usable:

1. Converge duplicate same-source provider imports into one logical `sessions` row.
2. Make provider-session lookup deterministic when all matches share the same capture source identity/path/root.
3. Add a native disambiguation command or error output that lists candidate `ctx_session_id` values with source metadata.

I locally prototyped option 2 as a compatibility fix:

- fetch a bounded set of provider-session matches
- collapse only when every matching session shares the same capture source identity/path/root
- keep genuinely distinct source matches ambiguous
- reuse the store/archive capture-source identity rule

That fixes the Claude repro above and keeps cross-source cases ambiguous, but it does not replace import-time convergence as the deeper identity model.

## Why It Matters

The CLI documents provider-session lookup, and downstream tooling can delegate native transcript reads to ctx only if:

```sh
ctx show session --provider <provider> --provider-session <provider_session_id>
```

is reliable for one logical provider transcript. Today same-source duplicate physical rows can make that path fail and require a `ctx_session_id` that callers do not naturally have.
