title: Post-v0.24 payload normalization change breaks reimport of existing indexes (`ProviderEventConflict`)
body:
## Summary

Commit `13e69e6d` ("De-overload provider retention metadata", #168) changed the normalized
provider payload shape. For events with no provider-supplied hash, the dedupe-key hash is
derived from that payload, so reimporting an event that an older binary already indexed now
produces a different hash for the same `(source_id, provider_index)`.
`reject_provider_event_hash_conflict` rejects that, and on the default import path the error
aborts the entire run.

Result: an index built before `13e69e6d` cannot complete an import afterwards. Reads keep
working, so the index just silently stops taking new sessions.

Bisected below. This is on `main`, not a released tag.

## Bisect

Same index copy (schema v46, never migrated), same Claude source tree, two adjacent commits:

| Build | Contains `13e69e6d` | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `a45c3956` (Merge #167) | no | **exit 0**, `imported_events: 1715`, `skipped_events: 472` |
| `6a95db1c` (Merge #168) | yes | **exit 1**, `ProviderEventConflict` |

```text
Error: store error: provider event conflict for provider-source/<source-uuid> at index 0:
existing hash fnv1a64:40b74f86ac45a7b4, new hash fnv1a64:8c201597ab2ffbfd
```

Both runs used `--data-root <scratch>` against a byte copy of the same pre-existing index, so
the only variable is the commit.

## Mechanism

1. `claude_event` (and the other providers touched by `13e69e6d`) changed the emitted payload
   keys. In `crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/providers/claude.rs`:

   ```diff
   -            "text": text,
   -            "truncated": truncated,
   +            "text": retained_text.text,
   +            "text_retention": retained_text.retention.as_json(),
                "content_preview": provider_capped_json(...),
   -            "content_retention": retention.as_str(),
   ```

2. `import_provider_capture_line` falls back to hashing that payload when the provider does
   not supply its own hash (`crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/importer.rs`):

   ```rust
   let event_hash = event
       .provider_event_hash
       .clone()
       .unwrap_or(compute_payload_hash(&payload)?);
   ```

3. The dedupe key is `provider-source:<source_id>:<provider_index>:<payload_hash>`, and
   `reject_provider_event_hash_conflict_from_rows` errors when a stored row has the same
   `(source_id, provider_index)` but a different `payload_hash`. The old rows carry the
   pre-`13e69e6d` hash; the reimport computes the post-`13e69e6d` hash.

So every already-indexed event of an affected shape conflicts on the next import, forever.

## Why one conflict kills the whole import

`import_provider_capture` only handles `ProviderEventConflict` on the non-default branch:

```rust
let was_present = if options.fast_event_inserts {
    // ...
    !store.insert_event_if_absent(&normalized_event)?   // ProviderEventConflict propagates
} else {
    match store.upsert_event(&normalized_event) {
        Ok(_) => {}
        Err(StoreError::Sql(rusqlite::Error::QueryReturnedNoRows)) => {}
        Err(StoreError::ProviderEventConflict { .. }) => {   // skipped, import continues
            summary.skipped_events += 1;
            summary.skipped += 1;
            summary.accepted_content_records += 1;
            return Ok(summary);
        }
        Err(err) => return Err(CaptureError::Store(err)),
    }
    was_present
};
```

`insert_event_if_absent` does `INSERT OR IGNORE` and then calls
`reject_provider_event_hash_conflict` when nothing was inserted, so it can raise the error.
`fast_event_inserts` defaults to `true` (`options.rs`), and native tree import sets it to
`true` explicitly.

This asymmetry predates `13e69e6d` and is not the root cause, but it is why a single
conflicting event aborts a multi-GiB import instead of being skipped the way the slow path
skips it. Same failure shape as #128.

## Repro

```sh
# with an index last written by a pre-13e69e6d binary
ctx import --provider claude --no-daemon
# Error: provider event conflict ... at index 0
# exit 1
```

A fresh index on the same binary imports the same sources fine (nothing stored to conflict
with), which is why this does not show up in clean-slate testing.

## Scope (what I did and did not establish)

Confirmed on one index for both Claude and Codex sources, each failing at its own
source/index. I have not established how broad the affected population is: it requires
pre-existing events whose fallback hash changes under the new normalization, so sources whose
provider supplies its own `provider_event_hash` should be unaffected.

I also did not check whether earlier sources commit before the run hits the conflict, so
"imports nothing" is what I observed for this invocation rather than a general claim.

Incidental note in case it saves you time: I first suspected the v47 repair (#174), since the
mandatory schema upgrade is what you hit immediately before the first import on new code. It
is not implicated. The conflict reproduces on an unmigrated v46 index using a build that
contains no v47 code at all, with the identical hash pair.

## Possible fixes

1. Re-hash or invalidate affected dedupe keys in a migration when the normalization changes.
2. Treat a same-identity/different-hash row as a legitimate update (payload changed) rather
   than a conflict, at least for the fallback-hash case where the hash is ctx's own output
   rather than provider-supplied.
3. At minimum, make the conflict non-fatal on the default path, matching the slow path, so
   one drifted event cannot take down the whole import.

## Environment

```text
built from main @ f208aa49 (`cargo install --path crates/ctx-cli --locked`)
```

`ctx --version` reports `0.25.0` at `f208aa49`, so it does not distinguish this 22-commit-post-tag
build from the v0.25.0 tag.

title: `--partial` removal silently breaks background import callers
body:
## Summary

#162 ("Make tolerant provider import the sole behavior") removed the `--partial` flag from
`ImportArgs`. Making tolerance unconditional is the right call, and it resolves the ask in
#128. But the flag now fails argument parsing rather than being accepted and ignored:

```text
$ ctx import --partial --quiet --no-daemon
error: unexpected argument '--partial' found

  tip: a similar argument exists: '--path'
$ echo $?
2
```

## Why this bites

`--partial` was the documented way to keep a long-lived index warm without one malformed row
killing the run, so it is exactly the flag you would expect to find in a background warmer.
Those callers tend to be written to never block or fail a foreground action:

```sh
ctx import --partial --quiet --no-daemon || true
```

With `|| true` the exit-2 parse failure is swallowed. The wrapper keeps reporting success
while the index quietly stops updating, and because reads keep working there is no symptom
until recall silently misses recent sessions. That is a slow, hard-to-attribute failure for
what is otherwise a clean simplification.

## Ask

Would a deprecation window be worth it: accept `--partial`, ignore it, and warn once that
tolerance is now unconditional? A release or two of that would let wrappers migrate without a
silent gap.

If a hard break is intended, that is a reasonable call too, but it is worth calling out in the
release notes under a heading that a wrapper author would actually grep for, since the failure
mode is silence rather than an error anyone sees.

## Environment

```text
built from main @ f208aa49
```

title: Bulk-import merge suppression can exceed FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT, aborting large first imports with `SQLITE_FULL`
body:
# Bulk-import merge suppression can exceed FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT, aborting large first imports with `SQLITE_FULL`

## Summary

Bulk mode sets `crisismerge = 1000000` on the event-search FTS5 tables
(`bulk_search.rs:372`) and holds it for the span of a whole source import. FTS5's
hard ceiling is `FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT = 2000`, so the suppression value is 500x
larger than the limit it has to stay under. On any single source large enough to
produce 2000 segments before the end-of-source compaction runs, `fts5AllocateSegid()`
sets `SQLITE_FULL` and the import aborts.

SQLite renders `SQLITE_FULL` as "database or disk is full", so the failure reads
as an out-of-disk condition on a machine with plenty free:

```text
Error: sqlite error: database or disk is full

Caused by:
    0: database or disk is full
    1: Error code 13: Insertion failed because database is full
```

This is not disk, not memory, and not corruption. Details under *Evidence*.

Encountered while rebuilding an index from scratch as a workaround for #176, but
it is an independent bug: it reproduces on a clean index with no pre-existing
rows to conflict with.

## Mechanism

`crates/ctx-history-store/src/bulk_search.rs`:

```rust
const FTS_AUTOMERGE_DEFAULT: i64 = 4;
const FTS_CRISISMERGE_DEFAULT: i64 = 16;
const FTS_BULK_CRISISMERGE: i64 = 1_000_000;   // :39
```

```rust
fn suppress_event_search_merges(store: &Store) -> Result<()> {   // :366
    for table in EVENT_SEARCH_FTS_TABLES {
        ...
        set_fts_config(store, table, "automerge", 0)?;                      // :371
        set_fts_config(store, table, "crisismerge", FTS_BULK_CRISISMERGE)?; // :372
    }
```

`automerge` is disabled outright and `crisismerge` is raised to 1,000,000. Both
are the mechanisms that would otherwise keep the segment count bounded during a
long insert run. Compaction is deferred to `merge_all_fts_tables_bounded()`,
which runs *after* the source completes.

The ceiling that is not deferred, in the vendored amalgamation
(`libsqlite3-sys-0.30.1/sqlite3/sqlite3.c`):

```c
#define FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT 2000                    // :232135

    if( pStruct->nSegment>=FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT ){    // :244594
      p->rc = SQLITE_FULL;
```

So for a source whose insert run creates >=2000 segments, hitting the cap before
the post-source compaction is structural, not a tuning accident.

## Evidence

Decoding the FTS5 structure record (`%_data` where `id=10`) on the aborted index:

| index | levels | segments |
|---|---:|---:|
| aborted mid-import | 2 | **2000** |
| healthy, fully merged | 65 | 2 |

Exactly 2000, i.e. the constant, not an approximate resource exhaustion.

Ruled out:

- **Disk**: 66-67 GiB free on the target filesystem, sampled every 15s across
  both runs. A 2 GiB `dd` to the same filesystem completes in ~1s. The failing
  database was 0.3-0.7 GiB.
- **Kernel `ENOSPC`**: `strace -f` over `write`/`pwrite64`/`ftruncate`/`fallocate`/`openat`
  for a whole failing run recorded **zero** `ENOSPC`. SQLite raises this
  internally; the kernel never reports a full device.
- **`temp_store = MEMORY`** (`connection.rs:225`): not implicated. An FTS5
  `optimize` on the aborted index fails in 0.0s with peak RSS 0.01 GiB under
  **both** `temp_store=MEMORY` and `temp_store=FILE`.
- **Page limit**: `max_page_count` is 4294967294 with `page_count` 181,886.
- **Corruption**: `PRAGMA quick_check` returns `ok`.
- **Memory**: 43 GiB available, no cgroup limit, no `ulimit`.

## Repro

Import a provider source large enough to create 2000 segments into a fresh data
root. Observed on one machine, importing from scratch:

| provider | source size | result |
|---|---:|---|
| opencode | 121 MiB | **ok** (447 sessions, 10,478 events) |
| claude | 1.0 GiB | `SQLITE_FULL` at ~523 MiB of database |
| codex | 2.0 GiB | `SQLITE_FULL` at ~703 MiB of database |

The same failure hits `ctx setup` over all sources at once (18,330 files,
3.1 GiB), aborting at ~303 MiB.

Note this does not reproduce on small fixtures, and it does not reproduce on
incremental imports against an already-merged index. Only a single source run
long enough to accumulate 2000 segments triggers it, which is why routine
warm-up imports never show it.

## Recovery

A plain FTS5 `rebuild` re-derives the index from `%_content` and collapses the
segments. `event_search` is an ordinary FTS5 table (not contentless, not
external-content), so this is non-destructive:

```sql
INSERT INTO event_search(event_search) VALUES('rebuild');
```

Measured: 2000 -> 19 segments in 1.4s, after which `optimize` succeeds where it
had failed.

Driving a large first import to completion is then possible by looping
import -> on-`SQLITE_FULL` rebuild -> resume. That took 4 passes for the 1.0 GiB
source and 11 for the 2.0 GiB one, which is consistent with the cap being hit
repeatedly rather than once.

## Possible fixes

1. Bound the suppression by segment count rather than by source boundary: run a
   compaction step when `nSegment` approaches `FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT`, so a long
   source cannot reach the ceiling.
2. Set `FTS_BULK_CRISISMERGE` below `FTS5_MAX_SEGMENT` instead of far above it.
   A crisis merge during a long run is presumably cheaper than aborting it.
3. At minimum, translate `SQLITE_FULL` from an FTS5 write into a diagnostic that
   names the segment cap. "database or disk is full" sends you to `df`, which is
   a long way from the actual cause.

## Scope

Established on one machine, one index, reproducing across three provider sources
and both the staged and combined import paths. I have not measured where the

title: Fix NativePath stalls and redesign index watch
body:
## Summary

- redraw `ctx index watch` in place on interactive terminals while preserving append-only redirected output and NDJSON for `--json`
- replace the internal-looking status block with a responsive dashboard: byte-weighted progress, indexed sessions, searchable records, measured throughput, ETA, semantic-search state, and actionable failure output
- adapt cleanly from wide terminals down to 24 columns; honor `NO_COLOR` and `TERM=dumb`; keep healthy daemon internals hidden
- add source-byte progress that preserves completed append-only prefixes and expose it as additive fields under `lexical` in machine output
- replace projection-impact queries that rescanned the complete event corpus for every imported source/session with index-driven `UNION ALL` branches
- replace source-generation retirement global union/sort scans with resumable owner-scoped keyset traversal
- add composite retirement indexes plus query-plan and lifecycle regression coverage
- treat malformed provider records as nonfatal data-quality rejections: indexing completes and the normal watch stays quiet, while durable aggregate diagnostics remain available through status/doctor JSON
- keep source-level import failures terminal: lexical state becomes `failed`, and both `ctx index watch` and `ctx index wait` stop promptly with an actionable error

## Root cause

The apparent 0/4,390 stall had two layers. The watch numerator represented finalized inventory units, which remain zero until NativePath root cutover, so it hid intermediate progress. More importantly, each source/session mutation ran broad `LEFT JOIN ... OR ... DISTINCT` impact queries over the entire event corpus. On the 13.6 GiB dogfood store this repeatedly scanned roughly 580k+ events, making cold import effectively quadratic and pinning one core.

The final stop at 97% was a separate lifecycle bug: valid and malformed records can coexist in a provider source, but rejected rows were treated as a daemon-wide failure. A later healthy source cycle could also overwrite the rejection count. Rejections are now nonfatal and tracked per source across cycles and restarts; real source failures remain terminal.

## Validation

- `scripts/check.sh --mode fast --force-rerun`: 47/47 Bazel release and repository checks passed; the post-rebase fast gate also passed 47/47
- Bazel `unit_tests`, `index_tests`, and `setup_sources_import_tests` passed
- Bazel Clippy for the CLI passed with warnings denied
- `cargo test -p ctx --test index`: 10/10 passed
- `cargo test -p ctx --test setup_sources_import`: 62/62 passed
- focused daemon-history unit coverage: 8/8 passed
- independent lifecycle re-review found no remaining issues after verifying terminal source failures and durable multi-source rejection diagnostics
- `cargo fmt --all --check`, `git diff --check`, docs, LOC policy, package audit, release construction, and performance smoke checks passed
- Windows GNU cross-check passed; release target-matrix checks passed
- JSON watch output parsed as NDJSON, included additive lexical byte fields, and contained no ANSI escapes
- live release-binary dogfood on the 13.7 GiB store at 80, 52, and 24 columns showed no wrapping and advanced records/throughput correctly
- query-plan tests prove indexed branches and no table scans/temp sorts for the repaired paths
- real-data resume on the same store advanced from 1,936 to more than 3,300 indexed sessions in minutes; the old 0.26.2 process had reached only 1,919 after about 87 minutes
- repeated SIGTERM/resume checks preserved progress and produced no failed units

title: fix(ingestion): admit empty existing Store targets to the cold builder
body:
## The defect

`ColdStoreBuild::begin_with_hard_link_probe` decided cold-build eligibility from a single `stat`:

```rust
match cold_target_state(&target_path)? {
    ColdTargetState::ExistingRegular => return Ok(None),   // ordinary incremental writer
    ColdTargetState::Absent => {}
}
```

The optimized cold builder — `journal_mode=OFF`, `synchronous=OFF`, `locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE`, FTS dropped during the load and rebuilt once at the end, atomic adjacent publication — was therefore reachable only on a brand-new install. `ctx setup`, and every import that admitted no content, leaves a `work.sqlite` behind, so the very next real import fell back to the ordinary writer even though the destination held nothing at all. On a 1.087 GB Codex corpus that is **8.6x wall time and 2.7x write amplification for byte-identical logical output**.

Eligibility is a property of the projection being written, not of whether the destination file happens to exist.

## Approach

Option 1 of the two candidates: **extend admission to an existing but wholly empty generation**, keeping the stage build and the publication primitive exactly as they are today.

I did not take the stage-and-merge option. Merging into a populated target changes what "canonical row" means during a bulk load — cursors, locator generations, source routes and dedupe identity all have to be reconciled inside the merge transaction — and none of that is needed to fix the reported defect. The empty-target case is the one every upgrading and newly set-up install actually hits.

Two deliberate departures from the issue's sketch:

**The admission predicate is strictly stronger than `fresh_provider_projection_eligible()`.** That predicate is safe on a stage this builder owns, but it tolerates catalog, artifact and summary rows, so using it to authorize destroying a destination the user owns would silently discard their rows. Admission now scans *every* table in the migrated destination and requires it empty outside a documented set: four control singletons, the FTS virtual and shadow tables (each a projection of a canonical table that must itself be empty), and `history_records`. A table nobody classified fails closed, so a projection added later cannot be discarded by a build that predates it. A test asserts the classification covers exactly the pristine schema.

**Control history records are carried, not dropped.** The import-control records an earlier run created move into the new generation before any provider content, bounded at 4096 records; a destination holding more than that is not a bootstrap state and stays on the ordinary writer. Publication therefore never loses a row the destination already held — the measured runs confirm the rebuilt generation has the same two `history_records` the ordinary writer produces.

Admission runs *after* `Store::open`, so a released v0.25 database is migrated before emptiness means anything, and a destination the ordinary writer would need to diagnose declines cold admission and is handed straight back to it.

## The exclusion invariant

The emptiness proof has to hold not just when it runs but through the install that follows it. A SQLite transaction the cold path opens and drops is **not** sufficient: ordinary `Store` writers do not participate in the cold-build lock, so a commit could land in the gap between a proof that ended and an install that had not started, and be replaced away. SQLite writes in place, so an inode check does not catch it either.

The invariant chosen instead is a **publication lease**, an adjacent `work.sqlite.ctx-store-publication.lock`:

* every writable `Store::open` takes it **shared** for the lifetime of the `Store`;
* the cold path takes it **exclusive** and holds it continuously across the emptiness proof, the retirement and the install.

While the lease is held exclusively no writable `Store` can exist, so no commit can reach the destination in that window. A writer that already holds the destination open holds the lease shared, so publication cannot start; when the writer finishes, the proof observes its rows and fails closed. Both directions are covered by tests, and both were verified to fail against a mutant that releases the lease immediately.

The lease is deliberately *not* the cold-build lock. That one is held for the whole multi-second build and only serializes cold builders against each other; taking it in `Store::open` would block every ordinary writer for the duration of a build. The publication lease is held for the milliseconds an install takes, so writers are excluded exactly when it matters. Admission takes the same lease non-blockingly as an early-decline probe: a live writable `Store` sends the import to the ordinary writer immediately rather than failing a completed build. `Store::open_read_only` does not take the lease; readers are unaffected.

**Both waits on the lease are bounded, in both directions.** An advisory lock outlives the *liveness* of the process holding it: a `SIGSTOP`ped process, a frozen cgroup (`cgroup.freeze = 1`, as a quiescing benchmark harness would use), an attached debugger, or a stalled filesystem all keep the lease held while making no progress. An unbounded wait on the open side would turn one wedged publication into a product-wide hang — daemon, import, search-with-refresh and Pro materialization alike — with nothing to point at.

* A writable open polls for **10s**, comfortably above a normal install and below the 30s SQLite busy timeout, then fails with `StorePublicationLeaseUnavailable`, which names the lease path and says a publication appears stuck.
* Publication polls for **5s** for shared holders to clear, then fails closed and leaves the import on the ordinary writer rather than publishing over a destination someone is holding open.

There is no cycle between the two bounds: publication waits only on live shared holders, and openers wait only on an actual exclusive holder.

## Preserving the `9e7d1b4f6` TOCTOU guarantee

That commit made admission absent-only and forced every install through an absent-target-only publication, closing a real overwrite race on zero-byte targets. Admitting an existing destination re-opens that door by construction, so it is closed several ways:

1. **The publication primitive is unchanged.** Both admissions still end in `create_absent_hard_link_with`, which fails closed the instant any other object owns the destination name. There is no new `rename`, no `RENAME_EXCHANGE`, and no clobbering path anywhere in the diff.
2. **The exclusive publication lease** spans the proof and the install, as above.
3. **The admitted state is re-proved immediately before publication**: the destination must still be the exact admitted `(device, inode)`, must still be empty, and its carried rows must still digest identically. The digest covers every column of every row, not just the id set, so an update that rewrites a record's contents in place is caught rather than replaced away.
4. **Retirement is identity-checked and reversible.** The admitted object is hard-linked aside before its name is removed, the removal only fires when the handle still matches, and a failed publication links the retired generation straight back — with the same absent-only primitive, so a concurrent winner is never overwritten by the rollback.

## Durability and recovery

The backup link is made durable **before** the only other name for the object is removed, and every subsequent directory mutation is synced before the next:

```
link_absent(target -> retired)
fsync_directory(parent)          # backup durable before the original name goes
remove_path_if_same(target)      # identity-checked
fsync_directory(parent)
install_same_filesystem(stage -> target)
fsync_directory(parent)
```

No crash can therefore leave the parent directory without a name for the admitted generation. Recovery runs under the cold lock before admission and never deletes a generation it cannot prove redundant:

* target absent, one retired name — the crash landed between the unlink and the install. Restore it, drop the backup name.
* target present and the *same object* as a retired name — the crash landed between the backup link and the unlink. The backup is a redundant second name for a live object, so drop it.
* target present and a *different* object — another owner took the destination. The retired generation is real data nothing else will claim: keep it, and decline the rebuild until it is resolved.

The orphan sweep no longer touches retired names at all. When a rollback cannot restore, the retired copy is **retained** and its path is reported through a dedicated `ColdStoreRetiredGenerationRetained` error that carries the underlying cause in its message.

## Measurements

Reproduced on this branch against a pristine `origin/main` build of the same tree. 1.087 GB / 32-file real Codex JSONL corpus, `taskset` pinned to 8 cores, `env -i` isolated, warm page cache, `--no-daemon`, Core-only, serialized through the shared benchmark lock. Medians of 5 runs unless noted.

| Arm | Wall | User CPU | Sys CPU | FS output blocks | Events | Final DB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| before — absent target | 18.03s | 26.70 | 1.87 | 1,722,328 | 142,950 | 682,266,624 |
| before — existing empty target | **156.79s** | 142.94 | 23.39 | 4,588,176 | 142,950 | 681,107,456 |
| after — absent target | 18.93s | 26.38 | 1.88 | 1,722,328 | 142,950 | 682,246,144 |
| after — existing empty target | **18.28s** | 26.93 | 2.01 | 1,722,360 | 142,950 | 682,237,952 |

before absent `[18.05, 18.03, 18.39, 17.98, 17.94]` · after absent `[19.41, 18.93, 19.53, 17.91, 17.79]` · after existing-empty `[18.28, 18.28, 18.47, 18.27, 18.60]`

- **8.6x wall, 5.3x user CPU, 11.6x system CPU, 2.7x fewer write blocks** on the existing-empty arm.
- The existing-empty arm is now **at parity** with the absent arm — 1.4% above the absent-target baseline median, and slightly below the absent arm on this branch.
- **The added synchronization costs nothing measurable.** The lease is taken twice per import — once non-blocking at admission, once for the install — against a ~18s build.
- No-op re-import against a populated target: 0.07s, unchanged.

### Absent-arm re-confirmation

The absent arm is the one that must not regress, so it was re-measured with the final build using **interleaved paired sampling** — baseline and branch run back to back inside each iteration, so both see the same background load and host drift cancels. 8 paired iterations:

| | min | median | max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline absent | 18.54s | 24.80s | 31.27s |
| branch absent | 18.48s | 18.80s | 27.81s |
| branch existing-empty | 18.21s | 20.36s | 26.74s |

Per-iteration delta (branch − baseline): `[-8.27, -9.95, -3.46, -0.09, -4.04, -0.05, -1.39, -0.39]` — **the branch was not slower in any of the 8 paired iterations.**

The absolute medians here are inflated by other work on the host, and the within-iteration ordering runs the baseline first, so the negative deltas are biased in the branch's favour; I read this as **no regression**, not as a speed-up. The minimums, which are the least-contaminated estimator, agree: 18.54s baseline vs 18.48s branch — equal. Write blocks are identical across all three arms (~1,722,400), and the existing-empty arm's minimum (18.21s) sits at the absent arm's (18.48s).

Worth noting for future measurement on this host: `taskset -c 24-31` is physical cores 8–15, the lower-binned CCD (mean `highest_perf` 183.5 vs 222.9 on cores 0–7), so contention there is real and asymmetric — one reason the paired design rather than raw medians is the right read.

Logical output is identical across both arms and matches the ordinary writer:

| | after absent | after existing-empty | before existing-empty |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PRAGMA integrity_check` | ok | ok | ok |
| foreign-key violations | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| sessions / events / edges / runs | 32 / 142950 / 17 / 1085 | 32 / 142950 / 17 / 1085 | 32 / 142950 / 17 / 1085 |
| capture sources / locators / cursors | 32 / 32 / 32 | 32 / 32 / 32 | 32 / 32 / 32 |
| rejected records | 16 | 16 | 16 |
| `history_records` | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| ordered event + session row digests | equal | equal | equal |
| FTS `event_search MATCH` hits | 17157 | 17157 | 17157 |
| `ctx search` result set | equal | equal | equal |

The `history_records` column is the point of the carry: the existing-empty arm keeps the control record the seeding import created, exactly as the ordinary writer does.

## Platform matrix

- **Linux x86_64** — full build, the measurements above, the complete Rust test graph, and `scripts/check.sh --mode presubmit` (93/93 Bazel targets).
- **macOS / Windows** — validated by construction rather than execution; the C dependencies could not be cross-built here. Everything on the changed path is already cross-platform: `same_file::Handle` for identity, `fs::hard_link` (`CreateHardLinkW` on Windows) for both publication and retirement, `fs2` advisory locks for the lease, and the existing `link_count`/`fsync_directory` `cfg` split, where the Windows `link_count` returns `None` and the extra Unix link-count invariant is skipped. No `renameat2` is introduced — the primitive was already the portable hard link.
- Windows cannot unlink a database another handle holds open. Rather than discover that after a full build, admission runs a **retirability probe**: it performs the exact retire-and-restore sequence in microseconds, puts the admitted object straight back, and declines to the ordinary writer if any step fails. A read-only parent directory reproduces that refusal on Unix and is covered by a test.

## Tests

- existing-empty-target admission, end to end and at the CLI seam;
- existing-non-empty target correctly *not* taking the rebuild path — a real prior import, catalog rows the stage predicate would have tolerated, and a non-database file;
- **exclusion**: a writable `Store` cannot be opened while publication holds the lease; a writer that starts inside the proof-to-install window cannot commit there and lands in the published generation instead; a commit from a `Store` opened *before* the proof is never replaced away; a writer racing a full publication is never dropped in either ordering;
- **liveness**: a lease held past the open deadline fails a writable open in bounded time with the named `StorePublicationLeaseUnavailable` error, and a released lease lets writers open again;
- **durability**: a crash between the backup link and the unlink leaves a redundant name the next owner drops; a crash between the unlink and the install is restored; a retired generation that differs from a live destination is retained, never swept, and declines the rebuild; the retained path is named ahead of its cause;
- **content digest**: an in-place rewrite of a carried record's body, which leaves the id set identical, invalidates the admission;
- the concurrent-target-mutation race in both shapes; the retirability probe declining cleanly; schema-drift fail-closed against an unknown table with rows, with the classification asserted against the pristine schema.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` (no new warnings), `scripts/check-loc.sh`, and `scripts/check.sh --mode presubmit` all pass. Two mechanical moves keep files under the 1000-line source ceiling: the pre-existing `cold_store.rs` test module to `cold_store/tests.rs`, and the adjacent-name publication and recovery helpers to `cold_store/publish.rs`.

## Out of scope

Deliberately untouched: the ingestion architecture, canonical identities, cursors, locators, lifecycle classification, privacy rules, provider parsers, the ordinary incremental writer, and every existing bound. Stage-and-merge into a populated destination is not attempted here.

title: First setup takes multiple hours for a 4.5 GiB multi-harness corpus while CPU and disk remain mostly idle
body:
## Problem

A clean `ctx setup` on a real multi-harness history corpus is still running after almost two hours, despite the host no longer having meaningful disk contention. The process uses roughly half of one CPU core while system-wide I/O wait stays around 0-3%.

The new bounded-WAL behavior is working very well: the main WAL has remained below 56.2 MiB instead of growing into multiple gigabytes. This issue is specifically about first-import throughput, not WAL growth.

## Reproduction

- `ctx 0.26.0`
- commit `0185699b4c6662272a16fe22ac11e54a975bfab2`
- clean/disposable data store
- command:

  ```console
  /usr/bin/time -v ctx setup --no-daemon --wait --json --progress json
  ```

- discovered corpus: 5 history sources, 66 files, 4.5 GiB
- sources include Codex, Claude, OpenCode, and other supported local harnesses

## Observed profile

The initial Codex cold-store phase processed 3,561,444,338 bytes in 1,829.94 seconds:

```text
schema=0.558s
core=527.341s
journal=386.226s
indexes+fts=62.925s
validation=852.359s
  database=845.488s
  search=6.871s
install=0.040s
```

After that, setup inventoried the complete 4.5 GiB corpus and continued source-by-source. Claude was reported complete after another long pass. At 1h56m the command was still processing OpenCode:

```text
ctx process CPU:          ~53% of one core
system I/O wait:          0-3%
process read_bytes:       17,982,562,304
process write_bytes:       3,516,149,760
main database:             2,323,824,640 bytes
main WAL:                     58,878,952 bytes
temporary OpenCode DB:       920,432,640 bytes
temporary OpenCode WAL:        5,290,112 bytes
```

The process remains runnable and its counters continue to advance, so this does not look like a deadlock. It looks like a mostly sequential pipeline with repeated full reads and expensive validation.

## Expected

A 4.5 GiB first import should not require multiple hours while leaving almost all CPU capacity idle. Ideally, setup should avoid repeated full-corpus/database passes and should either:

- reuse work already performed by the cold-store phase;
- validate incrementally or once at the publication boundary;
- avoid rebuilding/scanning provider-specific temporary stores serially when safe parallelism is possible.

## Questions

1. Is the full database validation after each cold-store build intentional? In this run validation alone took 852 seconds and was almost entirely database validation.
2. Is the complete source inventory subsequently read again after the Codex cold-store phase?
3. Would a profile captured from this corpus be useful for identifying the highest-value optimization boundary?

I can add the final elapsed time and final status/pending counts once this same run completes.

title: fix: stop rejecting admitted NativePath groups so v0.25 upgrades import
body:
Importing into a database upgraded from v0.25 runs for about seven minutes and
then hard-fails. Every existing v0.25 user hits this on their first 0.26 import.

## The failure, reproduced

Populated a data root with the released v0.25 binary over the 1.087 GB real
Codex corpus, snapshotted it, then ran a release build of `origin/main` against
the same data root and corpus.

```
Error: store error: NativePath publication group uncompressed journal encoding
bytes accounting is 8392067; maximum is 8388608
```

Exit status 1 after 7:27.86 wall. The database grew 640,315,392 -> 1,253,744,640
bytes before aborting. Byte-identical to the two runs already on record.

| Arm, same 1.087 GB corpus | Wall | Total CPU | Outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| v0.25 -> v0.26, `origin/main` | 410.8s / 431.8s / **447.9s** | 418.1 / 438.5 / **446.1** | **fails** |
| v0.25 -> v0.26, this branch | **270.2s** | **276.7** | **ok** — 142,950 events, 32 sessions, 17 edges |
| repeat import after that | **0.06s** | 0.01 | ok — `"change": "no_op"`, 0 imported |

## Root cause

It is not what the journal encoding contains. It is *which* quantity the group
bounds versus which quantity it enforces.

A `NativePathPublicationGroup` is admitted up front, before any of its work
runs. `NativePathGroupAccounting` fixes the coordinator's pages, sources, and
retained page bytes; `charge_core_mutations` then charges each typed call before
it executes. But the group also enforced two quantities that only the Store can
measure, computed from content the coordinator sized by a different, approximate
measure. Those two can exceed their ceilings on a group the Store already
admitted, and there is no way back: the mutation has run, the group is poisoned,
the transaction rolls back.

**Instance one, journal bytes.** Admission bounds provider-serialized page bytes
at 8 MiB (`NATIVE_PATH_MAX_RETAINED_PAGE_BYTES`). The journal encoding of the
same rows was enforced against an equal 8 MiB ceiling, and it is always the
larger of the two — it carries the canonical observation, evidence, provenance
and digests, not the provider's raw bytes. So *every* group filled to the
admission ceiling overflows. I instrumented the collector and the coordinator
and ran the upgrade to the failure point:

```
DBG group-attempt   chunks=1 pages=165 bytes=8347003
DBG byte-overflow   records=1843 bytes=8385408 next_bytes=8389903 ...
DBG split-at-zero   pages=165 bytes=8347003
DBG group-attempt   chunks=1 pages=82  bytes=4216276     <- both halves commit
DBG group-attempt   chunks=1 pages=83  bytes=4130727
```

49 of 145 group attempts overflowed this way. Each one wrote its Core rows,
overflowed, rolled back, and was redone as two halves — about a third of all
group work, wasted, on the passing runs too.

**Why an upgraded store emits a journal record per event at all.** Credit to the
ordinary-writer agent for tracing this half: on a store that already holds the
rows, `reconcile_provider_event_inner` falls through to
`provider_event_with_same_identity`, and when the stored hash or authority
differs it takes `write_event` — the upsert path — which re-reads
`semantic_searchable_document_count_from_stored_event`, runs
`upsert_event_search_projection_for_event` as a delete-and-re-insert across
three FTS tables, and appends a projection-journal record. A v0.25→v0.26
normalization change that alters every stored event's hash therefore turns every
event into a full FTS rewrite plus a journal record. That is the mechanism
behind the 49 bulk overflows and a large share of the runtime.

**Why splitting could not rescue it.** The coordinator's only recovery is to
republish the group as smaller page splits, which works while journal volume
tracks the pages. The group that actually killed the import was not
record-per-event: it was fanout. `upsert_session` and `upsert_capture_source`
land on rows that already exist and re-journal *every* canonical observation
whose digest the mutation changed — volume that is a function of rows already
stored, and does not shrink when the page count does. The ladder walked all the
way down and gave up:

```
DBG group-attempt   chunks=1 pages=1 bytes=10566
DBG byte-overflow   records=1811 bytes=8380218 next_bytes=8392067
                    last_kind=Event last_op=Upsert last_rev=2 ...
DBG UNSPLITTABLE    pages=1 bytes=10566
```

One page of 10,566 provider bytes produced 8,392,067 bytes of journal across
1,811 records. A page carries at most 64 units, so those records cannot be the
page's own events — they are fanout, and `last_rev=2` confirms it: second
revisions of observations that predate the run. Re-journaled upserts, not
reconciliation or retirement entries; the original hypothesis was close but
named the wrong mechanism. A single page is the smallest unit the coordinator
has, so `split_at_page_boundary` returns `None` and the import aborts.

A fresh 0.26 import never sees this because it uses the cold builder, where the
journal is inactive during the load and one baseline is written at the end. An
import into an existing-but-empty store survives because its journal volume does
track its pages, so splitting converges.

**Instance two, Core bind bytes.** With the journal ceiling removed the same
upgrade ran 65 seconds and then failed at:

```
Error: store error: NativePath publication group Core bound-value encoding
bytes accounting is 8390314; maximum is 8388608
```

Same defect, second instance. `NATIVE_PATH_MAX_CORE_BOUND_BYTES` was also 8 MiB,
also compared against content admitted at 8 MiB of provider-serialized bytes,
and the exact SQLite bind encoding is likewise the larger of the two — it carries
canonical columns (`metadata_json`, source paths, identity columns) the provider
estimate does not model. Over by 1,706 bytes on 8 MiB. This one had no recovery
path at all; the split ladder only ever matched journal errors.

## The fix

The Store now enforces exactly the quantities admission fixes, and nothing else:

* `page_count`, `source_count`, `retained_page_bytes` — coordinator accounting,
  validated when the group opens, immutable afterwards;
* `attempted_mutation_units` — the coordinator counts typed calls exactly from
  its own pages, and the Store charges before each call runs.

Core bind bytes and journal records/bytes are still measured exactly and still
reported on `NativePathGroupReceipt`. They no longer reject. An admitted group
commits.

The 8 MiB constant is not raised. It is not replaced by a larger one either.
`NATIVE_PATH_MAX_JOURNAL_BYTES` and `NATIVE_PATH_MAX_JOURNAL_RECORDS` are gone
because no per-group ceiling on derived journal volume can be both hard and
non-failing: one admitted Core mutation's fanout is unbounded by construction,
and it must be atomic with the mutation that caused it or the published cursor
would carry a checkpoint claiming a consistency the journal does not have.

So the journal stays bounded where the resource actually is. `GroupJournalCollector`
buffered the whole group; it now writes each completed chunk into the same
publication transaction as soon as it fills, retaining one chunk. This is the
streaming shape `append_baseline` already uses for a whole-corpus baseline in a
single transaction. Resident journal memory goes from a whole group (up to 4,096
records / 8 MiB) to one page (64 records), so this is a strictly tighter memory
bound than the one it replaces, and it is hard by construction: the chunk is
flushed the moment the next record would cross `PROJECTION_JOURNAL_CHUNK_SIZE`
or `PROJECTION_JOURNAL_MAX_PAGE_BYTES`.

Invariants preserved. Every chunk insert happens inside the group's existing
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so Core + source-generation + journal + cursor publication
stay one atomic unit and an abandoned group still rolls its chunks back with the
rows that produced them. Crash recovery, deterministic record ordering, and
privacy are untouched.

With the Store no longer rejecting admitted groups, the Codex split ladder is
unreachable and is removed, along with the mid-source split cursor only it used
(`split_at_page_boundary`, `build_context_store_cursor`, and the four
`CodexPublicationContext` fields that cursor read).

## What is actually bounded per transaction, and what is not

Removing a ceiling on journal output is only safe if something else bounds the
work. Streaming bounds *memory*, not transaction size, so on its own it traded a
rejected group for an unbounded one. Precisely:

* **Group input** — bounded by the four admission limits.
* **Journal memory** — bounded by one physical chunk (64 records), tighter than
  the whole-group buffer it replaces, and hard by construction.
* **Journal work per transaction** — bounded by the group's own admitted content
  *while the group leaves its parent rows unchanged*, which is now the normal
  case. Most of the fanout was never necessary: `write_raw_core` re-asserts the
  same capture source and session once per publication group, so a session with
  E events published over G groups paid O(G·E) canonical-observation builds and
  SHA-256s that emitted nothing, because the recomputed digests matched. The
  instrumented 1.087 GB upgrade made 3,522,400 `append_entity` calls and
  discarded 2,978,880 of them. All three mutations whose journal impact fans out
  over stored rows — `upsert_capture_source`, `upsert_session` and `upsert_run`
  — now read the stored row before and after the write and skip the fanout when
  it did not change. `CaptureSource`, `Session` and `Run` cover every column of
  their tables and compare `metadata_json` as parsed JSON, so an equal row
  implies an equal result for every dependent read — the skip is exact, not a
  heuristic, and a changed row still fans out. Two unit tests pin both
  directions.
* **Journal work per transaction when a parent row genuinely changes** — **still
  unbounded, and this PR does not close it.** The fanout then re-journals every
  dependent observation of that parent, and it has to be atomic with the
  mutation or the published cursor would carry a checkpoint claiming a
  consistency the journal does not have. Closing it requires the fanout itself
  to become resumable across transactions: a durable dirty-entity queue drained
  in bounded pages, in the shape `retire_source_generation_page` already uses.
  That needs a new table, so a schema migration off the frozen v47 identity, and
  is deliberately not attempted in a release-blocker fix.

The bounds comment in `native_path_group.rs` now states exactly this rather than
asserting a bound the code does not deliver.

**Sequencing.** Once upgrades rebuild-and-replace a pre-0.26 provider projection
instead of publishing alongside it, re-derivation runs through the cold builder,
where the journal is inactive during the load and one baseline is written at the
end — so the unbounded case disappears from the upgrade path entirely, and what
remains is a genuine actor-identity change inside an ordinary incremental
import. My recommendation is: land this, land rebuild-and-replace, then do the
resumable drain as the third step with the schema change it needs. I would not
hold the release blocker for the drain, but it should not be dropped: without
it, one session whose lineage resolves late still writes its whole event set in
one transaction.

## The upgrade arm

Its absence is why this shipped: every benchmark and integration arm in the 0.26
program used a fresh `CTX_DATA_ROOT`.

The released-store shape is the diff between the current schema and a real
v0.25 database: no projection journal, no NativePath publication cursors, and
six tables v0.25 never had — provider source locators, capture-source provider
routes, source generations and entities, session and event aliases — plus a
bare-UUID `source_identity` and the released `role_hint` vocabulary.

`released_store_upgrade_import_publishes_and_then_replays_as_a_noop` builds that
shape, imports into it, and requires the next import to be a no-op plus
`PRAGMA integrity_check` ok and zero FK violations. **On the parent commit it
fails with `uncompressed journal encoding bytes accounting is 8397053; maximum
is 8388608`** — the same error, from the same limit, as the field failure.

That test proves *publication*. It deliberately makes no claim about the
canonical event set, because any count assertion it could make there would have
to be a floor, and a floor is exactly what a duplicating upgrade passes.

The canonical-set claim lives in a second test,
`released_store_upgrade_matches_a_fresh_install_canonical_set`, which imports
the same corpus into a fresh store as a control and requires the upgraded store
to hold **exactly** the control's events, sessions, edges and capture sources.
It is `#[ignore]`d with a reason naming the duplication defect and the re-derive
branch that owns the fix, so it cannot silently pass, and it must not be
weakened to a floor.

Getting that test to fail honestly took two corrections worth recording, because
both are traps for the re-derive work:

1. The first shape left the six identity tables in place, so the upgrading
   import resolved through routes and locators the setup import had just
   written, reconciled with its own rows, and the exact assertion **passed** —
   a green gate over a defect the field reproduces. Clearing them is what makes
   the store actually look released.
2. Even then a synthetic upgrade re-derives the very ids already present. The
   property that actually distinguishes a released store is that *another
   release derived different identities*. The canonical-set test therefore also
   re-keys released capture sources and events to ids this build cannot derive.
   With that it fails as it should: the upgraded store keeps **two capture
   sources where a fresh install has one**, the miniature of the 284,923 versus
   142,950 events measured on the real corpus.

The perf smoke matrix gets a matching `released_store_upgrade_import` arm. It
runs last so no earlier arm observes it, reshapes the data root, imports, and
requires the following repeat import to be a no-op. Candidate only, since v0.25
is the release it upgrades from. The mock CLI now creates the tables the reshape
touches so the harness self-test exercises the arm instead of skipping it.

## Verification

`v0.25 -> v0.26` on the 1.087 GB corpus, pinned to cores 24-31 under the shared
benchmark lock, page cache equalised:

* import exits 0 in 270.2s and imports 142,950 events / 32 sessions / 17 edges —
  the same event count a fresh 0.26 import produces;
* repeat import is a 0.06s no-op, `"change": "no_op"`;
* `PRAGMA integrity_check` = ok, `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` = 0 rows;
* FTS queryable (262,904 rows), `ctx search "cargo test" --refresh off` returns
  the expected Codex hits, `ctx status` reports initialized;
* all 32 cursors advanced.

Re-confirmed three more times on the same corpus and the same v0.25 snapshot —
after the fanout change, after rebasing onto `origin/main` with #192, and after
rebasing again onto #201/#202/#203 — every one exit 0 under a hard `timeout`,
every one 142,950 events / 32 sessions / 17 edges, every one with a
`"change": "no_op"` repeat, integrity ok and 0 FK violations.

All four runs leave **byte-identical** canonical and journal state: 284,923
events, 34 sessions, 94 capture sources, 32 cursors, 262,904 FTS rows, 4,342
journal chunks, journal high-water 275,572. That is the strongest evidence
available that skipping unchanged-parent fanout changes nothing observable.

Cost fell from 276.7s CPU to 133.1s, 109.3s and 110.8s, but those three arms ran
untimed on cores 0-7 under contention rather than under the benchmark lock, so
treat the trend as indicative rather than as a benchmark number. The host
currently cannot resolve below roughly 10%; this is well outside that.

Fresh install on the same corpus, rerun on this branch: 142,950 events /
32 sessions / 17 edges in 24.0s wall, repeat import `"change": "no_op"`. Same
counts and same no-op with the data root pre-created. (Untimed, cores 0-7 at
nice, not under the benchmark lock — these were checked for behaviour, not for
comparable timings.)

Append, rewrite, truncation, deletion, restart and existing-store paths are
covered by the 1,248 `ctx-history-capture` and 334 `ctx-history-store` unit
tests, all green.

**Producer-deadlock hygiene.** A separate defect on `origin/main`
(`CODEX_SOURCE_MAX_QUEUED_WINDOWS = 4` over-committing the producer byte budget)
hangs roughly one cold import in ten. This branch does not touch that constant
or the producer, and none of the runs above were affected: every one terminated
with a definite exit status and a JSON packet, none was killed or abandoned. The
re-confirmation runs since then use a hard `timeout --signal=KILL` and report a
wedge as a distinct outcome rather than as a slow run.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets`
clean with no new warnings (`origin/main` is warning-free and so is this branch),
`bazel test //crates/ctx-history-store:unit_tests
//crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests` both PASSED,
`scripts/public-ctx/perf-smoke_test.py` 11/11.

`cargo test -p ctx --bin ctx` has six failures on this branch
(`upgrade::install::lock_tests::*`, `upgrade::install::marker::tests::absent_and_corrupt_managed_markers_have_distinct_classifications`,
`semantic::daemon::telemetry_tests::post_lock_initialization_failure_retains_restart_intent`).
The same six fail identically on `origin/main` in this environment, so they are
pre-existing and unrelated to this change.

## Two things this PR does not fix

**The upgrade duplicates the corpus.** After the upgrade the store holds 284,923
events: 141,973 written by v0.25 plus 142,950 written by v0.26. v0.26 derives a
capture-source identity (`codex-nativepath:<uuid>`) that does not match the
v0.25 `source_identity`, so it creates new sources and new event identities
rather than reconciling with the released rows. Sessions *are* reused (34, not
68), so the session rows are rewritten while their old events stay attached.
This is pre-existing on `origin/main` — I reproduced it on a single-file corpus
before touching anything (13,878 released + 13,956 new = 27,834) — and it is the
reason the database roughly doubles. It needs a product decision, not a bug fix.

**The remaining runtime is not all the ordinary writer.** 270s of CPU for a
corpus a fresh cold import does in 18.6s is three costs stacked, only one of
which this PR removes:

1. *speculative group redo* — 49 of 145 groups wrote, overflowed, rolled back and
   were redone. Removed here.
2. *quadratic journal fanout* — 3,522,400 `append_entity` calls, of which
   2,978,880 produced no record because the content digest was unchanged. Also
   removed here, by the parent-row comparison described above; it was the same
   defect as the bound, seen as cost rather than as a failure.
3. *the duplication above* — the upgrade writes the whole corpus a second time.
   Not fixed here; owned by the re-derive branch.
4. *per-event FTS rewrites on the upsert path* — every event whose stored hash
   changed is a delete-and-re-insert across three FTS tables. Not fixed here;
   it lives in `events.rs`, which the ordinary-writer branch owns.

One smaller item found on the exact path this PR bounds, also left alone:
`native_path_group/accounting.rs::event_bind_bytes` serializes an event's
payload and metadata purely to measure their length, and `events.rs` serializes
both again to bind them. Worth roughly 0.30 CPU-seconds over the corpus, so not
worth churning a release-blocker fix for — and removing the second pass means
threading the serialized strings into the bind, which is an `events.rs` change.

## What here becomes unnecessary once upgrades rebuild-and-replace?

Nothing does, and one part becomes more urgent, not less.

* **The admission/enforcement fix is needed regardless.** It is not
  upgrade-specific by construction: any group filled to the retained-page
  admission ceiling produces a larger journal encoding and a larger Core bind
  encoding of the same rows. The upgrade path is only where it first became
  fatal, because that is where the split ladder stopped converging; on runs that
  *passed*, 49 of 145 group attempts still wrote, overflowed, rolled back and
  redid themselves. The Core-bind instance has no recovery path at all and is
  charged on the cold-builder path too, so it can fail a fresh install.
* **Journal streaming stays**, because it is a consequence of removing the
  journal ceiling rather than of the upgrade path. A group at the admission
  ceiling emits more than 8 MiB of journal in the ordinary-writer path whether
  or not the store was upgraded; without streaming that is buffered in memory.
* **The parent-row fanout skip stays**, and applies to every import into a
  non-empty store. After a rebuild-and-replace upgrade, subsequent incremental
  imports run through the ordinary writer and would pay the same O(G·E) without
  it.
* **The split-ladder removal stays** — it only ever handled an error that can no
  longer occur.
* **The test arms stay**, and one changes state: the ignored canonical-set test
  is exactly the acceptance gate for the re-derive work and should be
  un-ignored by it.

What rebuild-and-replace *does* change is the residual unbounded-fanout case:
re-derivation runs through the cold builder, so the largest instance — a session
whose whole pre-existing event set is re-journaled in one transaction — stops
happening on upgrade. That lowers the urgency of the resumable drain but does
not remove the need for it.

One handoff note for that branch: my released-store reshape keys off cleared
identity tables and a deactivated projection journal. If rebuild-and-replace
detects a pre-0.26 projection by some other marker, the reshape has to set that
marker too, or the perf arm will exercise the old path.

Sequencing: this PR should land **before or with** rebuild-and-replace, not
after. Rebuilding a large projection still publishes through groups, so a
rebuild that fills a group to the admission ceiling hits the same rejection this
PR removes.

## Overlap with #198

#198 also edits `crates/ctx-history-store/src/native_path_group.rs`: a six-line
deletion in `impl Drop for NativePathWriteScope` at the bottom of the file. My
edits to that file are the bounds constants and comment, the receipt doc
comments, `charge_core_mutations`, `validate_final_accounting`, and the removal
of `collector_overflowed`. Disjoint regions, and I verified rather than assumed
it: cherry-picking #198's commit onto this branch auto-merges with no conflict
and the result compiles. No resolution needed from either side; the two can land
in any order.

This branch is rebased onto current `origin/main`, which now includes #192, #201,
#202 and #203. #192 rewrote the impact queries from `LEFT JOIN ... OR` into
`UNION ALL` forms, so each fanout query is index-friendly; this PR removes most
of the fanouts entirely — complementary, not overlapping. #201 removed `--json`,
which the perf arm picks up automatically because it reuses `import_command`;
the only conflict was the harness's frozen source digest, which both sides bump,
and the last commit rebinds it to the merged value. All gates were re-run on the
rebased tree.

Unrelated to this PR but worth flagging: `origin/main` is currently not
`cargo fmt` clean — `crates/ctx-cli/src/pro/referral.rs` and
`crates/ctx-cli/src/pro/workos_device.rs` arrived unformatted with #202/#203.
Every file this PR touches is clean; I have not reformatted theirs.

## Does this foreclose eliding the journal when no Pro helper is installed?

No, and it makes the sequencing easier.

The streaming change is entirely inside the collector path, which `append_entity`
only reaches when the journal is already active; with an inactive journal it
returns before any of it. Gating materialization on Pro presence is orthogonal to
it.

Removing the journal ceilings from group admission actively helps. Under the old
code a group's admissible size depended on whether the journal was being written:
a group that overflowed with Pro would have committed without it, so Core-only
and Core+Pro had different effective group capacities and eliding the journal
would have silently changed which groups commit. They are now identical, so
elision changes only whether journal rows exist, not what publishes.

One coupling elision still has to unpick, which this PR neither creates nor
removes: `ensure_active_journal` activates the journal unconditionally on any
ordinary Codex import, and `publish_root_group_once` rejects a receipt whose
checkpoint is `None` unless the store is a cold stage
(`CodexNativeVerticalError::CanonicalJournalInactive`). Both call sites need to
change for elision. And elision would indeed have hidden this bug on Core-only
while leaving it in place for every Core+Pro user, which is why it is not the fix
here.
