title: fix(pro): support Linux without a persistent keyring
body:
## Summary

- treat a missing, session-only, or stale default Secret Service collection as unavailable during initial Linux backend selection
- let unselected read/delete paths report an ordinary miss without creating local state, so first-time sign-in can continue
- durably select the hardened owner-private file vault before the first mutation
- preserve fail-closed behavior for locked, denied, corrupt, ambiguous, and already-selected backends

## Validation

- `cargo test -p ctx pro::credential_vault -- --nocapture` — 34 passed
- `cargo clippy -p ctx --bin ctx --tests --no-deps -- -D warnings`
- `cargo check -p ctx --target x86_64-unknown-freebsd`
- isolated live Linux smoke against a running Secret Service with a stale default collection — selected the file vault with 0700 directories and 0600 files
- independent security/code review — green, no blocking findings

title: perf(store): keep NativePath statements cached across typed mutations
body:
## The defect

ctx has two write paths into the local store: the cold builder, used when the
target database does not exist yet, and the ordinary incremental writer, used
for every existing target. For byte-identical output on the same corpus the
ordinary writer costs about 5.6x the CPU and 2.7x the filesystem writes.

Reproduced on this branch's merge base, 1.087 GB of real Codex JSONL
(1,086,939,432 bytes, 32 files), 8 cores, warm page cache, `--no-daemon`,
Core only:

| path | wall | user CPU | sys CPU | fs out blocks | events | final db |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| cold builder | 18.96s | 28.26 | 1.95 | 1,722,304 | 142,950 | 682,246,144 |
| ordinary writer | 159.31s | 144.57 | 22.84 | 4,593,768 | 142,950 | 681,111,552 |

The two paths produce logically identical stores: every canonical column of
`events`, `sessions`, `session_edges`, `runs`, `files_touched` and
`event_search` hashes identically, and only the wall-clock `imported_at` stamp
inside `metadata_json` differs.

## What this changes

`NativePathWriteScope::drop` discarded the whole prepared-statement cache after
**every** typed mutation. On the ordinary path that meant `prepare_cached` never
hit: importing 142,950 events re-parsed the canonical `events` upsert, all three
FTS projection inserts, the semantic stat updates and the projection-journal
append roughly 143,000 times each. That is what put SQLite's LEMON parser and
name resolution (`yy_reduce`, `resolveExprStep`) on the hot path, and it is the
source of the prepare/finalize malloc traffic and the `pthread_mutex_lock` time
that SQLite's serialized-mode global allocator mutex adds on top of it.

The flush was there for a real reason and the reason still holds. A NativePath
group installs an authorizer whose write decision SQLite evaluates once, during
`sqlite3_prepare_v2`, and then bakes into the statement. A statement prepared
inside the group's typed write scope carries an "allow" decision that must never
be replayed by an out-of-route mutation.

Cold NativePath groups already solved this lazily instead of eagerly:
`Store::with_atomic_write` discards the cache when a group is open and the typed
write scope is *not* active, which is precisely the moment before an unowned
mutation could reuse a stale decision. This PR generalises that shipped
mechanism from cold groups to every group and stops flushing on write-scope
exit.

The lazy flush is complete for the public API: every write statement in the
Store that goes through `prepare_cached` is reachable from outside the group
only via `with_atomic_write`, and `Connection::execute` uses an uncached
`prepare`, so it re-runs the authorizer unconditionally.

`connection_tests.rs` gains a regression test for exactly the case the retained
cache creates: repeating the *same* canonical mutation out of route, so the
cached "allow" statement is the one that would be reused. It must still be
denied and must still poison the group. The test fails if the lazy flush is
removed.

## Measurements

All timed runs were serialised through `flock /tmp/ctx-nativepath-perf-benchmark.lock`
and pinned with `taskset -c 24-31` (one SMT thread from each of physical cores
8-15, all of CCD1 and its L3). Page cache was equalised before each arm. Arms
alternate **and rotate position** between reps, because a fixed order confounds
the arm with its slot: this host drifts measurably inside a single rep. The CPU
governor is `powersave`, which adds variance; I did not change it. The host is
shared and was running two other agents' builds and benchmarks throughout.

**146.7 MB / 22,277 events, 6 rotated interleaved reps** (the low-noise
measurement; each arm occupied each slot twice):

| arm | user CPU median | user CPU range | wall median |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| before | 19.07 | 18.83 - 24.60 | 18.77s |
| after | **16.82** | 16.70 - 18.79 | **16.52s** |

**-11.8% user CPU, -12.0% wall.** Excluding the single contaminated rep (a
concurrent job on the box) both arms spread under 2%.

**1.087 GB / 142,950 events, rotated interleaved pairs.** This host was running
two other agents' builds and benchmarks for the whole window, with 1-minute load
between 8 and 82, so a single 160-second arm carries roughly +-15% of noise and
these pairs are reported individually rather than as a median:

| pair | host load during rep | order | base user CPU | after user CPU | delta |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 8.6, rising | base, after | 148.54 | 147.60 | -0.6% |
| B | 66, falling | base, after | 159.32 | **138.15** | **-13.3%** |

The two pairs carry opposite position bias (in A the second arm ran as load rose,
in B as it fell), so they bracket rather than pin the true value. The per-event
scaling from the low-noise arm predicts about -10% here: the saving is a fixed
per-mutation cost, and the ordinary writer costs 0.86 ms/event at 22k events
versus 1.04 ms/event at 143k, so the same absolute saving is a slightly smaller
share of a larger total. Pair B's wall clock moved 178.20s -> 158.87s.

I could not get a quiet enough window on this shared host to tighten the
full-corpus figure further. The 22,277-event arm is the measurement I would
stand behind.

## Correctness

Baseline and fixed stores built from the full 1.087 GB corpus are logically
identical:

- identical counts for `sessions`, `events`, `session_edges`, `runs`,
  `files_touched`, `sync_cursors`, `capture_sources`, `event_search`,
  `event_search_scriptgram`, `event_search_lookup`, `provider_source_locators`,
  `capture_source_provider_routes`, `event_aliases`
- identical ordered SHA-256 row digests over the canonical columns of `events`,
  `sessions`, `session_edges`, `runs`, `files_touched` and `event_search`
  (the `events` digest also matches the cold builder's)
- `PRAGMA integrity_check` = ok and 0 foreign-key violations on both
- identical FTS hit counts for seven probe terms
- identical `ctx search` result sets and ordering for five queries
- the no-op repeat import stays at 0.05 - 0.10s on both arms
- cold-path timings unchanged

`cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` (clean),
`cargo test -p ctx-history-store --lib` (332 pass), the four ctx CLI import
integration suites, and
`bazel test //crates/ctx-history-store:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests`
all pass.

## Investigated and rejected

**Removing the per-mutation `SAVEPOINT`/`RELEASE` pair.** Inside a NativePath
group every failed typed mutation poisons the group and rolls the whole
transaction back, and the storage contract only requires that a failed chunk
publish no half-written rows, so the nested savepoint's partial-rollback
granularity is never actually used. Skipping it removes two statement
compilations and one statement journal per canonical row. Measured over the same
6 rotated reps it was worth **nothing**: 16.79 vs 16.82 median user CPU-seconds
against the cache fix alone. Reverted rather than carried. The savepoint SQL is
trivial to parse and `temp_store = MEMORY` keeps its sub-journal off disk, which
also explains why filesystem write volume was identical in every arm.

**Durability work (the 16% vs 6.3% kernel time).** I found nothing incidental to
remove:

- `PRAGMA synchronous = NORMAL` is set once when the connection is configured.
  There is no per-batch `synchronous` change anywhere in the workspace, and
  under WAL + NORMAL a commit does not fsync at all, so there are no redundant
  commit fsyncs to eliminate.
- The ~2.35 GB written for a 682 MB database is WAL append plus checkpoint
  writeback of the same pages into the main database. That is inherent to
  committing ~200 bounded chunks against a growing FTS5 index.
  `wal_autocheckpoint = 14000` (57 MB) fires well before the 64 MB
  `enforce_bulk_wal_bound` hard limit, so the explicit `checkpoint_wal_passive()`
  after each bounded maintenance slice usually finds an already-small WAL and is
  not meaningful duplicate work.
- The cold builder writes 881 MB because it stages one database, builds indexes
  and FTS in a single pass at the end, and installs by rename. It never rewrites
  a page it already wrote. Closing that gap means deferring the search
  projection, which is a schema/FTS change and out of scope here.

Filesystem write volume is unchanged by this PR (4,593,712 vs 4,594,048 blocks),
as expected.

**The mutex delta (3.11% vs 0.79%).** Consistent with SQLite's serialized-mode
global allocator mutex being taken on every allocation made during prepare and
finalize; ~143,000 full flush-and-re-prepare cycles is the allocation source, and
this PR removes the cycles. I could not re-profile to confirm the residual:
`perf record` is blocked on this host by `kernel.perf_event_paranoid=4`, and I
did not change that setting.

## Quantified, deliberately not implemented: JSON pass-through

`events.rs:239` and `:247` re-serialise `event.payload` and
`event.sync.metadata` with `serde_json::to_string` even though the content
arrived as JSON. `native_path_group/accounting.rs::event_bind_bytes` serialises
both **again**, purely to measure the bound-value length, so every event's
payload and metadata are serialised twice per import.

Measured on the exact committed values for this corpus (142,950 events,
170,144,777 bytes of `payload_json` and 89,045,342 bytes of `metadata_json`),
using the realistic build-once/use-once access pattern rather than a hot loop
over a pre-parsed vector:

| value | parse only | + 1 serialisation | + 2 serialisations | cost of today's 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| payload | 0.274s | 0.442s | 0.456s | **0.182s** |
| metadata | 0.168s | 0.230s | 0.288s | **0.120s** |

A borrowed-slice pass-through would remove essentially all of it: about
**0.30 CPU-seconds per full-corpus import**, which is ~0.2% of the ordinary
writer's ~166 CPU-seconds and ~1.0% of the cold builder's ~30. That is an order
of magnitude smaller than the 13.1% the profile attributed to this category, so
the attribution appears to have captured provider-side JSON *parsing* and the
allocator traffic underneath it rather than these two calls. Changing the row
contract for 0.3 CPU-seconds does not look worth it on this evidence, and it
belongs in its own PR either way.

## What still explains the remaining gap

Statement re-preparation is not the bulk of the 5.6x. The dominant remainder is
row-at-a-time FTS5 projection maintenance: the ordinary writer inserts into
`event_search`, `event_search_scriptgram` and `event_search_lookup` for every
event and runs bounded FTS merge maintenance every 8 groups, while the cold
builder skips all projection work during core load and builds indexes and FTS
once at the end. Secondary contributors are the per-event projection-journal
record (cold defers journal activation to a single baseline) and the WAL plus
checkpoint write amplification above. All of those are schema/FTS or cold-builder
territory and out of scope for this PR.

title: perf(codex): classify NativePath records before parsing them
body:
## Why

Codex rollout files are dominated by records Core never materializes. Over the
frozen 11.88 GB real Codex corpus (9,337,945 records) the reader projects
**nothing but a counter** from 83.87% of records and 40.02% of bytes.

Before this change every one of those records was still handed to
`classify_codex_record`, which runs a full `serde_json` walk of the record and
materialises borrowed `Cow<str>` envelope and payload fields — for state that is
dropped on the next line. The largest single class is `event_msg` /
`token_count`: about half of all records, pure telemetry counters.

## What this adds

`provider/codex/nativepath/record/prefilter.rs`: a per-record classification
step that runs on the raw record bytes **before** any parse, allocation, or
payload hash.

```rust
enum CodexRecordAdmission {
    NoProjection(CodexSkipProjection), // proven parseable; projects only counters
    Probe,                             // unchanged path
}
fn prefilter_codex_record(record: &[u8]) -> CodexRecordAdmission
```

It allocates nothing, builds no `String`, and never falls back to a parse in
order to classify. String bodies are scanned eight bytes at a time with SWAR
word tests, the same idiom `record/structural/visitor.rs` already uses.

### The keep/skip set, and how it stays in sync with the reader

The skip set is not a hand-written list of type names. It is derived from the
reader:

* `record.rs` now exposes `codex_record_class(record_type, item_type)` — the one
  function that maps a discriminator pair onto `CodexRecordClass`. The
  structural probe calls it and the prefilter calls it.
* `codex_skip_projection(class)` names the classes whose entire projection is a
  counter bump:
  * `CodexRecordClass::Ignored` → `ignored_records`
  * `CodexRecordClass::ExcludedResult(kind)` with `!kind.is_eligible_output()`
    → `native_result_records` + `native_result_record_bytes`, exactly the two
    counters `process_output` advances before it reads anything the probe
    decoded.
* Every other class reaches parsed state and stays on the probe path:
  `SessionMeta`, every `Retained(_)`, and the three eligible output kinds.

Concretely, the derived skip set is:

| stays on the probe path | skipped from raw bytes |
|---|---|
| `session_meta`, `compacted` | any envelope type the class function does not name (`turn_context`, `world_state`, `inter_agent_communication_metadata`, …) |
| `response_item`: `message`, `reasoning`, `function_call`, `custom_tool_call`, `web_search_call`, `tool_search_call` | `response_item`: anything else that is not result-like (`agent_message`, …) |
| `response_item`: `function_call_output`, `custom_tool_call_output`, `tool_search_output` | `event_msg`: `token_count`, `sub_agent_activity`, `agent_message`, `agent_reasoning`, `user_message`, `task_started`, `task_complete`, `turn_aborted`, `context_compacted`, `thread_*`, … |
| anything the byte walk cannot prove | result-like envelopes whose only projection is a counter (`patch_apply_end`, `exec_command_end`, `mcp_tool_call_end`, `*_output`/`*_result`/`*_response`/`*_end`) |

### Record types classified Keep defensively

A false Keep costs performance; a false Skip loses user data. Where I could not
prove a record projects nothing, it stays on the probe path:

* **`response_item/function_call_output` and `custom_tool_call_output`** — the
  two largest byte classes (26% of bytes on the large corpus). Core discards
  their *successful* bodies, but "successful" is only knowable after
  `probe_structural_output` reads the exit code, wall time and timeout markers.
  Keep.
* **`response_item/reasoning`** — 4.84% of records, 8.33% of bytes. The ones
  carrying only `encrypted_content` with an empty `summary` end at
  `ValidUnmaterializable`, so Core keeps nothing from them, but deciding that
  from raw bytes needs a predicate over `summary`, `summary_text` *and*
  `encrypted_content`, and getting it wrong converts an ignored record into a
  `malformed retained Codex reasoning` rejection. Ambiguous, so Keep.
* **`compacted`** — only some of these materialize (`is_source_only_compacted`
  sends the rest to `ValidUnmaterializable`), but `codex_record_class` maps the
  whole class to `Retained(Compacted)`, so Keep, with no attempt to guess which
  ones are source-only.
* **`session_meta`** — metadata only, but it is what establishes the scan's
  owner. Keep.
* **Envelope types with a payload the walk cannot read simply** — a non-ASCII or
  escaped key, a `\u` surrogate, a non-canonical number, nesting past 24: all
  return `Probe` rather than a guess.

`prefilter_skip_set_matches_what_the_reader_materializes` walks the cross
product of every envelope discriminator and every payload discriminator the
class function branches on (plus fall-through shapes) and asserts the prefilter
verdict equals `codex_skip_projection(classify_codex_record(..).class)` for each
one. The two cannot drift without that test failing.

### Rejections stay identical

A record that fails `classify_codex_record` is rejected as `malformed Codex JSON
record`, and `rejected_records` is published in the import report and in the
store cursor. A prefilter that skipped a malformed record would silently drop
that rejection — and the corpus does contain a spliced `token_count` record.

So the prefilter is not a prefix matcher. It walks the whole record against a
deliberately **strict subset** of the structural probe's grammar and returns
`Probe` the moment anything is unusual: an escaped or non-ASCII key, a `\u`
surrogate, a non-canonical number, nesting past 24, a duplicate
`type`/`payload`/`timestamp` (or payload `type`/`call_id`), a non-string `type`,
a `timestamp` that is neither string nor null, trailing bytes, a non-object
envelope, or a missing `type`. Every skip carries a proof that the probe would
have succeeded with that class; every non-proof falls back to the unchanged
path. Being too strict only costs a fallback parse.

Kept records do not pay for the walk twice: the prefilter abandons as soon as
the discriminators read so far rule a skip out, which in this corpus is inside
the first ~106 bytes.

## Measurement

This work is **producer-side**. In my own profiles the serial writer thread is
58.5% of all CPU and the parallel producer pool is 41.5%; the classifier only
touches the producers, and the producers are not the wall-clock critical path.
So the honest expected shape is **a meaningful total-CPU reduction and a much
smaller wall-clock reduction**, and that is what the numbers below show. CPU is
still worth buying on its own: it is battery, thermals, and headroom on a
laptop.

### 1. Work removed — deterministic, not a timing

Counted over every record, comparing the classifier's verdict against the
reader's own class function:

| corpus | records skipped | bytes skipped |
|---|---:|---:|
| 1.087 GB | 383,353 / 681,909 = **56.22%** | 239,944,445 / 1,086,939,432 = **22.08%** |
| 11.88 GB | 7,831,695 / 9,337,945 = **83.87%** | 4,755,590,967 / 11,881,555,752 = **40.02%** |

Those records now reach no parse, no allocation, and no payload hash.

### 2. The classification stage in isolation — no I/O, no writer, single core

424,324 real records (734 MB) held in memory:

| stage | CPU |
|---|---:|
| classify every record from raw bytes | **0.121 s** |
| structural probe on every record (before) | 7.256 s |
| structural probe on the survivors only (after) | 5.241 s |
| **stage total before** | **7.256 s** |
| **stage total after** (classify all, probe survivors) | **5.362 s** (**-26.1%**) |

The classifier costs 0.121 s to answer 424k records because kept records abandon
the walk at their discriminator, inside the first ~106 bytes in this corpus. The
structural-probe work it removes is 1.9 s per 734 MB.

### 3. End to end — wall and CPU reported separately

Host: Ryzen 9 7950X, `powersave`, `taskset -c 24-31`, isolated `env -i` data
roots, page cache equalised before each arm, arms interleaved A/B/A/B inside one
benchmark-lock acquisition, so only paired reps are compared. Both arms were
built from `294533946` with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG=1
CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_STRIP=none`; this branch was later replayed onto
`8c23d9205` with no conflicts and an identical diff.

The two benchmark binaries were verified distinct before the numbers were
believed:

| arm | SHA-256 | size | `record::prefilter` symbols |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| before | `ea02ddc542ae4911a01708f1b4d39103ccad7ca37287fee32a7958e372cf240e` | 290,631,760 | **0** |
| after | `5bc504877950fe00367cb083f81ab354d3a3627777638593998d6740f8cc5d28` | 290,684,248 | **4** |

The classifier's machine code in the measured "after" binary is
instruction-for-instruction identical to a fresh build of this branch's HEAD
(`Prefilter::skip_string` 231 insns, `simple_string` 217, `value` 348, all
matching; `decided_skip_with` byte-identical), so the benchmarked arm is the
committed classifier.

| corpus | metric | before (median) | after (median) | median paired delta | reps favouring |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.087 GB | **wall** | 28.3s | 27.3s | **+0.0%** | 1/3 |
| 1.087 GB | **total CPU** | 44.5s | 43.4s | **+0.7%** | 1/3 |
| 11.88 GB | **wall** | 176.0s | 184.7s | **-4.8%** | 4/7 |
| 11.88 GB | **total CPU** | 270.2s | 278.2s | **-5.8%** | 4/7 |

(Medians of the two arms and the median *paired* delta disagree in sign on the
11.88 GB row because the arms did not hit their slow reps on the same
iterations; the paired delta is the meaningful one.)

**This host cannot resolve a single-digit effect from timing alone.** Three
other agents share it; the load average moved between 11 and 40 during these
runs. Per-rep paired deltas on the 11.88 GB corpus span -32.6% to +51.8% on
wall, and the *same* baseline binary measured 33.3, 44.5 and 45.0 CPU-s on three
reps of the same 1.087 GB corpus. Read the 1.087 GB row as "no regression"
rather than as a win.

### 4. Sampled cycles over a full 11.88 GB import

`perf record -F 499`, both arms back to back inside one lock acquisition:

| arm | cycle samples | writer / producer split | sessions / events / edges | rejected | skipped |
|---|---:|---|---|---:|---:|
| before | 160,039 | 58.5% / 41.5% | 3,464 / 764,669 / 3,406 | 108 | 557,869 |
| after | 134,155 | 55.4% / 44.6% | 3,464 / 764,669 / 3,406 | 108 | 557,869 |

Identical outcomes at full corpus scale. The **-16.2% total cycles** is
corroborating rather than decisive: the serial writer thread, which this change
does not touch at all, also moved between the two runs, so some of that gap is
host drift rather than the classifier. It is a **total-CPU** number and is not a
wall-clock claim.

The remaining hot symbols are unchanged and all live in
`probe_structural_output`, which runs on records this change deliberately keeps:
`StructuralStringVisitor::feed_char` 9.04%, `CodexWallTimeParser::feed_bytes`
4.02%, `CodexExitCodeParser::feed_bytes` 4.01%,
`StructuralJsonVisitor::string_summary` 1.96% — about 19% of total CPU, still
character-at-a-time. The classifier itself is 0.59% of total CPU in the after
profile.

## Equivalence evidence

Two arms, byte-identical corpus paths, data-root paths, and file mtimes, run
through a seven-step lifecycle: fresh import, no-op repeat, append, truncate,
in-place rewrite, source deletion, restart.

* **Import reports byte-identical at every step**, including
  `imported_sessions`, `imported_events`, `imported_edges`, `skipped_events`,
  `rejected_records`, and the rejection list. The append step deliberately adds a
  truncated `event_msg`/`token_count` record — a record in the *skip* class — and
  `rejected_records` goes 1 → 2 in both arms, which is the malformed-rejection
  contract holding through the prefilter.
* **Logical row digests identical** for `events` (10,128 rows), `sessions`,
  `session_edges`, `runs`, `files_touched`, `catalog_sessions`,
  `capture_sources`, `event_search` (7,054 rows) and `event_search_lookup`
  (2,267 rows), at every one of the seven steps. Surrogate UUID keys and
  `imported_at` stamps are re-run volatile and are projected out; a
  baseline-vs-baseline control run establishes exactly which columns are volatile.
* `PRAGMA integrity_check` = `ok`, `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` = 0 rows, both arms,
  every step.
* `ctx search` output identical across eight queries (127,549 bytes byte-for-byte).
* `ctx show event --content complete` identical for 52 events across all five
  event types (760,806 bytes byte-for-byte after per-run UUIDs are projected
  out). Twelve of those carry a verified-content locator and report
  `stored_truncated: true`, `origin: provider_source`, `source_verified: true` —
  they reopen and verify the original record, and do so identically.
* `provider_source_locators` and `sync_cursors` differ — and differ **identically
  in the baseline-vs-baseline control**, because their source-revision string
  embeds the file observation token, which includes inode ctime.

Whole-corpus differential, comparing the classifier's verdict against
`codex_skip_projection(classify_codex_record(..).class)` for every record:

| corpus | records | disagreements | probe rejections routed correctly |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1.087 GB | 681,909 | **0** | 20 |
| 11.88 GB | **9,337,945** | **0** | 137 |

Gates: `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean, `cargo clippy --workspace
--all-targets` clean (no diagnostics), `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --lib`
1257 passed / 0 failed / 3 ignored, `bazel test //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests`
PASSED, `scripts/check-loc.sh` passed.

## What I did not take

* `response_item/reasoning` (Keep, see above) is the largest remaining
  opportunity in this lane: 8.33% of bytes that currently build a full
  `serde_json::Value` only to be discarded at `ValidUnmaterializable`.
* `read_bounded_record` runs three SHA-256 passes over every byte
  (`full_hasher`, `complete_hasher`, `record_hasher`) and discards
  `record_hasher`'s digest for every complete record — roughly a third of the
  scan's hashing done for nothing. Out of scope here.
* The hand-rolled character-at-a-time scanners in `probe_structural_output`
  (`StructuralStringVisitor::feed_char`, `CodexWallTimeParser::feed_bytes`,
  `CodexExitCodeParser::feed_bytes`) remain the largest single category of
  cold-path CPU. They run on records this change deliberately keeps.

title: perf(store): drop the two prefix-redundant events indexes
body:
**No schema version or identity moves.** `user_version` stays 47 and
`FINAL_SCHEMA_IDENTITY` stays `ctx-store-schema-47-final-v7`. See §4 — an
earlier revision of this PR did bump the identity, and measuring what that costs
is what argued it back out.

Based on `8c23d9205` ("Fix NativePath stalls and redesign index watch", #192).
That commit rewrote the projection-journal impact queries into indexed
`UNION ALL` branches and added five `*_source_generation_retirement` keyset
indexes, so the `events` index set is 14 B-trees, not 13. Every plan and every
measurement below was taken on top of #192; nothing here is carried over from an
earlier base.

This was scoped as two changes landing together: convert `event_search` to an
external-content FTS5 table over `event_search_lookup`, and prune the `events`
index set. **Only the second half survived contact with the data, and only two
of the five candidate indexes did.** Everything below is measured on the real
4.23 GB qualification database (764,669 events from the 11.88 GB Codex corpus),
not on synthetic rows.

---

## 1. External-content FTS5 over `event_search_lookup` is not implementable

`event_search_lookup` is not a second copy of `event_search`. It is a
**20.6% subset**, populated only for `event_type = 'message'` with
`role IN ('user','assistant')` (`semantic_lookup_event_parts`), because it
exists to feed the semantic lite-turn projection, not lexical search.

On the qualification database:

| table | rows |
|---|---:|
| `events` | 764,669 |
| `event_search` | 735,006 |
| `event_search_lookup` | 151,173 |

Declaring `event_search` with `content='event_search_lookup'` silently drops
every row that has no matching content row. Broken down by what
`event_search` actually indexes:

| bucket / role | rows | rows lost | indexed text | text lost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `tool_call` / assistant | 414,274 | 414,274 | 170.7 MB | 170.7 MB |
| `summary` / assistant | 156,906 | 156,906 | 14.8 MB | 14.8 MB |
| `message` / assistant | 85,418 | 0 | 83.6 MB | 0 |
| `message` / user | 65,755 | 0 | 36.1 MB | 0 |
| `message` / system | 12,653 | 12,653 | 14.7 MB | 14.7 MB |
| **total** | **735,006** | **583,833** | **319.8 MB** | **200.2 MB** |

**79.4% of rows and 62.6% of indexed text.** Concretely, the searches that
disappear are the ones users actually run against tool output:

| query | hits today | hits after | lost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `"cargo clippy"` | 1,820 | 67 | 96.3% |
| `taskset` | 184 | 4 | 97.8% |
| `"cargo fmt"` | 5,041 | 326 | 93.5% |
| `"git worktree"` | 2,013 | 504 | 75.0% |
| `rustfmt` | 2,263 | 564 | 75.1% |
| `"bazel test"` | 3,278 | 1,393 | 57.5% |

This is not a schema optimization; it is data loss, and it fails the
identical-search-behavior gate on the first query. **Not implemented.**

### What the 510 MB actually costs, and what would recover it

`event_search_content` is 510 MB because FTS5's private content table stores
all six column values per row: 319.8 MB of `preview_text` plus 91.6 MB of
`event_id`/`history_record_id`/`session_id`/`role`/`rank_bucket` text, plus
page overhead. Any *external* content table has to store the same bytes, so
external content over a widened content table moves the cost rather than
removing it — and adds a TEXT primary-key autoindex (~37 MB at 735k rows)
that the FTS5 `%_content` table does not have.

The only shape that removes the copy is **contentless FTS5**
(`content=''`, `contentless_delete=1`). I built all three shapes from the real
735,006-row corpus:

| shape | `%_content` | `%_data` | `%_docsize` | `%_idx` | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| current, 6 columns, internal content | 510.3 MB | 197.1 MB | 11.2 MB | 0.64 MB | **719 MB** |
| contentless, 6 columns | 0 | 197.1 MB | 13.1 MB | 0.64 MB | 211 MB |
| contentless, `preview_text` only | 0 | 142.5 MB | 9.4 MB | 0.43 MB | **152 MB** |

That is **567 MB, 13.4% of the whole database**, and ranking is unaffected:
across 45 real-shaped queries (single terms, phrases, `OR`, `AND`) the
1-column contentless table returned **identical rowid sets, identical order,
and bit-identical `bm25()` scores** to the current 6-column table.

It is not in this PR because it is a different change with a much larger blast
radius, and shipping it half-verified is worse than not shipping it:

- `preview_text` is derived from `events.payload_json` by a Rust function
  (`event_search_preview_from_payload`), so it cannot be recomputed in SQL. A
  contentless table forces preview derivation to read time. That is cheap —
  `event_search_hit_sql` already selects `e.payload_json` for cursor
  extraction — but it moves a materialized value to a computed one.
- `crates/ctx-history-store/src/records.rs:312` filters and ranks on
  `event_search.history_record_id` directly. Contentless returns NULL for
  every column, so record search needs a join back through
  `events`/`runs`/`sessions` to reproduce the projection-resolved value.
- The v47 canonical-projection verifier
  (`search/projections/validation.rs`) proves exact row-for-row equality by
  reading `event_search`'s columns. It would need a different proof strategy.
- Deletes must become rowid-addressed, which means committing `events.seq` as
  the FTS rowid.

Recommendation: worth doing, as its own PR, with the contentless equivalence
harness in this PR's evidence as the gate.

---

## 2. Index prune: 2 of 5 candidates are redundant, 3 are load-bearing

`EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` was run against the real 4.23 GB database, first brought
up to the post-#192 index set by a writable open, using the bundled SQLite
(libsqlite3-sys 0.30.1). Every query is planned twice — once with the current
index set, once inside an open transaction with the five candidates dropped and
rolled back, so the database is never modified. The database carries no
`sqlite_stat1`, so plans are shape-determined and reproduce on a fresh Store.

**36 queries planned, and the set deliberately includes the NativePath
ingestion/publication write path, not only read-side queries.** An index no user
query touches can still be load-bearing for every publication group, so the
corpus covers: the three #192 journal impact statements verbatim
(`SOURCE_EVENT_IMPACT_SQL`, `SESSION_EVENT_IMPACT_SQL`,
`SESSION_FILE_TOUCH_IMPACT_SQL`) and each of their `UNION ALL` branches in
isolation; `run_mutated` event fanout; the event identity probe; the keyset
generation-retirement page (including its `INDEXED BY
idx_events_source_generation_retirement` hint), its next-owner probe and its
owner-recovery query; the dedupe-key point probe and the provider hash-conflict
range scan; the `seq` identity probe; the two protocol-validity `EXISTS`
predicates; session reparenting; the record delete guard; the
`GROUP BY history_record_id` count; the blob reference guard; locator route
authority; and the canonical observation stream.

Result: **19 plans identical, 12 changed with no scan and no sort introduced,
5 regressions — all five in the three `idx_events_live_message_*` indexes,
which this PR therefore keeps.** No publication-path query regressed.

#192's own guard, `projection_journal::impact::tests::
impact_queries_use_indexed_union_branches`, independently confirms this on a
fresh Store. It pins each impact statement's plan by index name *and* asserts
`!contains("SCAN ")` and `!contains("TEMP B-TREE")`. Those two structural
assertions — the ones that actually guard the quadratic — pass unchanged. Only
the pinned name for the session-scoped branches moves from
`idx_events_session_id` to `idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms`, which this PR
updates in place with a comment explaining why. **That guard test is the one
file this change touches outside `schema/`, and it is deliberate: leaving it
pinned to a dropped index would have hidden the plan change rather than
documenting it.**

### Dropped: `idx_events_history_record_id` (39.6 MB)

Strict left prefix of `idx_events_history_record_occurred_at_ms`.

```
### records.rs:136 record delete guard
  SELECT 1 FROM events WHERE history_record_id = ?1
  BEFORE: SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_history_record_id (history_record_id=?)
  AFTER : SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_history_record_occurred_at_ms (history_record_id=?)

### events.rs max_events_per_history_record
  SELECT COALESCE(MAX(event_count), 0) FROM (
      SELECT COUNT(*) AS event_count FROM events GROUP BY history_record_id)
  BEFORE: CO-ROUTINE (subquery-1)
          SCAN events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_history_record_id
          SEARCH (subquery-1)
  AFTER : CO-ROUTINE (subquery-1)
          SCAN events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_history_record_occurred_at_ms
          SEARCH (subquery-1)

### events for record ordered by time
  SELECT id, payload_json FROM events WHERE history_record_id = ?1 ORDER BY occurred_at_ms
  BEFORE / AFTER (identical):
    SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_history_record_occurred_at_ms (history_record_id=?)

### record links: events for record, newest first
  SELECT id FROM events WHERE history_record_id = ?1
  ORDER BY occurred_at_ms DESC, seq DESC LIMIT 50
  BEFORE / AFTER (identical):
    SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_history_record_occurred_at_ms (history_record_id=?)
    USE TEMP B-TREE FOR LAST TERM OF ORDER BY
```

Same access shape (`SEARCH`/covering `SCAN`), no temp B-tree introduced
anywhere.

### Dropped: `idx_events_session_id` (40.5 MB)

Strict left prefix of `idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms`.

```
### sessions.rs:246 reparent events by session
  UPDATE events SET history_record_id = ?1 WHERE session_id = ?2
  BEFORE: SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
  AFTER : SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)

### session event count
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM events WHERE session_id = ?1
  BEFORE: SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
  AFTER : SEARCH events USING COVERING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)

### ctx_events public view filtered by session
  SELECT ctx_event_id, event_seq FROM ctx_events WHERE ctx_session_id = ?1 ORDER BY event_seq
  BEFORE: SEARCH e USING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
          USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY
  AFTER : SEARCH e USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)
          USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

### transcript page: session events ordered by time
  SELECT id, payload_json FROM events WHERE session_id = ?1 ORDER BY occurred_at_ms, seq LIMIT 200
  BEFORE / AFTER (identical):
    SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)
    USE TEMP B-TREE FOR LAST TERM OF ORDER BY

### projection_journal session_mutated fanout
  SELECT DISTINCT e.id FROM events e LEFT JOIN runs r ON r.id = e.run_id
  WHERE e.session_id = ?1 OR r.session_id = ?1 ORDER BY e.id
  BEFORE / AFTER (identical):
    SCAN e USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_events_1
    SEARCH r USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_runs_1 (id=?) LEFT-JOIN
```

Where a temp B-tree appears it appeared before the change too (`ctx_events`
sorts on `event_seq`; the transcript page sorts the trailing `seq` term).
Nothing regressed to a table scan.

### Publication path: every changed plan keeps its access shape

The queries #192 introduced are the ones most at risk, because they run once
per mutated entity inside a publication group. They are unaffected:

```
### [publication] journal session_mutated event impact (SESSION_EVENT_IMPACT_SQL)
  BEFORE: COMPOUND QUERY / LEFT-MOST SUBQUERY
          SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
          UNION ALL
          SEARCH run USING INDEX idx_runs_session_id (session_id=?)
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_run_id (run_id=?)
  AFTER : COMPOUND QUERY / LEFT-MOST SUBQUERY
          SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)
          UNION ALL
          SEARCH run USING INDEX idx_runs_session_id (session_id=?)
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_run_id (run_id=?)

### [publication] journal source_mutated event impact (SOURCE_EVENT_IMPACT_SQL)
  BEFORE: SEARCH events USING INDEX idx_events_capture_source_id (capture_source_id=?)
          UNION ALL
          SEARCH session USING INDEX idx_sessions_capture_source_id (capture_source_id=?)
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
          UNION ALL
          SEARCH run USING INDEX idx_runs_source_id (source_id=?)
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_run_id (run_id=?)
  AFTER : identical except
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)

### [publication] journal session_mutated file-touch impact (SESSION_FILE_TOUCH_IMPACT_SQL)
  BEFORE: SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_session_id (session_id=?)
          SEARCH file USING INDEX idx_files_touched_event_id (event_id=?)
          ... three further UNION ALL branches ...
  AFTER : identical except
          SEARCH event USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=?)

### [publication] generation retirement keyset page (INDEXED BY idx_events_source_generation_retirement)
### [publication] generation retirement next-owner probe over events
### [publication] generation retirement owner recovery over events
### [publication] dedupe probe / hash-conflict range scan / seq identity probe
### [publication] protocol validity EXISTS over events.run_id and events.capture_source_id
### [publication] locator route authority for event
### [publication] canonical observation stream by capture source
  all IDENTICAL PLAN
```

Every `SEARCH … (session_id=?)` stays a `SEARCH`. Nothing becomes a `SCAN`, and
no `USE TEMP B-TREE` appears that was not already there. The #192 `UNION ALL`
shape — the thing that fixed the previous quadratic — is preserved exactly,
because the wider composite index has the same leading column.

### Kept: all three `idx_events_live_message_*` partial indexes

The premise was that these three overlap heavily. They do not: they lead with
different columns (`event_type`, `run_id`, `session_id`) and serve three
disjoint access shapes in `search/projections/semantic_document.rs`. Dropping
any of them costs an ordered scan.

```
### semantic recent anchor page (no run/session filter)   -- recent_event_embedding_documents
  BEFORE: SEARCH anchor USING INDEX idx_events_live_message_role_occurred_seq (event_type=? AND role=?)
          SEARCH anchor_search USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_event_search_lookup_1 (event_id=?)
  AFTER : SCAN anchor USING INDEX idx_events_source_generation_retirement   <-- 764,669-row scan
          SEARCH anchor_search USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex_event_search_lookup_1 (event_id=?)
          USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

### semantic next_user candidate scoped by run_id
  BEFORE: SEARCH candidate_user USING INDEX idx_events_live_message_run_role_occurred_seq
          (run_id=? AND event_type=? AND role=? AND occurred_at_ms>?)
  AFTER : SEARCH candidate_user USING INDEX idx_events_run_id (run_id=?)
          USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY      <-- sort per anchor row, LIMIT 1 no longer short-circuits

### semantic next_user candidate scoped by session_id (run_id IS NULL)
  BEFORE: SEARCH candidate_user USING INDEX idx_events_live_message_session_run_role_occurred_seq
          (session_id=? AND run_id=? AND event_type=? AND role=? AND occurred_at_ms>?)
  AFTER : SEARCH candidate_user USING INDEX idx_events_session_occurred_at_ms (session_id=? AND occurred_at_ms>?)
          USE TEMP B-TREE FOR LAST 2 TERMS OF ORDER BY

### semantic assistant candidate scoped by run_id          -- same regression as next_user
### semantic assistant candidate scoped by session_id      -- same regression as next_user
```

These two subqueries run once per anchor row inside the lite-turn CTE, so a
per-row sort is not an acceptable trade for 67.8 MB. **Kept.**

### Also checked and kept (plans identical before and after)

`idx_events_capture_source_id` (40.5 MB — deliberately streams the canonical
observation feed one source at a time), `idx_events_run_id`,
`idx_events_dedupe_key` (enforces a uniqueness constraint),
`idx_events_payload_blob_id`, and the FTS hit join
`JOIN events e ON e.id = event_search.event_id`.

---

## 3. Measured effect

### Index bytes on the real database (`dbstat`)

`dbstat` before, on the untouched final-v7 qualification store, and after, on
the same store migrated by this branch:

| object | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| accounted pages | 4,234,485,760 | 4,154,331,136 |
| `idx_events_history_record_id` | 39,649,280 | — |
| `idx_events_session_id` | 40,505,344 | — |
| freelist | 8,192 | 80,162,816 |

**−80,154,624 bytes of live index pages (1.89% of the database), to the byte.**
Every other object is byte-identical: `events` 2,292,715,520,
`event_search_content` 510,341,120, `projection_journal_chunks` 390,873,088,
`event_search_data` 196,595,712, `event_search_lookup` 185,016,320, and all nine
retained `events` indexes unchanged.

Per event insert this removes 2 of the 14 `events` B-tree maintenance
operations, and specifically the two whose keys are random 36-byte UUID text —
the ones with the worst page locality. (The `dbstat` numbers above are from the
released final-v7 store, which predates #192's
`idx_events_source_generation_retirement`; that index is present in both arms of
every measurement and is not affected by this change.)

### Isolated write path

765k rows streamed from the real corpus into the exact `events` schema, WAL,
`synchronous=NORMAL`, indexes present up front, `taskset -c 24-31`, serialised
through the shared benchmark lock, arms alternated within each rep. **These
three reps predate the rebase onto #192, so they carry the 13-index set without
`idx_events_source_generation_retirement`.** That index is in neither arm here
and in both arms of the cold A/B below; it does not interact with the two
dropped prefixes, but treat these numbers as directional and the cold A/B as
authoritative.

| rep | current wall | pruned wall | Δ | current CPU | pruned CPU | Δ |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 63.33 s | 53.45 s | −15.6% | 51.58 s | 40.69 s | −21.1% |
| 2 | 63.16 s | 41.41 s | −34.4% | 47.70 s | 33.28 s | −30.2% |
| 3 | 40.77 s | 36.48 s | −10.5% | 33.27 s | 30.75 s | −7.6% |

Absolute numbers drift because this host runs several concurrent agents; reps 1
and 2 ran at load average ~45, rep 3 at ~9. **Rep 3 is the least contended and
therefore the most conservative reading: −10.5% wall, −7.6% CPU.** Every rep
favours the pruned set, and arms alternate within a rep so drift is shared.

Resulting file: 2,715,004,928 → 2,635,059,200 bytes, **−79,945,728 (−2.9%)**,
matching the `dbstat` index sizes above. Peak RSS is unchanged (22–23 MiB both
arms) — dropping indexes does not change SQLite's working set.

### Whole-pipeline cold import — not yet measured

The end-to-end cold-import A/B on the real corpus (released binary vs this
branch, 3 reps alternating, `taskset -c 24-31`) is scripted but never acquired
the shared benchmark lock across ~70 minutes of waiting. Part of that is simply
five or six agents contending. Part of it is probably not: a separate
investigation has since found a real producer deadlock on `main`
(`CODEX_SOURCE_MAX_QUEUED_WINDOWS = 4` over-commits the producer byte budget,
wedging roughly 1 cold import in 10 with parked producer threads and a 0-byte
staged DB), and a wedged import holds both the benchmark lock and the store's
`EventSearchBulkGuard` indefinitely. **Treat the whole-pipeline number as
outstanding, and re-run it against a host where that fix has landed, with a hard
`timeout` on each import so a wedge is recorded as a wedge rather than as a slow
run.**

What is *not* outstanding is the safety question it would answer. The risk with
dropping an index during Core publication is that a publication lookup silently
degrades to a scan and turns group commits quadratic. That is answered directly
and at the mechanism level in §2: every publication-path statement — including
all three #192 journal impact statements and the keyset generation-retirement
queries — was planned before and after, and none introduced a scan or a sort.
#192's own `impact_queries_use_indexed_union_branches` guard, whose
`!contains("SCAN ")` and `!contains("TEMP B-TREE")` assertions are exactly that
check, passes unchanged.

---

## 4. Migration: reconciliation, not a versioned migration

The prune ships the way `idx_events_seq` and the three legacy
`idx_events_*_role_occurred_seq` indexes already ship: two
`DROP INDEX IF EXISTS` lines in `INDEXES_SQL`, which `migrate_to_latest` runs at
the end of every writable open. There is no gated migration step and no
identity bump.

**Crash-safe.** `DROP INDEX` is a single atomic statement. A machine losing
power mid-open comes back with either index present or absent, and the next
writable open re-runs `INDEXES_SQL` and finishes the job. There is no state a
torn write can produce that a reopen does not resolve.

**Bounded.** Catalog work plus freelist bookkeeping. No table rewritten, no FTS
index rebuilt, no projection recomputed; peak memory is the page cache,
independent of index size.

**Safe in both directions.** An older binary's `INDEXES_SQL` recreates both
indexes on its own writable open; a newer binary drops them again. No store
version becomes unreadable, no read-only command fails, and a mixed-version
window costs only the index rebuild on each writable open by the older binary.
`an_older_binary_recreating_the_indexes_is_reconciled_on_the_next_open` walks
that cycle three times and asserts convergence, unchanged rows and unchanged
sibling indexes every time.

**Reversible.** Two `CREATE INDEX` statements. The prune removes no row, no
column and no projected byte, so nothing has to be recovered from anywhere
else. `prefix_prune_is_reversible_by_recreating_the_narrow_indexes` pins it.

### Cost on the real 4.23 GB database

A copy of the qualification store, carrying the post-#192 index set, opened by
the branch binary three times with an identical no-op `ctx import` over the
11.88 GB corpus. The first open applies the prune; the second and third find it
already applied, so the difference is the reconciliation and nothing else.
`taskset -c 24-31`, page cache pre-warmed.

| run | wall | user CPU | sys CPU | peak RSS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **first open** — applies the prune | 1.50 s | 0.86 s | 0.41 s | 87,792 KiB |
| second open — already pruned | 1.22 s | 0.76 s | 0.35 s | 88,188 KiB |
| third open — already pruned | 1.22 s | 0.81 s | 0.36 s | 88,268 KiB |

**0.28 s of wall clock, +0.07 s user and +0.05 s system CPU, and no change to
peak RSS** — 87.8 MiB on the applying open versus 88.2 MiB on the two that do
nothing, i.e. marginally *lower*, and set by the ordinary import path rather
than by the 80 MB of index being freed. For scale the released binary's own
qualification run reports `full_repeat_max_rss_kib=88004` for the same no-op
import.

Afterwards the store reports 12 `events` indexes, neither prefix index present,
and `freelist_count * page_size = 80,154,624` — the dropped index bytes exactly.

**Note on file size:** dropping an index returns its pages to the freelist; it
does not shrink an existing file. A migrated 4.23 GB store stays 4.23 GB on disk
with 80 MB of reclaimed free pages that subsequent writes reuse instead of
extending the file. The size win is a smaller file on newly built stores and
suppressed growth on existing ones. No `VACUUM` — a multi-GB rewrite for a 1.89%
file-size gain is not worth it.

### Why there is no identity bump (this changed during review)

An earlier revision of this PR moved `FINAL_SCHEMA_IDENTITY` to
`ctx-store-schema-47-final-v8` with a gated, single-transaction migration in
`final_v47.rs`, following the v2 -> v7 chain. Measuring the consequence argued
it back out.

`Store::open_read_only` calls `verify_final_schema_identity`, so **every
read-only command hard-fails between installing the new binary and the first
writable open.** Measured on a final-v7 copy of the qualification store with
that revision's binary:

```
$ ctx status --json
Error: open read-only ctx store .../work.sqlite
Caused by:
    history store schema 47 is not the released final shape
    (identity: ctx-store-schema-47-final-v7)
```

The same failure applied to `ctx sql`, `ctx show`, `ctx locate`,
`ctx index status`, and `ctx search --refresh off`; only `ctx setup`,
`ctx import` and `ctx search` at its default `--refresh background` take the
writable path. That is the established contract for a *structural* identity
change, and `open_existing_store_read_only` does not even map
`UnsupportedSchemaIdentity` to actionable guidance the way it maps
`UnsupportedSchemaVersion`. Paying it for an index-set change that is
intrinsically safe in both directions, in exchange for 1.89%, is a bad trade.
The repo's own precedent agrees: index-set changes here have always been plain
`INDEXES_SQL` reconciliation.

---

## 5. Search equivalence

Two copies of the real 4.23 GB qualification store, identical byte for byte at
the start, each given the same no-op `ctx import` over the 11.88 GB corpus,
both on the post-#192 base:

- **arm A** — `8c23d9205` binary, 14 `events` indexes.
- **arm B** — this branch's binary, 12 `events` indexes.

Both stores stay at identity `ctx-store-schema-47-final-v7`; the only difference
is the two indexes.

Both end at 764,669 `events` rows and 735,006 `event_search` rows. The corpus
is 194 cases run through each arm, one output file per case:

- 112: 56 single-term queries drawn from the actual user-role preview
  vocabulary of this corpus (`home`, `worktree`, `codex`, `rustfmt`,
  `environment_context`, `task-slug`, …), each in both default
  session-diverse and `--events` dense mode;
- 16: 8 phrase queries, both modes;
- 3 multi-term `--term` OR merges;
- 7 filter dimensions that reach an `events` access path:
  `--event-type message|tool_call|summary`, `--provider codex`, `--since 30d`,
  `--include-subagents`, `--workspace`;
- 6 depth/limit shapes: `--limit 1`, `5`, `50`, `120`, `200`, plus `--verbose`;
- 1 `--backend lexical`;
- 10 public-view `ctx sql` queries over `ctx_events`, `ctx_sessions`,
  `ctx_files_touched`, `ctx_sources`, including the `GROUP BY ctx_session_id`,
  `GROUP BY history_record_id`, and `WHERE ctx_session_id = ?` shapes that
  specifically exercise the two pruned columns;
- 18 `ctx show session` (lite, `--mode full`, `--content complete`) and
  20 `ctx show event` (indexed and `--content complete`) — complete-content
  retrieval reads back through the recorded provider sources.

Outputs are compared byte for byte after normalising the data-root path and the
`generated_at` wall-clock stamp — the only two fields that legitimately differ
between two runs. Result sets, ordering, `bm25` scores, previews, snippets,
citations, pagination cursors, and exit codes are all inside the compared
bytes.

```
identical=194 differing=0 missing=0 rc_mismatch=0
```

**194 of 194 byte-identical.** Four host-volatile fields are normalised before
comparison and nothing else: the data-root path, `generated_at`, `elapsed_ms`,
and `available_memory_bytes` — plus the echoed `since` boundary for the one
`--since 30d` case, which is `now - 30d` evaluated at process start and
differed by the 1.75 s between the two invocations (its result set was already
identical).

---

## 6. Checks

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` — no warnings, no new lints.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-store` — 341 pass, 0 fail (6 of them new, in
  `schema::tests::prefix_redundant_event_indexes`), including #192's
  `impact_queries_use_indexed_union_branches`. Re-run after the identity bump
  was removed.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture` — pass.
- `bazel test //crates/ctx-history-store:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests`
  — both PASSED on the post-#192 base
  (`ctx-history-capture` 224.1 s, `ctx-history-store` 123.6 s).
- `cargo test --workspace` — 7 failures in `ctx --bin ctx`
  (`upgrade::install::lock_tests` ×4, `upgrade::install::marker::tests` ×2,
  `semantic::daemon::telemetry_tests::post_lock_initialization_failure_retains_restart_intent`).
  All 7 reproduce identically on the merge base with an unmodified tree: they
  contend on machine-global installation locks and the canonical executable
  path, which this shared build host perturbs. Not caused by this change.

### New tests

`crates/ctx-history-store/src/schema/tests/prefix_redundant_event_indexes.rs`

- `composite_indexes_absorb_every_prefix_lookup_with_the_same_access_shape` —
  asserts the plan for each absorbed lookup names the composite index and never
  falls back to a table scan.
- `released_store_reopen_drops_prefix_indexes_without_data_loss` — the
  reconciliation path, with rows and every other `events` index asserted
  unchanged.
- `an_older_binary_recreating_the_indexes_is_reconciled_on_the_next_open` —
  three full recreate/drop cycles, the mixed-version window.
- `every_same_version_identity_upgrade_lands_on_the_pruned_index_set` — v2
  through v7 entry identities all converge, since nothing is identity-gated.
- `released_v46_upgrade_lands_on_the_pruned_index_set` — the released-version
  upgrade path.
- `prefix_prune_is_reversible_by_recreating_the_narrow_indexes` — rollback.

---

## 7. Recommendation

**Adopt the index prune. Do not attempt external-content FTS5 over
`event_search_lookup` — it is not implementable.**

The two halves of the original plan do not have to land together, because the
premise that tied them together does not hold: external content over
`event_search_lookup` is not a smaller version of the FTS index, it is a
79.4%-smaller *corpus*. There is nothing to combine.

What is left is a small, self-contained, fully reversible change:

- **−80,154,624 bytes** of live index pages, verified to the byte three
  independent ways (`dbstat` object sizes, `dbstat` accounted-total delta, and
  freelist growth).
- **Two fewer random-UUID-keyed B-tree writes per event**, out of 14.
- **Zero query-plan regressions** across 36 statements including the whole
  NativePath publication path, and **194/194 byte-identical** CLI outputs on the
  real corpus.
- Reconciliation costing **0.28 s and no extra memory** on a 4.23 GB store, with
  no version move, no unreadable-store window, and rollback in two
  `CREATE INDEX` statements.

The identity bump an earlier revision carried has been removed (§4). Measuring
it showed it bought auditability in exchange for hard-failing every read-only
command until the first writable open — a bad trade for 1.89% on a change that
is intrinsically safe in both directions. What ships is four files, no version
move, and a reconciliation that already has precedent in this file.

**Separately: contentless FTS5 is the real prize** — 567 MB, 13.4% of the
database, with `bm25()` proven bit-identical on 45 queries over the real
corpus. It is a bigger change than this one and belongs in its own PR (§1).

title: Remove the --json CLI flag
body:
## Summary

- remove public `--json` output aliases and make `--format` the sole output selector
- use `--format jsonl` for streaming `index watch` output and rename import’s input selector to `--input-format`

- add public-help regression tests that reject the removed flags

Prepares ctx 0.26 Local Pro for fixed staging and production commercial channels.

- pins pro.ctx.rs and pro-staging.ctx.rs trust records
