title: fix(pro): refresh auth while Checkout polls
body:
## Summary
- refresh a rejected WorkOS access token noninteractively during long Checkout polling
- keep account and subject identity pinned across refresh
- zeroize superseded access tokens and reuse the refreshed credential for entitlement issuance
- bound transient and fatal refresh behavior with regression coverage

## Production finding
A real unreleased-CLI Checkout dogfood remained open beyond the short WorkOS token lifetime and failed at approximately six minutes with HTTP 401. This patch keeps the supported 30-minute Checkout wait viable.

## Validation
- `bazel test //crates/ctx-cli:unit_tests --config=ci`
- focused Checkout polling tests
- `git diff --check`

title: fix(upgrade): re-derive pre-0.26 provider projections instead of doubling them
body:
> Based on `main`. This change is independent of #196, which fixes an unrelated journal-byte
> accounting bound that makes v0.25 upgrade imports abort outright; either can merge first. It was
> originally stacked on #196, but that branch is being rebased repeatedly while it is finished, so
> this is cut from `main` to stay reviewable. Both were verified together: the reproduction below was
> taken on `origin/main` + #196.

## The defect

Upgrading a ctx 0.25 index to 0.26 silently indexes the user's entire history a second time.

v0.26 derives a capture-source identity that v0.25 never wrote, so an upgrading import creates new
capture sources and new event identities instead of recognising the rows already present. Sessions
*are* reconciled — the existing `v47_provider_session_repair` migration dedupes those — so the old
events stay attached to the rewritten sessions and nothing looks obviously broken. The database
roughly doubles and search returns every hit twice.

### Reproduced on `origin/main` (+ #196), independent of this change

Released `ctx 0.25.0` over a 116 MB / 6-file slice of the launch corpus, then one `ctx import` with
`origin/main`+#196 over the same slice:

| | events | sessions | edges | capture_sources | user_version |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| v0.25 index | 10,031 | 8 | 5 | 12 | 46 |
| after one v0.26 import | **20,157** | 8 | 5 | 18 | 47 |
| clean v0.26 install, same corpus | 10,126 | 6 | 0 | 6 | 47 |

20,157 = 10,031 + 10,126. Exactly one extra copy.

On the 1.087 GB launch corpus the same arithmetic holds against measured endpoints: the pristine
v0.25 snapshot carries **141,973** events, a clean 0.26 import of that corpus produces **142,950**,
so an upgrade lands at **284,923**.

It compounds. `event_search MATCH 'wait'` on the small corpus went 2,423 (v0.25) → 38,969 after the
upgrade import plus the ordinary search-triggered refreshes: every subsequent provider refresh
appends another full copy.

## Strategy: re-derive, do not reconcile

The ctx database is a reconstructable representation of local provider data, not an archive, and
complete-content retrieval already fails closed when a source has vanished or changed identity.
Identity reconciliation would mean writing and maintaining a mapping from every retired provider
identity to every current one, per provider, forever — a permanent compatibility surface for rows we
can rebuild exactly from the bytes still on disk. Rejected.

So: **on detecting a pre-0.26 provider projection, discard the derived provider data and re-derive
it from the provider sources.**

## Build alongside, then swap. Never delete then rebuild

Auto-upgrade and background maintenance are both default-on, and the Codex ingestion path has a
known intermittent deadlock (see *Known hazard* below), so this has to be safe when it is killed at
an arbitrary point.

1. **Preflight disk.** Refuse rather than fill the disk (below).
2. **Re-derive into a staging root** at `<data_root>/.ctx-provider-rebuild/`. The destination is
   absent, so the Codex session tree takes the cold builder's one-shot path exactly as a fresh
   install does; everything after it uses the ordinary incremental writer, exactly as
   `ctx import --all` does today. The installed index is untouched and fully searchable for the
   whole re-derivation.
3. **Validate before installing.** Reopen the staged file from scratch through
   `Store::open_read_only` (schema version + final schema identity), then `integrity_check`,
   `foreign_key_check`, non-zero session/event counts, a recorded projection generation that is not
   superseded, and a real `MATCH` query against all five FTS tables.
4. **Install atomically** through the existing cold-store publication primitive. `cold_store.rs`
   gains `publish_over_existing_store(staged, target, retired)`: it retires the current index with
   one `rename`, then publishes the staged object with the same absent-target-only hard link
   `ColdStoreBuild::finish` already uses, verifies the published name resolves to the exact staged
   inode, and `fsync`s the directory. The window in which the index path does not resolve is one
   `rename` wide. If the link fails after the retirement, the original is renamed straight back.
5. **Recover on the next run.** A retired generation with no index present is renamed back; a
   retired generation with an index present is a completed publication and is removed. An abandoned
   stage directory is deleted before the next attempt starts.

An exclusive lock file admits one rebuild per data root across processes.

### Failure matrix

| Interrupted at | Installed index | Left behind | Next run |
|---|---|---|---|
| preflight / before staging | untouched | nothing | retries |
| insufficient disk | untouched | nothing | refuses again with the same message |
| during re-derivation (incl. the ingestion deadlock) | untouched, searchable | stage dir | stage cleared, retries |
| during validation | untouched, searchable | stage dir | stage cleared, retries |
| between retire and link | absent for one `rename` | `work.sqlite.ctx-superseded` | renamed back, then retries |
| after link, before cleanup | new generation installed | `work.sqlite.ctx-superseded` | retirement removed, no-op |
| after cleanup | new generation installed | nothing | no-op (`AlreadyNative`) |

Measured, not argued: `ctx index rebuild` on the 1.087 GB corpus was `SIGKILL`ed at 2 s, 6 s, 12 s,
20 s, 28 s and 33 s (publication lands at ~30 s). Every time the installed index survived with
**141,973 events / 34 sessions**, `integrity_check ok`, `0` foreign-key violations and a queryable
FTS, and `ctx search` still answered from it. Every retry then completed to the fresh-install result
and compared digest-equal to the control.

## Disk headroom

Both generations exist at once, so the rebuild needs roughly a second copy of the index. Required is
`1.25 x` the installed index and WAL, with a 256 MiB floor; available comes from the filesystem
holding the data root. Roughly 4.2 GB of index per 12 GB of corpus, so a 70 GB corpus needs about
50 GB transiently.

If it does not fit, the rebuild refuses before creating a stage and names both numbers:

```
not enough free disk space to rebuild the provider index: 52.5 GiB required, 3.0 GiB available
on /home/you/.ctx (49.5 GiB short). The rebuild is built alongside the current index of 42.0 GiB
and only replaces it once it is complete, so both exist at the same time. Free space and run the
rebuild again; the current index is untouched.
```

`ctx status --format json` reports `required_bytes`, `available_bytes` and `sufficient_disk` while a
rebuild is pending, so the shortfall is visible before the user runs anything.

## Scope question 1 — what is preserved, what is re-derived

Only `work.sqlite` is replaced. Nothing else in the data root is read, moved or rewritten.

**Re-derived** (all of it provider-derived canonical output): `events`, `sessions`, `session_edges`,
`runs`, `capture_sources`, `files_touched`, `catalog_sessions`, `provider_source_locators`,
`capture_source_provider_routes`, `sync_cursors`, the import `history_records`, the FTS/search
projection, and the projection journal.

**Preserved**, because it lives outside the index file: `config.toml` (daemon opt-out, analytics
opt-out, `search.semantic`, auto-upgrade mode), `device.json`, `install.json`, `usage.sqlite` (local
usage — a separate database), `vectors.sqlite` (semantic sidecar), `semantic-model-cache/`,
`objects/` (content-addressed; the stage's objects are merged in, and an existing name is the same
bytes by construction), `plugins/`, `runtime/`, `daemon/`, and the Pro helper with its credential
vault / keyring entries.

`rebuild_keeps_every_local_file_except_the_provider_index` seeds every one of those paths with
recognisable bytes, runs a real rebuild, and asserts each survives byte for byte while the index
itself changes — and that neither the stage nor the retired generation is left behind.

## Scope question 2 — the trigger

A **recorded provider-projection generation**, written once per store into
`ctx_provider_projection_generation`.

`run_migrations` records it before any migration touches the rows that prove it, using the
`user_version` the previous binary left behind:

- row already present → never re-evaluated;
- `user_version >= 47` → native;
- otherwise, any row in `capture_sources` / `sessions` / `session_edges` / `runs` / `events` /
  `files_touched` → **superseded**;
- otherwise → native.

Why not the alternatives. The schema version alone cannot work: by the time anything downstream
looks, the store is already migrated to the current version and the evidence is gone — and the
version keeps moving for unrelated reasons. A row probe alone cannot work either: after one
upgrading import the rows carry both identities, so the probe stops being able to tell. Recording
the decision at the one moment it is knowable, and never revisiting it, is what makes it fire
exactly once.

Fires exactly once, never on a fresh install, never twice:

- a fresh install enters `run_migrations` at `user_version = 0` with empty tables → native, no extra
  work on the fresh path at all;
- an upgraded store is marked superseded and stays marked across reopens and across an interrupted
  migration;
- the re-derived store is built by the cold builder from nothing, so it is native by construction —
  the flag clears because the *file* is replaced, not because anything writes "done". A second
  `ctx index rebuild` returns `AlreadyNative` and changes no rows.

Constants live in `ctx-history-store`, keyed to `NATIVE_PROVIDER_PROJECTION_SCHEMA_VERSION = 47`,
deliberately independent of `SCHEMA_VERSION` so a future migration bump does not silently retarget
the trigger.

While a store is superseded, every provider write is fenced. The fence sits at the top of
`run_import_internal` (so the user gets the reason before a single provider file is read) and in
`ensure_search_projection_ready_for_provider_import`, the one funnel every provider write into an
existing store passes through — which covers the daemon's background refresh and the
search-triggered refresh. `upgraded_store_is_fenced_out_of_provider_imports` asserts a refused
import adds zero canonical rows.

## Scope question 3 — consent and visibility (recommendation, not a fait accompli)

Implemented as **announce and defer**, and that is what I recommend:

- detection is automatic and free;
- reads keep working — `ctx search`, `ctx show`, `ctx locate` all serve the existing index;
- writes fail closed with the reason and the exact command, so nothing duplicates in the meantime;
- `ctx status` reports `provider_projection: rebuild_required | rebuild_running | native | unknown |
  uninitialized`, plus the disk numbers and a one-line notice, so a user who wonders why imports
  stopped gets an answer instead of an unexplained stall;
- the re-derivation itself only runs when the user runs `ctx index rebuild`.

The rebuild is written so it *could* be driven unattended — idempotent, disk-preflighted, resumable,
one lock per data root, and it never leaves the index worse than it found it. I did not turn that on
because a multi-minute-to-multi-hour rebuild of the user's history, plus a transient second copy of
a database that can be tens of GB, is not something a background daemon should start without being
asked. **The daemon-driven variant is a one-line policy change and a product decision — please make
it explicitly**, and please not before the ingestion deadlock below is fixed, because a wedged
unattended rebuild would sit pending forever with nobody watching.

## Scope question 4 — semantic index and Pro graph

Both are derived, both recover on their own, neither is deleted here.

**Semantic sidecar.** `vectors.sqlite` is untouched. A re-derived store is an independently
initialised store, so it carries a new `canonical_semantic_projection_state.store_identity`; the
daemon's `prepare_semantic_reconciliation_version` sees an identity that does not match what the
vector store acknowledged and re-arms a full reconciliation sweep, which enqueues missing or changed
documents and prunes anchors that no longer exist. Semantic search degrades to stale coverage while
that runs, then converges. No new code — `rebuild_reproduces_a_fresh_install_of_the_same_corpus`
asserts the identity actually changes, which is the signal the sweep keys on.

**Pro graph.** Pro entitlement, credentials and the helper binary live outside the index and are
untouched. The graph itself is materialised from the projection journal. A superseded store never
activates a journal under 0.26 — the fence stops the import that would have — so the helper has no
checkpoint against it, and after the rebuild the next materialisation takes a full baseline from the
new journal generation. Automatic, no user action.

## Upgrade equals fresh install — evidence

1.087 GB launch corpus. Left: the pristine v0.25 snapshot upgraded and rebuilt. Right: a clean 0.26
import of the same corpus into an empty data root.

| | rebuilt from v0.25 | fresh 0.26 install |
|---|---|---|
| events | 142,950 | 142,950 |
| sessions | 32 | 32 |
| session_edges | 17 | 17 |
| runs | 1,085 | 1,085 |
| capture_sources | 32 | 32 |
| files_touched | 1,261 | 1,261 |
| catalog_sessions | 32 | 32 |
| sync_cursors | 32 | 32 |
| provider_source_locators | 32 | 32 |
| capture_source_provider_routes | 32 | 32 |
| event_search | 131,452 | 131,452 |
| event_search_lookup | 16,237 | 16,237 |
| projection_journal_chunks | 2,075 | 2,075 |

Not just counts: **ordered row digests over all 15 canonical tables are equal**, after excluding
values a second build cannot reproduce —

- wall-clock stamps of the import run: `created_at_ms` / `updated_at_ms` / `cataloged_at_ms` /
  `indexed_at_ms` / `last_imported_at_ms` / `last_synced_at_ms`, `imported_at` inside
  `metadata_json`, and the activity stamps on the import `history_records` row;
- the projection journal's `cumulative_digest`, which is seeded from those stamps;
- `canonical_semantic_projection_state.store_identity`, which is per-store *by design* and is
  exactly how the semantic sidecar detects it must reconcile.

Everything else matches byte for byte, including every canonical id, every capture-source identity,
every NativePath cursor and every provider event hash — those are derived from the provider bytes,
so a correct re-derivation has to reproduce them, and it does.

`integrity_check` ok, `0` foreign-key violations, all five FTS tables queryable, `COUNT(*) =
COUNT(DISTINCT id)` on `events`, and `ctx search refactor` returns 15 hits / 15 distinct ids.

## Re-derivation time

| corpus | index | re-derivation | clean 0.26 import, same corpus |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.087 GB, 32 sessions, 142,950 events | 640 MB → 682 MB | **28–34 s** (eight completed runs) | 23.2 s |
| 11.88 GB, 3,464 sessions, 764,669 events | 4.23 GB → 4.23 GB | **246 s** (312 s wall incl. the one-time v46→v47 migration of the old 4.2 GB index) | 230 s |

The 11.88 GB arm confirms the sizing assumption directly: 11.88 GB of corpus produced a 4.234 GB
index, so a rebuild of that store needs about 4.2 GB transiently on top of the 4.2 GB already
installed. It also reproduced the equivalence at scale — 764,669 events / 3,464 sessions / 3,406
edges / 3,464 capture sources, and ordered row digests equal to the clean-install control across all
15 canonical tables, `integrity_check ok`, `0` foreign-key violations, FTS queryable.

The re-derivation is a fresh cold import plus validation and one publication, so it costs about what
a clean install of the same corpus costs. Notably it is *faster* than the broken upgrade import it
replaces: that path drives the incremental writer over an existing 640 MB store, which on this host
never finished at all.

## Known hazard, not introduced here

The Codex NativePath producer has an intermittent deadlock on `origin/main`
(`CODEX_SOURCE_MAX_QUEUED_WINDOWS` over-committing the preparation byte budget): every worker parks
in `futex` with zero CPU and zero I/O and never returns. I hit it repeatedly on both the upgrade
import and the cold rebuild — six kill/retry runs on the 1.087 GB corpus needed 3, 1, 2, 3, 3 and 2
attempts. It is owned elsewhere and is **not** fixed here.

It is the reason the design in this PR is what it is: a wedged rebuild holds the store's bulk-search
guard forever, and the only acceptable answer is that the installed index is untouched and a retry
works. Both are asserted above. Anyone driving this unattended should apply a timeout and treat a
wedge as a distinct outcome.

## The handoff gate in #196

#196 leaves `released_store_upgrade_matches_a_fresh_install_canonical_set` `#[ignore]`d, naming this
branch as owner. **It stays ignored, and it should be re-pointed rather than un-ignored.** As
written it drives `import_codex_native_session_root` straight into the released store and asserts
that *the upgrading import itself* leaves the fresh-install canonical set. That is the reconciliation
contract the product owner rejected: it can only pass if this build learns to resolve retired
identities in place. Under the chosen strategy the upgrading import does not reconcile — it is
refused, and a separate re-derivation replaces the store file, which a function taking `&mut Store`
cannot do to its caller's file.

Its *intent* — an exact set, never a floor — is the gate this PR is measured against, one layer up,
at the store lifecycle where the fix lives: `rebuild_reproduces_a_fresh_install_of_the_same_corpus`
asserts the upgraded store ends holding exactly a fresh control's events, sessions, edges and
capture sources, and the two real corpora above assert the same thing with ordered row digests.
Moving the ignored test's assertion to that level is a small edit inside a file this branch does not
own, so I have left it alone.

I did adopt both traps it documents. My fixture clears the six tables v0.25 never had, strips this
build's NativePath change token from the catalog rows (a real v0.25 catalog carries exactly six
metadata keys — checked against the snapshot), re-keys sources and events to identities this build
cannot derive, and re-keys the event dedupe key, which embeds the capture-source id and silently
reconciles if it is left behind. `superseded_fixture_duplicates_without_the_trigger` is the standing
proof that this is not vacuous: with the trigger disabled and the fence bypassed, the same fixture
produces `released + fresh` capture sources *and* `released + fresh` events — the miniature of
284,923 against 142,950. Every other assertion in the file rests on that.

## Tests

New:

- `ctx-history-store`: six tests over the recorded generation — fresh store, released store with and
  without provider rows, a store already at the native version, survival across an interrupted
  migration, and read-only unknown.
- `ctx-history-store`: five tests over `publish_over_existing_store` — retire-and-install, install
  over an absent target, rollback when the link fails after retirement, refusal of a missing stage,
  refusal of an occupied retirement path.
- `ctx-cli`: twelve tests over the orchestration — the fixture-honesty proof above, the fence,
  fresh-install equivalence, preserved local state, no-op on repeat and on a fresh install,
  publication-window recovery, retirement cleanup, abandoned-stage cleanup, end-to-end disk refusal,
  the headroom formula, and recorded-root replay for sources discovery never finds. Discovery and
  free space both have test-only seams so no test reads the developer's own provider history or real
  disk.

`cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean over the files this branch touches, `cargo clippy -p ctx -p
ctx-history-store --all-targets` no new warnings, and
`bazel test //crates/ctx-history-store:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests` — both
`PASSED`.

`cargo test -p ctx --bin ctx` reports 872 passed and 7 failed here; the same seven
(`upgrade::install::lock_tests::*`, `upgrade::install::marker::tests::*`,
`semantic::daemon::telemetry_tests::post_lock_initialization_failure_retains_restart_intent`) fail
identically on a clean `origin/main` checkout, so they are pre-existing and unrelated. Nothing in
this branch touches the upgrade installer or the daemon.

title: Document the macOS Developer ID / Team ID used to sign release binaries
body:
Installing ctx 0.25.0 on macOS (arm64, hosted installer) and registering the `rs.ctx.maintenance` LaunchAgent triggers a macOS Background Task Management notification reading:

> "legacy publisher" added a login item

That name is the code-signing organization on the shipped binary:

```
Authority=Developer ID Application: legacy publisher (SJSNARH4TG)
Authority=Developer ID Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA
TeamIdentifier=SJSNARH4TG
```

The binary itself verifies cleanly:

- `spctl -a -vvv -t install` → `accepted`, `source=Notarized Developer ID`
- `codesign --verify --deep --strict` → valid on disk, satisfies its Designated Requirement
- Hardened runtime enabled (`flags=0x10000(runtime)`)
- SHA-256 matches the release receipt written by the installer to `ctx.install.json`, which points at the official `cli.ctx.rs` artifact URL

So provenance is fine. The issue is naming: the signing org doesn't match the publisher named on ctx.rs ("© 2026 ctx engineering, inc."), and I couldn't find the Team ID documented in the repo, the embedded docs (`ctx docs`), or `SECURITY.md`.

**Two asks:**

1. Can you confirm that Team ID `SJSNARH4TG` / "legacy publisher" is your signing identity?
2. Would you consider publishing it — README, `SECURITY.md`, or the install docs?

An unexpected company name in a macOS login-item prompt reads as a compromise indicator, and it's the kind of thing that sends people hunting for malware on their own machine. A documented Team ID lets users verify with `codesign -dv --verbose=4` instead of guessing.

Since `SECURITY.md` already scopes the local-machine trust boundary, the signing identity seems like a natural thing to pin down there.

**Environment:** ctx 0.25.0 (source commit `228e05f`), `macos-arm64`, stable channel, installed via the hosted installer from https://ctx.rs/install

title: Fresh Codex setup fails with SQLite foreign key constraint on a real corpus
body:
## Problem

A fresh setup from current `main` reproducibly fails while indexing Codex history with SQLite error 787. This is a clean install into an empty data root, not a v0.25 database upgrade.

## Version

- commit: `103c0105` (`Merge pull request #203`)
- binary reports: `ctx 0.26.0`
- previous locally deployed `ctx 0.25.0` can read and search its existing index normally

## Reproduction

```console
$ ctx setup --data-root /tmp/ctx-v026-repro --no-daemon --wait --format json --progress json
{"message":"codex","phase":"indexing","total_bytes":3645068564,...}
Error: store error: sqlite error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed

Caused by:
    0: sqlite error: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
    1: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
    2: Error code 787: Foreign key constraint failed
```

The command was run twice against two independently empty data roots. Both attempts failed in the Codex phase:

- run 1: 3m21.96s, exit 1
- run 2: 3m20.08s, exit 1

The second run used about 306s user CPU, 7s system CPU, 156% aggregate CPU, and reached roughly 1.1 GiB of cold-stage SQLite data before failure. The staging database was automatically removed after the error.

## Expected behavior

A malformed or otherwise unusual record in a real Codex corpus should either be rejected with the nonfatal data-quality accounting introduced in #192, or produce a diagnostic identifying the affected source. It should not abort the entire clean setup with an unqualified FK error.

## Initial scope / possible area

This appears to happen during Codex NativePath cold-store construction or finalization: progress never advances to another provider, and the temporary `work.sqlite.ctx-native-cold-*.sqlite` disappears after the error. I have not identified the exact FK, so this is only a scope hint rather than a root-cause claim.

The corpus is real multi-year Codex history (~3.65 GB reported by setup). I can run a focused diagnostic or test a candidate patch against it if that would help.

title: feat!: make provider history authoritative with Tantivy and flat-F32 search
body:
## Summary

This PR replaces ctx’s legacy canonical `work.sqlite` history Store with the storage and retrieval architecture for ctx 1.0.

Provider-native history files and databases now own transcript content. ctx’s Core history data plane consists of rebuildable projections tied to a verified source generation:

```text
provider history
  → stable identities and typed source locators
  → immutable Tantivy lexical generation
      ├─ exact source hydration for search, show, locate, and MCP
      ├─ relational.sqlite metadata projection
      ├─ optional flat-F32 semantic generation
      └─ optional generation-bound Pro materialization
```

The PR:

- Replaces `ctx-history-store` and `ctx-history-search` with dedicated source-backed index and relational projection crates.
- Converts native providers, custom JSONL, and history-source plugins to stable identities, typed locators, and exact provider hydration.
- Builds immutable Tantivy candidates privately, verifies their source manifest and policy identity, and publishes them atomically.
- Stores searchable text as indexed terms without retaining message bodies or display previews in Tantivy.
- Replaces the production `sqlite-vec` path with immutable, memory-mapped F32 vector segments.
- Adds generation-bound lexical, semantic, relational, and Pro catch-up with explicit stale, partial, and unavailable states.
- Moves refresh ownership to the persistent daemon, including provider discovery, event-driven refresh, semantic work, recovery, and query-service supervision.
- Rewires setup, import, search, show, locate, SQL, status, doctor, MCP, SDK contracts, and release construction around the new generation model.
- Starts a fresh 1.0 history epoch and removes the old Store only after a new Tantivy generation has been verified and activated.

## Why Tantivy replaced SQLite FTS

The matched lexical bakeoff used the same 998 source files, 5.44 GB of history, and 371,017 searchable events:

| Metric | SQLite contentless FTS5 | Tantivy |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Cold build wall time | 30.60 s | **7.65 s** |
| Main index size | 209.0 MB | **117.4 MB** |
| Total filesystem output | 3.87 GB | **240.8 MB** |

The SQLite writer was occupied for 30.587 of the 30.601 seconds, while 16 producers accumulated 304.4 seconds waiting to submit work. Removing copied bodies reduced storage, but it did not remove the single-writer bottleneck.

The query comparison showed the same split:

- Rare term: SQLite 0.885 ms, Tantivy 1.092 ms.
- Medium-frequency term: SQLite 28.83 ms, Tantivy 1.413 ms.
- Broad term: SQLite 115.23 ms, Tantivy 1.178 ms.

SQLite remained competitive for selective queries. Tantivy won decisively for cold construction, index size, write parallelism, and frequent-term retrieval—the workloads that dominate a large local history corpus.

These numbers compare the lexical data planes rather than claiming a fourfold improvement for every end-to-end command. The production implementation adds source verification, exact hydration, publication recovery, projections, and user-facing contracts on top of the measured engine.

## Why flat-F32 replaced sqlite-vec and ANN

The semantic bakeoff began from an existing embedding corpus and compared storage and query backends across 466,000 chunks:

| Backend | Build time | Query p50 | Storage | Recall |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| sqlite-vec F32 | 5.83 s | 305 ms | 800 MB | exact baseline |
| USearch F32 | 116 s | 30 ms | 785 MB | 100% |
| USearch BF16 | 61 s | 17 ms | 427 MB | 99.45% |
| Flat mmap F32 | **1.10 s** | **21.7–24.2 ms** | **716 MB** | **100%** |

Flat F32 also matched sqlite-vec exactly on the retained real-E5 query set. At this corpus size, an exact scan under 25 ms left too little latency to justify HNSW’s graph construction, tuning, approximate recall, and roughly 916–1,796 CPU-seconds of build work.

Immutable flat segments fit ctx’s ownership model:

- vectors are written sequentially and published through a checksummed manifest;
- readers pin one generation and scan it through mmap;
- queries retain a bounded top-k without loading a database or graph;
- interrupted writes leave the previous generation readable;
- model or projection changes invalidate and rebuild derived data cleanly;
- macOS, Windows, and Linux builds no longer need to compile and load a SQLite vector extension.

Embedding generation still dominates cold semantic ingestion. Flat exact search therefore remains the correctness baseline until measured corpus size or query concurrency demonstrates a need for an ANN accelerator. A future ANN layer can be generated from the flat generation without becoming the sole copy.

## Where SQLite still fits

SQLite remains in the parts of ctx that benefit from relational or transactional storage:

- `relational.sqlite` provides disposable metadata and stable read-only `ctx_*` views for `ctx sql`;
- `usage.sqlite` stores bounded, content-free local usage aggregates;
- provider-owned SQLite histories remain supported and are read through verified snapshot paths.

SQLite no longer owns canonical transcript content, lexical retrieval, or semantic vectors. That boundary preserves SQL inspection without making one database responsible for source authority, full-text indexing, vector search, rendering, and migration.

## User-visible behavior

Search candidates come from the active Tantivy generation, while snippets and complete transcripts are hydrated from the exact provider record identified by that generation’s locator. A source that moved, changed, disappeared, or became unsupported produces a typed availability error. ctx does not silently return a stale database copy.

The daemon owns bounded refresh and projection catch-up. Foreground queries read committed generations instead of becoming history writers. Relational, semantic, and Pro consumers can catch up independently, but they must match the active Core generation before their results are admitted.

Semantic search remains opt-in. Lexical search stays available without a model, while hybrid search uses semantic evidence only when its flat-F32 generation has compatible, complete coverage.

## Migration

ctx 1.0 builds a fresh source-backed epoch from current provider history. It does not migrate, read, or fall back to the legacy canonical Store.

Old history artifacts are deleted only after the replacement Tantivy generation reopens and verifies successfully. Failed or interrupted publication retains the previous safe state and completes through the next fix-forward setup or refresh. title: Cold mixed-provider import rejects valid OpenCode and active Hermes SQLite sources
body:
## Problem

A cold import of a real mixed-provider history corpus fails on valid OpenCode and active Hermes sources unless three local workarounds are applied.

The corpus used for validation contains:

- 3,935 sources from Claude, Codex, Hermes, and OpenCode
- about 3.83 GB of certified source data
- about 520,000 events
- an ordinary OpenCode SQLite database of about 943 MiB

This is not a synthetic stress test; it is accumulated agent history from normal use.

## Reproduced blockers

### 1. A valid OpenCode SQLite database exceeds the snapshot admission limit

The 943 MiB database is rejected by the 512 MiB SQLite snapshot cap. Raising the bounded limit to 2 GiB admits this source while preserving a finite guardrail.

### 2. OpenCode provider event types can escape into `EventRole`

An OpenCode event with role/type `agent-switched` reaches the relational projection as a role and aborts the transaction:

```text
invalid EventRole value: agent-switched
```

Provider-specific event types should be normalized to the canonical role vocabulary. In the local fix, tool-like event kinds map to `tool`; unrecognized kinds such as `agent-switched` map to `unknown`.

### 3. Active SQLite sources can fail revision revalidation without committed data changes

Two cases caused false source-change failures:

- a zero-length SQLite WAL appeared or disappeared;
- unrelated siblings changed in the source directory while the Hermes database itself remained the same object.

Observed errors included:

```text
provider source changed while its authority handle was retained
complete inventory authority hermes/ctx.document-tree changed during final precommit revalidation
```

A zero-length WAL contains no committed transactions, so the local fix treats it as revision-neutral. For Hermes parent directories, the local fix revalidates directory object identity while continuing to strictly revalidate the SQLite database and non-empty WAL leaves.

## Validation

With those minimal changes and focused regression tests, the same corpus completed a clean import:

- 4 providers
- 4,564 sessions
- 520,000+ events
- full cold pass in about 6 minutes
- relational SQLite about 1.3 GB
- relational WAL peaked around 1.1 GB and checkpointed back to zero
- two subsequent forced incremental passes completed in about 2.1 seconds each
- catalog, lexical, relational, and refresh all reported `ready`

The latest `main` was checked before filing this issue. The recent bounded incremental relational-validation change fixes a separate 10-second validation timeout we had observed, so that problem is intentionally not included here.

I have the changes split into small local commits with focused regression tests and can open a PR after confirming the intended limits and normalization behavior.

title: daemon --once can exit 0 while core refresh state remains pending or stale
body:
## Problem

After a daemon is interrupted after the lexical generation has committed but before its refresh receipt is published, a later forced one-shot run can exit successfully while the index is still not usable as a fully refreshed snapshot.

Observed immediately after the interrupted cycle:

```text
catalog: pending
lexical: ready
relational: stale
refresh: pending
daemon: stale_lock
lock active: false
```

In an earlier reproduction, `ctx daemon run --once --force` returned exit 0 in about 1.4 seconds while catalog remained pending and relational remained stale. The actual lexical generation had advanced, but the persisted refresh receipt was still `running` and referenced the previous generation.

This makes exit 0 unsafe for automation: the caller cannot treat a successful one-shot run as proof that catalog, lexical, relational, and refresh have converged.

## Expected behavior

On startup, the daemon should reconcile a refresh receipt left in the committed state against the actual published lexical generation. A forced one-shot run should then execute all required core catch-up work, including relational projection, before reporting success.

Optional Pro work should not consume the only scheduler opportunity and starve required core relational catch-up.

Either:

1. `--once` exits 0 only when all required core projections are `ready`; or
2. it exits non-zero with structured details identifying every remaining pending/stale projection.

## Validation of a local fix

I tested a small local change that:

- repairs a committed-but-unpublished refresh receipt during restart reconciliation after verifying the real lexical generation;
- schedules required relational catch-up before optional Pro catch-up;
- preserves independent relational retry behavior.

Focused restart/retry tests pass. On a real mixed-provider index with 4,564 sessions and about 520,000 events, the recovery pass completed in about 8 seconds and left:

```text
catalog: ready
lexical: ready
relational: ready
refresh: ready
daemon running: false
lock active: false
```

The latest `main` was fetched immediately before filing. Its recent bounded incremental relational-validation change fixed a separate 10-second SQL-validation timeout, but it does not contain the receipt-reconciliation and scheduler-ordering changes described here.

I can send the local commit and regression tests as a focused PR.

title: Small Claude event is rejected by shared hydration capacity accounting
body:
## Problem

`ctx show event` rejects a small Claude event as exceeding the 64 MiB aggregate hydration budget. The same event fails in both `complete` and `indexed` content modes.

```bash
ctx show event <event-id> \
  --before 0 \
  --after 0 \
  --content complete \
  --format json
```

```json
{
  "detail": "source hydration exceeds the aggregate byte budget",
  "error": "hydration_budget_exceeded/content_too_large",
  "error_code": "hydration_budget_exceeded",
  "failure_kind": "content_too_large",
  "retryable": false
}
```

This is reproducible with a one-event window. `ctx locate event` reports:

- locator family: JSONL
- source record `byte_length`: 3,456 bytes
- complete content available: true
- entire source JSONL: 150,925 bytes
- longest line in that JSONL: 28,574 bytes

Therefore neither the selected record nor its entire source approaches 64 MiB.

## Likely cause

The common hydration accounting admits the returned provider body using both its length and allocation capacity. For exact JSONL locators, `provider_body_is_admitted` compares the returned `Vec` capacity against a maximum derived from the source record byte length.

A provider can legitimately parse and normalize a small record into a short string whose spare allocation capacity is larger than `byte_length + overhead`. That allocator detail is then surfaced as `hydration_budget_exceeded`, even though retained content and the operation-wide budget are small.

This should be fixed in the shared hydration accounting rather than in the Claude adapter. Capacity may be relevant to peak-memory accounting, but unused capacity should not be treated as response content or rejected against the exact source-record length without an opportunity to release/re-account it.

## Expected behavior

- A single 3.4 KiB event hydrates successfully.
- The common hydration path remains bounded for every provider.
- `indexed` mode provides bounded indexed content when complete source hydration cannot be admitted, rather than failing identically.
- A genuine oversized response reports measured/reserved sizes so a client can make a useful decision.

This blocks a daily-timeline consumer because skipping the event would silently create a worklog gap, while parsing the located provider JSONL would break the public CTX abstraction.

## Related integration friction

These are not blockers of the same severity, but they appeared while integrating exclusively through the public CTX 1.0 CLI.

### `--max-columns` constrains stable-view expansion

This two-column query fails with `--max-columns 12` and succeeds with `--max-columns 64`:

```sql
SELECT e.ctx_event_id, s.root_ctx_session_id
FROM ctx_events AS e
LEFT JOIN ctx_sessions AS s ON s.ctx_session_id = e.ctx_session_id
LIMIT 1
```

The error is `too many columns in result set`. It appears that the SQLite limit is applied while the stable views are expanded, rather than only to the final projected columns. Either the limit should describe this behavior, or it should constrain only the public result shape.

### Event-window bounds are absent from help

`ctx show event --help` does not state that `--before` and `--after` accept only `0..50`. The constraint is shown only after an invalid request.

### Generation races are not consistently structured

Generation changes can surface as plain CLI errors, for example:

```text
the lexical generation changed while a verified reader was opening
```

A stable JSON error code with `retryable: true` would let clients use one retry policy for SQL and hydration operations.

## Environment

- CTX 1.0.0
- projection contract 4
- Linux
- real mixed-provider index: about 520,000 events and 3,900 sources

The current upstream `main` and open issues/PRs were checked immediately before filing. No matching issue or newer hydration fix was found.

title: Continuous source writes can starve multi-call SQL consumers
body:
## Problem

On a continuously active multi-user host, several humans and coding agents append to supported runtime histories around the clock. Every refresh can advance the source-backed Core generation. The relational projection catches up shortly afterward, but `ctx sql` refuses reads whenever its ready generation is older than the newly active Core generation.

A consumer that performs an explicit import and then reads a day through several public `ctx sql` calls can therefore starve even though a complete, internally consistent relational projection is already available. Retrying does not reliably help: by the time a slower query or the next page starts, another active session may have produced another Core generation.

Observed with CTX 1.0 on a host with multiple concurrent Codex sessions:

1. `ctx import --all --no-daemon` succeeds through an already running daemon.
2. `ctx status` briefly reports matching ready generations.
3. A paginated read from `ctx_events` / `ctx_sessions` either fails with a generation mismatch, a generation-change error, or completes after the next refresh has already made the projection stale again.
4. A bounded consumer with three full-snapshot retries can exhaust every attempt without obtaining a complete day.

Representative errors include:

```text
source-backed SQL projection is not ready for Core generation <new>;
active generation is Some(<last-ready>) with status ready; wait for daemon catch-up
```

and:

```text
the lexical generation changed while a verified reader was opening
```

This is not exceptional source churn. It is the normal operating state of an agent-history service on an active shared server.

## Desired behavior

Read-only consumers should be able to finish against the latest fully published, internally consistent snapshot while a newer generation is being built or projected. Fresh events may appear on the next idempotent import; they do not need to invalidate an in-progress historical read.

Possible contracts include:

- let `ctx sql` read the last ready relational generation while Core is ahead, and report both generation IDs/staleness in structured output;
- expose a public snapshot/generation token that subsequent SQL and hydration calls can pin;
- publish Core plus its read projections atomically from the consumer's perspective.

The important property is bounded progress: continuous writers must not make a complete read or import impossible. Slightly stale but explicitly identified results are preferable to starvation, provided each returned snapshot is internally consistent.

## Consumer context

The motivating consumer builds a daily timeline exclusively through CTX's public interfaces. It runs an explicit import, selects event metadata from the stable `ctx_*` SQL views, then hydrates selected event IDs through bounded `ctx show event` calls. It intentionally does not open CTX storage or provider files directly.

title: OpenCode metadata table hides populated message and part history
body:
## Problem

OpenCode NativePath schema selection can prefer a populated `session_message` table even when that table contains only metadata, hiding the actual conversation stored in populated `message` and `part` tables.

This occurred on a real OpenCode database with:

- `session_message`: 29 rows containing metadata such as `agent`, `model`, and `time`, but no conversational role/type;
- `message`: 30,852 rows;
- `part`: 140,039 rows.

CTX selected `session_message` and imported only 29 `notice` events with an unknown role. The user and assistant history in `message + part` was absent from the index.

## Expected behavior

Schema precedence should be based on whether a candidate table contains conversation-bearing rows, not merely whether it exists and is populated.

A metadata-only `session_message` table should not hide a populated `message + part` schema. An explicitly present but empty current table can remain authoritative if that is the intended migration contract.

## Validation of a local fix

A small local change probes `session_message` for canonical conversation markers (`role` or conversational `type`) before giving it precedence. If it contains only metadata, CTX falls through to populated `message + part`.

On the same database, the isolated import then produced:

| event | role | count |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| message | assistant | 68,931 |
| summary | assistant | 28,045 |
| message | user | 5,371 |
| command_output | tool | 1,116 |
| tool_output | tool | 901 |
| tool_call | assistant | 22 |

The resulting mixed-provider projection contained about 628,000 events and remained queryable. A regression test with metadata-only `session_message` plus populated `message + part` selects the latter schema.

## Scope

This is distinct from SQLite snapshot admission and role normalization in #215. The source is admitted successfully; the wrong valid schema family is selected, silently omitting most OpenCode history.

Environment: CTX 1.0.0 on Linux, current `main` checked before filing.

title: Source capability identity changes cannot replace an existing registered source
body:
## Problem

An existing source-backed index cannot refresh a registered source after CTX changes the source's schema/capability identity.

This was observed while validating a corrected OpenCode schema selection. A fresh data root imported the source successfully, but an existing data root containing the same registered path under the previous capability fingerprint could not replace it.

Both an explicit import and daemon-owned refresh failed with:

```text
authoritative inventory still contains the source proposed for deletion
```

The full error retained the prior generation rather than corrupting it, but the source could not advance. Rebuilding the disposable data root made the same binary and provider database work.

## Reproduction shape

1. Build an index with a provider source under capability/schema identity A.
2. Change CTX schema detection so the same provider path is correctly represented by identity B.
3. Run a refresh against the existing data root.
4. The candidate generation treats A as deleted and B as added, but deletion certification rejects A because the authoritative inventory still contains it.

The failure reproduced both through `ctx import --provider opencode --path <database>` and through the periodic daemon refresh, so it was not only command/daemon contention.

## Expected behavior

CTX should atomically replace the old source identity with the new identity when the authoritative provider inventory still describes the same source location/lineage under a changed capability contract.

At minimum, the error should identify this as an unsupported source-identity migration and provide a structured recovery action. Requiring an undocumented full data-root rebuild makes otherwise compatible provider fixes unsafe to ship to existing indexes.

## Why this matters

Provider schema detection and normalization will evolve. If a capability digest is part of source identity, every correction can otherwise strand existing indexes even though the underlying provider database is valid and a fresh import succeeds.

Environment: CTX 1.0.0 on Linux, current `main` checked before filing.

title: Repeated SQLite refresh accumulates deleted lexical documents and generation manifests
body:
## Problem

Repeated refresh of a large, actively changing SQLite source causes substantial transient and retained storage amplification before the existing Tantivy merge policy compacts it. Full generation manifests also continue to accumulate without an apparent retention bound.

This was observed on a real mixed-provider index with about 628,000 live events. The largest changing source was an OpenCode SQLite database of about 900 MiB.

## Observed lifecycle

After several refreshes in less than an hour, `meta.json` reported:

```text
active segments:   9
max documents:     1,528,854
deleted documents:   900,522
live documents:      628,332
deleted ratio:          58.9%
```

The data root had grown from roughly 2.1 GiB shortly after the cold import to roughly 3.1 GiB:

- relational projection: about 1.5 GiB, with zero freelist pages;
- lexical index: about 1.5 GiB;
- generation manifests: 8 files at about 24 MiB each (about 187 MiB total).

CTX does have lexical compaction. The writer configures Tantivy `LogMergePolicy` with a minimum fan-in of 8 segments and invokes managed-file garbage collection when constructing a writer. During a later maintenance cycle, the merge completed:

```text
active segments:   4
deleted documents: 257,312
live documents:    628,470
```

The total data root temporarily fell to about 1.8 GiB. A simultaneous SQLite `VACUUM` reclaimed only about 31 MiB, so the large reduction came from the built-in Tantivy merge rather than SQLite compaction.

The reduction was not stable under continuing refreshes. Shortly afterward the index was again at 5 segments with 385,982 deleted documents, while the data root was about 2.7 GiB. Generation manifests had increased to 11 files (about 257 MiB) even though only the current generation ID was referenced by current lexical metadata and daemon receipts on disk.

The relational WAL was also not the persistent cause: a passive checkpoint reduced it from about 189 MiB to zero.

## Expected behavior

- Repeated replacement of a large SQLite source should have a bounded and documented peak-storage amplification.
- Merge scheduling should consider deletion density or replacement volume where appropriate, not only segment fan-in, so a heavily replaced source does not repeatedly approach a multi-GiB peak before compaction.
- Generation manifests should have an explicit bounded retention policy that preserves generations still required by active or pinned readers and recovery, then removes older manifests.
- `ctx status` or `ctx doctor` should expose pending/reclaimable lexical and manifest storage when meaningful.

## Why this matters

This is normal service operation, not a synthetic benchmark: multiple agent runtimes continuously update history while the daemon refreshes it. The current compaction mechanism eventually works, but storage oscillates by roughly a gigabyte while the live event count changes only slightly, and manifests continue growing across successful publications.

This issue is separate from temporary provider SQLite snapshot cleanup and from relational WAL growth.

Environment: CTX 1.0.0 on Linux, current `main` checked before filing.

title: `--content complete` silently truncates Codex tool-call arguments to preview length
body:
## Problem

`ctx show event --content complete` can silently return a truncated Codex tool-call payload while reporting that the content is complete, source-verified, and not truncated.

This was reproduced with two real `function_call` records whose `arguments` values are valid JSON strings of 6,720 and 6,811 characters. The complete source JSONL records are 9,205 and 9,368 bytes.

For both events:

```bash
ctx show event <event-id> \
  --before 0 \
  --after 0 \
  --content complete \
  --quiet \
  --format json
```

returned event text of 4,016 and 4,015 characters. After removing the `<tool-name>: ` prefix, the retained argument text was exactly 4,000 and 3,999 characters. Both JSON objects ended in the middle of a string and were invalid.

At the same time, the response described the result as:

```json
{
  "complete": true,
  "complete_content_available": true,
  "origin": "provider_source",
  "source_verified": true,
  "stored_truncated": false
}
```

`ctx locate event` pointed to the correct source record and byte range, so the underlying provider data was present and readable.

## Likely cause

The current Codex NativePath tool-call projection builds display text through `codex_tool_arguments_preview` and then applies `PROVIDER_MAX_PREVIEW_CHARS` again in `build_tool_call`.

That is appropriate for indexed/display text, but the source-backed complete-content path appears to reuse the same preview projection. The exact provider record is successfully hydrated and verified, then its tool arguments are reduced to the 4,000-character preview before being returned as complete content.

## Expected behavior

- `--content complete` returns the full verified provider payload when it is within the complete-content byte budget.
- Preview limits used by the lexical/display projection do not apply to complete-content hydration.
- If any limit or retention policy is applied, the response must report truncation and must not claim `complete: true`.
- Structured tool arguments should not be silently converted into invalid partial JSON.

## Impact

Public-interface consumers cannot distinguish the result from genuinely complete content. In the observed case, identifiers near the end of the tool arguments were lost, so an analytics consumer had to fail closed and omit otherwise deterministic observations.

## Scope

This is separate from the aggregate hydration accounting problem in #218. The source record is small, hydration succeeds, and the response is returned; only the supposedly complete content is silently preview-truncated.

Environment: CTX 1.0.0 on Linux. Rechecked against current `main` at `b9da2c47`; no matching issue or pending fix was found.

title: macOS: symlink-ancestor and socket rejection silently degrade to raw IO errors in root_handle
body:
## Problem

On macOS (and other BSD-derived kernels), the root-authorized descriptor walk in `common/io/root_handle/unix.rs` silently weakens two of its rejection checks compared to Linux.

`open_component` opens each path component with `openat(parent, name, O_NOFOLLOW | O_DIRECTORY | ...)` and classifies the failure by `errno`:

- a symlinked ancestor is expected to fail with `ELOOP` and map to `AuthorityOpenError::Rejected`
- a non-regular special file (FIFO, device node, socket) is expected to fail with `ENXIO`/`ENODEV` and also map to `Rejected`

On macOS/BSD, `openat(..., O_NOFOLLOW | O_DIRECTORY)` against a symlinked ancestor returns `ENOTDIR` instead of `ELOOP`, and a bound Unix-domain socket returns `EOPNOTSUPP` instead of `ENXIO`/`ENODEV`. Neither errno is handled in `open_component`'s match, so both cases fall through to the catch-all arm and surface as a raw `std::io::Error` passthrough instead of the intended `Rejected` classification.

This was found while fixing two macOS-only tests in `complete_content/source_access/nanoclaw_snapshot.rs` that had been left on a stale call signature of `open_provider_sqlite_readonly`. The function gained a `data_root` parameter in `4f7ec06c` (fix(storage): secure selected roots and SQLite snapshots), but the macOS-gated tests were not updated, so `cargo test` does not catch this on Linux CI. Passing the missing argument to run the tests on macOS uncovered the errno-handling gap above.

## Impact

The symlink-ancestor and special-file rejection checks are part of the provider-source authority walk used to keep source access confined to trusted roots. On macOS, both checks degrade to a generic IO error rather than the specific `Rejected` outcome, which is what downstream resolver code (`provider_sources::resolvers::path_presence`, in one observed case) expects to classify the path correctly.

## Suggested fix

- add the missing `data_root` argument to the two stale macOS test calls
- add `EOPNOTSUPP` alongside `ENXIO`/`ENODEV` for the special-file case
- for `ENOTDIR`, disambiguate with an `fstatat(AT_SYMLINK_NOFOLLOW)` probe: reclassify to `Rejected` only when the component is confirmed to be a symlink, since `ENOTDIR` is also the legitimate error for a non-symlink component (e.g. a plain file standing in for a directory ancestor), which must keep surfacing as a raw IO error for existing callers

title: Cold import repeats slow OpenCode scans and loses all work on active Hermes change
body:
## Problem

On current `main` (`850fa66a`), a cold all-provider import on an actively used host performed repeated expensive scans, then discarded all work when an active Hermes SQLite source changed.

This regresses the active-SQLite and mixed-provider behavior previously reported in #215 and closed by #235.

## Environment

- isolated `ctx 1.0.0` binary built from `850fa66a`
- isolated empty data root
- daemon started manually for that data root
- ordinary live sources discovered for Codex, Claude, OpenCode, and Hermes
- OpenCode SQLite database: approximately 900 MiB
- Hermes SQLite database: approximately 328 MiB

The installed ctx binary and production data root were not involved.

## Reproduction

Start the daemon for a fresh isolated data root, then request a full import:

```text
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> daemon run
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import --all --no-daemon --format json --progress plain
```

Running the import without an available daemon immediately returns:

```text
the ctx daemon is unavailable for source-backed refresh; no foreground writer was started
```

## Observed behavior

1. Starting the daemon immediately began a periodic Core refresh.
2. The explicit import became a coalesced manual request, but did not reuse or publish the nearly completed work.
3. The first pass spent approximately 12 minutes on the 900 MiB OpenCode database and reached the final Codex source.
4. A second request then started from the first sources and scanned OpenCode again for approximately another 12 minutes.
5. After 26 minutes 26 seconds, the explicit import exited 1:

```text
invalid capture payload: daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed:
run capture-owned all-provider source-backed refresh:
source-backed scan failed for hermes: InvalidSource:
SQLite source file changed while its read snapshot was active
```

6. No Core generation was published. The isolated data root returned to approximately 21 MiB with `history_epoch.status=pending` and zero indexed events/sessions.
7. The daemon immediately started a third periodic full refresh from the beginning. I stopped that isolated daemon to avoid another unproductive pass.

During each OpenCode scan, status exposed only the source-level state:

```json
{
  "completed_sources": 2,
  "current_source": "~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db",
  "phase": "refreshing",
  "total_sources": 6
}
```

The process remained active, used roughly one CPU core and peaked around 900 MiB RSS, so this was slow processing rather than a dead process.

## Why this is operationally severe

- Approximately 900 MiB of local SQLite input took around 12 minutes per scan.
- Coalescing caused that expensive scan to be repeated.
- A late change in one active provider invalidated the work for every provider.
- Automatic retry started the same full cycle again with no published generation available to readers.
- Source-level progress gives no indication whether a long SQLite scan is advancing.

On a host where agents continuously write Codex and Hermes history, waiting for all sources to become quiescent is not practical.

## Expected behavior

- An explicit import arriving during an equivalent daemon refresh should attach to or upgrade that work, not restart a full cold scan.
- Active SQLite sources should use a stable snapshot/retry strategy that does not invalidate already completed providers.
- Failure or revision churn in one provider should not discard a valid generation assembled from the other providers indefinitely.
- Automatic retries should be bounded and should not immediately repeat a 20+ minute cold cycle without publishing usable state.
- Long source scans should expose useful row/byte progress.
- A 900 MiB local OpenCode database should not require approximately 12 minutes to scan on a modern host.

## Additional context

The same real corpus family completed a mixed-provider cold import in about six minutes under the implementation documented in #215. The current behavior is therefore both a correctness regression for active Hermes and a substantial cold-import performance regression.

title: One `image_generation_end` record fails the entire Codex source with `unsupported Core body shape`
body:
`ctx import --provider codex` exits 1 and imports nothing when any rollout file in the tree contains an `event_msg` record whose `payload.type` is `image_generation_end`:

```
Error: publish provider inputs through the Core refresh engine

Caused by:
    daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed: run capture-owned all-provider
    source-backed refresh: source-backed refresh completed with source failures
    but no usable source route: source-backed scan failed for codex:
    invalid_source (invalid capture payload): system invariant failed:
    Codex output has an unsupported Core body shape
```

The source is reported as `"source_failure_class": "unreadable"` with `imported_sessions: 0`.

Version: `ctx 1.0.0` built from `main` @ `b534eb8d`, Linux x64, Cargo source install.

## Why this is worse than it looks

Search keeps working and keeps returning Codex hits, because the separate `codex_history_jsonl` prompt-history source still imports. So `ctx search --provider codex` looks healthy while every Codex *transcript* is missing. On my machine that was 19,404 of 19,406 files (about 18k sessions) silently reduced to one-line prompts, from **two** offending records in **two** files.

## Minimal repro

Two synthetic lines, no real content, 12-byte `result`:

```json
{"timestamp": "2026-05-31T20:33:07.000Z", "type": "session_meta", "payload": {"id": "019e7d2a-0000-0000-0000-000000000000", "timestamp": "2026-05-31T20:33:07.000Z", "cwd": "/tmp/repro", "originator": "codex_cli_rs", "cli_version": "0.0.0", "instructions": null}}
{"timestamp": "2026-05-31T20:33:10.000Z", "type": "event_msg", "payload": {"type": "image_generation_end", "call_id": "ig_repro", "status": "generating", "revised_prompt": "a red square", "result": "iVBORw0KGgo=", "saved_path": "/tmp/repro/img.png"}}
```

Save as `$HOME/.codex/sessions/2026/05/31/rollout-2026-05-31T20-33-07-019e7d2a-0000-0000-0000-000000000000.jsonl` in an otherwise empty HOME and run:

```bash
ctx --data-root /tmp/ctx-repro import --provider codex
```

Fails as above. Delete that one line and the same import publishes.

## Isolation

Hardlinked the Codex tree into an isolated `HOME` (so auto-discovery could not overlap the real one) and bisected against a scratch `--data-root`:

| Scope | Result |
|---|---|
| 2026/01 - 2026/04, 2026/07, 2026/08 | ok |
| 2026/05 (3,912 files), 2026/06 (4,033 files) | FAIL |
| 2026/05, by day | 30 days ok, `05/31` (288 files) FAIL |
| `05/31`, by file (binary search) | one file |

Then removing payload types from that file one at a time:

| Variant | Result |
|---|---|
| minus `image_generation_call` + `image_generation_end` | ok |
| minus `tool_search_call` + `tool_search_output` | FAIL |
| minus `custom_tool_call` + `custom_tool_call_output` | FAIL |
| only `image_generation_call` (plus `session_meta`) | ok |
| only `image_generation_end` (plus `session_meta`) | **FAIL** |

So the `response_item` / `image_generation_call` sibling is handled; only the `event_msg` / `image_generation_end` end-event is rejected. Its shape:

```json
{
  "timestamp": "...",
  "type": "event_msg",
  "payload": {
    "type": "image_generation_end",
    "call_id": "ig_...",
    "status": "generating",
    "revised_prompt": "<string>",
    "result": "<base64 png>",
    "saved_path": "<path>"
  }
}
```

## Asks

1. **Accept or skip the record, don't fail the source.** The CLI reference states "Imports always commit valid records and report rejected records ... A source with valid content and rejections completes with an explicit `completed_with_rejections` outcome." An unsupported body shape in one record currently takes the whole source down instead, which contradicts that contract. This is the part that matters: whatever new payload type Codex adds next will do the same thing again.
2. **Handle `image_generation_end`** (even as an ignored record type).
3. **Name the offending record in the error.** It currently names neither the file nor the line nor the payload type, so isolating it took a month-day-file bisect. Path + line + `payload.type` would have made it a one-minute fix.

## Side note

The auto route and the explicit route fail differently. `ctx import --provider codex --path <dir>` on a subdirectory of an already-registered source returns:

```
Error: explicit codex/codex_session_jsonl authority is already enabled at <dir>;
```

title: Cursor worker.sock socket blocks all provider history refresh
body:
## Problem

`ctx setup --wait` starts the daemon but publishes no history or lexical generation, so `ctx search` returns nothing, even though Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Zed, Copilot CLI, and Auggie sources are all available.

The live Cursor tree contains `worker.sock`, a Unix-domain socket. The Cursor authority walk correctly refuses to open the socket, but the traversal treats every `open_child` failure as a fatal symlink rejection. That invalidates inventory completion, classifies the whole Cursor source as `unknown`, and the daemon then raises a terminal coverage failure for the entire multi-provider refresh. A single optional provider that happens to sit beside a socket takes down search for every provider.

## Reproduction

```
ctx sources --provider cursor --format=json
cat ~/.ctx/daemon/jobs/core-refresh.json
find ~/.cursor/projects ! -type d ! -type f -print
```

`ctx sources --provider cursor` reports Cursor as `unknown`, and the core refresh job records a terminal coverage error naming Cursor.

## Impact

Any user whose Cursor installation keeps a bound `worker.sock` under its projects tree loses all `ctx search` results, not only Cursor results, until the socket is removed. Removing or renaming the live socket is not an acceptable workaround.

## Suggested fix

Skip non-regular entries (Unix sockets, FIFOs, device nodes) during Cursor transcript traversal as a non-fatal issue instead of invalidating discovery completion. Keep the safe rejection behavior, and report the provider as available when its usable transcript files can be read. Genuine symlink and IO errors should remain fatal.

This is distinct from #230 (fixed), which corrected the low-level errno classification for the socket rejection on macOS but left the higher-level refresh still blocked by any single `unknown` optional-provider source.

title: fix(cursor): skip non-regular source entries without failing discovery
body:
## Summary

A live Cursor `worker.sock` Unix-domain socket sitting beside valid transcripts made `ctx setup --wait` publish no history or lexical index, so `ctx search` was unavailable for every provider even though Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Zed, Copilot CLI, and Auggie sources were present.

The Cursor authority walk opens each child with `open_child`. A non-regular entry (socket, FIFO, device node) is correctly refused with a `Rejected` error, but `visit_directories` treated every `open_child` error as a fatal symlink rejection. That invalidated inventory completion, classified the whole Cursor source as `unknown`, and made the daemon report a terminal coverage failure for the entire multi-provider refresh.

The refusal already carries a stable reason string. This change adds a shared `is_non_regular_source_rejection` classifier and skips those entries as a non-fatal `SpecialFile` issue, while keeping genuine symlink and IO errors fatal. Valid transcripts beside a special file now complete discovery, the provider reports available, and the full refresh publishes the lexical generation for all providers.

The safe rejection behavior is unchanged: the socket is still never opened or read, it is only no longer treated as coverage failure.

This is the higher-level counterpart to #230 (merged), which corrected the low-level socket errno classification on macOS but left the refresh still blocked by any single `unknown` optional-provider source.

## Validation

`cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --lib cursor_special_file_beside_transcript_is_skipped_without_failing_discovery` passes. The new regression test discovers a valid transcript alongside a non-regular special file and asserts completion is preserved, the transcript is still found, and the skipped entry is recorded as a non-fatal issue. It uses a FIFO to exercise the identical `NON_REGULAR_PROVIDER_SOURCE_REASON` rejection path without the platform `sun_path` length limit; the socket-specific errno mapping is covered by the existing `root_handle` unix tests.

`cargo clippy -p ctx-history-capture --all-targets` is clean for the changed surface.

Fixes #248.

title: factory-ai-droid no longer discovers ~/.factory/sessions automatically
body:
## Problem

`ctx import --provider factory-ai-droid` without `--path` fails even when `~/.factory/sessions` exists and contains importable session JSONL files:

```
factory-ai-droid has no official automatic history location established: no official automatic Factory history location is established; use an exact user-authorized --path; use `ctx import --provider factory-ai-droid --path <path>`
```

`ctx sources --provider factory-ai-droid` likewise reports the provider with a "no established automatic history location" issue.

This is a regression. #107 (merged) established automatic discovery of `~/.factory/sessions` through `FACTORY_DROID_DEFAULTS`, and the provider worked like the other CLI harnesses with a fixed default root. The v0.26 platform foundation rework (e3a40966) emptied `FACTORY_DROID_DEFAULTS` in `crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider_sources/specs.rs` and moved the provider into the manual-unsupported resolver lane, where `resolve_factory` emits `InsufficientOfficialEvidence` and zero sources.

## Impact

Every Factory AI Droid user must pass `--path ~/.factory/sessions` explicitly. `ctx setup` and bare `ctx import` never pick up Droid history, unlike peer harnesses with a fixed default root (Junie, Kimi Code CLI, and others).

## Suggested fix

Restore the default location spec (`~/.factory/sessions`, format `factory_ai_droid_sessions_jsonl`) and move the provider back to the simple fixed-root resolver lane, platform-gated like its peers. The default-location import probe (`has_jsonl_file_under_matching`) and the explicit-path format mapping already support the provider, so only resolver wiring is needed.

title: factory-ai-droid import aborts with duplicate event identity when a tool call is cancelled and retried
body:
## Problem

Factory AI Droid reuses a message `id` when a tool execution is cancelled and retried: the retry record keeps the same `id` and references it through `parentId`. The direct JSONL projector derives each event identity from the native record id alone, so both records mint the same stable event id inside one session and the whole import fails closed with `duplicate event identity <uuid> in one candidate generation`.

## Reproduction

```bash
work=$(mktemp -d)
mkdir -p "$work/sessions/project"
cat > "$work/sessions/project/demo.jsonl" <<'EOF'
{"type":"session_start","id":"demo","timestamp":"2026-07-14T09:30:00Z","cwd":"/workspace","model":"factory/droid"}
{"type":"message","id":"dup","timestamp":"2026-07-14T09:30:13Z","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"Execute_1","is_error":false,"content":"first"}]}}
{"type":"message","id":"dup","timestamp":"2026-07-14T09:30:23Z","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"tool_result","tool_use_id":"Execute_2","is_error":true,"content":"Error: Tool execution cancelled by user"}],"visibility":"user_only"},"parentId":"dup"}
EOF
ctx import --provider factory-ai-droid --path "$work/sessions"
```

Got: the import aborts with `duplicate event identity ... in one candidate generation`.

Want: both records retained as distinct events.

## Impact

Any Droid session containing a cancelled and retried tool call makes the whole factory-ai-droid import fail, so no Droid history is imported at all. Real session logs hit this routinely, because cancelled executions are normal Droid usage.

## Suggested fix

Mint an occurrence suffix per (native record id, subrecord) pair, the same disambiguation the Cursor provider already uses. Occurrence zero must keep the exact current identity so previously imported events never move, and certified-suffix append scans must probe the base event identity lookup so appended retries continue the occurrence sequence instead of colliding with the imported prefix.

title: fix(factory-ai-droid): retain retried records that reuse one native id
body:
Fixes #261.

## Summary

- Factory AI Droid reuses a message `id` when a tool execution is cancelled and retried (the retry keeps the `id` and references it through `parentId`). The direct JSONL projector derived each event identity from the native record id alone, so the retry collided with the first occurrence and the whole import failed closed with `DuplicateEventIdentity`.

- Certified-suffix append scans probe the base event identity lookup (exponential then binary search) so appended retries continue the occurrence sequence instead of colliding with the imported prefix.

## Validation

- New unit test `factory_droid_reused_record_ids_mint_distinct_stable_event_identities`: two records sharing one native id mint distinct event ids, the first occurrence keeps the pre-fix identity, and replays are deterministic.
- New CLI end-to-end test `factory_droid_import_retains_retried_records_that_reuse_one_native_id`: importing a session with a reused id retains both records, and a certified-suffix append reusing the same id refreshes incrementally.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture` and `cargo test -p ctx --test native_providers` failure sets are byte-identical to a clean `upstream/main` checkout (pre-existing environment-dependent sqlite and warp failures only).
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-capture -p ctx --all-targets` introduces no new warnings.
- Manual acceptance on macOS with a real `~/.factory/sessions` tree containing multiple sessions with reused record ids: `ctx import --provider factory-ai-droid` publishes successfully, cancelled-retry records are searchable, and a repeat import refreshes incrementally without identity errors.
