title: daemon cannot start after upgrade when the active publication predates source-refresh metadata
body:
## Problem

`ctx daemon enable` and `ctx daemon run` fail at startup with:

```text
recover interrupted Core refresh before daemon readiness: recover exact terminal refresh receipt from Core publication metadata: active Core publication has no source-refresh metadata
```

In `recover_interrupted_publication` (`crates/ctx-cli/src/semantic/source_backed_refresh_coordinator/coordinator_state/request_lifecycle.rs`), a job whose `request_state` is `published` but whose `previous_generation` differs from the active generation falls through to the pointer-advanced branch, which decodes `SourceBackedPublicationMetadata` with `?`. Publications written by binaries from before the refresh routing control-plane commits (3ae9c766, d17953a5) carry no such metadata, so the decode error aborts daemon startup. There is no legacy fallback and no CLI recovery flag (`ctx daemon run --force` does not bypass it).

## Impact

After upgrading across the control-plane commits, any daemon restart (including autostart) fails permanently while search keeps serving the old generation. Background maintenance and incremental refreshes stop until the user rebuilds the data root by hand.

## Reproduction

1. Install a build from before the control-plane commits and run `ctx setup --wait` to publish a generation.
2. Upgrade to a build containing 3ae9c766 / d17953a5.
3. Restart the daemon (`ctx daemon disable` then `ctx daemon enable`), or let it autostart.

Got: permanent startup failure with the metadata error; `ctx doctor` still reports "No problems found".

Want: a publication without source-refresh metadata is treated as terminal-complete (or triggers one cold refresh) so the daemon starts.

## Suggested fix

In the pointer-advanced branch, distinguish absent metadata from malformed metadata: when the verified publication simply has no source-refresh metadata (legacy binary), bind the terminal success from the job receipt or enqueue one cold refresh instead of propagating the decode error. Keep failing closed for present-but-malformed or mismatched metadata.

## Workaround

Move `~/.ctx/daemon/jobs/core-refresh.json` aside so recovery returns `Ok(false)` and the daemon starts. If the following refresh reports carried-route conflicts against the retained generation (`carried source route ... cannot mutate retained source ...`), rebuild the derived data root: `mv ~/.ctx ~/.ctx.backup && ctx setup --wait`.

title: fix(daemon): recover legacy publications without source-refresh metadata
body:
## Summary

- `recover_interrupted_publication` aborted daemon startup when the active Core generation was published by a binary from before the refresh routing control plane (3ae9c766, d17953a5): those publications carry no source-refresh metadata, and the pointer-advanced branch decoded it with `?`.
- When the verified publication has no source-refresh metadata at all, recovery now accepts the verified generation as terminal-complete and installs any queued successors instead of propagating the decode error.
- Publications with present-but-malformed or mismatched metadata keep failing closed; the next scheduled refresh publishes with metadata, so exact receipt recovery resumes from there.

## Validation

- New regression test `legacy_publication_without_source_refresh_metadata_does_not_block_restart`: a bare committed generation (no metadata) plus a `published` job with an advanced pointer recovers with `Ok(false)`; verified it fails with the #275 startup abort when the fix is reverted.
- `cargo test -p ctx --bins source_backed_refresh_coordinator`: 88 passed, 0 failed (macOS note: the suite needs a symlink-free `TMPDIR`, e.g. `TMPDIR=/private/tmp`, because the private-directory walk opens each component with `O_NOFOLLOW`).
- `cargo clippy -p ctx --bins`: no new warnings; `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: clean.
- Real-data acceptance on macOS: a data root published by a pre-control-plane build aborted `ctx daemon enable` exactly as in #275; with this fix the same root starts the daemon and serves its endpoint (the root's remaining refresh error is unrelated same-machine generation skew).

Fixes #275.

title: tests fail on macOS with ENOTDIR under the default symlinked TMPDIR
body:
## Problem

On macOS, running the test suite with the default per-user `TMPDIR` fails every test that calls `establish_private_data_root` with `Os { code: 20, kind: NotADirectory }` (28 failures in `cargo test -p ctx --bins source_backed_refresh_coordinator` alone, all at test setup).

macOS sets `TMPDIR` under `/var/folders/...`, and `/var` is a symlink to `/private/var`. `walk_private_directory` (`crates/ctx-history-core/src/platform_security/unix_private_directory.rs`) opens each path component with `openat(..., O_NOFOLLOW | O_DIRECTORY)`, so the symlinked `var` component is rejected and setup fails before the test body runs. `tempfile::tempdir()` follows `TMPDIR`, so every affected test inherits the symlinked root. `absolute_data_root_path` normalizes lexically but never canonicalizes, so the symlink survives into the walk.

## Impact

Any contributor running the suite on macOS sees dozens of failures unrelated to their change. It reads like a regression and costs review time; hit while validating #276.

## Reproduction

1. On macOS with the default environment: `cargo test -p ctx --bins source_backed_refresh_coordinator`.
2. Observe ENOTDIR panics at `establish_private_data_root` call sites.
3. `TMPDIR=/private/tmp cargo test -p ctx --bins source_backed_refresh_coordinator` passes 88/88.

## Suggested fix

Any of: canonicalize the data-root path in `absolute_data_root_path` before the walk (resolving `/var` to `/private/var`); have the affected tests canonicalize their tempdir; or at minimum fail with a clear "path contains a symlinked component" error instead of a bare ENOTDIR so the cause is obvious. The first option also helps real users who point `CTX_DATA_ROOT` at a symlinked path.

## Workaround

Run tests with a symlink-free temp dir: `TMPDIR=/private/tmp cargo test ...`.

title: Manual import repeats a running cold daemon refresh instead of joining its result
body:
## Problem

A manual all-provider import arriving while the daemon is already running a cold all-provider refresh is serialized as another complete pass instead of joining and reusing the in-flight result.

A fresh isolated reproduction on `504a9e4e` showed:

1. daemon startup admitted a periodic cold refresh;
2. `ctx import --all --no-daemon` arrived while that refresh was running;
3. the request reported `coalesced_requests: 0`;
4. ctx performed a second full provider pass and a second 1,020 MiB OpenCode online backup.

`--no-daemon` prevents autostart here; the explicit import still uses the already-running daemon endpoint.

Field evidence: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/236#issuecomment-5171589000

## Current gap

The coordinator already has one active publisher, but its current attempt model conflates three things: the caller's logical freshness request, the physical executor pass, and terminal publication.

At current main, `ctx import --all` uses the automatic refresh request shape. A manual request admitted during an already-running cold refresh is conservatively forced into a successor chiefly by `fresh_after_admitted_snapshot`. Catalog `Some`/`None` mismatch is the analogous failure mode for explicit-path imports. In both cases, admission is decided from request metadata rather than semantic route coverage.

Relevant code:

https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/6312f7f85aa9acf3916d0234eee25ec268d37ed3/crates/ctx-cli/src/semantic/source_backed_refresh_coordinator/coordinator_state/request_lifecycle.rs#L338-L385

This is not an index-writer mutual-exclusion failure: only one publisher runs at a time. It is a single-flight coverage failure that repeats already completed work.

## Expected behavior

All refresh triggers should use one coordinator and one active publisher. A newer manual freshness request should attach to the running attempt. After publication, ctx should determine whether that result covers the requested catalog and admission-time freshness boundary:

- covered: reuse the same published generation and publication receipt, while recording the caller's own durable terminal request resolution;
- not covered: run only the uncovered or post-snapshot route delta;
- never repeat every provider merely because trigger metadata differs.

## Acceptance criteria

- A running periodic cold `All` refresh plus a concurrent explicit `import --all` launches one full executor and one large SQLite backup.
- The explicit caller receives its own durable terminal resolution, bound to the generation that satisfies its request.
- Provider writes after the running attempt snapshot create only a bounded delta successor.
- Duplicate waiters share terminal success and failure outcomes across daemon restart.
- No path weakens the single authoritative publisher or atomic generation publication contracts.

title: Active provider writes can keep the daemon in an immediate refresh loop
body:
## Problem

On a continuously active host, provider filesystem changes observed during a long refresh can immediately schedule more periodic work after publication. In the reported isolated run, ctx completed two expensive passes, published a partial generation, and then immediately started a third refresh with:

```text
trigger: periodic
trigger_provenance: daemon_scheduler
```

Field evidence: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/236#issuecomment-5171589000

The prior reproduction observed the same behavior after a successful publication: a new full refresh began about 20 seconds later while provider histories were being written normally.

## Why this matters

Some follow-up work is legitimate when bytes were appended after a route snapshot. However, a long refresh should not turn normal continuous writes into an effectively permanent all-provider import loop. This repeatedly consumes CPU, I/O, scratch space, and large SQLite backup bandwidth.

## Expected behavior

Background maintenance should be generation- and route-aware:

- publication should satisfy watcher observations already covered by each certified route snapshot;
- only changes newer than that route snapshot should remain dirty;
- follow-up work should target exact changed routes rather than defaulting to another full pass;
- sustained writes should be debounced and rate-limited without disabling explicit freshness requests;
- retries should remain bounded and distinguish source-local failure from systemic failure.

This issue does not presuppose removing provider watchers. The product may retain background freshness, but it must have a bounded convergence and resource policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- Keep representative provider writers active throughout a cold all-provider refresh.
- After publication, ctx does not immediately start another full all-provider pass.
- A post-snapshot append schedules only its exact route after the documented debounce or cadence.
- Events already covered by the published route certificate do not recreate dirty work.
- Sustained writes cannot produce an unbounded tight refresh loop.
- An explicit wait/freshness request can still bypass background cadence and obtain a truthful request-bound result.

title: Active Codex append can fail session-tree import during lineage scanning
body:
## Problem

A normal append to an active Codex session can fail the Codex source-backed route with:

```text
provider source changed during bounded capture
```

The session-tree route otherwise has an append-tolerant contract: it certifies a frozen prefix and defers newer suffix bytes to the next refresh. The lineage helper currently reopens an ancestor session and requires exact file-observation equality before and after scanning it. An append during that scan is therefore promoted to a source failure.

Field evidence: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/236#issuecomment-5171589000

Conflicting code paths:

- strict lineage scan: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/6312f7f85aa9acf3916d0234eee25ec268d37ed3/crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/codex/nativepath/source_backed/lineage.rs#L116-L164
- append-tolerant route contract: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/6312f7f85aa9acf3916d0234eee25ec268d37ed3/crates/ctx-history-capture/src/provider/source_backed/registration/families/jsonl/codex.rs#L376-L390

## Expected behavior

Each Codex source should have one admitted file identity and frozen EOF for a refresh. Ctx should parse and certify exactly that prefix, allow append-only growth beyond it, and derive lineage from the same captured authority rather than requiring a second quiescent read of the live file.

Rewrites, truncation, object replacement, and mutations within the certified prefix must still fail closed. Ordinary suffix growth must succeed and be caught up incrementally later.

## Suggested direction

Capture the tool-call and parent-session facts needed for lineage during the primary bounded parse, or spool those facts into bounded ctx-owned temporary storage. Resolve lineage from that generation-local captured data. A second read, if retained, must use the same frozen-prefix authority and append-tolerant prefix proof.

## Acceptance criteria

- Deterministically append to an active parent or ancestor session during lineage processing; the refresh publishes the certified prefix successfully.
- The next refresh imports the deferred suffix exactly once.
- Lineage results match a quiescent import of the same frozen bytes.
- In-prefix rewrite, truncation, source replacement, and invalid append proof remain source failures.
- Ambiguous or malformed lineage metadata is handled at the narrowest safe record/relationship boundary rather than failing an otherwise valid Codex source.

title: OpenCode online backup can fail as malformed after copying the full database
body:
## Problem

An active OpenCode source using the new logical online-backup path completed another approximately 1,020 MiB private copy and then failed as a source with:

```text
sqlite error: database disk image is malformed
```

The run preserved and published the healthy providers, so source-failure isolation worked. The OpenCode source remained unavailable after paying the full backup cost.

Field evidence: https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/236#issuecomment-5171589000

## What is known and unknown

The symptom is reproducible evidence of an unsuccessful OpenCode snapshot/import path, but the current diagnostic does not establish whether:

- the admitted live source view was already corrupt;
- the private online backup was inconsistent;
- a specific ordinary or virtual table was corrupt;
- the failure occurred during snapshot validation, schema observation, ordering, or row projection.

The implementation should not assume the backup API caused corruption until source and backup evidence distinguishes those cases.

## Expected behavior

A healthy WAL-active OpenCode database should yield a transactionally consistent private snapshot that remains readable for discovery, projection, and terminal certification while writers continue. If the provider source itself is corrupt, ctx should report that distinction with the failing phase and SQLite extended error while preserving other providers.

## Suggested investigation and direction

- Record the exact operation/phase and SQLite primary plus extended error code.
- In an isolated reproducer, run bounded integrity evidence against the admitted source view and private backup to identify where corruption first appears.
- Validate the private backup before beginning the expensive logical projection.
- Retain a safe opt-in diagnostic artifact or receipt sufficient to inspect a failed isolated backup without exposing provider content by default.
- If retry is appropriate, bound it and avoid immediately repeating a full 1 GiB copy indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria

- Repeated backups of a healthy WAL-active OpenCode fixture remain valid while a writer commits concurrently.
- A source-corrupt database and a backup-corrupt database produce distinct phase-specific diagnostics.
- Projection uses one certified private snapshot from discovery through commit.
- Provider DB, WAL, SHM, and directory entries are not modified by ctx.
- Failure remains source-local, preserves the prior/readable generation, and cannot trigger an unbounded backup loop.

title: Fix coordinated refresh and active-source snapshot integrity
body:
## Summary

This PR fixes four related active-source coordination and snapshot-integrity failures while retaining one authoritative publisher and atomic generation publication.

- **#281:** separates durable logical refresh demands from immutable physical attempts. A manual import can join a running cold refresh, evaluate that verified generation against its own admission fence, and schedule only an exact uncovered-route successor.
- **#282:** records monotonic route watermarks at watcher ingress and binds cleanup to exact verified-generation coverage. Automatic refreshes use bounded debounce, cooldown, and route-local retry instead of immediately rescanning active writers.
- **#283:** derives Codex lineage from the same admitted frozen-prefix scan that emits records. Ordinary suffix growth publishes the certified prefix and is imported once on the next refresh; lineage state stays bounded, task-local, disposable, and non-authoritative.
- **#284:** never opens the live provider SQLite family with SQLite. DB/WAL bytes are copied and certified through retained file authority into ctx-owned storage, the private logical backup is independently certified, and failures retain phase/artifact/code/cleanup provenance.

## Important boundaries

- There is still only one physical publisher. Explicit freshness can bypass background cadence, but it cannot create a second writer.
- Indeterminate, changed, or unavailable coverage fails closed to exact successor work; it is never treated as fresh.
- Codex lineage uses bounded in-memory facts and creates no durable sidecar or second source of truth.
- SQLite acceptance preserves the complete provider-directory name-to-bytes map, including DB, WAL, SHM, missing sidecars, and unrelated entries.
- SQLite resource exhaustion remains typed `ResourceUnavailable`; non-exhaustion `EIO` remains `Internal`.
- The removed dead `snapshot/online_backup.rs` path is not restored.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p ctx --bin ctx`: **1,462 passed, 3 ignored**
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture`: **1,070 passed, 1 ignored** across unit and integration targets
- Codex-focused capture: **172 passed, 1 ignored**

title: Large Codex corpus exhausts fixed lineage working-set budget and aborts cold import
body:
## Problem

The Codex lineage implementation added by #291 has a fixed task-local budget that is too small for a real, long-lived Codex corpus. A cold all-provider refresh spends roughly nine minutes scanning the first Codex route and then fails systemically with:

```text
ResourceUnavailable: Codex lineage working set exceeded its bounded task-local capacity
```

The current limits are:

```rust
const MAX_LINEAGE_FACTS_PER_TASK: usize = 262_144;
const MAX_LINEAGE_FACT_BYTES_PER_TASK: usize = 64 * 1024 * 1024;
```

## Environment

- release build from current `main` at `5df35cf6243b8daac6dada47d2f09d6ca60c9ac1`
- fresh isolated data root and manually started isolated daemon
- 37 discovered routes / 6 provider sources
- several Codex sessions were actively appending during the run
- installed production ctx and its data root were not involved

## Reproduction

```text
ctx setup --data-root <isolated-root> --catalog-only --no-daemon
ctx daemon run --data-root <isolated-root> --force
ctx import --data-root <isolated-root> --all --no-daemon
```

The daemon-owned periodic cold refresh reached `<home>/.codex/sessions`, used approximately one CPU core, and failed after about nine minutes. The isolated root had grown to approximately 634 MiB, but no generation was published.

The durable refresh receipt reported:

```json
{
  "status": "failed",
  "progress": {
    "completed_sources": 0,
    "phase": "failed",
    "total_sources": 6
  },
  "retryable": true,
  "retry_after_ms": 10000,
  "last_error": "run capture-owned source-backed refresh: source-backed scan failed for codex: ResourceUnavailable: Codex lineage working set exceeded its bounded task-local capacity"
}
```

The retry is not useful for this failure: the corpus deterministically exceeds the same fixed budget.

## Expected behavior

- A valid corpus should not become unimportable merely because its accumulated lineage facts exceed a compile-time task budget.
- Memory must remain bounded, but excess lineage data should spill/partition/compact or degrade only the affected relationships to `Unproven` rather than failing the entire Codex route.
- A deterministic capacity failure should not be classified as immediately retryable with the same inputs and limits.
- Progress should expose useful Codex record/byte counters during the long scan; this run showed zero bytes and zero records until failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- A fixture exceeding 262,144 lineage facts publishes its otherwise valid Codex records with bounded memory.
- Lineage remains correct for facts retained across any partition/spill boundary.
- Exhaustion at the narrowest relationship boundary cannot discard the entire cold generation.
- An unchanged deterministic capacity failure cannot enter an automatic retry loop.

title: Timed-out import remains admitted and launches an orphaned full refresh successor
body:
## Problem

During an active cold refresh, `ctx import --all --no-daemon` can time out waiting for the daemon response and exit 1, while the daemon has nevertheless durably admitted that logical demand. The abandoned demand later runs as another expensive full successor.

This leaves the caller with a failure while background work continues, and it prevents the coalescing guarantee from #281/#291 from working through the public CLI path.

## Environment

- release build from current `main` at `5df35cf6243b8daac6dada47d2f09d6ca60c9ac1`
- fresh isolated data root
- isolated daemon already running a periodic cold `All` refresh
- installed production ctx and its data root were not involved

## Reproduction

While the daemon's durable receipt showed a running periodic `All` refresh, run:

```text
ctx import --data-root <isolated-root> --all --no-daemon --format json --progress plain
```

Two attempts returned after 3.3 and 4.0 seconds with exit 1:

```text
request daemon-owned source-backed refresh
read daemon query response
wait for daemon query response readiness
daemon query response read timed out
```

The daemon endpoint identity already reported `available: true` and the daemon process remained healthy and busy.

After the running periodic attempt terminated, its receipt contained both timed-out CLI requests as queued manual successors:

```json
{
  "coalesced_requests": 0,
  "queued_successors": [
    {
      "status": "running",
      "trigger": "search",
      "trigger_provenance": "manual",
      "progress": { "phase": "queued" }
    },
    {
      "status": "running",
      "trigger": "search",
      "trigger_provenance": "manual",
      "progress": { "phase": "queued" }
    }
  ]
}
```

The first orphaned successor immediately began another full discovery pass even though its caller had already received a terminal error. I stopped only the isolated daemon to avoid repeating the expensive scan.

## Expected behavior

- Endpoint readiness should mean that a refresh request can receive an acknowledgement within the public response deadline, even while discovery/scan work is active.
- A request that was durably admitted should return its request ID/accepted state rather than a transport failure.
- If the client truly abandons or fails before admission is acknowledged, ctx must have an explicit cancellation/ownership policy; it should not silently perform unobserved expensive successor work.
- An equivalent `All` demand should join the running attempt as promised by #281, not appear as a full successor solely because the response path timed out.

## Acceptance criteria

- Submit a manual `All` import while a periodic cold `All` refresh is in discovery and scan phases; the CLI receives a timely durable acknowledgement and waits on its own request-bound result.
- The receipt records one physical full executor and a coalesced logical demand.
- For a deliberately disconnected client, the documented policy deterministically cancels or retains the demand without reporting a contradictory terminal transport failure.
- The daemon query endpoint stays responsive during long provider discovery and capture work.

title: Active Codex append still fails final verification and triggers an automatic refresh loop
body:
## Problem

On a continuously active multi-agent host, current `main` can still fail a
Codex follow-up refresh when an admitted transcript is appended during final
verification. The daemon then immediately starts another automatic refresh,
so a host with several continuously writing Codex sessions may never become
quiescent enough to finish the cycle.

This was reproduced on `4eb528b70b237a4b9b06da448f5de0a597f1c8a8`,
which includes the append-tolerant lineage fix from #291.

## Environment

- release build of `ctx 1.0.0` from current upstream `main` (`4eb528b7`)
- fresh isolated data root and isolated daemon
- production binary and production data root were not involved
- six discovered source families
- several Codex sessions remained active throughout the test
- Codex input: 4,012 JSONL files, 3.66 GiB

## Reproduction

Start a daemon against a fresh isolated root, then request an explicit import
while its initial periodic refresh is running:

```text
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> daemon run --force
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import --all --no-daemon --format json --progress plain
```

Keep one or more Codex sessions writing normally during the refresh.

## Observed behavior

1. The initial periodic refresh completed after 44m33s and successfully
   published generation
   `6b463ec271e08866d13f063814b40fec9c52668477fd826dd49ddcfe250e9eab`.
2. The explicit request was durably admitted while that refresh was running:
   `coalesced_logical_demands: 1`, `fresh_after_admitted_snapshot: true`.
3. The follow-up was incremental rather than a complete reindex. It processed
   approximately 68,820 Codex records and entered `verifying`.
4. It then failed. The explicit import exited 1 after 1h03m38s total:

```text
invalid capture payload: daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed:
run capture-owned source-backed refresh: source-backed scan failed for codex:
InvalidSource: invalid provider transcript path
"2026/07/23/rollout-2026-07-23T16-40-36-019f8ec7-08ef-7e62-80a5-ed03ab92ac7b.jsonl":
provider source changed while its authority handle was retained;
retained generation
6b463ec271e08866d13f063814b40fec9c52668477fd826dd49ddcfe250e9eab
```

5. The already published generation remained readable and a search against it
   succeeded.
6. Immediately after the failed follow-up, the daemon automatically started a
   third refresh. It reached OpenCode before I stopped the isolated daemon to
   avoid an unbounded retry loop.

## Why this remains a blocker

The host is intentionally never quiescent: multiple interactive Codex sessions
append to their transcripts throughout the day. Requiring the complete set of
Codex files to remain unchanged across a long scan and final verification makes
successful catch-up probabilistic. Automatic retries amplify the problem into
continuous CPU and disk consumption.

The first published generation is an improvement over the all-or-nothing
failure from #236, but the daemon still cannot converge reliably to a fresh
generation on this workload.

## Expected behavior

- Append-only growth after an admitted frozen EOF should not invalidate the
  certified prefix during final verification.
- The next refresh should import the deferred suffix exactly once.
- Rewrites, truncation, replacement, and mutations inside the certified prefix
  should continue to fail closed.
- A retryable source revision should not cause immediate unbounded full-daemon
  refresh cycles.
- The explicit attached request should receive a structured retryable outcome
  rather than waiting over an hour and exiting with a generic failure.

Related: #236, #283, #291.

title: Cold 4 GiB refresh takes 44 minutes and attached progress remains opaque
body:
## Problem

A cold local refresh of approximately 4 GiB of agent history took 44m33s on
current `main`. The attached incremental follow-up then ran for another 19
minutes before failing, for a total explicit-import wall time of 1h03m38s.

This makes a full refresh operationally expensive even before accounting for
the active-source correctness failure reported separately.

Tested commit: `4eb528b70b237a4b9b06da448f5de0a597f1c8a8` (`ctx 1.0.0`).

## Corpus and environment

- fresh isolated data root and isolated daemon
- production CTX was not modified
- six discovered source families
- Codex: 4,012 JSONL files, 3.66 GiB
- Claude projects: approximately 59 MiB
- OpenCode storage plus a live SQLite source whose snapshot reported
  1,138,959,432 bytes
- ordinary SATA SSD, 16 GiB RAM
- several agents continued writing history during the run

The beginning of the test overlapped other container work and showed 62-72%
I/O wait. After those builds subsided, I/O wait fell to 14-21%, but the refresh
still required tens of minutes. The ctx daemon generally consumed around
66-84% of one CPU and reached approximately 2 GiB RSS.

## Timings

- release build (context only): 9m54s
- initial cold refresh: 44m33s
- incremental successor: approximately 19m05s before failure
- explicit `ctx import` wall time: 1h03m38s
- isolated data root peaked around 3.7 GiB and settled around 3 GiB

The cold refresh did successfully publish a searchable generation. The
performance measurement is therefore not merely time spent before an early
failure.

## Progress-reporting friction

For most of the initial refresh, the attached CLI repeatedly printed:

```text
Refreshing local history (0 / 0 sources; phase admission pending).
```

The physical daemon job was making progress, but the attached request did not
surface it. Codex frequently reported `completed_bytes: 0` even after hundreds
of thousands of records. During final verification, the CLI printed only:

```text
Verifying refreshed history (0 / 6 sources).
```

That phase remained unchanged for roughly nine minutes, with no route, byte,
record, or verification-step detail. The user cannot distinguish slow progress
from a deadlock without inspecting private daemon receipts and OS process
metrics.

## Expected behavior

- A roughly 4 GiB local corpus should complete in minutes rather than around
  45 minutes on an otherwise ordinary development host.
- The daemon should expose phase timings that separate discovery, provider
  parsing, snapshot copy, projection/index construction, verification, commit,
  and publication.
- An attached/coalesced request should display the physical job's progress
  instead of `0 / 0` for most of its lifetime.
- Record and byte counters should remain meaningful for Codex and SQLite
  providers.
- Long verification should identify the route and verification step currently
  consuming time.

Related performance and scheduling history: #236.

title: Failed refresh can be replaced by a false-ready empty generation
body:
## Problem

After a source-backed refresh fails final verification, the daemon can immediately publish an empty generation and report the index as ready.

This is worse than preserving the failed/unavailable state: clients see a healthy search service but receive no results.

## Reproduction sequence

1. Start from an isolated, empty CTX data root.
2. Register and cold-import a real 3.7 GiB Codex sessions tree.
3. Let final verification fail with:

   ```text
   session relationship graph is invalid: session chain disagrees on root identity
   ```

4. Leave the daemon running and inspect the next periodic refresh plus `ctx status` / `ctx doctor`.

Observed on current `main` at `9fcd9b4fb9cd7f0eacb05cb3bd7e2a4f15afa83f`.

## Observed behavior

The failed request returned exit 1 after 1,928 seconds. The daemon then completed a periodic request in about 0.6 seconds and published a new generation as healthy:

```text
request_state: published
refresh.status: ready
lexical.status: ready
generation_matches: true
completed_sources: 38
```

However, the active generation was empty:

```text
indexed_documents: 0
certified_source_bytes: 0
sources: []
segments: []
```

The periodic receipt simultaneously reported all 38 catalog routes as unsupported, `source_count: 0`, and still used outcome `completed`. A search returned zero results, and the complete data root had shrunk to roughly 124 KiB.

## Expected behavior

- A failed refresh must retain the last non-empty certified generation when one exists.
- With no previously valid generation, status must remain unavailable/failed rather than claiming search is ready.
- A periodic scan in which all known routes are unsupported must not replace a non-empty candidate or publish an empty healthy generation without an explicit destructive intent.
- Readiness should require a generation consistent with the catalog's expected active sources, not merely a physically valid empty Tantivy index.
- Status/doctor should make `zero documents / zero certified sources` conspicuous when catalog routes exist.

## Why this matters

Operational consumers treat `ctx status` readiness as authority. A false-ready empty generation silently converts an explicit import failure into apparent success and can cause downstream tools to conclude that historical records do not exist.

title: Codex cold refresh fails final relationship verification after full capture
body:
## Problem

A cold refresh of a real Codex session corpus completes capture and then fails final verification with:

```text
session relationship graph is invalid: session chain disagrees on root identity
```

This makes the current upstream build unusable for this corpus even when importing only the native Codex sessions tree. The failure is unrelated to `history.jsonl` and still reproduces with PR #322 applied.

## Reproduction

Tested on an otherwise idle Linux host with low, but non-zero, concurrent Codex activity.

- source: one native Codex sessions tree (`~/.codex/sessions`)
- source size at start: 3.7 GiB
- isolated binary, data root, daemon, and config
- no OpenCode, Claude, or prompt-history source in the catalog
- semantic indexing disabled

```bash
ctx daemon run --force
ctx import \
  --provider codex \
  --path ~/.codex/sessions \
  --no-daemon \
  --format json \
  --progress none
```

## Results

### Current `main`

- commit: `9fcd9b4fb9cd7f0eacb05cb3bd7e2a4f15afa83f`
- elapsed: 1,928 seconds (32:08)
- capture reached about 786k records and completed the single source
- final verification failed
- command exit: 1

### Current `main` plus PR #322

- commit: `14701e38917e4792a4a0ee07679d170df25cc559`
- elapsed: 2,033 seconds (33:53)
- capture reached about 810k records and completed the single source
- final verification failed with the same error
- command exit: 1

The record-count difference is expected because the source is append-active. Both runs used one logical request without a restart from zero.

The structured outcome reports `source_refresh_failed`, class `internal`, `retryable=true`, and marks every affected route retryable, but retrying performs another expensive full pass and cannot repair a deterministic relationship-graph invariant failure.

## Expected behavior

- A malformed or ambiguous relationship observation should not invalidate the entire otherwise readable corpus.
- The diagnostic should identify the conflicting session/records and the two root identities, without exposing message content.
- If the ambiguity can be handled safely, relationship classification should fail open or quarantine only the affected relationship/session.
- If the refresh must fail, it should fail before spending more than 30 minutes building an index that cannot be published.

## Additional performance observation

On the idle host, both variants used roughly one CPU core for most of capture and spent several long CPU-only merge phases with no record-counter movement. Search readiness was reported during the run, but the exposed generation contained zero indexed documents until final publication. Full cold refresh therefore remains roughly 32-34 minutes for a 3.7 GiB Codex corpus.

title: copilot_cli source unreadable when session files/ checkouts contain symlinks
body:
## Problem

One symlink anywhere under a Copilot CLI `session-state/<id>/files/` checkout makes the entire `copilot_cli` source unreadable, so `ctx import --provider copilot-cli` publishes no Copilot history at all.

Copilot CLI stores a checked-out working copy of the conversation's repository under `~/.copilot/session-state/<uuid>/files/`. Real repositories legitimately contain symlinks (commonly `CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md`, and linked binaries such as `bun`). These entries sit beside the transcripts but can never hold one: the Copilot CLI selector only admits `<session>/events.jsonl`.

The authority walk correctly refuses to follow the link (`symlinked provider source path components are rejected`), but the direct-JSONL discovery traversal, the JSONL membership fence walk, and the format-neutral source inventory each treat that refusal as fatal for the whole source instead of skipping the entry, in the spirit of #248 (a Cursor `worker.sock` socket invalidated all provider history until #249).

## Reproduction

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/copilot-demo/session-state/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/files/checkout
printf '{"id":"s1","timestamp":"2026-08-01T10:00:00Z","type":"session.start","data":{"sessionId":"demo","startTime":"2026-08-01T10:00:00Z","selectedModel":"gpt-5-mini","context":{"cwd":"/workspace"}}}\n{"id":"u1","timestamp":"2026-08-01T10:00:01Z","type":"user.message","data":{"content":"hello from copilot"}}\n' > /tmp/copilot-demo/session-state/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/events.jsonl
touch /tmp/copilot-demo/session-state/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/files/checkout/AGENTS.md
ln -s AGENTS.md /tmp/copilot-demo/session-state/11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555/files/checkout/CLAUDE.md
ctx import --provider copilot-cli --path /tmp/copilot-demo/session-state
```

Observed: `Error: inspect explicit source ...` caused by `invalid provider transcript path ".../files/checkout/CLAUDE.md": symlinked provider source path components are rejected`. No Copilot session is imported.

Expected: the symlinked working-copy entry is skipped (never followed), and the valid `events.jsonl` transcript imports and becomes searchable.

## Impact

Any Copilot CLI session whose working copy contains a symlink silently drops out of `ctx search`. Because source classification marks the whole source unreadable, all Copilot sessions share the failure once one `files/` checkout contains a link.

## Suggested fix

Skip link-like and non-regular entries during provider source walks when the entry cannot hold a selected transcript, and keep selected transcript paths fail-closed (a symlinked `events.jsonl` must still abort). Concretely: add an `is_symlink_source_rejection` classifier next to `is_non_regular_source_rejection` (#249), apply the skip in the direct-JSONL discovery traversal for non-selected entries, in the JSONL membership fence walk (route-set comparison still catches a transcript that turns into a link after admission), and in the format-neutral source inventory whose contract already states links are never followed.

title: fix(copilot-cli): skip link-like session files entries without failing the source
body:
Fixes 362.

## Summary

- A Copilot CLI `session-state/<id>/files/` checkout containing a symlink (for example `CLAUDE.md -> AGENTS.md`) made the whole `copilot_cli` source unreadable, so no Copilot history imported or was searchable.
- Adds `is_symlink_source_rejection` (plus the shared `SYMLINK_PROVIDER_SOURCE_REASON` and Windows `REPARSE_PROVIDER_SOURCE_REASON` constants) next to the `is_non_regular_source_rejection` helper from #249.
- The direct-JSONL discovery traversal now skips link-like and non-regular rejections for entries the provider selector can never select; a selected transcript path (a symlinked `events.jsonl`) stays fail-closed.
- The JSONL membership fence walk skips the same entries, keeping opening and closing observations consistent; a transcript route that turns into a link after admission still drops out of the observed route set and fails the membership comparison as a source change.
- The format-neutral source inventory (`inventory_provider_jsonl_paths` / `inventory_provider_regular_paths`) skips link-like and non-regular entries instead of erroring, matching its documented "links are never followed" contract; its unit tests now assert the outside target of a symlink never leaks into the inventory.
- The shared walks also harden the other direct-JSONL family providers (Windsurf, Qwen Code, Qoder, Tabnine, Antigravity, Factory AI Droid) against the same layout.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` clean.
- `cargo test -p ctx --test native_providers copilot_cli_import` green: `copilot_cli_import_skips_symlinked_session_files_checkout` imports and searches a session-state tree whose `files/` checkout contains a symlink, including a second import that exercises the membership fence; `copilot_cli_import_still_rejects_symlinked_transcript` proves a symlinked `events.jsonl` still aborts.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture --lib common::io` and the `source_backed::family::jsonl` / `native_jsonl` unit tests green.
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-capture -p ctx --all-targets -- -D warnings` reports no findings in the files this PR touches; the workspace currently carries pre-existing clippy 1.96 findings in unrelated crates (for example `ctx-protocol`, `ctx-history-index`, `ctx-cli/src/upgrade`) that reproduce on unmodified `main` with this toolchain.
- Real-data check: with this patch applied on top of 49932564, `ctx import --all` against live history including a `~/.copilot/session-state` with symlinked `files/` checkouts completes cleanly and `ctx search --provider copilot-cli` returns Copilot sessions. Note: current `main` cannot complete any refresh on this machine's real history due to an unrelated regression ("session relationship graph is invalid: session chain disagrees on root identity", reproduced with a pristine d462376b binary on a fresh data root), so the real-data check was run on the last-known-good base; the patch itself is base-independent.

- Preserve positive copied-origin proof while treating absence or ambiguous duplicate identity as `unknown`; repository outcomes and file attribution now require a positive `UniqueToSession` origin.
- Keep Hermes discovery as a stable, typed detection-only route. Current `state.db` schemas lack a provider-owned, transactionally maintained per-session content revision, so Hermes reports `unsupported` / `importable: false`; imports fail with `unsupported_schema` without opening or modifying the database, have no override, and retain same-epoch last-good records as stale.

title: fix(codex): admit valid nested child sessions
body:
## Summary

- remove the invalid Codex equality/quarantine between provider `session_id` root advisory and the direct parent
- admit every nested child from its own certified bytes with no ancestor lookup, traversal, liveness dependency, scheduling, or reprocessing
- remove the now-dead terminal rejected-source plumbing while preserving ordinary malformed JSONL rejection
- replace obsolete conflict tests with depth-1, depth-2, deep-chain, missing/changed/deleted parent, incremental independence, cardinality, search, show, and zero-source-failure coverage

## Root cause and staging evidence

This is a residual correctness regression in the lineage work associated with #306. Codex emits valid chains such as:

- A: self A, root advisory A
- B: self B, direct parent A, root advisory A
- C: self C, direct parent B, root advisory A

Current main set the child-local normalized root to the direct parent, then `quarantine_root_conflicts_v0` compared the top-level advisory against it and rejected C because A differs from B.

A realistic fresh-install staging refresh reported 2,538 Codex source failures. All 39 retained diagnostics inspected mapped to real depth-2-or-deeper sources, and all 39 had the expected top-level advisory differing from the direct parent. Their unique child content was omitted from search.

## Resulting semantics

Self ID, direct parent ID, and provider top-level advisory remain separate. The advisory is non-authoritative for admission. Each child is indexed from only its own bytes, so parent absence, arrival, append, rewrite, truncation, deletion, or restoration does not invalidate or reprocess an unchanged child.

`CODEX_PARSER_REVISION` remains v27 because normalized output for already-admitted sources is unchanged. The fix admits sources that were rejected before projection and therefore had no successful v27 certificate to migrate.

## Validation

All commands were governed by `ctx-build-governor` through the repository wrapper where applicable.

- `scripts/bazelw test //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests --test_arg=codex_child_independence --test_output=errors` — 11 passed
- `scripts/bazelw test //crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-refresh:unit_tests //crates/ctx-cli:native_provider_rejections_tests --test_output=errors` — capture 1,216 passed / 1 ignored; refresh 156 passed; CLI 16 passed
- `scripts/bazel-affected.sh origin/main` — all 146 selected targets passed
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` — passed under the governor light lane
- `git diff --cached --check` — passed under the governor light lane

An independent fresh read-only review approved the exact commit with no must-fix findings, including the shared rejected-leaf cleanup, source-local identity/security invariants, v27 decision, O(n) cardinality, and test adequacy.

title: fix(codex): restore exact repository result origin
body:
## Summary

- Restore invocation-local positive origin for exact Codex commit and pull-request results.
- Require bounded exact one-call/one-result uniqueness for direct and continued results before publishing repository outcomes.
- Keep copied, unknown, mismatched, ambiguous, and overflowed evidence fail-closed, with no parent-triggered descendant work.

## Root cause

Commit `0128fdeb2` removed the positive `UniqueToSession` result origin while the post-parse repository gate continued to admit only that state, so every exact repository outcome was cleared. The existing 256-entry terminal authority could also be exhausted by unrelated display results before a later repository-capable invocation appeared.

This change carries invocation-local origin through calls, results, continuations, pending context, and checkpoints. It uses a 16,384-entry ephemeral exact occurrence cache with fail-closed overflow, keeps the persisted repository-candidate domain capped at 256, and bounds append-first-admission recounts to the already certified prefix.

## Validation

- `//crates/ctx-history-capture:unit_tests`: 1,235 passed, 1 ignored diagnostic benchmark.
- `//crates/ctx-history-capture:codex_direct_result_tests`: 11 passed.
- Active-source contract inventory passed.
- Rust format, source diff, docs, provider-matrix, and crate-size unit gates passed.
- Exact crate ratchets: `ctx=140169`, `ctx-history-capture=206843`; `hard_limit` remains 20,000 with only the two existing offender entries.
- Stamped merged-head canary (`4e6235de9c172c848e86dc71c30f3770d892b851`, tree `12579a942a5f35df4bf7908c072d2de0ebf2c14a`): exactly 7 sources / 233,092,337 bytes, 109 exact commit events, 7 exact PR events, and PR #203 returned 3 matches / 3 evidence records including both `contains_commit` and `merged_as`.

## Bounded cost

Cold parsing retains one source read; uniqueness adds no second full parse, hydration, or parent work. The 16,384-entry cache has an estimated maximum footprint of about 0.91 MiB and abstains on overflow. A short same-fixture comparison measured 20.85s / 17,408 KiB for the corrected path versus 16.04s / 17,152 KiB for the broken 0-commit/0-PR control; that delta includes restored repository hydration and certification, so it is behavior-and-cost evidence rather than isolated uniqueness overhead.

The 19GB corpus and broad release matrix were intentionally not run for this focused correction.

title: README lists Hermes as supported although its history is detection-only
body:
## Problem

The README currently lists **Hermes Agent** as `Supported`.

The same section defines support as being able to discover or read persisted history and import it into the local search index. In the current implementation, however, the default Hermes source is explicitly detection-only:

- `source_kind: ProviderSourceKind::DetectionOnly`
- `import_support: ProviderImportSupport::Unsupported`

The reported reason is that current Hermes `state.db` schemas do not provide a provider-owned, transactionally maintained per-session content revision.

As a result, ctx can discover `~/.hermes/state.db`, but it cannot import Hermes sessions. Calling this simply "Supported" makes users expect those sessions to be searchable.

## Expected documentation

Please distinguish between:

- providers whose histories are currently importable;
- providers that ctx can only detect and report as unsupported.

For example, the Hermes row could say **Detection only / current state.db schema unsupported**, or Hermes could be moved to a separate section for recognized but non-importable providers.

This issue is only about aligning the documentation with current behavior, not about requesting a particular implementation for restoring Hermes import support.

title: Incompatible active generation fails daemon startup as an interrupted refresh instead of triggering its documented rebuild
body:
## Summary

This is the same failure shape as #275, in the same function, one branch earlier.

`generation_incompatibility_requires_rebuild` documents its errors as "structurally incompatible with this build and therefore must be replaced from source authority". `open_published_generation` honours that by mapping all of them to `Ok(None)`. `recover_interrupted_publication` then reads that `None` as an invariant violation, because the journal's last job is terminal, and fails daemon startup with:

```text
recover interrupted Core refresh before daemon readiness: interrupted source refresh
advanced Core without an active generation
```

The rebuild never happens, `daemon.recoverable` is `false`, and the message names a subsystem that is not involved.

#275 fixed the neighbouring case, a verified publication carrying no source-refresh metadata, by adding `recover_legacy_published`. This case never reaches it: there is no verified publication to inspect, so the `ok_or_else` on the active generation fires first.

## Environment

ctx 1.0.0 built from `main` @ `c69cf1e2`, Linux x86-64, source install. Previous build `b534eb8d`, which predates `f3c918251` by about seven hours. Data root 4.7 GiB, 22,669 sources / 24,403 sessions / 922,709 events, healthy immediately before the upgrade. The stale data root still reproduces on demand, so this is a property of the store rather than transient daemon state.

## Reproduce

Any data root whose active generation this build considers incompatible, plus a refresh journal whose last job is `request_state: "published"`, so any store that has completed one refresh. The path I took:

1. Index on a build at or before `b534eb8d`, so `search/lexical/active-generation.json` is written at `version: 1`.
2. Rebuild the CLI at `c69cf1e2` and restart the daemon.

```text
$ ctx status
✗ History status: failed
A verified search index is not available.
Search    unavailable (generation verification failed)
Refresh   stale (published generation mismatch)

$ ctx daemon enable
✗ ctx daemon did not become ready: recover interrupted Core refresh before daemon
  readiness: interrupted source refresh advanced Core without an active generation.
  Run `ctx daemon status --format json`, then `ctx daemon run` for details

$ ctx daemon run
✗ recover interrupted Core refresh before daemon readiness
interrupted source refresh advanced Core without an active generation
(exit 1, no additional detail)

$ ctx doctor
! ctx found 4 issues
  [1] History is unavailable          The component is not ready.
  [2] Search index is unavailable     The component is not ready.
  [3] History source catalog is still preparing
  [4] History refresh is stale
  (no repair offered)
```

`ctx setup --no-daemon` returns in 0.2s with "Setup completed, but no verified search index is available."

## Where the signal is dropped

`f3c918251` ("fix(index): verify Core before publication") bumped `ACTIVE_GENERATION_POINTER_VERSION` 1 to 2 and added `physical_integrity_digest` to `GenerationSlot`. That part works as intended: `load_active_generation_pointer` rejects the older pointer at the explicit version gate with `UnsupportedActiveGenerationPointer(1)`, and `crates/ctx-history-index/src/tests/integrity_certification.rs:103` asserts exactly that.

`generation_incompatibility_requires_rebuild` (`crates/ctx-history-index/src/lib.rs:252`) lists that error alongside `UnsupportedCommitPayload`, `UnsupportedManifest`, `GenerationContractMismatch`, `CoreRecordPolicyRevisionMismatch`, `GenerationPolicyMismatch`, `SchemaMismatch`, `IndexSettingsMismatch` and `ChecksumMismatch`, under a doc comment saying such a generation must be replaced from source authority.

`open_published_generation` (`crates/ctx-history-refresh/src/publication.rs:185`) collapses all of them:

```rust
Err(error) if generation_incompatibility_requires_rebuild(&error) => Ok(None),
```

The arm directly above it does not collapse. `MissingActiveGenerationPointer` consults the journal first and, when a published generation is named, bails with a message that says what is actually wrong ("verified Core generation X is missing from Y"). The incompatibility arm has no equivalent, so "must be replaced from source" and "there is nothing here" become the same value.

`recover_interrupted_publication` (`crates/ctx-history-refresh/src/engine/request_lifecycle/recovery.rs:85`) receives that `None`, sees a terminal `published` job, and raises the error above.

`mark_active_generation_for_rebuild` and `active-generation-rebuild-required.json` (`crates/ctx-history-index/src/writer_support.rs:25-49`) already exist for this decision, and `classify_active_integrity_failure` already routes a different failure class into them via `ActiveGenerationNeedsRebuild`.

## Scope

- Not specific to the upgrade mechanism. `ctx upgrade` manages the binary, config and semantic worker caches; it does not migrate, reset or rebuild the index, so an automatic upgrade for a managed install reaches the same state as a source rebuild. `ctx upgrade status` reports `Automatic upgrades  apply` by default.
- Not specific to upgrades at all. Every error in that list lands here, so a `ChecksumMismatch` or a `SchemaMismatch` on a store that was never upgraded fails the same way.
- Symmetric across versions: a v2 pointer read by a pre-`f3c918251` build fails the same gate from the other side.

## Workaround, and what it shows

#275's workaround applies unchanged, and I verified it against the stale data root:

```bash
mv ~/.ctx/daemon/jobs/core-refresh.json ~/.ctx/daemon/jobs/core-refresh.json.aside
```

Recovery then returns `Ok(false)`, the daemon starts, and it immediately begins building a replacement generation from source, which is what the incompatibility was supposed to trigger in the first place. So the machinery downstream of this gate is fine; only the gate stands in the way.

That also sets the real blast radius: the store is not damaged and the history is not lost. Nothing in the CLI says so. `ctx doctor` reports four not-ready components and offers no repair, and the daemon error names an interrupted refresh, so the reachable conclusion from the tool alone is that the data root has to be discarded.

## Ask

Give the incompatibility arm the journal-aware treatment the `MissingActiveGenerationPointer` arm already has, so recovery can tell "this generation must be replaced" apart from "there is nothing here" and drive the existing rebuild marker instead of failing startup. That is the same shape as the `recover_legacy_published` fallback added for #275.

Failing that, the message should name the real condition and the command that clears it, rather than reporting an interrupted refresh with `recoverable: false` and pointing at `ctx daemon run`, which re-prints the same line.

title: Incremental refresh selects all routes for a few live Codex appends
body:
## Use case

Several Codex sessions run on this host throughout the day, so transcripts are almost always changing. CTX search is used only once or twice per day.

## Verified behavior

I ran two consecutive refreshes against an already healthy published generation. The second started immediately after the first, so very little new material had accumulated.

That second run found only 3 changed sessions and 13 new messages, but it selected all 38 source routes and reported processing about 4.6 GiB. The refresh took about 80 seconds, used about two minutes of CPU time, and peaked at about 3 GiB of memory.

It also published more than once during the same finite-daemon run: the final receipt's previous generation was newer than the generation active when the process started. Continuous Codex writes appear to trigger another catch-up before the daemon can become idle.

## Question

Is this the expected incremental behavior for a multi-session live host?

The merged live-append qualification in #397/#398 completed in seconds without reprocessing existing descendants, but this real multi-provider run still selects every route and reports processing the full corpus for a handful of new events.

A cheap incremental path seems important here: a persistent daemon otherwise repeats expensive work while CTX is rarely queried, while an on-demand refresh makes the user wait before searching.

title: Finite daemon continuously re-arms refresh on an active multi-session host
body:
## Use case

Several Codex sessions run on this host throughout the day, so transcripts are almost always changing. CTX is queried only once or twice per day, and a finite daemon is used to refresh history without keeping maintenance running permanently.

## Current-main validation

I tested current `main` at `a09a546cf55d1e120f16098d8e2590ff52b2352b` against an isolated copy of an already healthy generation. Production CTX was not involved. The daemon was started with:

```text
ctx daemon run --force --idle-exit-seconds 60
```

The unchanged-JSONL optimization from #510 worked: each incremental pass identified only 4-5 changed sources, and all routes completed without source failures.

The remaining problem is lifecycle convergence on a live host:

- an explicit `ctx import --all --no-daemon` attached to an in-progress refresh and correctly waited for an exact successor;
- both publications succeeded, and the explicit import exited 0 after about three minutes;
- the successor contained only 6 changed sessions, 8 messages, and 34 tool calls, and reported about 1.5 minutes elapsed;
- immediately after that successor completed, the finite daemon started a third periodic refresh instead of entering its 60-second idle window;
- the third pass was still committing after more than 2.5 minutes and was stopped to avoid keeping the host busy indefinitely;
- across the observation, the daemon ran for 7m40s, consumed about 5m40s of CPU, and peaked below 500 MiB RSS.

The last successfully published generation remained healthy: lexical search worked and `ctx show event` returned complete Codex content.

## Question

Is a finite daemon expected to keep re-arming periodic refreshes whenever live provider files change?

On a host with continuously active sessions, source activity can prevent the daemon from ever reaching its idle-exit condition. For an on-demand refresh workflow, it would be useful for one explicit demand to converge to a usable generation and then allow the daemon to exit, leaving later appends for the next explicit invocation.

title: perf(index): bind publication safety to construction
body:
## Summary

- replace exhaustive Core/body/projection/lineage replay during writer publication with a compact event-identity term/posting audit
- capture session identity and relationship authority from the exact prepared Core record, validate changed sessions at construction time, and bound route rollback state
- keep metadata-only republish physical and structural
- seal raw writer, document-conversion, and active-generation Searcher/Index escapes from all shippable feature surfaces
- retain explicit deep scrub and adversarial corruption coverage outside the publication hot path

## Complexity contract

- no-op publication performs zero logical passes
- cold publication scans live event identity terms/postings once
- incremental publication inspects changed identity terms against bounded segments
- changed-session capacity checks are constant time on first insertion
- route rollback visits only sessions inserted by that route

## Performance

Controlled cold publication, 4096-byte bodies:

| Documents | Commit | Compact identity |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 16,384 | 3.141s | 84.5ms |
| 32,768 | 6.208s | 165.1ms |

Identity terms/postings doubled exactly, logical/projection/lineage replay stayed zero, and peak RSS was 173.61 MiB. The final safety changes were 5-6% faster than the prior candidate in the least-contended run and remained below the old 176.03 MiB RSS baseline.

The physical Rust crate-size gate is currently blocked by baseline drift on `origin/main`: `ctx-history-capture` is 133,922 CLOC while its ledger ratchet is 133,921. The repository policy rejects raising that ratchet from a feature branch, so this PR does not weaken the gate; it needs a base/main maintenance fix.

An earlier complete `scripts/check.sh --mode ci --force-rerun` run had 179/191 checks passing. The remaining failures were current-main/stale-inventory failures and disk-pressure failures while broad tests fetched crates and created SQLite scratch data; the focused build and qualification checks above are green.

## Dogfood

I completed a real headless DeepSeek Harness run using `@deepseek-ai/dsh@0.1.0-rc.6` with a custom `codex-load-balancer` provider, streamed OpenAI Responses API, and model `gpt-5.6-sol` served by the local Codex load balancer. The harness returned the exact marker `DSH_LB_LIVE_OK` and persisted a valid `session.jsonl.zstd` containing the provider/model metadata, Responses replay state, response id, and usage accounting (`193` input / `11` output tokens).

The load balancer deployment rejects the Responses `max_output_tokens` field, while the upstream pi-ai adapter always emits it. For this dogfood run only, a task-local localhost relay removed that one incompatible field and forwarded the request/stream unchanged otherwise; the actual LLM request and response went through the Codex load balancer. A direct load-balancer canary also returned `LIVE_OK` before the harness run.

The upstream headless startup segfaulted when its model-unrelated native process/SQLite/code/tool plugins were enabled in this environment, so those unrelated plugins were disabled for the isolated harness run. This did not affect the provider request, streamed response, or persisted transcript format exercised by ctx.

## Review

An independent review was run after implementation. It found and the branch fixes later-header attribution, rejected-row diagnostic line indexing, packed coordinate validation, and timing-dependent cancellation synchronization.

title: Persistent-only daemon continuously refreshes active multi-session hosts
body:
## Use case

Several Codex sessions run on this host throughout the day, so provider transcripts are almost always changing. CTX is queried only once or twice per day. In this workload, continuous maintenance costs more than the occasional search it serves.

## Context

#523 reported this lifecycle problem for a finite daemon. #529 fixed it by letting one explicit demand converge and then preventing later provider appends from re-arming automatic refresh before idle exit.

Current `main` later removed the finite idle lifetime in `4ff926a85`, leaving only the persistent daemon profile. The unchanged-JSONL optimization from #510 is still working; this report is about lifecycle behavior, not all-route rescanning.

## Current-main observation

I tested the production build from current `main` at `d40721a320977877513cdac9579256c61158df46` against an already healthy generation while several Codex sessions were active.

Within about three minutes after `ctx daemon enable`:

- at least three distinct refresh requests ran sequentially as live transcripts changed;
- the daemon averaged roughly three quarters of one CPU core;
- process I/O accounting increased by roughly 3 GiB read and 2 GiB written;
- each pass handled only a small number of changed sessions, confirming that the incremental source-selection fix is active;
- `ctx search --refresh off` did not complete within 15 seconds during refresh;
- after `ctx daemon disable`, the same search completed in under one second.

The daemon was still running another refresh when I stopped the observation. The published generation remained healthy.

## Product question

What lifecycle should a continuously active development host use when CTX is queried infrequently?

Would you consider restoring a bounded explicit-convergence mode, or another supported policy where one requested catch-up publishes a usable generation and later appends wait for the next demand? A persistent daemon that can quiesce or apply a configurable cooldown could also address the same workload.

The important property is that continuously changing transcripts should not imply continuous indexing when no consumer is querying CTX. Query reads should also remain responsive while background maintenance is active, consistent with the documented foreground-query preemption behavior.

title: fix(index): pin generations across concurrent publication

## Summary

title: Manual-mode first import fails under umask 0002 because writer lock is created as 0664
body:
## Problem

On a host with the common user `umask 0002`, a first import in manual indexing mode fails before publishing its initial Core generation.

CTX creates `search/lexical/.ctx-generation-writer.lock` with mode `0664`, then rejects that same file because it is not owner-private.

## Reproduction

Tested on Debian at upstream commit `dce1381d380492d93a0c35dc83f99d007a3b5678` using a clean data root and a controlled Codex transcript:

```bash
umask 0002

ctx --data-root /tmp/ctx-umask-repro daemon disable
ctx --data-root /tmp/ctx-umask-repro import --all --format json --progress none
```

The import exits with status 1:

```text
the durable generation-retention lease is malformed, non-canonical, or not owner-private; resolve the unfinished lease owner before publishing Core
```

The file created by CTX is group-writable:

```text
664 alice:developers /tmp/ctx-umask-repro/search/lexical/.ctx-generation-writer.lock
```

The failure reproduced on a second, entirely fresh data root. Running the same lifecycle under `umask 0077` creates mode `0600` control files and succeeds.

## Expected behavior

CTX should create security-sensitive control and lock files with explicit owner-private permissions, independent of the caller's ambient umask. A normal `umask 0002` should not make CTX produce a file that violates its own validation rules.

## Impact

This blocks first import and therefore blocks adoption of the new manual/on-demand indexing lifecycle on otherwise normally configured multi-user development hosts.

title: Custom-source filtered search (--provider-key / --source-format) is ~100x slower than unfiltered — 50s vs 0.5s on the same query
body:
### Summary

Filtering a search to a custom history source (`--provider-key`, `--source-id`, or `--history-source`) takes ~50s wall / ~20s user CPU where the identical unfiltered query returns in ~0.5s — including the same custom-source events, correctly ranked. The index clearly contains the events; only the filtered path is slow. Timings are stable across repeated runs and query terms, so this is not cold-cache, term-dependent, or a one-time segment merge.

### Environment

- ctx 0.25.0 (`ctx-macos-arm64` release binary), macOS 15 arm64 (M4), 16 GB RAM
- Index: 16,114 native sessions / 334,369 events (codex, claude, opencode, pi, gemini) — `work.sqlite` ≈ 6.4 GB
- Custom source: Amp (Sourcegraph) thread history via a history-source plugin (`ctx-history-jsonl-v1`), `provider_key=amp`, 248 sessions / 35,661 events
- Maintenance daemon disabled (`daemon_running: false`); idle `ctx mcp serve` processes present (read-only); no imports running; all searches `--refresh off`

### Reproduction

Query text is irrelevant — any term reproduces it; only the custom-source filter matters:

```console
$ time ctx search "<term>" --limit 5 --refresh off
# matches include the custom-source events, ranked correctly
real  0m0.492s   user 0m0.063s   sys 0m0.051s

$ time ctx search "<term>" --provider-key amp --limit 5 --refresh off
# correct results
real  0m54.117s  user 0m20.225s  sys 0m8.403s

$ time ctx search "<other terms>" --provider-key amp --limit 3 --refresh off
real  0m50.598s  user 0m20.080s  sys 0m8.017s
```

### Expected

Filtered search ≈ unfiltered cost: the docs say custom-source filters imply `--provider custom`, and provider filtering for native providers (`--provider codex` etc.) shows no comparable penalty on this index.

### Observed / hypothesis

~20s user + ~8s sys, CPU-bound and roughly proportional to the 6.4 GB store, suggests the custom-source filter path scans/decodes stored records rather than applying the filter as an index term the way unfiltered ranking does. Unfiltered search proves the custom events are in the lexical index with correct ranking, so only the filter routing seems affected. (Guess from the outside — happy to be corrected.)

### Synthetic repro (no real data needed)

```bash
python3 - <<'EOF' > /tmp/synthetic.jsonl
import json, random
print(json.dumps({"record_type":"manifest","schema_version":"ctx-history-jsonl-v1"}))
print(json.dumps({"record_type":"source","source_id":"s1","provider_key":"synthetic","source_format":"synthetic-v1"}))
words = ["alpha","parser","migration","rollback","cursor","index"]
for s in range(250):
    sid = f"sess-{s}"
    print(json.dumps({"record_type":"session","source_id":"s1","session_id":sid,"started_at":"2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"}))
    for e in range(140):
        txt = " ".join(random.choices(words, k=12))
        print(json.dumps({"record_type":"event","source_id":"s1","session_id":sid,"event_index":e,"event_type":"message","role":"user","occurred_at":"2026-01-01T00:00:01Z","payload":{"text":txt},"preview":txt}))
EOF
ctx import --format ctx-history-jsonl-v1 --path /tmp/synthetic.jsonl
time ctx search "alpha" --refresh off                            # fast
time ctx search "alpha" --provider-key synthetic --refresh off   # slow
```

Can attach `--json` outputs or run instrumented builds on the affected corpus if useful. Found while integrating Amp (Sourcegraph) thread history via the history-source plugin system — which otherwise worked exactly as documented, cursor handoff included.

title: `ctx import --provider/--path` still refreshes every discovered provider
body:
## Problem

`ctx import --provider <provider>` is documented as importing one provider, and `--path` appears to narrow that further to one exact native source. On current `main`, both forms still refresh every automatically discovered provider.

This makes it impossible to use the public import CLI to maintain a deliberately scoped index, for example Codex and Claude Code only, on a host that also happens to contain OpenCode or Hermes data.

## Environment

- Debian Linux
- release build from `3eacc4a35e57449d815da07a5a48c56274047654`
- fresh isolated data roots
- live Codex, Claude, OpenCode, and Hermes sources present
- installed production binary and data root were not involved

## Reproduction

On a fresh data root:

```console
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> daemon disable
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import \
  --provider codex \
  --path ~/.codex/sessions \
  --format json \
  --progress plain
```

The same behavior also occurs without `--path`:

```console
ctx --data-root <another-isolated-root> import \
  --provider codex \
  --format json \
  --progress plain
```

## Observed behavior

Although Codex was the only selected provider, progress and daemon status reported a six-source, multi-provider refresh:

```json
{
  "providers": ["codex", "claude", "opencode", "gemini", "hermes"],
  "total_sources": 6,
  "current_source": "/home/alice/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db"
}
```

The refresh copied and scanned the OpenCode SQLite database. Because that unrelated live database changed during the second run, the requested Codex import published as partial:

```text
opencode: SQLite source file changed while its read snapshot was active
```

`ctx doctor` then reported `History refresh is partial`, even though the explicitly selected Codex source was usable.

The behavior also matches the current application path: `run_automatic` validates the selected provider, but then calls the all-provider preflight and refreshes without a provider-scoped admission.

## Why this matters

- `--all` already exists for callers that want every discovered provider.
- A host may contain histories that are intentionally outside a particular CTX index.
- An unrelated active or malformed source can degrade an explicitly requested provider import.
- Scanning large unrelated SQLite histories adds substantial time, CPU, I/O, and storage cost.

In our real isolated run, the first all-provider refresh took 10m59s. A subsequent refresh took 1m48s but became partial solely because the unrelated OpenCode database changed.

## Expected behavior

- `ctx import --provider codex` refreshes only automatically discovered Codex sources.
- Adding `--path ~/.codex/sessions` refreshes only that exact Codex source.
- `ctx import --all` remains the explicit way to refresh all discovered providers.
- Failures in unselected providers do not affect the selected import outcome.

If refreshing the full automatic catalog is intentional under the new generation model, the CLI should reject these selectors or document that they validate/register a source without limiting refresh scope. The current help text, `Import one provider`, implies actual scoping.

title: fix(opencode): ignore empty derived strings
body:
## Problem

A valid OpenCode SQLite source can contain empty derived metadata, for example a failed
tool call whose `state.input.command` is `""`. The OpenCode projection emitted that value
as a `ProviderDeclaredFact`, Core validation rejected the empty field, and the error escaped
the record projection. The result was that the complete OpenCode source was reported as
unreadable and none of its otherwise valid history became searchable.

## Change

- Skip exactly empty OpenCode fact values while preserving whitespace-only values, matching
  Core's existing `is_empty()` contract.
- Treat empty call-id, tool, status, and output-role strings as absent derived metadata.
- Preserve the complete structured source body and invocation arguments, including an empty
  command; only the invalid derived field is omitted.
- Bump the OpenCode parser revision to v10 so existing indexes are reprojected consistently.

## Validation

- Targeted Rust checks passed in the Microsoft Rust DevContainer.
- A release build imported an unchanged 1.5 GB OpenCode SQLite source into a fresh data root:
  168,782 searchable events across 1,504 sessions, with zero source failures.
- `ctx doctor` returned clean and provider-scoped lexical search returned OpenCode results.
- A production `import --all` then completed with Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Gemini, and Hermes
  present: 1,251,793 searchable events across 5,797 sources.
- The final diff received GO verdicts from two independent reviewers and a separate premium
  adversarial review.

title: Legacy OpenClaw JSONL history is silently omitted from sources and import --all
body:
## Problem

CTX advertises OpenClaw as a supported provider, so I expected an existing OpenClaw archive to be included in `ctx import --all`.

On a host with a readable legacy archive at:

```text
~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions/*.jsonl
```

`ctx sources --all` does not mention OpenClaw at all, and `ctx import --all` silently publishes a generation without those sessions. There is no warning that supported history exists but requires an explicit path.

This was surprising in practice: I only discovered much later that the OpenClaw conversations I expected to search were absent from the index.

## Real-world result

The archive contained 531 JSONL sessions (about 64 MiB). Explicit import worked correctly:

```console
ctx import \
  --provider openclaw \
  --path ~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions
```

It imported:

- 531 sessions
- 10,704 messages
- 5,605 tool calls
- 0 skipped OpenClaw records

The conversations were immediately searchable with `--provider openclaw`.

## Current contract

The provider matrix explains that legacy OpenClaw JSONL remains importable only by exact explicit path, while automatic discovery checks the newer per-agent SQLite layout and reports that layout as unsupported.

That distinction is reasonable as an internal compatibility policy, but it is not visible from the normal CLI workflow. For a user, `Supported` plus silent omission looks like a successful complete import.

## Suggested minimum behavior

When readable legacy OpenClaw session JSONL files are present, could CTX at least report them as detected but requiring explicit import?

For example, `ctx sources --all` or `ctx import --all` could show something like:

```text
openclaw  manual  ~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions
Legacy OpenClaw JSONL history was detected but is not imported automatically.
Run: ctx import --provider openclaw --path ~/.openclaw/agents/main/sessions
```

Automatic import would also solve the surprise, but a clear diagnostic and recovery command would be sufficient. The important part is that a nominally successful `--all` import should not silently omit a supported archive that CTX can already parse.
