title: Windows: every hosted install fails — the install transaction and install.ps1 disagree on the marker's install_path form, and the ctx Pro pair step rejects both forms
body:
## Environment

- Windows 11 Home 26200, x64, NTFS
- PowerShell 7.6.5 (`pwsh`)
- ctx **1.1.1** (stable), `install.ps1` fetched from `https://ctx.rs/install.ps1` on 2026-08-27 (104,785 bytes)
- Install dir: `C:\Users\ichik\.local\bin` (no reparse points, no case mismatch, owner `ichik`)

## Symptom

Every hosted install fails:

```
install.ps1: ctx could not complete its crash-recoverable hosted install transaction
```

This reproduces on a completely clean machine state (no `ctx.exe`, no marker, no `~/.ctx`, no leftover lock files).

Below are five distinct defects found in one install attempt. They are reported together because they are sequential blockers in the same code path: fixing any one alone still leaves the installer unable to complete.

---

## 1. The install transaction requires the extended-length `install_path`; `install.ps1` writes the plain form

`Invoke-HostedInstallTransaction` runs:

```
ctx.exe upgrade --hosted-transaction install \
  --install-path <path> --attempt-id <id> --marker-source <file> --binary-sha256 <sha>
```

The child's actual error (discarded by the installer — see §5):

```
Error: hosted install marker does not bind the signed executable and target
```

**A/B test.** Same staged binary, same `--attempt-id`, same `--binary-sha256`, same directory. The *only* difference is the form of `install_path` inside the marker source:

| marker `install_path` | `--install-path` | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `C:\Users\ichik\ctxtest2\ctx.exe` | plain | exit 1 — `does not bind the signed executable and target` |
| `\\?\C:\Users\ichik\ctxtest2\ctx.exe` | plain | **exit 0 — `"status": "committed"`** |
| `\\?\C:\Users\ichik\ctxtest2\ctx.exe` | `\\?\...` | **exit 0 — `"status": "committed"`** |
| `C:\Users\ichik\ctxtest2\ctx.exe` | `\\?\...` | exit 1 |

`install.ps1` writes the plain form:

```powershell
$marker = [ordered]@{
    ...
    install_path = $installPath          # C:\Users\ichik\.local\bin\ctx.exe
```

so as shipped this can never succeed on Windows.

**It is not field validation.** I varied the marker source ten ways — dropping `installed_at`, `install_attempt_id`, `channel`, `source_commit`, `published_at`, both URLs; a minimal 6-field marker; `platform` changed to `windows-x86_64` — and every one produced the byte-identical error. Only the `install_path` form changes the outcome.

## 2. `install.ps1`'s own verification cannot accept the marker ctx writes

When the transaction does commit, ctx writes the on-disk marker itself, in extended form:

```json
{
  "install_path": "\\\\?\\C:\\Users\\ichik\\.local\\bin\\ctx.exe",
  ...
}
```

`Test-InstalledTargetIdentity` then checks:

```powershell
[IO.Path]::GetFullPath($installedMarker.install_path) -ceq $installPath
```

`[IO.Path]::GetFullPath('\\?\C:\x\y.exe')` returns `\\?\C:\x\y.exe` unchanged, so this comparison is always `False`. The same `GetFullPath(... .install_path) -cne $installPath` shape appears at four more sites (`Read-ExistingManagedInstall`, the upgrade-result validators, the transaction-proof validator).

So §1 and §2 have to be fixed together — whichever form is chosen, the two sides currently disagree.

## 3. The managed-pair (ctx Pro) step rejects the marker in **both** forms, and it is fatal

With the Core transaction committed, the next step is:

```
ctx.exe --ctx-core-hosted-pair-install-v1 <envelope> <staged core> <ctx-pro.exe> <marker source>
Error: hosted install marker does not own this Core path
```

Tested with the marker in the plain form **and** in the extended form — same error both times. (Note this is the opposite requirement from §1, or at least a different one: the form that makes the transaction commit does not satisfy this step.)

`install.ps1` treats it as fatal:

```
install.ps1: ctx Pro installation failed; the verified Core install was retained. Retry by rerunning this installer command
```

Retrying does not help — it is deterministic.

**This blocks users who do not want ctx Pro at all.** The installer aborts here, before `ctx setup`, before `ctx integrations install skills`, and before the semantic runtime step. `$managedPair` is derived solely from `CTX_RELEASE_MANAGED_PAIR_ENVELOPE_windows_x64` in the release metadata; there is no parameter and no environment variable to skip it (`-NoProTrial` only declines the *trial offer*, it does not skip the companion install).

Please either make the companion step non-fatal for the Core install, or provide a documented `-NoPro` switch.

## 4. The install-directory precheck message contradicts the implementation

```
Error: verify hosted transaction install directory

Caused by:
    private state ACL is not owner-only
```

Measured on a fresh directory:

| directory ACL | result |
| --- | --- |
| inherited (`SYSTEM`, `Administrators`, owner) | rejected |
| **owner only** — `icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "*<user-sid>:(OI)(CI)F"` | **rejected** |
| `SYSTEM` + owner, no inheritance | accepted |

So the actual requirement is "SYSTEM + owner, not inherited", but the message tells you to make it owner-only, which is rejected. Anyone following the message gets further from a working state.

## 5. `install.ps1` discards the child process output, so all of the above look identical

```powershell
function Invoke-ExecutableCaptured(...) {
    ...
    & $Executable @Arguments *> $commandOutputPath
    ...
}
...
if ($transaction.ExitCode -ne 0) {
    Fail "ctx could not complete its crash-recoverable hosted install transaction"
}
```

The captured output is never printed on the failure path, and `$tempRoot` is removed in `finally`, so nothing survives to inspect. Defects §1, §3 and the semantic-runtime failure I filed separately **all surface as the same single line**, with no way for a user to tell them apart.

Every error message quoted in this report was obtained only by patching a local copy of `install.ps1` to add:

```powershell
Write-Host ([IO.File]::ReadAllText($transaction.OutputPath))
```

before each `Fail`. Please print the captured child output when a step fails.

I think this is also why fixes can look ineffective from the outside: #642 was closed as fixed, and that *specific* failure is indeed gone, but the same user-visible one-liner still appears because a different defect took its place.

## 6. The two marker validators disagree with each other

A marker with the **plain** `install_path` is accepted at runtime. With a hand-placed binary and such a marker:

```json
"install": {
    "install_path": "\\\\?\\C:\\Users\\ichik\\ctxtest\\ctx.exe",
    "managed": true,
    "marker": "valid",
    ...
}
```

`ctx upgrade status` reports `managed: true` / `marker: valid` for exactly the marker that `upgrade --hosted-transaction install` rejects as not binding the target. Whatever the intended canonical form is, these two paths should share one normalizer.

---

## Reproduction

```powershell
# clean state: no ctx.exe, no ctx.exe.install.json, no ~/.ctx
irm https://ctx.rs/install.ps1 -OutFile install.ps1
pwsh -NoProfile -File .\install.ps1 -Semantic -NoProTrial
```

To see the real error, add the `Write-Host` from §5 before the `Fail` in `Invoke-HostedInstallTransaction`.

## Suggestion

A Windows CI job that runs `install.ps1` end to end against a clean profile would have caught §1, §3 and §4 immediately. #638, #639, #640 and #642 were all Windows-only path/IO/ACL defects in this same script, and none of them are the sort of thing a unit test reaches.

Happy to test a patch — I have the reproduction scripted.

title: Windows: semantic runtime never installs — ctx runs its generated extract.ps1 without binding -Destination
body:
## Environment

- Windows 11 Home 26200, x64
- ctx **1.1.1** (stable), managed install at `C:\Users\ichik\.local\bin\ctx.exe` (`upgrade status` → `managed: true`, `marker: valid`)
- Fresh data root (`~/.ctx` created by this install)
- ONNX Runtime sidecar artifact: `runtime-7fc0ed292117a84373268fd68e4c7f1dbdcb06fa5057c7ce44579b918dbe36c3.artifact`, 5,940,650 bytes, `VERSION_NUMBER` = `1.27.0`

## Symptom

The semantic runtime can never be installed. Any semantic-enabled upgrade/repair ends with:

```
Error: extract ONNX Runtime sidecar: Join-Path : Cannot bind argument to parameter 'drive' because it is null.
At C:\Users\ichik\.ctx\.ctx-upgrade-downloads\runtime-7fc0ed29...e36c3.extract.ps1:100 char:39
+ ... -Item -ItemType Directory -Path (Join-Path $Destination 'lib') -Force ...
    + CategoryInfo          : InvalidArgument: (:) [Join-Path], PSArgumentNullException
    + FullyQualifiedErrorId : ArgumentNull,Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.JoinPathCommand
```

(The original is localized Japanese; the parameter named in the message is `drive`, i.e. `Join-Path` received `$null` for `-Path`.)

Through `install.ps1` the same failure surfaces as:

```
install.ps1: ctx Semantic runtime repair failed
```

## Cause: ctx invokes its generated `extract.ps1` without binding `-Destination`

The generated script declares four parameters:

```powershell
param(
  [string]$ArchivePath,
  [string]$Destination,
  [string]$ExpectedVersion,
  [long]$MaxExpandedBytes
)
```

**`$ArchivePath` and `$ExpectedVersion` are bound; `$Destination` is not.** That is provable from where it fails: the script opens the archive, enumerates entries, and passes the strict version gate at line 97

```powershell
if ($versionText -cne ($ExpectedVersion + [char]10)) {
    throw "runtime VERSION_NUMBER is not exactly $ExpectedVersion"
}
```

before dying at line 100 on `Join-Path $Destination 'lib'`. An unbound `[string]` parameter is `$null`, which is exactly what `Join-Path` reports. If the arguments were positional and one were missing, the version gate would have thrown first — it does not.

**The generated script itself is correct.** I captured it before ctx deletes it and ran it by hand against the same `.artifact`, with all four parameters supplied by name:

```powershell
& .\extract-captured.ps1 -ArchivePath <the .artifact> -Destination <empty dir> `
    -ExpectedVersion '1.27.0' -MaxExpandedBytes 400000000
```

It completes successfully and produces exactly the expected tree:

```
LICENSE
MICROSOFT_VC_RUNTIME_LICENSE.rtf
ThirdPartyNotices.txt
VERSION_NUMBER
GIT_COMMIT_ID
lib\onnxruntime.dll
lib\msvcp140.dll
lib\msvcp140_1.dll
lib\vcruntime140.dll
lib\vcruntime140_1.dll
```

So the defect is in the invocation, not in the script.

## Reproduction

```powershell
$env:CTX_SEARCH_SEMANTIC = '1'
ctx upgrade --channel stable --format=json
```

Reproduces with and without `CTX_RELEASE_METADATA_URL` / `CTX_RELEASE_METADATA_SIGNATURE_URL` pointed at a local metadata file (which is what `install.ps1`'s semantic repair step does), so it is not related to the metadata override.

Note that ctx deletes `<hash>.extract.ps1` after the failure while leaving `<hash>.artifact` behind, so the generated script has to be captured while it exists.

## Impact

Semantic search cannot be enabled on Windows at all on a clean install. It also aborts `install.ps1` at the semantic repair stage, so the install never reaches `ctx setup` or the skill install.

## Relation to #642

#642 was a different failure in this same path (the spawned `extract.ps1` could not open the `.download` file it was handed, because the downloader still held it). That specific failure is gone in 1.1.1 — the archive opens fine here. The extract path is still broken, now because of the unbound `-Destination`.

Happy to test a patch.

title: fix(upgrade): pass non-verbatim paths to the Windows extraction helper
body:
Fixes the Windows semantic-runtime install failure reported in #767.

## What is happening

`extract_runtime_archive` drives the embedded ONNX Runtime extraction script through `System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe`. The `-Destination` it passes is `staged_path` from `stage_downloaded_runtime_artifact`, which descends from `semantic_runtime_root(data_root)`. When the data root has been canonicalised — `std::fs::canonicalize` yields the verbatim `\\?\` form on Windows — every path below it inherits that prefix.

Windows PowerShell's provider cmdlets cannot resolve a drive for a verbatim path, so the script's first `Join-Path $Destination 'lib'` fails and the whole semantic runtime install aborts:

```
extract ONNX Runtime sidecar: Join-Path : Cannot bind argument to parameter "drive" because it is null.
At C:\Users\<u>\.ctx\.ctx-upgrade-downloads\runtime-<hash>.extract.ps1:100 char:39
+ ... -Item -ItemType Directory -Path (Join-Path $Destination 'lib') -Force ...
```

`-ArchivePath` survives the same treatment because the script consumes it through `[System.IO.Compression.ZipFile]::OpenRead`, which accepts verbatim paths. Only the *provider* cmdlets reject them. That is why `$ArchivePath` and `$ExpectedVersion` bind and work while `$Destination` looks unbound — the script gets far enough to open the archive and pass the `VERSION_NUMBER` gate before dying.

The user-visible effect is that `runtime/onnxruntime/<version>/` is created and `<platform>` never appears, so semantic search can never be provisioned on Windows.

## Evidence

Windows 11, `System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe`, same machine and session:

```
Destination = C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim
  Join-Path $Destination 'lib'  ->  C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim\lib

Destination = \\?\C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\ctx-verbatim
  Join-Path $Destination 'lib'  ->  Cannot bind argument to parameter "drive" because it is null.
```

Feeding the real generated extractor a verbatim `-Destination` reproduces the production failure exactly, down to the same location (`extract.ps1:100 char:39`). The same script with an identical but non-verbatim destination extracts the expected tree (`lib/onnxruntime.dll`, `lib/msvcp140.dll`, …, `VERSION_NUMBER`, `LICENSE`).

## The change

One file. A `powershell_path_argument` helper that converts `\\?\C:\…` to `C:\…` and `\\?\UNC\server\share` to `\\server\share`, leaves every other path untouched, applied to the two path arguments handed to the helper.

## Tests

`cargo test -p ctx-upgrade-engine --lib` on Windows 11, cargo 1.98.0:

| | passed | failed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 84 | 3 |
| after | 88 | 3 |

The four added tests cover verbatim drive paths, verbatim UNC paths, ordinary paths, and a non-drive device path that must be left alone.

The three failures are pre-existing on this platform and unrelated to this change — I confirmed by stashing the patch and re-running:

```
upgrade::install::transaction::tests::coreml_clean_install_journals_exact_fallback_composition_and_paths
upgrade::install::transaction::windows::tests::failed_replace_repairs_missing_executable_before_any_wait
upgrade::state::tests::only_trusted_automatic_active_state_admits_the_recovery_daemon
```

For what it is worth they are also canonical-path shaped — one reports `install transaction data root is not canonical: C:\Users\<u>\AppData\Local\Temp\.tmpXXXXXX\data-root`.

## End-to-end

Verified on Windows 11 with a release build of this branch installed into a throwaway `BinDir` with a valid hosted-install marker and a scratch `CTX_DATA_ROOT`. The extraction step completes and the staged runtime tree is written in full, including ctx's own `ctx-runtime-install.json`. Details, including one caveat about a later unrelated-looking check, are in a comment below.

## Related

This is the same underlying issue as the marker-path mismatch reported in #766: the internal canonical `\\?\` form reaching a consumer that cannot accept it. A single normalisation applied wherever a path leaves ctx for an external consumer would cover both, and possibly the three failing tests above. I kept this PR to the one defect.

## Optional follow-up

`scripts/test-windows-runtime-upgrade-extractor.ps1` supplies `-Destination` from the test itself, so it validates the embedded script text but cannot catch a caller that hands over an unusable value — which is exactly this bug. Adding an `Assert-EmbeddedExtractorSuccess` case with `-Destination "\\?\$runtimeDestination"` would fail on current `main`; making it pass would also mean hardening the embedded script to use `[System.IO.Path]::Combine` / `[System.IO.Directory]::CreateDirectory` instead of `Join-Path` / `New-Item`. Happy to add that here or as a separate PR, whichever you prefer.

Fixes #767

title: Same-version semantic repair cannot publish a missing ONNX Runtime sidecar: the legacy path label requires a ctx binary replacement in the same transaction
body:
## Summary

A same-version `ctx upgrade` — the documented semantic repair path — cannot publish a missing ONNX Runtime sidecar, because the install-transaction validator only accepts that path label when the transaction also replaces the `ctx` binary. The repair therefore fails for the one case it exists to serve: the runtime is missing and the CLI is already current.

This is the blocker immediately behind #767. It is only reachable on Windows once #767 is fixed (before that, extraction dies first), but the validator itself is not Windows-specific.

## Environment

- Windows 11 Home 26200, x64
- ctx 1.1.1 (stable), managed install, `marker: valid`
- Live data root `~/.ctx` with `[search] semantic = true`, runtime absent
- The binary used was a local build of `main` carrying the #768 fix, with the workspace version pinned to `1.1.1` so the run reaches semantic provisioning

## What happens

```
$env:CTX_SEARCH_SEMANTIC = '1'
ctx upgrade --channel stable --format=json
->  Error: install transaction has an unexpected path count
```

Extraction succeeds — the staged tree is complete, including ctx's own manifest:

```
runtime\onnxruntime\1.27.0\.windows-x64.ctx-upgrade-<id>.new\
    ctx-runtime-install.json
    VERSION_NUMBER  LICENSE  GIT_COMMIT_ID  ThirdPartyNotices.txt  MICROSOFT_VC_RUNTIME_LICENSE.rtf
    lib\onnxruntime.dll  lib\msvcp140.dll  lib\msvcp140_1.dll  lib\vcruntime140.dll  lib\vcruntime140_1.dll
```

The persisted journal (`.ctx.exe.upgrade-install-transaction.json`) then holds exactly one entry:

```json
{
  "phase": "prepared",
  "paths": [
    {
      "label": "ONNX Runtime sidecar",
      "staged": "\\\\?\\C:\\Users\\<u>\\.ctx\\runtime\\onnxruntime\\1.27.0\\.windows-x64.ctx-upgrade-<id>.new",
      ...
    }
  ]
}
```

## Why it cannot succeed

`validate_paths_for_platform` in `crates/ctx-upgrade-engine/src/upgrade/install/transaction/journal.rs`:

```rust
if !(2..=6).contains(&journal.paths.len()) {
    return Err(anyhow!("install transaction has an unexpected path count"));
}
```

one path fails the lower bound. Relaxing the bound does not help, because the next gate is:

```rust
let runtimes = journal.paths.iter().filter(|p| p.label == "ONNX Runtime sidecar").collect::<Vec<_>>();
if runtimes.len() > 1 || (!runtimes.is_empty() && binary.is_none()) {
    return Err(anyhow!("install transaction has invalid runtime paths"));
}
```

A journal carrying the legacy `ONNX Runtime sidecar` label is publishable **only** alongside a `ctx binary` path. A same-version repair has no binary path by construction, so the runtime can never be published that way.

## Why this matters

The docs advertise exactly this path:

> Running `ctx upgrade` again at the same CLI version repairs a missing or hash-mismatched selected semantic asset from the signed catalog without changing the CLI version.

On this machine that repair selects the legacy `plan.metadata.onnxruntime` artifact — `stage_downloaded_runtime_artifact` runs and produces the legacy label — rather than a signed-catalog `Semantic *` asset. So the documented repair is structurally unavailable here.

**It also explains a failure in #766.** `install.ps1` installs the CLI and then runs its "Semantic runtime repair" step as `ctx upgrade --channel <channel> --format=json` with `CTX_SEARCH_SEMANTIC=1`. At that moment the CLI it just installed is already current, so the repair transaction has no binary path and hits this gate. That is the

```
install.ps1: ctx Semantic runtime repair failed
```

I reported there. So on Windows the hosted installer cannot provision semantic even after #767 and the marker issues in #766 are fixed.

## What I am unsure about

Whether the correct fix is to let a runtime-only transaction publish, or to make same-version repair select the signed-catalog `Semantic *` assets instead of the legacy sidecar. That looks like a selection/policy decision rather than something I should guess at, which is why I am filing rather than sending a patch.

The validator is not `#[cfg(windows)]`, so the gate applies on every platform; whether other platforms reach it depends on whether their repair also selects the legacy artifact, which I cannot test here.

## Repro material

I have the full JSON envelopes, the journal file, and directory listings from both a scratch data root and a live one, and can retest a patch quickly.

title: upgrade artifact download rejects RFC 2544 fake-IP (198.18.0.0/15) before TUN routing
body:
## Environment

- macOS arm64
- Official managed installation
- Current CLI: `ctx 1.1.1`
- The same behavior is still present in the `v1.2.0` source

## Failure

`ctx upgrade` fails while downloading the official artifact:

```text
GET artifact: https://cli.ctx.rs/storage/v1/object/public/releases/artifacts/stable/1.1.1/ctx-macos-arm64: Dns Failed: resolve dns name 'cli.ctx.rs:443': artifact host resolved to a private or local address
```

On this network, the normal resolver result is:

```text
$ dig +short A cli.ctx.rs
198.18.8.39
```

The address is from the RFC 2544 benchmarking range (`198.18.0.0/15`) and is used here as a fake IP that the TUN layer routes. It is not an on-LAN or private service in this setup.

As a transport check, `curl --noproxy '*'` against the artifact URL obtained from the same signed release metadata succeeds:

```text
http_code=200 remote_ip=198.18.8.39 size_download=42208720
```

The failure therefore occurs before the TUN routing path can carry the HTTPS request.

## Why this happens

The artifact client explicitly disables proxy discovery and installs `public_only_resolver`:

- [`artifact_agent`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/fbf73c77c90f10b01a78e10a4add051c1101df09/crates/ctx-cli/src/net.rs#L246-L253) calls `try_proxy_from_env(false)` and `resolver(public_only_resolver)`.
- [`public_only_resolver`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/fbf73c77c90f10b01a78e10a4add051c1101df09/crates/ctx-cli/src/net.rs#L255-L269) rejects the result if any resolved address is non-public.
- [`is_public_ipv4`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/fbf73c77c90f10b01a78e10a4add051c1101df09/crates/ctx-cli/src/net.rs#L323-L341) classifies `(198, 18..=19, _)` as non-public.

This fail-closed check also rejects the RFC 2544 fake-IP transport scheme before the operating system and TUN layer can route it.

## Requested narrow mitigation

Please consider a default-off escape hatch, for example:

```toml
[upgrade]
allow_rfc2544_fake_ip = true
```

The exception should remain deliberately narrow:

1. Apply only to the compile-time production artifact authority (`https://cli.ctx.rs/storage/v1/object/public/releases/artifacts/...`), not to arbitrary metadata URLs, hosts, or general CLI HTTP.
2. Permit only `198.18.0.0/15` at DNS-resolution time when the explicit opt-in is enabled.
3. Keep HTTPS-only enforcement, signed metadata verification, artifact SHA-256 verification, bounded and validated redirects, and rejection of all other private, local, or reserved targets unchanged.
4. Keep the current secure behavior as the default.

Another direction worth discussing is an explicit, constrained proxy transport for the pinned official artifact authority, allowing the proxy to resolve the target hostname instead of resolving it locally and rejecting the fake IP before connection. The existing HTTPS, signature, hash, authority, and redirect protections should remain in place.

Re-running the managed installer is not a durable workaround: managed installations return to `ctx upgrade` for subsequent releases, so the same resolver gate is encountered again.

Thank you for considering this.

title: Large archival OpenClaw source leaves automatic refresh stuck in repeated watch recovery
body:
## Problem

On a live Debian host, a clean ctx 1.2.0 setup successfully publishes a usable lexical generation, but automatic refresh does not reach a terminal state when a large, inactive OpenClaw archive is discovered.

The OpenClaw archive is no longer being written to. Several Codex sessions are active concurrently on the host.

## Reproduction

Using the official ctx 1.2.0 Linux binary and a fresh, isolated data root:

```console
ctx setup --wait --progress plain
```

Automatic discovery selected seven sources, including Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, OpenClaw, and Hermes.

## Observed behavior

The initial scan completed all seven sources and published a usable lexical generation after approximately four minutes:

- 4,429 sessions
- 156,353 messages
- 126,424 tool calls
- approximately 2.1 GiB processed

However, the refresh remained in `watch_recovery` instead of completing.

During recovery, daemon status showed:

- more than 1.2 million ignored access events;
- more than 8,700 watcher ingress overflows;
- `forced_rearms` increasing from 1 to 3;
- `consecutive_failures` increasing from 1 to 3;
- no completed work cycles;
- sustained CPU usage of roughly three cores.

The last ignored access path was inside the archival OpenClaw sessions directory. The counters continued increasing until the isolated run was stopped after approximately eight minutes.

The published generation itself was healthy: lexical search with `--refresh off` returned results in about 0.3 seconds.

## Expected behavior

Reading a provider archive should not cause enough watcher pressure to invalidate the same refresh.

Watcher recovery should converge after bounded work, allowing `ctx setup --wait` and the owning refresh request to complete even when other provider sources remain active.

## Additional context

PR #783 appears to bound callback processing and memory growth, but on this corpus the repeated overflow -> rearm -> recovery sequence still does not terminate.

title: Setup fails when daemon startup takes more than five seconds
body:
## Problem

With the official ctx 1.1.1 build, `ctx setup` can stop before the daemon becomes ready. It reports `ctx daemon did not become ready: timed out waiting for live daemon lifecycle readiness`. The daemon continues its startup work and later reports a healthy lifecycle state.

## Reproduction

- Use a source set that makes startup reconciliation take more than five seconds
- Run `ctx setup`
- After the timeout, run `ctx status --format json` until the daemon reports `ready`

## Expected behavior

The [v1.2.0 source](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.0/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs#L38-L39) sets the handoff timeout to five seconds. `ctx setup` must wait for a terminal startup result or return a non-error progress state.

title: Semantic catch-up fails after an incremental lexical refresh
body:
## Problem

Semantic search reaches `ready` after a full rebuild. The ONNX runtime loads correctly. After the next automatic incremental refresh, semantic catch-up stays `pending` with `generation_not_acknowledged`. The job fails with `source-backed semantic manifest identity does not match its verified index`.

## Reproduction

- Start with lexical and semantic indexes in the `ready` state
- Add one event to a supported provider transcript
- Wait for automatic indexing
- Run `ctx status --format json` after the lexical generation changes

## Expected behavior

The failure occurs at this [v1.2.0 comparison](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.0/crates/ctx-semantic-index/src/vector_store/source_projection.rs#L114-L119). Semantic reconciliation computes a manifest generation ID, then compares it with the verified index generation. Catch-up must process the published incremental generation and acknowledge the current lexical generation.

title: Large Codex tool output drops the complete transcript route
body:
ctx 1.2.0 drops a complete Codex transcript route when one `custom_tool_call_output` contains inline `image_url` data and the encoded Core record is larger than 8 MiB. `ctx doctor` reports `JSONL semantic page exceeds the 8388608 byte limit`. The lexical generation then contains no events from that rollout.

To reproduce, create an isolated Codex rollout with `session_meta`, `custom_tool_call`, and `custom_tool_call_output` records. Set the output to an array with text and a 9 MiB base64 data URL. Run `ctx --data-root /tmp/ctx-repro import --provider codex`, then run `ctx --data-root /tmp/ctx-repro list events --provider codex --source-format codex_session_jsonl --content none --limit 1`; the import reports a source failure, and the list returns no events.

The Codex projector accepts content up to 16 MiB, but the shared JSONL publisher limits a semantic page to 8 MiB. Compare the encoded Core record with the shared page limit before publication. If it is too large, retain the event identity and metadata, mark its content as omitted, and publish its siblings normally.

title: fix(codex): preserve bounded oversized semantic rows
body:
## Summary

- keep the shared JSONL semantic page limit at 8 MiB
- split Codex semantic output into bounded pages before publication

## Why

This change keeps the ordinary 8 MiB limit for generic and multi-record pages. It uses Codex's existing `MAX_CODEX_SOURCE_BACKED_SINGLE_ROW_PAGE_BYTES` contract only for a single record. This preserves the full event instead of omitting valid content.

title: OpenCode import fails "one-snapshot bounded-work contract" after a complete scan
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #755 (closed). The terminal-revalidation fix is confirmed working:
the `source_changed` failure no longer occurs on v1.2.x. The same OpenCode
database now fails one layer deeper, with an internal invariant instead:

```text
Internal: OpenCode-family lifecycle violated its one-snapshot bounded-work contract
```

The scan itself reads the complete importable corpus every time; the failure is
at publication. This looks like the same underlying non-reproducibility that
#755's revalidation misattributed to a source change — now detected honestly by
a stricter guard.

## Environment

```text
ctx v1.2.0 and v1.2.1 (GitHub release binaries ctx-macos-arm64) — identical failure on both
run side-by-side against a data root otherwise served by managed 1.1.1
macOS arm64 (Apple M4)
source: ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db — 4,916,953,088 bytes, WAL mode
```

The data root was fully rebuilt from scratch on 1.1.1 (no legacy state; see
#755 evidence rows 4–5). The source database is the same one from #755,
unchanged, with no `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars present and no OpenCode processes
running during imports.

## Reproduction

```bash
ctx import --provider opencode
```

Output (v1.2.1; v1.2.0 byte-identical except attempt id):

```text
History refresh failed

Agent histories  OpenCode
Sessions         5,247
Messages         325,260
Tool calls       150,738
Data scanned     3.2 GiB
Elapsed          2m 29s
Remaining        complete
✗ publish provider inputs through the Core refresh engine
daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed (code=source_refresh_failed, class=internal,
retryable=true, attempt=01a048d4-a762-7571-97d1-2664726e202c,
affected_routes=["bf58ee684bdc19dbd0d052a9d93f15c1aac1065dac9be31a6127f33ff57d8e81"],
retryable_routes=["bf58ee684bdc19dbd0d052a9d93f15c1aac1065dac9be31a6127f33ff57d8e81"],
blocked_routes=[], retained_generation=None, retry_advice=Some("retry_request")): run capture-owned
source-backed refresh: source-backed scan failed for opencode: Internal: OpenCode-family lifecycle
violated its one-snapshot bounded-work contract: Internal: OpenCode-family lifecycle violated its
one-snapshot bounded-work contract
```

Notes:

- `retry_advice: retry_request`, but the failure is deterministic — every retry
  produces identical scan totals and the identical error.
- The evidence base from #755 still applies: source byte-frozen during runs,
  failure reproduced after complete state resets, sidecar-less at rest, small
  WAL-less SQLite sources (Zed) import cleanly on the same machine.

## The scan is complete, not truncated

Scan totals are identical across six-plus runs on 1.1.1, 1.2.0, and 1.2.1:
5,247 sessions / 325,260 messages / 3.2 GiB. Checked against the source:

```text
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM session;                        -- 5,295
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT session_id) FROM message;      -- 5,247
```

5,247 is exactly the number of sessions containing at least one message; the
other 48 are metadata-only and correctly skipped by the conversation gate.

The byte accounting also closes. The 4.58 GiB file decomposes as:

```text
message + part payloads (conversation stream)   3.68 GiB   scanned (reported 3.2 GiB decoded)
event table (internal event-sourcing log)       0.39 GiB   correctly not a conversation source
freelist (dead pages, never vacuumed)           0.10 GiB   empty space
indexes + page overhead + small tables         ~0.41 GiB   structure
total: 1,200,428 pages x 4 KiB                  4.58 GiB   matches the file exactly
```

So the lifecycle reads the complete importable corpus, then violates the
one-snapshot bounded-work contract during publication — the failure is in
post-scan evidence derivation, not in reading.

## Requests

1. Make the error say **which lifecycle step demanded work beyond the single
   bounded snapshot** and what it observed — `class=internal` with a generic
   contract name is undebuggable from outside.
2. The offer from #755 stands: this machine can run an instrumented or patched
   build against the real 4.9 GB database with minutes of turnaround.

## Related (will report separately if useful)

First start of a 1.2.0 binary against this root also failed on recovery of a
1.1.1-written `daemon/jobs/core-refresh.json` receipt
(`published daemon source refresh catalog binding route is absent from
route_results`) — cleared manually. Anyone upgrading with a failed route in
their last refresh may hit that wall; happy to file it as its own issue.

title: Daemon hot-retries a deterministically failing source route — new 4.6 GB snapshot every ~4 minutes, no backoff or quarantine
body:
## Summary

With `indexing mode auto`, the daemon retries a deterministically failing source route in a hot loop: each failure is followed by a fresh full snapshot and rescan of the same 4.9 GB SQLite source within about a minute, indefinitely, with no visible backoff, cap, or quarantine.

One permanently failing source (in this case the OpenCode route from #799) turns automatic maintenance into an unbounded background cost: ~3 minutes of heavy I/O plus a 4.6 GB temp write per cycle, on a battery-powered laptop. The only escape is `ctx index mode manual`, which sacrifices automatic freshness for every other provider because of one bad route.

## Environment

```text
ctx 1.1.1 (managed install), macOS arm64 (Apple M4, laptop)
indexing mode auto, daemon enabled
failing route: ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db — deterministic internal failure, see #799
```

## Observation

Timeline after `ctx index mode auto` brought the daemon up (poll interval 60 s, watching `tmp/provider-sqlite/` snapshot directories and daemon CPU time):

```text
t+1m  snapshot=provider-sqlite-snapshot-HN7WTk  cpu=00:17   ← first scan running
t+2m  snapshot=provider-sqlite-snapshot-HN7WTk  cpu=00:20
t+3m  snapshot=provider-sqlite-snapshot-HN7WTk  cpu=00:23
t+4m  snapshot=provider-sqlite-snapshot-03I7A0  cpu=00:24   ← NEW snapshot: second scan began
```

The first scan takes ~2.5–3 minutes, fails with #799's `one-snapshot bounded-work contract` error (`class=internal`, `retry_advice: retry_request`), and a new private snapshot appears within roughly 60 seconds. Each cycle writes ~4.6 GB into `tmp/provider-sqlite/` and reads 3.2 GiB of source payload.

The failure is deterministic — the same source has failed identically across many runs and versions (#755, #799) — so every retry is guaranteed wasted work.

## Expected behavior

Some combination of:

1. **Failure-class-aware retry policy.** `class=internal` deterministic failures should not be retried on the same schedule as transient errors (`source_changed`, I/O). After N identical failures with an unchanged source fingerprint, quarantine the route until the source changes or the binary version changes.
2. **Backoff with a cap.** Even for retryable classes, immediate re-snapshot of a multi-GB source is expensive; exponential backoff would bound the cost.
3. **Per-route disable.** There is still no way to exclude one source/route from automatic maintenance (`ctx sources` is read-only, no config key). `mode manual` is the only lever, and it is global.
4. **Visibility.** `ctx status` shows `Refresh pending` while this loop runs; nothing surfaces "route X has failed N times, retrying every M minutes."

## Context

- #799 is the failing route; this issue is about the retry policy around any such route.
- #215 introduced duplicate-identity quarantine, so a quarantine concept already exists in the codebase; it does not appear to cover deterministic internal scan failures.
- `daemon/wakeup.json` advertises `scheduled_retry_wakeups`, suggesting scheduled retries exist — but the observed behavior is an immediate hot loop.

title: Post-publication verification remains in watch_recovery for over an hour
body:
## Problem

A clean setup on current `main` publishes a usable lexical generation, but the owning refresh request does not reach a terminal state.

Tested commit: `da53d1475b6fb9d74c22d74742dd52d88f8734ff`.

## Environment

- Debian host
- 16 GiB RAM
- ordinary SATA SSD
- fresh isolated data root and isolated daemon
- several Codex sessions actively appending
- seven discovered sources across Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Gemini, OpenClaw, and Hermes
- production CTX was not involved

## Observed behavior

`ctx setup --wait --progress none` successfully processed all seven sources:

- approximately 10.8 GB of source data
- 9,858 sessions
- 321,968 messages
- 548,944 tool calls

The lexical generation was published after approximately 12 minutes and was immediately usable. A lexical search with `--refresh off` returned results successfully.

However, the owning request remained in:

```text
request_state=running
phase=watch_recovery
completed_sources=7/7
```

It was still nonterminal after one hour.

During that time:

- eight `ctx-generation-*` worker threads continued consuming CPU;
- the daemon accumulated more than 3.5 CPU-hours;
- RSS varied between approximately 3 and 6 GB;
- the reported refresh elapsed time stopped advancing after publication;
- no verification progress or ETA was exposed.

Unlike #790, this run did not experience watcher pressure:

```text
ignored_access_events=0
ingress_overflows=0
forced_rearms=0
raw_events=0
```

So the watcher-event feedback loop appears fixed, but a different post-publication path still prevents convergence.

## Expected behavior

Once a generation has been published and verified sufficiently for search, the owning request should reach a terminal state within bounded time.

If additional generation verification is required, CTX should expose its phase, progress, and eventual completion. It should not remain indefinitely under the generic `watch_recovery` phase while consuming several CPU cores.

## Related issues

- #790 — watcher access-event storm; the counters from that report remain zero in this reproduction.
- #690 — post-publication generation work and repeated exhaustive maintenance.
- #306 — cold-refresh performance and opaque verification progress.

title: Daemon does not stop on SIGTERM or SIGINT during generation verification
body:
## Problem

A daemon performing post-publication generation verification did not stop after receiving either `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT`.

Tested commit: `da53d1475b6fb9d74c22d74742dd52d88f8734ff`.

This was observed during the isolated reproduction reported in #804. The daemon had already published a usable lexical generation but remained busy with eight `ctx-generation-*` threads.

## Observed behavior

I sent `SIGTERM` directly to the daemon PID and waited 30 seconds. The process continued running and consuming CPU.

I then sent `SIGINT` and waited another 20 seconds. The process again continued running.

`SIGKILL` was required to terminate it.

Because the parent `ctx setup --wait` process was still alive, it briefly spawned another daemon before the parent command itself was interrupted.

## Expected behavior

`SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` should initiate bounded graceful shutdown even while generation verification is running.

Long-running verification workers should observe cancellation, release their resources, and allow the supervising command to exit without respawning another daemon during shutdown.

If graceful shutdown cannot complete within a bounded interval, CTX should expose that state rather than silently continuing to consume CPU.

title: Semantic lite-turn projection drops intermediate assistant messages
body:
## Problem

`ctx 1.2.1` builds one semantic document for each user message. It adds only the last nonempty assistant message before the next user message. Agent sessions often contain several assistant messages around tool calls. An intermediate message can contain the only copy of a decision or finding. Lexical search retains that message. The semantic document omits it because [`semantic_lite_turn_assistant`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.1/crates/ctx-history-index-query/src/execution/lookup.rs#L43-L54) overwrites [`latest_assistant`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.1/crates/ctx-history-index-query/src/execution/lookup.rs#L153-L162).

## Reproduction

- Import a supported transcript with these records: user `Run check A`, assistant `The amber falcon owns relay 47`, assistant `Done`, user `Continue`
- Enable semantic search and wait for `ready`
- Run `ctx search "amber falcon" --backend lexical --events`; it returns the first assistant message
- Build the lite-turn document for the first user message; it contains `Run check A` and `Done`
- Query the unique finding through the semantic backend; no vector document contains `amber falcon owns relay 47`

## Expected behavior

Preserve all discovery-eligible assistant text in each user turn, subject to the existing byte and page limits. A possible fix is to collect assistant sections until the next user message, then apply deterministic truncation. If ctx keeps one assistant message, semantic status and documentation must state that coverage rule.

title: Semantic --refresh wait stops before daemon catch-up in auto mode
body:
## Problem

With automatic indexing enabled, `ctx search --backend semantic --refresh wait` can finish Core refresh and return `semantic_generation_not_acknowledged`. The JSON error has `retryable: true`. The same command succeeds after the daemon catches up. The v1.2.1 [`run_search`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.1/crates/ctx-history-cli/src/source_index/search.rs#L300-L317) path selects foreground semantic reconciliation only when the daemon is disabled. In auto mode, `wait` stops at the Core receipt and semantic preflight can see an older projection. #792 fixed generation identity during catch-up, this report covers the wait boundary after a valid publication.

## Reproduction

- Enable automatic indexing and semantic search, then wait for `ctx semantic status` to report `ready`
- Append one event to a supported provider transcript
- Immediately run `ctx search "new event" --backend semantic --refresh wait --format json`
- Observe `semantic_generation_not_acknowledged` for the new Core generation
- Wait for daemon catch-up and run the same command again. The semantic query succeeds

## Expected behavior

Wait for semantic acknowledgment of the pinned Core generation when a query requires semantic evidence. A possible fix is a daemon wait request after the Core receipt and before query preflight. If Core publishes a newer generation during the wait, repin within the same bounded deadline.

title: OpenCode file parts are rejected without record diagnostics
body:
## Problem

`ctx 1.2.1` rejects current OpenCode `part.data` records with `type: file`. [`is_retained_type`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.2.1/crates/ctx-history-providers-sqlite-logical/src/providers/opencode/native_path/json/output.rs#L60-L81) does not admit this type. A source with valid text and file parts reports `completed_with_rejections` and `rejected_record_total: 1`. Its `rejection_diagnostics` array is empty. Filename, MIME type, source path, and text attachment metadata are absent from search. Aggregate rejection counts also contain known duplicate carriers and blank placeholders, which hides this coverage loss.

## Reproduction

- Create a current OpenCode message-part SQLite source with one valid `text` part
- Add `{"type":"file","mime":"text/plain","filename":"example.txt","url":"file:///tmp/example.txt","source":{"type":"file","path":"example.txt"}}` as a second part
- Run `ctx import --provider opencode --path ./opencode.db --reset-cursor --format json --progress none`
- Observe `outcome: completed_with_rejections`, `rejected_record_total: 1`, and `rejection_diagnostics: []`
- Run `ctx search "example.txt" --provider opencode`. The file record is absent

## Expected behavior

Retain bounded metadata for OpenCode file parts. Do not index data URLs or binary bytes. A possible fix is to admit `file` and project `filename`, `mime`, `source.path`, and `source.text.value`. If the record stays unsupported, emit a bounded diagnostic and keep that rejection separate from ignored duplicate or placeholder records.

title: fix(opencode): handle file parts without indexing payloads

- treat OpenCode-family message file parts as known ignored carriers before generic output routing
- keep attachment bytes, data URLs, filenames, MIME metadata, and source paths out of searchable Core content

- cover scanner, adapter, CLI import, projection-limit, and privacy behavior

## Provider consistency

Existing providers use mixed attachment behavior: explicit media is commonly ignored, while some generic tool JSON paths retain embedded values. None of the audited providers dereference attachment files or perform OCR. This change keeps OpenCode on the safer explicit-media boundary.

title: Live sources keep setup and manual import in repeated exhaustive refresh after publication
body:
## Problem

On a live multi-session host, both automatic setup and an explicit manual import keep starting exhaustive refresh passes after publishing usable generations. The owning command does not reach a terminal state while Codex sessions continue appending.

Tested commit: `53c4784cf9b6f99b558c251a12212d27e2fb7ee3` (`ctx 1.2.3`).

## Environment

- Debian host with 16 GiB RAM and an ordinary SATA SSD
- fresh isolated binary, daemon, and data root
- production CTX was not involved
- several Codex sessions actively appending
- seven discovered sources across Codex, Claude, OpenCode, Gemini, OpenClaw, and Hermes
- semantic indexing disabled

## Automatic setup reproduction

```console
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> setup --wait --progress none
```

The first pass processed all seven sources without source failures:

- approximately 10.9 GB of provider input
- 9,927 sessions
- 323,334 messages
- 552,443 tool calls

An active lexical generation was published. Unlike #790, watcher-pressure counters remained zero throughout the run:

```text
ignored_access_events=0
ingress_overflows=0
forced_rearms=0
raw_events=0
```

The expensive post-publication deep verification reported in #804 is also gone.

However, the same setup request then entered an exhaustive recovery pass across all seven sources. That pass completed and advanced the active-generation pointer, but the request returned to admission and started another exhaustive pass. After the third publication it started a fourth pass from Codex again.

The command was still nonterminal when stopped after approximately 29 minutes.

## Manual mode reproduction

I stopped the isolated automatic daemon, switched the same isolated data root to manual mode, and ran the same path used by my production timer:

```console
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> index mode manual
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import --all --progress none --quiet
```

The finite worker also selected `reconciliation_demand=exhaustive`. It published a generation, reset progress under the same import request, and started another exhaustive pass instead of completing. The owning `import` command remained nonterminal until interrupted after 5m40s.

## Expected behavior

Publishing a bounded snapshot should satisfy the owning setup or explicit import request even when live sources advance again immediately afterward.

New changes may be scheduled as a later incremental maintenance request, but they should not prevent the current command from ever reaching a terminal state. This must also hold for manual mode, where an explicit finite import is expected to finish and leave no worker behind.

## Additional observation

After interrupting the repeated recovery passes and stopping the worker, `search --refresh off` did not return within 30 seconds. I am including this only as a recovery-state symptom, not claiming a separate search root cause yet.

title: Ctrl-C leaves the finite import worker running as an orphan
body:
## Problem

Interrupting an explicit manual import with Ctrl-C exits the client but leaves its finite daemon worker running as an orphan.

Tested commit: `53c4784cf9b6f99b558c251a12212d27e2fb7ee3` (`ctx 1.2.3`).

This was reproduced on a fresh isolated data root while investigating the repeated-refresh behavior reported in #819.

## Reproduction

```console
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> index mode manual
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import --all --progress none --quiet
```

While the finite Core worker was actively refreshing, I sent Ctrl-C to the owning `import` command.

## Observed behavior

- the `import` client exited with code 130;
- the finite daemon worker continued running and consuming CPU;
- the worker was reparented to PID 1;
- no client remained to report its state or clean it up.

Sending `SIGTERM` directly to the orphaned worker stopped it in approximately one second. This confirms that the bounded daemon signal handling from #812 works; the missing behavior is cancellation propagation and child reaping by the owning CLI command.

## Expected behavior

Ctrl-C on an owning finite operation should forward cancellation to its worker, wait for the bounded shutdown, and reap the child before returning control to the shell.

An interrupted `ctx import` must not leave an unobserved daemon consuming CPU in the background.

## Related work

- #805 / #812 — direct daemon `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` handling

title: Allow daemon-free semantic queries from ready projections during passive refresh
body:
## Summary

The daemon-free semantic contract in #725 is still incomplete after #726 and #772. A ready semantic projection cannot be queried by `ctx search --refresh off` or the default `--refresh background` path when the daemon is disabled.

On ctx 1.2.2, strict semantic search fails with:

```text
semantic_daemon_disabled
local semantic search requires automatic indexing or an available daemon query service
```

Hybrid search falls back to lexical even when the active Core generation has a compatible ready semantic projection.

## Reproduction

1. Configure manual indexing with semantic search enabled and no persistent daemon.
2. Run `ctx search "first query" --backend semantic --refresh wait` to publish Core and reconcile semantic state.
3. Confirm the finite worker exits.
4. Run `ctx search "follow-up" --backend semantic --refresh off`.

Expected: query the ready semantic generation locally, without starting a worker or changing projection state.

Actual: `semantic_daemon_disabled`.

The default background path has the same gap: it remains refresh-inert, but cannot use the ready semantic generation locally.

## Proposed behavior

- In manual mode, `off` and `background` use a read-only foreground query adapter.
- Exact-generation preflight must succeed before model loading or vector search.
- Query embedding may load only verified cached model assets.
- These paths must not download a model, reconcile semantic coverage, or write projection state.
- Missing or stale semantic state must return the existing typed semantic readiness error.
- `wait` keeps its current bounded reconciliation behavior.
- MCP and daemon-backed query behavior remain unchanged.

This restores the `off` and `background` portion of the contract described in #725.

## Why

The passive paths still reported `semantic_daemon_disabled` or fell back to lexical.

title: Default daemon-free foreground Core ML execution to CPU on macOS
body:
## Problem

On macOS, a daemon-free foreground semantic search can stall during implicit Core ML accelerator setup.

With the stock signed v1.2.3 binary, a finite `--refresh wait` search using the default Core ML compute selection remained in Core ML/ANE model compilation and loading for more than eight minutes. The process had to be interrupted.

The same binary and semantic index completed the search in 29.41 seconds when Core ML was explicitly restricted to CPU:

```sh
CTX_INTERNAL_SEMANTIC_BACKEND=coreml \
CTX_SEMANTIC_COREML_NATIVE_COMPUTE=cpu \
ctx search "semantic search" --backend semantic --refresh wait
```

The successful run reported semantic as effective and ready, completed freshness reconciliation, returned a result, and left no ctx process running afterward.

This matters for manual installations that intentionally run without a daemon and only synchronize when `ctx search` is invoked.

## Expected behavior

When no Core ML compute override is set, finite foreground semantic execution should use a reliable compute mode and avoid implicit ANE compilation.

Explicit compute overrides should continue to be honored. The daemon's existing default should not change.

## Proposed scope

- Default only foreground Core ML acquisition to `CPUOnly` when no compute mode was explicitly selected.
- Preserve explicit `all`, `cpuAndNeuralEngine`, `cpuAndGPU`, and `cpuOnly` selections.
- Preserve the daemon's existing compute default.

Related context: #726 recorded a long fresh Core ML/ANE load, while #820 tracks finite workers that survive interruption. This issue is specifically about the implicit compute choice for foreground semantic execution.

title: Make explicit import finish enabled semantic indexing
body:
## Summary

When semantic search is enabled, an explicit `ctx import` currently waits only for Core/lexical publication. In manual indexing mode the finite worker performs Core work only, so the command can report success while semantic indexing is still behind. Semantic catches up only when a later semantic or nonzero-weight hybrid search uses `--refresh wait`.

This is separate from #821. That issue is about querying an already-ready semantic projection without a daemon. This issue is about making an explicit import leave enabled indexes ready before it returns.

## Expected behavior

For an explicit `ctx import` when semantic search is enabled:

1. Publish the requested Core/lexical generation.
2. Reconcile semantic coverage for that exact generation.
3. Return success only when both are ready.
4. If semantic work fails, preserve the valid lexical publication but return a clear typed semantic failure.

The same contract should apply in manual and automatic indexing modes. Automatic background refresh should remain asynchronous, and `--refresh off` should continue doing no work.

When semantic search is disabled, import behavior should remain unchanged.

## Acceptance coverage

- manual-mode import completes Core and semantic sequentially;
- automatic-mode explicit import waits for daemon semantic acknowledgement;
- semantic failure is visible rather than reported as full import success;
- empty semantic-eligible generations do not load a model unnecessarily;
- the semantic generation must exactly match the Core generation published for the import;
- background refresh remains non-blocking.

title: fix(daemon): cancel only owned finite foreground workers
body:
Fixes #820

## Root cause and fix

Finite manual workers used the persistent-daemon detached launch path. That discarded direct-child ownership, so an interrupted foreground command could not safely stop and reap only the worker it started.

This preserves direct-child authority only for the finite worker that actually wins singleton startup. On interruption, the foreground owner targets that worker's private process group, waits for it, and reaps the exact child; joined or persistent daemons remain observational and are never killed by this path. If graceful Ctrl-Break delivery fails on Windows, the bounded fallback terminates and reaps only that retained child handle.

The implementation keeps one interrupt broker at the foreground wait boundary and reuses the existing lifecycle model; it does not add a second process manager or broader kill mechanism.

## Provenance

The branch preserves Luca King's original contribution and authorship, then applies maintainer integration, test, and size-split commits on post-#821 `main`.

- exact candidate: `b5a260cb830cc54670052c10410cfbb07349ad12`

title: fix(refresh): make verified publication request-terminal
body:
Closes #819

## State-machine remediation

- cap production route coverage at the admission watermark when a newer exhaustive marker reappears; the original UUID remains terminal and the newer dirty revision is owned by a distinct exhaustive maintenance UUID
- restore exhaustive ownership for retryable routes after recovery from a crash between durable failed-terminal persistence and route finalization
- make `request_not_retained_after_restart` non-resubmittable and truthful: the acknowledged outcome is unknown and no longer observable, with no daemon restart or replay across client versions
- use strict publication ownership for ordinary Published and every metadata-owned Running recovery: request ID, operation, scope, generation, and receipt; metadata-free Published remains compatible and metadata-free Running replays conservatively
- remove production typed-unknown reenqueue machinery while retaining only cfg(test) lost-ack helpers

## Final-review remediation

- validate physical publication generation and receipt before decoding a logical Published `request_outcome`; a proven no-op binds to the physical receipt/generation and may carry a different logical request ID, operation, and scope
- keep every Running journal strict: terminal-only `request_outcome` data—null, malformed, or valid foreign data—fails closed before all recovery branches
- persist `route_finalization_pending: true` in the first durable Published/Failed terminal image and install that exact marker-bearing snapshot as the bounded durable-root owner under the engine lock, before queue advance, unlock, coverage sampling, or route disposition changes
- make admission, progress/status, retry, and scheduler persistence always publish that exact owner plus current successors during the ownership window; no writer can regenerate a markerless terminal from the mutable attempt
- let only the route-finalization writer project the second markerless image. The owner clears only after that image commits; failure atomically converts the same bounded owner into `FinalizationOnly`, retried before successors with no recapture, reexecution, Core reinstall, queue advance, or route refinalization
- preserve deferred `did_work` and coverage proof so generation notification/provider events occur exactly once after the corrected final image is durable
- on restart from a pending Failed image, conservatively rearm provisional stale automatic pauses and normalize the durable image without recapture
- align the daemon CLI assertion and stale client commentary with `request_outcome_unknown_after_acknowledgement`
- preserve legacy metadata-free Published compatibility, metadata-free Running replay, SelectedImport Exhaustive semantics, and the no-terminal-archive design

The finalization barrier coverage is split at the real crash boundary. In the pre-second-write test, the hook runs after the marker-bearing terminal write, the original writer panics before route finalization, and the test joins that terminated writer and drops the original engine before constructing a fresh engine. It then verifies the durable marker/original UUID, every successor, exact route dispositions and exhaustive obligations, one execution, one recovery finalization transition, and no duplicate notification. A separate post-second-write test lets the original writer complete and be dropped before restart. Together they cover Published/Failed x existing-successor/no-existing-successor x crash-before/crash-after (8 cases), including concurrent admission plus ordinary status, retry-status, and scheduler writers. The existing second-write failure matrix covers Published/Failed x successor/no-successor and proves one finalization-only retry with one notification.

The changed daemon wire remains schema v1 and is covered by inline old/new-client recovery fixtures. No metadata-version constant changed; the accepted v1-v4 metadata matrix remains in `ctx-history-refresh-execution`.

## Overflow stability root cause

The reproducible failure was test synchronization, not a product lost-wakeup race. Production first installs the synchronous overflow uncertainty fence, then retains the wake in the existing coalescing wake state/condvar; the dirty-route ledger retains maintenance ownership independently. The old test flooded a real filesystem callback backend and polled wall-clock state without an authoritative callback receipt, so OS scheduling could delay the overflow past its deadline.

The test now drives the exact production callback ingress through a small doc-hidden seam: one event blocks the worker at the existing barrier, exactly `WATCH_EVENT_QUEUE_CAPACITY + 1` further events establish one overflow synchronously, and the existing wake receipt must carry the fenced boundary before one recovery/admission/publication. There is no polling loop, retry loop, or enlarged success timeout; the remaining three-second wait is only a deadlock watchdog on the authoritative wake handoff.

## Red/green evidence

Focused red before remediation:

- exact old head `35cbd9aa55`: Bazel overflow test with `--runs_per_test=20 --cache_test_results=no` — 3 passed / 17 failed, all waiting for `overflow recovery and maintenance publication`
- `refresh_all_to_import_exact_no_op_restart_restores_queued_successor` — 0 passed / 1 failed: physical Refresh/All metadata was incorrectly compared with logical Import/Exact ownership
- `post_route_finalization_write_failure_retries_once_before_optional_successor` — 0 passed / 1 failed: successful pending retry refinalized routes and produced four terminal writes instead of the bounded three
- the previous crash-before barrier test was rejected on credibility because it recovered while the original writer was still blocked and later allowed that writer to perform the second write; the replacement terminates and drops that writer before recovery
- while tightening route-obligation assertions, the first exhaustive fixture run was 0 passed / 2 failed because the test had admitted an incremental periodic root; changing the fixture to a real exhaustive dirty-route admission made the asserted recovery obligation match the production contract

Focused green:

- `marker_terminal_recovers_after_true_pre_finalization_writer_termination` and `finalized_terminal_recovers_after_writer_completes_before_restart` — 2 passed / 0 failed, 8 internal barrier/crash cases

- `publication_metadata_ownership_rejects_table_driven_mismatches_for_terminal_and_running_recovery` — 1/1

title: fix: keep daemon-free semantic queries passive
body:
Closes #821.

Supersedes contributor PR #822 while preserving Yusoof Moh's authored replay as commit `64acb97154713ad130edfb0be13acb80ad5a0f64` (`Yusoof Moh <yusoofsh@users.noreply.github.com>`).

Rebased directly onto `89f751634a2518a227b2820fce11fe36ad310e09` (including #823, #836, #831, and #819). #830 remains separate.

## Remediation

- Daemon-free exact semantic preflight now holds the existing flat-store coordination lock read-only from sidecar inspection through immutable SQLite control/schema reads and flat-generation pinning. It refuses WAL and rollback-journal state, canonicalizes symlinked parent components, rejects a symlink final DB, preserves exact `OsString` sidecars, and never creates the coordination file.
- Ordinary daemon/Reconcile preflight remains WAL-aware. Executor fingerprint validation occurs inside the reconcile boundary immediately after lazy resolution and before acquisition, HTTP, writable store opens, embedding, or mutation. `ReadyEmpty` resolves no executor.
- Built-in passive loading is cache-only: CoreML consumes validated compiled artifacts (Auto canary failure falls back to cached CPU), Windows ML consumes an already-ready provider, and ONNX consumes an existing cache. Typed configuration/unavailable errors retain code/reason/retryability through CLI fallback policy.
- #823's foreground CPU default remains lazy and built-in-only; selected HTTP executor/auth is preserved. Passive mode performs no import completion or reconciliation.
- CLI/semantic executor/storage/daemon contract documentation now distinguishes passive snapshots from ordinary daemon reads.

title: Windows: source-backed refresh fails with ERROR_ACCESS_DENIED (os error 5) on the Codex prompt-history source, silently freezing the index
body:
## Summary

On `windows-x64`, every source-backed refresh fails with a bare `os error 5` originating from the Codex **prompt-history** source (`~/.codex/history.jsonl`, `source_format: codex_history_jsonl`, `schema_variant: codex-prompt-history-jsonl-v1`).

The failure is not a permissions problem. It reproduces with a **byte-identical copy of the file in a directory with no Deny ACEs**, and on a **virgin data root**.

Because the whole refresh aborts, **no new generation is ever published**. The index silently stops advancing while `ctx status` continues to report `Search ready`. On this machine the index sat frozen for three days before anyone noticed — `ctx search` kept answering, just with data that stopped at the moment of install.

## Environment

```
ctx           1.2.4 (also reproduced on 1.1.1)
platform      windows-x64
OS            Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200
install       managed: true, marker: valid
data root     C:\Users\<user>\.ctx
```

## Reproduction

Minimal case — a single 86-byte file is enough:

```bash
# 1. copy the codex prompt-history file somewhere with a plain, inherited ACL
cp ~/.codex/history.jsonl /tmp/codexclean/history.jsonl

# 2. import only that file into a data root
ctx --data-root /tmp/ctxtest import --path /tmp/codexclean/history.jsonl --provider codex --format json
```

Result:

```
Error: publish provider inputs through the Core refresh engine

Caused by:
    daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed (code=source_refresh_failed, class=internal,
    retryable=true, affected_routes=["4165f48f24d0b5b0d1f4727660c4584f4db2399ddab8ee0bc4ab47d223d7db79"],
    retryable_routes=[...], blocked_routes=[],
    retry_advice=Some("retry_request")):
    run capture-owned source-backed refresh: アクセスが拒否されました。 (os error 5)
```

(`アクセスが拒否されました` = "Access is denied" — the message is localized because it is a raw
Windows error surfaced through `std::io::Error`.)

The file content is a single valid line:

```json
{"session_id":"<uuid-redacted>","ts":<epoch-redacted>,"text":"/login"}
```

It also reproduces on a **fresh data root** with normal discovery (no `--path`): `ctx setup` indexes
Claude Code and Codex sessions successfully (495 sessions / 9,362 messages / 30,147 tool calls /
761 MiB), then fails on the prompt-history route and pauses it:

```json
{
  "status": "failed",
  "error_code": "source_refresh_failed",
  "last_error": "run capture-owned source-backed refresh: アクセスが拒否されました。 (os error 5)",
  "automatic_retry": {
    "state": "paused",
    "reason": "repeated_internal_failure",
    "confirmation_limit": 2,
    "routes": {
      "c635e6148bb3f3dede59fa1ef7671c23f40c8e46b8c0e18080e5abe46a8e9f6d": {
        "state": "paused", "matching_failures": 2, "build_version": "1.2.4"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

The route identity `c635e614…` is deterministic: it is the same id in a virgin store and in the
long-lived one, and the generation record attributes it to

```json
"sources": [{ "provider": "codex",
              "source_format": "codex_history_jsonl",
              "schema_variant": "codex-prompt-history-jsonl-v1" }]
```

## What this is not

Each of these was tested and ruled out:

| Hypothesis | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| File ACL / Deny ACEs | Byte-identical copy in a directory with **0 Deny ACEs** | **Still fails** (new route id) |
| File permissions | Opened all 800 files under the source trees with `FileShare.ReadWrite` | 800 openable, 0 failures |
| The file is locked by Codex | `File.Open` with share `None`/`Read`/`ReadWrite`/`Delete` | All succeed |
| Corrupted/stale store | Virgin data root built from scratch by 1.2.4 | **Still fails** |
| Single-file vs directory source | Imported the same copy via its **directory** path | **Still fails** |
| Disk / AV | 442 GB free; Defender Controlled Folder Access disabled | Not a factor |
| Caller identity | File owner is the invoking user, who holds `FullControl` | Not a factor |

## Impact

1. **Silent staleness.** The refresh aborts before publishing, so the last good generation keeps
   serving. `ctx status` shows `Search ready` with a full record count. The only hint is a
   `Refresh unavailable` / `partial` line. Users have no reason to suspect their history stopped
   three days ago.
2. **Wasted I/O.** Each attempt re-reads the full corpus (~600–790 MB) and writes a complete
   ~325 MB Tantivy generation, then discards it because certification never runs. On `auto` mode
   this repeats every few minutes, indefinitely.
3. **One route takes down every route.** 43 of 44 routes reconcile fine; the single failing route
   aborts the whole publication. This looks like the same class of problem as #664
   ("Claude route fails whole-tree on one bad file; Codex quarantines per file"), but on the
   publication path rather than the parse path.

## Diagnosability

The error carries **no path and no operation** — just `run capture-owned source-backed refresh:`
plus a raw OS error. There is no `RUST_LOG`/tracing hook in the shipped binary, and the daemon's
Windows Task Scheduler registration clears the environment down to 11 variables, so no env-based
diagnostic reaches the process that actually fails.

Identifying the responsible source required parsing
`search/lexical/ctx-generations/<generation>.json` by hand to map the route id to a source
descriptor. Attaching the offending path and the failing syscall to this error would have made
this a one-minute diagnosis.

## Suggested direction

- Wrap the failing filesystem call so the error names the path and operation.
- Consider quarantining a route that fails publication instead of aborting the whole generation,
  matching the per-file quarantine behavior Codex sources already have on the parse path (#664).
- Clarify the intended behavior once a route is paused. Observed here: one generation *was*
  published with the failing route's provider simply absent (Claude Code only, 304 sessions —
  Codex missing entirely), and after that every subsequent refresh failed again, so the index
  never advanced past that point. The result is a store that looks healthy, silently omits one
  provider, and stops taking updates.

I am happy to run further instrumented builds on this machine — it reproduces 100% of the time.

title: Reconsider the integrations and relations/cross-linking between the skill, mcp and cli
body:
Directly dumping the conversation, as I found my agent using the skill but not the MCP (and it is available).

```
  ❯ side question: I am curious, why you used "ctx" in shell, and not via the MCP tool? If it is not worth      10:43   ┃
    having the MCP I will uninstall it for ctx.                                                                         ┃
 ⌄ Thought for 13s                                                                                                      ┃
 │ I need to clarify the recommendation: Keep the MCP if the user wants an agent that can autonomously manage history,  ┃
 │ perform structured searches, and avoid shell parsing. If they only want to manually invoke context and minimize tool ┃
 │ usage, then uninstalling makes sense. Specifically, for context, the skill alone won’t execute history searches,     ┃
 │ but MCP allows that. It's worth noting that the overhead from tool descriptions is minimal. The user seems to be     ┃
 │ asking a conceptual question here.                                                                                   ┃
                                                                                                                        ┃
 ● I used the  ctx  shell command because the ctx skill explicitly documents and recommends the CLI workflow ( ctx      ┃
   status ,  ctx search ,  ctx show , and  ctx blame ). That was reasonable from the skill’s instructions, but given    ┃
   that a ctx MCP integration is available, it was not the best choice for this particular history lookup. I should     ┃
   have preferred the MCP tool first and used the CLI only if the MCP result was insufficient or unavailable.           ┃
                                                                                                                        ┃
   For  ctx , the distinction is:                                                                                       ┃
                                                                                                                        ┃
   • Skill only: gives the agent instructions for when and how to search history, but does not provide an executable    ┃
     history-search capability.                                                                                         ┃
   • MCP enabled: gives the agent structured history search, session/event inspection, provenance lookup, and           ┃
     potentially blame operations without shelling out or parsing CLI output.                                           ┃
   • CLI fallback: still useful for troubleshooting, commands not exposed by MCP, or when the MCP service is            ┃
     unavailable.                                                                                                       ┃
                                                                                                                        ┃
   My recommendation is to keep the ctx MCP enabled if you want agents to autonomously use prior conversation history.  ┃
   The system-context cost of the MCP description is generally much smaller than loading history content, which only    ┃
   happens when a tool is called. Uninstall it if you deliberately want history access to be manual-only or want to     ┃
   enforce that agents cannot search prior sessions by default.                                                         ┃
```

So if there are real benefits of using the MCP tool instead of shell 'ctx' executions (this statement requires proofs), the skill should suggest using the MCP first (if available).

ACs:
- Proofs the MCP is worth (token efficiency, robustness, ease of use) compared the CLI
- Proper "integration"/cross-linking between the Skill and the MCP (not only the CLI). Watch out because some users might not install the MCP.

title: Normalize OMP parentSession fork lineage
body:
## Problem

OMP 18.0.10 writes `parentSession` in two native forms: ordinary forks store the source session ID, while path-based branches store the source session path. The Pi adapter currently ignores both forms, so ctx publishes the child content but loses the normalized fork relationship.

Sanitized authentic OMP records reproduce both forms. They also confirm that an external or unavailable parent is a normal input shape, so treating unresolved lineage as a route failure would regress independent child publication.

## Impact

OMP fork and branch sessions appear unrelated in ctx even when both sides are present in the imported inventory. Historical navigation cannot recover the direct fork edge, and downstream consumers cannot distinguish a forked session from an independent session.

## Suggested fix

- Resolve a non-path `parentSession` only when it names one unique native session ID in the currently admitted Pi inventory.
- Resolve an absolute path only when its strict platform path identity names an admitted file and the OMP filename session ID agrees with the admitted header.
- Project `parent_session_id` with the `Forked` relationship, without inferring `root_session_id` or `agent_scope`.
- Abstain from lineage for missing, external, malformed, duplicate-key, oversized, self-referential, or cyclic claims while continuing to publish child content.
- Recompute the resolved edge from every admitted inventory so parent addition, removal, or replacement updates the child projection.

## Owner question

Would you agree with this bounded direct-edge contract for OMP, specifically that unsafe or unresolved claims should omit lineage rather than reject child content?

## Validation

A draft implementation includes sanitized authentic OMP 18.0.10 fixtures for ID forks, path branches, and missing parents, plus qualification coverage for resolution, deletion, ambiguity, cycles, oversized claims, and path/header identity mismatch.

title: feat(pi): normalize OMP fork lineage
body:
## Summary

- normalize OMP 18.0.10 `parentSession` ID forks and path branches against the admitted Pi inventory
- project a direct `Forked` relationship without inferring root or subagent metadata
- preserve child publication by abstaining on missing, malformed, ambiguous, oversized, self-referential, or cyclic claims
- add sanitized authentic OMP fixtures and advance the Pi parser revision

## Contract

ID claims resolve only to a unique admitted native session ID. Absolute path claims resolve only to an admitted strict platform path identity whose OMP filename suffix agrees with the admitted header session ID. The raw claim remains cache-only, while the resolved parent identity participates in the leaf binding so inventory changes replace affected child projections.

## Scope

This change is local to Pi source-backed discovery and projection. It does not infer transitive roots, classify OMP forks as subagents, preserve title values, or expand OMP source discovery.

Fixes #856.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-providers-jsonl-shared -p ctx-history-capture-composition-qualification --all-targets -- -D warnings`
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture-composition-qualification --test jsonl_publication` (47 passed)
