title: fix(platform): resolve managed root from home only
body:
## Summary

- Resolve the managed ctx lifecycle root with the platform home/profile API only.
- Stop requiring unrelated Windows roaming and local-app-data known folders when only the profile path is needed.
- Preserve the existing separation between custom CTX_DATA_ROOT commands and the canonical managed daemon root.

## Root cause

title: Manual incremental import scans ~12 GB and rereads the generation for a 325-event delta
body:
## Problem

A clean manual incremental import on current `main` still performs work proportional to the full corpus even when the actual delta is very small.

Tested commit: `d0296baa081f027d12657486e11ef9811b73c0a4`.

The isolated index already contained a successfully published generation. No previous worker was running or interrupted before this measurement.

## Environment

- Debian, 16 GiB RAM, ordinary SATA SSD
- isolated binary and data root; production CTX was untouched
- semantic search disabled
- manual indexing mode
- approximately 12.6 GB of certified source data
- 9,028 sources and 10,806 sessions
- Codex sessions were actively appending

## Observed behavior

A second clean:

```console
ctx --data-root <isolated-root> import --all --progress none --format json
```

completed successfully and published a new generation, but:

- total command wall time was 5m39s;
- the finite worker reported 11.7 GB `processed_bytes`;
- all 47 routes were scanned;
- only 6 sessions, 37 messages, and 143 tool calls were processed;
- the resulting index delta was only 325 searchable events and 0 sessions;
- the worker reached `published` after approximately 2m34s;
- the parent `ctx import` then remained active for roughly another three minutes;
- during that terminal phase, `/proc/<client-pid>/io` reached approximately 12.7 GB of physical reads.

One live Hermes SQLite source changed during its snapshot and was carried forward from the previous generation. The other 46 routes completed, and the new generation was published successfully.

A previous incremental run against the same generation family showed the same full-corpus scan and took approximately 15 minutes with a cold filesystem cache.

## Why this matters

Manual mode is intended for infrequent, demand-driven refreshes. On an active development host, only a handful of sessions may have changed, but each request still reads approximately the entire source corpus and then appears to reread a generation-sized amount of data during terminal verification.

This makes refresh cost primarily dependent on total retained history rather than the size of the delta.

## Expected direction

Could unchanged routes and already certified generation data avoid full byte-level rescanning during an incremental refresh?

It would also help if progress or phase attribution distinguished:

- source change detection;
- changed-source parsing;
- generation construction;
- post-publication or retained-generation verification.

This is separate from the old cold-import performance report in #306: cold-import performance has improved substantially. The remaining concern is the steady-state cost of a small incremental update.

title: Semantic search hard-fails for minutes after every Core generation on a busy auto-index machine
body:
## Problem

On ctx **1.2.4** with automatic indexing + semantic enabled, every new Core generation makes `--backend semantic` hard-fail until flat-F32 is pinned to that generation. Catch-up does succeed. The window is minutes, not a brief flicker, and it repeats as often as live agent transcripts publish a new Core gen.

This is **not** #658 (ONNX `dlopen` / `model_load_failed`). Runtime here is CoreML `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small`; after catch-up, `ctx semantic status` is `ready` and semantic queries return hits.

This is **not** #792. Catch-up acknowledges the new generation; there is no stuck `source-backed semantic manifest identity` failure.

It is the leftover of #814 / #826. v1.2.4 notes say search now waits for semantic catch-up "avoiding a brief window where search could use the previous generation." On a machine that ingests Claude/Cursor/OpenCode continuously, that window is the common case, and there is no way to use the previous pinned projection while catch-up runs.

## Environment

- ctx 1.2.4, macOS arm64, daemon mode `full`, indexing `auto`, semantic enabled, `local_only`
- Model: `e5-small-v1:mean-pool:l2:query-passage`, CoreML (`coreml-native:0.2.0`)
- Corpus at last ready state: ~836 sessions, ~9.9k semantic docs, ~9.0k projected events

## What happens

1. Live ingest publishes Core generation `N`.
2. `semantic.status` / `flat_f32.status` stay `pending` until catch-up pins flat-F32 to `N`.
3. `ctx search --backend semantic` returns `semantic_generation_not_acknowledged` (flat-F32 missing, stale, partial, or not pinned to `N`). Lexical still works.
4. A later Core generation `N+1` can publish before `N` is ever acknowledged, so that generation is skipped rather than served.

Measured on 2026-09-01 (KST):

| t | event |
|---|---|
| 20:19:28 | Core gen `579ed7b6` published |
| 20:22:29–20:26:17 | semantic queries fail (`semantic_generation_not_acknowledged`, not pinned to `579ed7b6`); ~10 samples over ~4 min |
| 20:30:09 | Core gen `aeef8985` published (`579ed7b6` never acknowledged; superseded after ~10.7 min) |
| 20:30:22 | semantic catch-up ready; subsequent `--backend semantic` returns 10 hits |

Same error on this machine: 2026-08-23 (gens `df9cbe0c`, `2a6cb67d`) and 2026-08-30 (gen `87d81a66`).

`flat_generation` moved 1631 → 4733 over ~6 days (~every 5–6 min on average). That increment tracks real Core publications from live ingest, not no-op source retries.

There is no config to delay Core publish until semantic is pinned, or to serve the previous pinned generation during catch-up.

## Expected

One of:

1. **Stale-while-revalidate** — while catch-up is in progress, `--backend semantic` (and hybrid) serve the last pinned generation, with a warning that results may lag the latest Core gen. `--refresh wait` can still block until the new pin.
2. **Pin-before-publish** — do not make Core gen `N` the active search generation until flat-F32 is pinned to `N`.
3. **Typed fallback** — if exact-generation preflight fails only because catch-up is running, default hybrid should use lexical (or the previous pin) instead of failing the whole query. Strict `--backend semantic` can keep the typed error if that must stay exact.

Right now a busy auto-index install is semantically unavailable for several minutes after each ingest, which agents then report as "semantic is broken."

## Reproduction

1. `ctx index mode auto` + semantic enabled, wait until `ctx semantic status` is `ready`.
2. Produce new events in a supported provider (Claude Code / Cursor / OpenCode session write).
3. As soon as `ctx status` shows a new Core generation, run:
   `ctx search "probe" --backend semantic --refresh off --format json`
4. Observe `semantic_generation_not_acknowledged` until catch-up completes (here: 2–11 min). Repeat on the next ingest.

## Related

- #814 / PR #826 — wait for catch-up after refresh (ships in 1.2.4). Fixes the wait boundary; does not restore availability during the wait on a high-churn corpus.
- #792 / PR #795 — generation identity during catch-up (not this failure).
- #658 — ONNX `dlopen` on Tahoe (not this machine).

title: Move telemetry delivery out of interactive command paths
body:
Interactive commands should not perform telemetry network I/O. Even a short HTTP deadline couples command latency and shutdown behavior to a remote service.

## Required behavior

- Interactive commands only append an already-normalized event with a stable event ID to a durable local outbox, then continue without opening a telemetry connection.
- The daemon/background owner is the sole delivery owner and drains the outbox asynchronously.
- Each delivery attempt has one deadline covering the whole HTTP operation (connect, request, response, and body handling), not separate unbounded phases.
- Retry handling distinguishes permanent from retryable failures, honors bounded `Retry-After`, and uses capped exponential backoff with jitter.
- At-least-once delivery is harmless through stable event IDs and server idempotency.
- The outbox has explicit size/age bounds, crash-safe writes, single-owner locking, opt-out/delete behavior, and deterministic shutdown/interrupt behavior.
- Tests cover offline operation, restart recovery, duplicate delivery, malformed records, backpressure, `Retry-After`, deadline expiry, and opt-out.

## Out of scope

- Changing telemetry event content or opt-in policy.
- Replacing the server-side durable ingestion queue.
- Blocking interactive commands on a successful telemetry upload.

title: Small incremental refresh still performs generation-sized copy work
body:
## Problem

#863 fixed the post-publication predecessor rehash reported in #859, and #510 fixed the route-selection problem reported in #507. Both improvements are visible on the current build: a small refresh identifies only the changed sessions, publishes successfully, and no longer leaves a long terminal tail.

However, creating the next generation for a very small delta still appears to perform work proportional to the retained generation rather than to the delta.

Tested commit: `370ab3948cb05a05d3c1207e113ffb47912ff58a` (`ctx 1.3.0`).

## Environment

- Debian box with 16 GiB RAM and a SATA SSD
- semantic search disabled
- manual refresh, persistent daemon disabled
- about 13 GB of certified source data
- about 11,000 sessions and 1.6 million searchable documents
- several Codex sessions can be actively appended while CTX refreshes

## Reproduction

Starting from a healthy, fully imported generation, run:

```console
ctx import --all --progress none --quiet
```

Only four changed sessions were processed. The published result added one session and 109 searchable events.

## Observed

- refresh completed successfully in about 4 minutes
- it consumed about 3 minutes of CPU time
- cgroup peak memory was about 6 GiB
- the receipt reported about 12 GB of `processed_bytes`
- `scan_stage` accounted for about 2 minutes 37 seconds
- progress spent substantial time in `source_family_copy`, including retained provider data
- before exit, the parent process had accumulated about 4 GB of physical reads

For comparison, the cold import of the same 13 GB corpus completed in about 12 minutes. A delta of 109 searchable events therefore cost roughly one third of a cold import.

There was no correctness failure in this run: all routes completed, the new generation was published, search used the new data, and no worker was left behind.

## Question

Is generation-sized `source_family_copy` work expected for every incremental publication?

The source qualification and predecessor-validation fixes now correctly narrow the changed input. The remaining cost seems to be in materializing the next immutable generation. Could unchanged source families or index segments be reused by reference, reflink, hard link, or another copy-on-write mechanism so refresh cost scales closer to the changed data?

If a full logical copy is currently required by design, it would also help for progress and receipts to distinguish logical retained bytes from bytes physically read or rewritten. At present, `processed_bytes` makes a tiny delta look like a full source reprocessing pass even though route selection itself is working correctly.

title: Prevent active-generation search races during continuous publication
body:
## Problem

When automatic daemon maintenance publishes immutable lexical generations while a search is opening the active generation, ordinary CLI and MCP reads can repeatedly fail with the retryable `active_generation_race` response instead of pinning one stable published generation.

This reproduced on `main` commit `85785ca6c` with a fresh daemon whose executable identity matched its lock. Eight bounded `--refresh off` searches during normal continuous publication produced six successes and two caller-visible generation races. The affected index reader and generation code is unchanged at current `main` commit `4848bd04f`.

## Impact

Read-only search becomes intermittently unavailable during ordinary background indexing. Retrying at the caller can lose the same race again, and compact or human presentation can independently race while opening the retained peer.

## Expected behavior

A reader should select and retain one immutable published generation for its complete lifetime, including any retained peer needed for compact identity presentation. Publication may make results slightly stale, but it should not reclaim a generation from a live reader.

## Suggested fix

- Give active and exact `VerifiedIndex` readers process-scoped generation read leases.
- Acquire the selected active generation and its retained peer as one reader-owned pair.
- Retry the active selection window once when publication evicts the target or holds its reclamation range, then preserve the existing typed generation-change error as the bounded fallback.
- Open compact presentation peers through the reader-owned lease instead of mutable active-pointer state.
- When pointer-bound certification races with managed hard-link topology changes, verify the immutable leased slot directly against its published physical digest.

## Validation

A focused implementation adds deterministic coverage for active and exact reader lifetime, publication during selection and verification, reclamation-lock conflicts, retained-peer lifetime, and machine, compact, and human reads across two rotations. On the optimized build, 64 equivalent searches against an owner-verified automatic daemon completed successfully with zero generation races or timeouts.

title: fix(index): lease active generation readers
body:
## Summary

- retain process-scoped leases inside active and exact `VerifiedIndex` readers
- select and lease the retained compact/human presentation peer with the target reader
- retry the generation-selection window once only when the observed publication pointer changes
- transfer the peer lease into the returned peer reader and verify/certify its immutable bytes before use
- remove the old unleased peer-opening path and keep retry policy inside `VerifiedIndex`

## Scope

This is reader lifecycle wiring around the existing generation lease primitive. It adds no daemon, protocol, journal, background worker, persistent state, or caller-level retry loop.

Fixes #870.

title: Manual import waits about a minute after successful publication and finite-worker exit
body:
## Problem

With the persistent daemon disabled, a successful manual import can remain active for another 60–95 seconds after the refresh receipt is already terminal and the finite worker reports itself stopped.

This is distinct from the predecessor rehash fixed by #863 and the unchanged SQLite source copies fixed by #869. The new generation is already published and searchable during the remaining wait.

Tested commit: `4848bd04f63b4ee601514f23d35d9aba5dc48572` (`ctx 1.3.0`).

## Environment

- Debian box with 16 GiB RAM and a SATA SSD
- manual indexing mode
- persistent daemon disabled
- semantic search disabled
- about 13 GB of certified source data
- several Codex sessions actively appending

## Reproduction

Starting from a healthy published generation:

```console
ctx import --all --progress none --quiet
```

## Observed

Four consecutive small-delta imports completed correctly, but two isolated runs and two production runs showed a long terminal wait:

| Run | Receipt elapsed | Command wall time | Wait after receipt |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Isolated data root | 1m28s | 2m35s | about 67s |
| Isolated data root, `CTX_ANALYTICS_ENABLED=false` | 1m10s | 2m34s | about 84s |
| Production data root via a oneshot systemd unit | 1m16s | 2m22s | about 66s |
| Production data root with process-tree I/O sampling | 1m07s | 2m44s | about 93s |

All runs exited 0. The sampled production run processed five changed sessions and 35 messages, reported no source failures, and left the service successful.

During the isolated run, the finite worker's lifecycle status was already `stopped` while the foreground `ctx import` process continued waiting. The exited child was briefly visible as a zombie and was reaped only when the foreground command returned.

A 200 ms cgroup process-tree sampler confirmed that the terminal wait is active I/O rather than an idle wait. After the receipt became `completed`:

- the foreground `ctx import` process performed about 6.1 GiB of physical reads and 6.7 GiB of syscall-level reads;
- sequential file-position movement attributed about 5.1 GiB to the current lexical index generation;
- the finite worker performed only about 32 KiB of physical reads in the same phase.

Disabling analytics did not remove the delay, so this does not appear to be telemetry delivery. The I/O attribution also suggests that the expensive read happens in foreground post-publication cleanup or shutdown rather than in the finite refresh worker.

## Expected

After the requested generation has been published and the owned finite worker has stopped, the foreground import should reap it and return promptly without rereading a generation-sized portion of the lexical index.

Could this post-publication read be avoided, or at least attributed in progress or diagnostics?

title: First read after refresh revalidates the retained generation
body:
## Problem

On current `main`, the foreground import now returns promptly after publication, so the lifecycle delay from #872 is fixed. However, the generation-sized verification cost can reappear on the first read after refresh.

In particular, `ctx search --refresh wait` completed its refresh and published a new generation, then spent about another 90 seconds before returning search results. During that interval, the retained predecessor's physical certification was rewritten and a generation-sized amount of index data was read.

Tested commit: `b575c6ca6` (`ctx 1.3.1`).

## Environment

- fresh isolated data root
- manual indexing mode
- semantic search disabled
- about 13 GiB of certified agent-history sources
- about 7 GiB lexical index
- several Codex sessions actively appending
- Debian, 16 GiB RAM, SATA SSD

## Reproduction

Starting from a healthy data root with an existing published generation:

```console
ctx import --all --progress none
ctx search "generation-sized copy work" --refresh wait
```

## Observed

The incremental refresh triggered by the search processed six changed sessions and about 13,500 new messages:

- refresh receipt reached `completed` in about 2m25s;
- the foreground search returned in about 3m54s;
- the additional post-receipt delay was about 90s;
- the retained predecessor's certification sidecar was rewritten when the search finally returned;
- no worker or zombie process remained afterward;
- `ctx doctor` remained clean.

The same behavior was visible more directly after the preceding incremental import. The first `ctx show event` took about one minute and accumulated about 5.8 GiB of physical reads while opening the lexical generations. The retained predecessor certification appeared at completion. Repeating the identical `ctx show event` immediately afterward took 2.8 seconds.

This suggests that the safe full-verification fallback is still reached when a reader spans generation publication, possibly because the read lease or reclamation changes the retained predecessor identity. That is an inference from the timing, I/O, and certification-sidecar lifecycle rather than a confirmed code-level cause.

## Expected

Certification preserved across publication and reclamation should remain reusable by the first post-refresh reader. `search --refresh wait` should proceed to search shortly after the refresh receipt becomes terminal instead of paying another generation-sized verification cost.

Could the retained-reader/reclamation path preserve the predecessor certification in this case, or expose why it deliberately falls back to full verification?

title: test(daemon): stabilize terminal upgrade event observation
body:
## Summary
- replace the one-shot sink read with one shared-deadline observation of durable applied state, replacement ownership, the attempt-matched terminal event, and original-child exit
- retain exact `count == 1`: reject duplicate matches within either transport and accept one delivered/outbox overlap only for the same nonempty event ID and exact complete raw JSON record bytes
- bound the test-owned `ctx daemon disable` child with explicit spawn, `try_wait`, direct-child kill, and reap deadlines before continuing through the identity-verified daemon fallback
- use one explicit daemon data root for launch, observation, identity verification, disable, fallback signals, panic cleanup, and artifact cleanup
- explicitly stop and prove the replacement dead before the final event recount
- test-only change; no runtime, daemon, upgrade, release, pipeline, threshold, or unrelated-test behavior changes

## Root cause
`finalize_automatic_applied` durably records `applied`, resumes the daemon handoff, and only afterward emits the terminal upgrade event. Event emission durably appends the batch to the analytics outbox. The replacement drains that outbox asynchronously; the file transport writes the body and newline separately, flushes, and only then can reconciliation remove the queued entry.

The old harness read analytics once. Its sink-first fallback could let an already-created sink mask the attempt terminal event still in the durable queue. A queue-to-sink transition could also be sampled between those states, while a concurrent body/newline append could expose partial JSON. This is a harness observation race; production behavior is unchanged.

## Final independent findings closed
1. The cleanup path no longer calls unbounded `.output()`. It converts the prepared test command to a direct `std::process::Command` with null stdio, polls its owned `Child` for 12s, calls `Child::kill()` on expiry, and polls for at most 1s to reap it. Spawn, poll, kill, or reap failure is explicit. Even when that bounded command fails or times out, cleanup continues through the existing daemon fallback. The fallback verifies current lock owner, data root, recorded binary, and live executable before TERM and re-verifies before KILL; there is no unverified PID-only signal path.
2. Delivered records retain the exact complete line bytes while also parsing JSON for event matching. String-backed outbox entries retain the exact queued payload bytes while parsing separately. A delivered/queued overlap collapses only when both event IDs are identical and nonempty and both exact raw byte sequences match. A legacy object-backed queue entry has no recoverable original byte sequence and therefore cannot collapse against a delivered record. Same-source duplicates remain errors. The focused contract proves that semantically equal JSON with different key order and whitespace is rejected.

## Previously closed safeguards retained
- `DaemonTestRoot` owns `<temp>/data`; replacement status, active lock identity, disable, guarded TERM/KILL, Drop, and artifact removal all use that stored root.
- The observed replacement PID must equal the active lock PID and its live executable must match `ctx-test-copy` before normal cleanup.
- `waitpid(WNOHANG)` reaps only a child. `ECHILD` is accepted only after an independent liveness check proves the already identity-checked PID is gone.
- Delivered-file observation retries a snapshot with a partial trailing record. Queue-first observation remains race-safe because successful delivery flushes before outbox reconciliation.
- The final terminal-event recount occurs only after replacement stop and death/reap proof.

## Truthful timeout bounds
All harness polling waits are finite. The main durable-state/replacement/event/original-exit observation uses one shared 45s deadline.

For normal cleanup, the bounded disable child contributes at most 12s, plus at most 1s only when it must be killed and reaped. A normally exited disable command can be followed by at most 5s cooperative daemon-exit wait, 1s after identity-verified TERM, and 5s after identity-reverified KILL. Those branches make the maximum configured normal cleanup wait 23s, so observation plus normal cleanup is at most 68s of configured waits.

If disable is stuck acquiring `DaemonLifecycleControlLock`, it is killed and reaped by 13s and skips the cooperative 5s wait; the verified TERM/KILL fallback adds at most 6s, for a 19s configured stuck-lock cleanup bound. The immediate ECHILD liveness proof adds no wait. The panic worst case is 45s observation + 23s first guard cleanup + 5s direct-child reap + 23s root-guard retry = 96s of configured waits. The Bazel target has a 900s medium timeout.

title: Semantic asset catalog is unpublished on every platform at 1.3.1, so built-in provisioning never starts
body:
## Observation

`ctx semantic enable --executor builtin` succeeds on 1.3.1, then parks at `pending` with `Reason lexical_generation_unavailable`, and no model or runtime assets ever appear under the data root. Verified on a throwaway `CTX_DATA_ROOT` so no earlier state was involved.

The stable metadata document publishes no semantic keys at all:

```console
$ curl -sS https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v1/releases/stable/ctx-release-metadata.env | grep -ciE 'onnx|semantic'
0
```

The families that are published are `CTX_RELEASE_{SCHEMA_VERSION,CHANNEL,VERSION,ARTIFACT_*,SHA256_*,MANAGED_PAIR_*,SELF_*,AUTO_*,BASE_URL,SOURCE_*,PUBLISHED_*}`. The `beta` channel returns an empty document.

Both key families the provisioning path needs are missing. `scripts/semantic-release-assets.py` emits:

```
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_ASSETS
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_AUTHORITY_
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_SCHEMA_VERSION
```

and the installed 1.3.1 binary reads those alongside the older sidecar set:

```console
$ rg -ao 'CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_[A-Z_]*|CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_[A-Z_]*|ctx-onnxruntime-[a-z0-9-]*' ~/.local/bin/ctx | sort -u
CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_ARTIFACT_
CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_SHA
CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_VERSION
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_ASSETS
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_AUTHORITY_
CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_SCHEMA_VERSION
ctx-onnxruntime-linux-x64-cuda12
ctx-onnxruntime-windows-x64
```

`ctx-release-metadata.env` under `functions/v1/releases/<channel>/` is the only metadata path in the binary, so there is no alternate catalog for it to read.

At 1.1.1 the same endpoint listed six `CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_ARTIFACT_*` entries with `.tar.gz` names, while HEAD builds `.tar.zst`. That reads like a catalog scheme migration whose publication step has not landed rather than a plain omission, but I cannot tell from outside which it is.

## Upgrade side effect

Upgrading 1.1.1 to 1.3.1 failed closed:

```text
release 1.3.1 is newer than this ctx build but has no complete ONNX Runtime sidecar metadata; refusing a downgrade-compatible legacy update
```

`ctx upgrade status` reported `state error` while `ctx upgrade check` reported an available release, so `upgrade.auto = "apply"` stalled quietly for about a week. Recovery needed `ctx daemon disable --prepare-uninstall`, moving the executable and its marker aside, then rerunning the hosted installer. A plain installer rerun first refused with `prior managed integration ownership is not bound to its marker`.

If the absence is intentional for now, a typed unavailable reason from `ctx semantic enable` and `ctx semantic status` would be clearer than the current `lexical_generation_unavailable`, which points at history rather than at asset availability.

## Request for `linux-x64-cuda12` when the catalog is published

This follows #717. Detection is no longer the gap: #749 recognizes WSL2 GPU forwarding, and the pipeline at HEAD still targets the accelerator. `scripts/construct-semantic-release-catalog.sh` enumerates `linux-x64-cuda12` in its platform loop, `scripts/onnxruntime-sidecar/release_manifest.sh` gives it `runtime_backend="cuda"`, `catalog_role="accelerator"`, `catalog_backend="ort-cuda"`, bundled CUDA provider libraries, and NVIDIA license documents, and the catalog validates a separate `ctx-multilingual-e5-small-onnx-o4-fp16-1.0.0.tar.xz` accelerator model variant.

From the outside the remaining step looks like publication alone. On this host the CUDA execution provider measured 21x faster than the CPU provider at seq=128 and 5x at seq=512 against the same cached `model.onnx` (numbers and method in #717), so the accelerator entry is the difference between semantic indexing that keeps up with daily use and one that does not.

## Environment

ctx 1.3.1, Linux x64 under WSL2 (kernel 6.18), hosted installer, channel stable, 14,403 sessions and 5.19M searchable events in the lexical index.

Released payload-v2 envelopes include publication metadata and can exceed the current payload limit. The current decoder rejects those envelopes before reporting their unsupported version, preventing source-authoritative index recovery.

Recognize the bounded released envelope as an unsupported payload so the existing recovery path builds a current generation from provider sources. title: fix(import): preserve direct JSONL order and valid result records
body: Direct JSONL session order follows physical records and result-block order while event identities remain stable. Oversized native event keys reject their physical record without stopping valid neighboring history. title: Use positive filters to skip unrelated lexical postings
body:
A lexical search scoped to a small session could exhaust its candidate budget on earlier body matches outside that session in the same index segment. Required positive filter postings now supply a lower bound for metered body seeks, so unrelated intervals do not consume the candidate budget. In a 17-document single-segment fixture with normal budgets, the selected-session query examines 17→1 candidates and makes 17→2 body cursor movements; broad-query work is unchanged. With CandidateDocs capped at two, the baseline instead admits two candidates and returns empty with budget exhaustion; the fix admits one candidate and returns the expected scoped event exhaustively.

Preserve OR membership within each positive group, intersections across fields, negative and substring predicates, corpus-wide scoring, deterministic ordering, and all existing work ceilings. Every posting probe, seek and advance remains charged before execution. Five focused tests cover independent expected membership, early OR/AND convergence, disjoint and missing groups, ranking parity, and finite posting/candidate exhaustion boundaries.

Validation: the test-only baseline reproduced the small-budget failure after physical topology and normal-budget membership controls passed. The fix passed nine query unit tests and 141 writer integration tests with strict Clippy. All 108 graph-selected targets passed on the original tested inputs. Both later rebases preserve the complete query crate and patch bytes; seven direct consumers passed on the intermediate base, and four CLI/setup/refresh targets passed on the latest base. Independent source review found no interaction between the later setup, companion-routing or refresh-terminal changes and the preserved lexical traversal evidence.

title: Repair interrupted managed-pair publication copies
body:
A process interruption during managed-pair publication can leave a partial temporary file that prevents every repair retry. Recovery now recreates empty or matching-prefix temporaries from retained verified inputs under the installation lock, while retaining rejection of unrelated content, links, and unsafe files.

Validated with the owning 18-test suite and a Linux process-termination regression: the baseline retains a 128-KiB partial copy and fails recovery; the candidate completes the same retained attempt. Coverage includes every publication slot, already-current targets, invalid retained inputs, and temporary-file rejection. This does not claim Windows/macOS native or power-loss qualification.

title: Preserve refresh journal errors and report effective retry status
body:
Unreadable or malformed refresh journals now propagate an error during recovery instead of being treated as an absent queue. This preserves unknown admitted work until the journal can be read again, using the existing strict reader.

Status and retry advice now reflect the current indexing policy and running owner. With a running manual worker, status recognizes already-admitted work, including queued successors retained beneath a terminal root. When no worker is running, it recommends an explicit request. Historical retry checkpoints remain available without promising unscheduled automatic work.

Validation: the original journal/status failures and the terminal-root successor regression reproduced before the fixes. The three owning suites passed 570 tests, and owning Clippy passed. The changes add no scheduler or new persistence protocol.

title: Bound history-source header reads before buffering
body:
History-source imports could buffer an entire oversized header line before
rejecting it. Cap each read at the smaller of the remaining 1 MiB header
budget and the 256 KiB line budget, plus one byte to detect overflow. Rejection
stops reading immediately; a valid early header still permits a large export.

Counting-reader tests exercise the production validation loop, including exact
and overflowing line/total boundaries, EOF, and an early header with an 8 MiB
body. Application-port and CLI tests verify rejection before source admission
and without Core publication.

Validation: the old loop failed the two byte-consumption regressions while 215
CLI unit cases passed. With the cap, all 217 CLI units, four request-parity
cases, and five plugin CLI contracts passed. The oversized-line case now
consumes 262,145 bytes, with at most one fixed buffer of physical prefetch.
The retained history CLI Cargo, Bazel, and source boundary check also passed.
All 78 normal graph-selected targets passed across preserved admitted runs.
The SDK package passed its exact default-Debug retry; an upgrade fixture retry
passed after removing the artifact harness's global semantic-runtime override.
Both original failures and the environment-only correction are retained in the
validation packet; no product assertions or source were changed for those retries.

Preserve those values in the Rust, TypeScript, Python, Go, JVM and .NET SDKs, including Rust complete and paged session paths. Rust protocol decoding now distinguishes a present JSON null from an absent field.

Preserve producer retry decisions and structured diagnostics under details.producerError. Place search options before the literal query terminator in SDK arguments and generated CLI followups. Clarify that ctx honors explicitly configured external semantic execution.

Each queued analytics batch is now owned by the existing random data-root identifier. Enqueue, delivery, targeted purge, and delivery-health counters use that owner. The uploader rechecks the current identity and consent before each request, so an enabled root only delivers its own batches. An in-flight request may finish.

title: fix(swift): preserve event payloads, retry errors, and literal queries

Swift shown events now retain opaque `activity` and `structuredContent` values, including original keys and present JSON nulls. CLI failures preserve the producer error object and its retryability. Search queries follow all options and `--`, and leading-hyphen option values remain literal.

The patch adds regressions at the existing injected-runner and DTO boundaries. The unmodified shared activity fixture is checked through event, window and session responses; malformed producer diagnostics retain the standard process-error fallback.

Remove the obsolete Swift compatibility exceptions from the Swift and shared contract documentation.

title: Preserve durable refresh identity and pending setup status
body:
Concurrent refresh callers could receive another caller's ID, and automatic background responses could appear accepted without a durable request. Each accepted caller now retains its original identity. Compatible callers admitted before a full-catalog capture share its verified publication, with durable completion recorded separately for each caller.

A strictly typed forgotten response permits one retry with the original ID and parameters. Optional background search can read an existing committed generation when the eight-request queue is full, reporting `admission_rejected` without an accepted ID or receipt. Wait/import and searches without a readable generation still fail on overload; malformed or unconfirmed responses remain errors. Setup reports active background work as pending when its captured freshness is pending.

Validation: `bash scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` passed the physical Rust crate-size preflight, Clippy build, and all 211 CI test targets (207 executed, four cached). Owning regressions cover real discovered-source captures, distinct caller IDs, late appends and generation pins, persistence failures and restart, bounded recovery, overload, and setup readiness. Durable admission adds per-caller persistence work; restart can repeat physical work within the existing receipt-retention bounds.

title: Make ctx doctor show actionable information
body:
By default I get this useless message:

```bash
>  ctx doctor
! ctx found 1 issue

Configuration
Automatic upgrades  apply

Issues
[1] History refresh is partial
  The component is not ready.

Hint: Resolve the issues above, then check again.

Next

```

However, when I output in JSON mode I find that the cause is "provider SQLite scratch has insufficient free-space headroom... : required 16019288989, available 7329218560" with the given provider. _That_ I can act on.

title: Remove generic locality fields from status and all seven SDKs
body:
Generic status returned a `local_only`/`localOnly` property even though status alone cannot establish where configured semantic execution runs. Remove that property from CLI/MCP status and setup, usage/error receipts, index readiness/mode/wait, daemon command receipts, and all seven SDK DTOs and normalizers. Older status payloads lose both spellings only at the generic status root; semantic diagnostics and opaque captured JSON retain their existing handling.

This is a breaking cleanup. Raw status/setup moves to schema 3; the affected usage/error, index, and daemon envelopes move to schema 2. The experimental in-repo `agent-history-v1` contract retains schema 1 with an explicit documented exception to its required-field rule. Callers must remove property reads, constructor arguments, and required-field checks, and update CLI schema-version checks. Standalone semantic execution diagnostics, stats, uninstall receipts, stored visibility/sync values, and privacy controls retain their separate contracts.

Validation: three targeted baseline regressions compiled and failed at the intended CLI/SDK/protocol assertions. Fixed Rust/protocol/presentation and both Go owners passed; TypeScript passed 39 tests plus typecheck, Python passed 40 tests, and ordinary JVM and .NET owning suites passed. Native Swift XCTest passed 25 tests with five existing Darwin-only skips. The normal affected selector chose 88 tests. The initial run passed 83; five suites had stale schema expectations. Those expectations were corrected, and all five owning suites plus four docs/policy/format checks passed. The final selector chose the same 88 targets; unaffected passing evidence was retained. title: Route stable upgrades through the bridge and complete the first managed pair

Stable clients use the v2 update endpoint so the original endpoint can remain on a frozen bridge release. Staging keeps its existing route and signature verification uses the existing trust key.

Hosted installations that reached the bridge without a companion can now finish their first managed pair through ordinary upgrade, including when the offered version equals the installed version. title: Retire pre-bridge upgrade handling from current releases

The preserved 1.3.2 bridge takes clients from the original stable feed onto v2. Advance current source to 1.3.3 and remove the v0.25 startup adapter, historical daemon takeover paths, obsolete dependencies and fixtures. Current upgrades keep managed-pair recovery, all-root daemon handoff and digest-verified process handling.

title: fix(semantic): prevent tokenizer truncation of document chunks
body:
Semantic indexing split documents by character count, allowing complete prepared inputs to exceed the built-in model's 512-token limit and lose body text to tokenizer truncation.

Fit built-in chunks against the loaded tokenizer, preserve fitting windows, and use bounded smaller windows when needed. Check again before inference, reuse compatible vectors before fitting, and rebuild derived built-in semantic indexes under the revised policy. Original history and HTTP executor preprocessing remain unchanged.

Validated owning and affected tests and actual-model coverage regressions.

title: Claude session titles show as - and --title returns 0 (thorough fix)
body:
## Problem Statement

As a ctx user browsing Claude Code / Claude Desktop history, I see `-` in the Session Title column for sessions that visibly have a title in the native transcript, and filtering by that title returns nothing. The concrete witness is a TradingAgents session titled `Trading agents candidate review` (662-line transcript, 32 title rows from line 11 onward): it is indexed and full-text searchable, but its session title is absent on every event and `--title` never matches it. Users cannot rely on session lists or title search for Claude, while Codex and Antigravity titles work.

## Solution

From the user's perspective: after the fix, any Claude session that declares a title anywhere in its transcript shows that same title on the session in `sessions` output and is found by title-substring search, on par with Codex. Re-importing after the fix backfills titles without manual per-file work. Title-only rows remain non-searchable records (as today) but still contribute the session title.

## User Stories

1. As a Claude Desktop user, I want my custom session title to appear in the session list, so that I can recognize past work.
2. As a Claude Code user, I want AI-generated titles to appear when I did not set a custom title, so that untitled sessions are still distinguishable.
3. As a CLI user running sessions with no query, I want titled Claude sessions to show titles instead of `-`, so that scanning is useful.
4. As a CLI user running sessions with a free-text query, I want the matched Claude session to still show its title, so that context is preserved.
5. As a CLI user running search with a title filter, I want title-substring matches to include Claude sessions, so that title search works across providers.
6. As a user with a long session where the title is declared mid-file, I want early messages to carry the final title too, so that the session has one stable title.
7. As a user with subagent sessions, I want parent and child sessions to each resolve their own titles correctly, so that delegation does not leak titles.
8. As a user re-importing after upgrade, I want existing Claude sources to be recertified automatically, so that I do not need manual reset.
9. As an import operator, I want title-only rows to stay rejected as records while still contributing titles, so that rejection diagnostics stay clean.
10. As a Codex user, I want no regression in Codex title behavior, so that the fix is Claude-scoped.
11. As an Antigravity user, I want no regression in first-prompt/checkpoint title fallbacks, so that provider parity holds.
12. As a daemon operator, I want background refresh to pick up the fix without source-changed failures when Claude is idle, so that rollout is smooth.
13. As a downstream consumer of session JSON, I want `session_title` present whenever the provider declared one, so that automation can rely on it.
14. As a user with 10k+ untitled Claude transcripts, I want untitled sessions to keep showing `-` rather than invented titles, so that absence stays truthful.
15. As a support engineer, I want a clear distinction between content matches and title matches in results, so that debugging is straightforward.

## Implementation Decisions

- Treat the Claude session title as session-scoped metadata, not row-sequential state: the final adjudicated title for the source applies uniformly to all retained events in that source, matching the existing Codex owner-title semantic.
- Observe title metadata before applying record-shape rejection in both the preflight planning pass and the source-backed projection pass, so title-only declarations are never lost to the empty-row rejection path.
- Preserve the existing title tier priority (custom over AI-generated over agent name) and same-tier timestamp tie-break; no change to adjudication semantics, only to coverage and timing.
- Keep the existing Core activity fact category for session titles and the existing indexed title field; no schema or wire-format change. Session-level display continues to read from the event fact, which becomes consistent once all events share the final title.
- Keep title-only declarations as rejected records for search purposes; only their metadata side-effect changes.
- Bump the Claude provider parser revision as part of the change so already-certified sources are recertified on next import instead of staying as a no-op generation.
- No change to bare-title fallback, agent-scope handling, duplicate-identity planning, or Codex/Antigravity title paths.

## Testing Decisions

- A good test asserts external behavior (import a transcript, then read/search it), not internal observation order or private session state.
- Primary seam (single, highest): end-to-end composition seam covering ingest, index, and read — synthesize a Claude transcript with a pure title declaration after several messages plus messages after it, import it, then assert every session event carries the title, title-substring search finds the session, and the session list shows the title. This one seam covers preflight, projection, indexing, and shaping together.
- Secondary regression pin only if the primary seam proves too coarse: provider-level projection pin asserting a pure title row with empty body still updates session metadata despite record rejection.
- Prior art: existing title-priority adjudication test, SQLite/JSONL title fallback tests, Antigravity checkpoint/first-prompt tests, provider lifecycle publication tests, and read-application search shaping tests.

## Out of Scope

- Ingesting the Desktop UI metadata directory as a new source type; the fix stays on the existing projects transcript tree.
- Backfilling titles for providers that store titles only as native-session display strings without title facts (e.g. task-docs/SQLite display titles).
- Changing tier semantics, inventing titles for untitled sessions, or redesigning session-champion ranking.
- Semantic/hybrid title ranking changes; lexical title-substring parity only.
- UI column layout or new CLI flags.

## Further Notes

- Witness transcript has its first title at line 11 of 662 with 32 repeated title rows, yet a 22-event lite transcript shows zero title facts today; post-fix the same fixture should show uniform titles.
- In the wild only a small minority of Claude transcripts declare any title, so most `-` rows are correct absence and must remain `-`.
- Title-row rejections in import diagnostics are expected before and after the fix.

title: fix(build): require executable Cargo target owners
body:
Cargo tests and binaries could pass the target inventory check when their source belonged only to a Rust library. Require an executable owner of the correct kind, and match the test harness setting while retaining the existing contract test macros.

Validated with the inventory unit and live repository Bazel checks, including checker entrypoint regressions for compile-only owners, custom test contracts, source matching, and harness settings.

title: Semantic indexing permanently fails when the Flat-F32 manifest reaches 16 MiB
body:
## Why

On a large local history corpus, built-in semantic indexing eventually becomes permanently unavailable while lexical search remains healthy. Restarting the daemon and rebuilding the derived semantic index do not provide a durable recovery: the rebuilt Flat-F32 manifest grows back to the same limit and the semantic job fails again.

This leaves `semantic = true` configured but every hybrid search falls back to lexical and every semantic-only search fails.

## Reproduction

1. Use ctx 1.3.1 with automatic indexing and the built-in semantic executor.
2. Import a corpus large enough to select approximately 234k semantic documents.
3. Enable semantic indexing with built-in throttling enabled.
4. Let the daemon perform repeated bounded semantic catch-up runs while provider history continues to publish Core generations.
5. Observe the semantic manifest grow to 16.0 MiB.
6. Inspect `ctx semantic status` and `daemon/jobs/semantic-index.json`.

This reproduced twice on the same corpus:

- first on the pre-existing semantic sidecar;
- again after removing only derived lexical/semantic search storage, rebuilding Core from provider histories, and starting a clean semantic backfill.

The clean rebuild reached semantic progress sequence 8116 before the failure was observed. That field is reported as a sequence value, not assumed to be a count of completed records or cycles.

## Expected / Actual

- Expected: Semantic maintenance compacts or otherwise bounds Flat-F32 manifest growth before the storage safety limit, eventually publishes a generation matching the active Core generation, and keeps semantic search usable across subsequent incremental Core refreshes.
- Actual: The semantic job enters retryable `failed`, resets its progress sequence for the new failed attempt, and repeatedly reports:

```text
invalid flat F32 input: manifest exceeds the safe size limit; compact first
```

Observed state after the clean rebuild failed:

```text
ctx semantic status
Status      failed
Background  running
Executor    builtin
Reason      daemon_semantic_job_failed
```

```json
{
  "consecutive_failures": 3,
  "failure_class": "retryable",
  "last_error": "invalid flat F32 input: manifest exceeds the safe size limit; compact first",
  "semantic_progress_sequence": 1,
  "status": "failed"
}
```

The two retained active/previous manifest files are each reported as 16.0 MiB. The semantic sidecar is approximately 817 MiB. Lexical Core publication succeeds independently.

## Environment

- ctx 1.3.1, official installer-managed binary
- macOS 26.5.1, Apple Silicon arm64
- built-in `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small` executor
- CoreML backend, canary passed
- built-in throttling enabled
- approximately 10.9k indexed sources, 11.1k sessions, and 1.9M searchable Core events
- approximately 234k selected semantic documents
- more than 50 GiB free on the data filesystem when reproduced

## Severity / Priority

- Severity: High for semantic users with large or high-churn corpora. Semantic retrieval remains unavailable indefinitely; lexical retrieval remains available.
- Priority: High because the documented recovery (rebuilding derived search storage) reproduces the same terminal condition and the error requests compaction without exposing a compaction command.

## Completion criteria

- A regression test uses a reduced test-only manifest bound and enough bounded semantic maintenance transactions to cross it without the fix.
- Semantic maintenance compacts or rebases before a transaction would exceed the manifest safety limit.
- A clean backfill larger than the threshold reaches `ready` and a semantic-only query succeeds.
- Subsequent incremental Core generations catch up without unbounded manifest growth or recurrence of the error.
- Recovery remains crash-safe and preserves the currently pinned generation for readers until the replacement is durably published.

## Non-goals

- Adding query-time `--since` filtering; it does not reduce semantic projection size.
- Introducing an index-time recent-history retention policy.
- Changing the embedding model or executor protocol.
- Addressing unrelated provider source rejections.

## Related

- #860 covers temporary semantic unavailability while catch-up follows frequent Core generations; this report is different because catch-up terminates at the manifest safety limit and does not recover.
- #792 covers semantic generation identity mismatch after incremental refresh.
- #318 describes the Flat-F32 compaction/recovery ownership during the semantic index crate extraction, but was closed unmerged and states behavior preservation.
- #222 covers analogous manifest/storage growth in the lexical index, not the semantic Flat-F32 sidecar.

## Technical notes

Hypothesis: bounded semantic duty cycles and repeated Core-generation reconciliation create many small Flat-F32 segments, but compaction is not triggered early enough to keep the serialized manifest below its hard safety bound. The exact compaction policy and transaction boundary should be confirmed in the implementation; this hypothesis is separate from the observations above.

title: fix(codex): preserve distinct item and call identities
body:
Codex tool calls and results can carry distinct response-item IDs alongside their shared call ID. Preserve both typed activity envelopes and the native item identities while retaining id-only fallback and duplicate/conflicting-selector rejection.

Rotate the parser revision so importing unchanged session files replaces the previous normalized records once, followed by a no-op.

Validation: Codex provider unit tests, scanner/store identity and rewrite regressions, and the JSONL parser-revision replay test.

title: Confirm terminal refresh journal durability before completion
body:
Terminal refresh results now wait for confirmed journal persistence before completion. Later status overlays use the same boundary, and failed persistence retries keep the exact result pending without repeating capture or advancing queued work.

On Unix, the existing data-root creator confirms new directory links before descending, and journal initialization confirms its owned directory boundaries. Failed synchronization remains retryable. After initialization, running updates in existing directories retain file sync and replacement without an added directory flush.

Validation: owning refresh, daemon, and platform tests; Linux filesystem syscall ordering, error/retry and concurrent creation cases.

title: fix(search): show and cite the winning semantic passage
body:
Semantic search can match text in a paired assistant reply while displaying only the user prompt. Preserve the winning passage through result selection, verify it against stored content, and show a snippet with citations to the messages that contributed it. Result IDs and session grouping remain unchanged.

Passage citations identify the displayed message ranges. Unicode clipping preserves complete graphemes; a passage that cannot fit a complete grapheme returns an empty, truncated snippet.

Validation: the regression executes the search application API and human renderer with a deterministic embedding fixture. Its semantic implementation dependency is limited to tests and enforced by exact build inventory checks. Focused owners pass: CLI 230, read application 97, semantic index 131 (one existing ignored test), index query 141, and daemon query adapter 43. Coverage includes semantic/hybrid output, pairing, tied winners, Unicode limits, citations, and integrity failures. The 26 boundary mutation tests, live dependency checks, and repository policy also pass.

title: test(performance): measure startup-owned cold refresh
body:
## What changed

Measure the first startup-owned cold refresh from before daemon launch through its completed publication. A search queued behind that work may legitimately finish as a same-generation no-op; it must not replace the cold job being measured.

The test now binds the cold request and receipt, corroborates them with status, and checks the later search against the same live generation and full corpus. CPU affinity is inherited at launch so the serial comparison is serial from the start. Existing corpus, worker, CPU-overlap and speedup assertions remain; no product scheduler or refresh behavior changes.

Adds ten focused regressions and their existing Bazel target input. Continuous-family callers retain their measurement behavior.

## Validation

- Uncached performance suite passed: 18 checks passed, one existing filesystem-dependent skip. The cold test passed with 2.18x parallel speedup.
- Uncached continuous-family suite passed all three checks.
- The separate forced-serial control failed the intended parallel-worker assertion.
- Full canonical CI passed: size preflight, CI build and all 211 selected tests, all executed. No release qualification or publication is claimed by this PR.

title: test(daemon): capture lifecycle output without pipe backpressure
body:
## What changed

The persistent-daemon lifecycle harness waited for a child to exit before reading its stdout and stderr. A full pipe could therefore stop the child from exiting and cause a test timeout.

Finite command output is now captured to owned temporary files from launch and read through bounded, independent snapshots. The original nine lifecycle cases, command and signal deadlines, interactive MCP pipes, and daemon behavior remain unchanged. Cleanup reuses the existing child-termination helper.

New regressions cover both large output streams and their tails, exit codes, concurrently launched children, timeout/cancellation cleanup, oversized capture, read failures, and retained output handles. A Linux control reproduces the old wait-before-drain blockage.

## Validation

- The uncached owning target passed all 16 checks, including the original failing lifecycle case and the old-pipe control.
- Canonical CI passed: size preflight, build, and all 211 selected tests (29 executed and 182 cache hits).
- No factory or release qualification is claimed by this change.

title: Hosted installer fails with unrecognized managed-pair argument on 1.3.1
body:
Running the hosted installer on Linux x86_64 fails when it invokes an internal command that the downloaded executable does not recognize.

### Reproduction

On a machine without an existing ctx installation:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install -o /tmp/ctx-install.sh
sh /tmp/ctx-install.sh \
  --semantic \
  --no-pro-trial \
  --no-skill \
  --no-modify-path
```

### Actual result

```text
Installing ctx 1.3.1...
ctx child output:
error: unexpected argument '--ctx-core-managed-pair-apply-v1' found

Usage: ctx [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

For more information, try '--help'.
error: ctx managed-pair installation did not complete; rerun this installer command to retry safely
```

The installer exits with status 1. No ctx executable was installed at the selected default location.

### Expected result

The hosted installer successfully installs ctx with semantic support, or detects an incompatible release artifact before invoking its internal installation interface.

### Environment and additional evidence

- Linux x86_64.
- Hosted installer selected version 1.3.1.
- Subsequently downloading the Linux x64 binary from GitHub Release v1.3.1, verifying it against the published `SHA256SUMS`, and installing it manually succeeded.
- The manually installed binary reports `ctx 1.3.1`.

This suggests a compatibility mismatch between the hosted installer and the artifact it selected, but the underlying cause has not been confirmed.

title: Semantic enable reports preparing when runtime is missing
body:
On Linux x86_64, enabling semantic search after a direct GitHub release installation reports that search is preparing, but background model loading fails because ONNX Runtime is missing. The supported way to provision CUDA for this installation is unclear.

### Environment

- ctx 1.3.1, installed from the GitHub release's Linux x64 Core binary.
- NVIDIA GPU visible to `nvidia-smi`.
- Built-in semantic executor, automatic indexing enabled.
- Direct installation was used after the hosted installer failed as reported in #947.

### Observed behavior

After running:

```sh
ctx setup
ctx semantic enable
ctx semantic status
```

The human-facing output says:

```text
Semantic search is preparing
Model acquisition or semantic indexing is still in progress.
```

Once initial history indexing reached model loading, detailed daemon status showed:

```text
last_run_reason: model_load_failed
last_run_status: skipped
last_error: no ONNX Runtime dynamic library candidates were found for linux-x64; set an absolute path with CTX_ONNXRUNTIME_DYLIB, ORT_DYLIB_PATH, CTX_ONNXRUNTIME_DIR, CTX_ONNXRUNTIME_CACHE_DIR, or CTX_RUNTIME_DIR
```

The high-level semantic status continued to report pending/preparing. This makes an actionable missing dependency look like ordinary background progress.

### CUDA provisioning evidence

The v1.3.1 source expects ONNX Runtime 1.27.0 and the CUDA asset `ctx-onnxruntime-linux-x64-cuda12.tar.zst`. The accelerator loader validates a canonical runtime layout, an installation manifest, and bundled dependencies:

- [Runtime version and CUDA asset selection](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.3.1/crates/ctx-semantic-model/src/model_runtime/onnx.rs)
- [Accelerator runtime validation](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.3.1/crates/ctx-semantic-model/src/model_runtime/onnx/verified_runtime.rs)

During investigation:

- The GitHub v1.3.1 release assets contained Core executables and `SHA256SUMS`, but no runtime sidecars.
- Stable metadata at `https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v1/releases/stable/ctx-release-metadata.env` contained no `CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_` or `CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_` fields.
- Requesting `ctx-onnxruntime-linux-x64-cuda12.tar.zst` under that metadata's artifact base, `https://cli.ctx.rs/storage/v1/object/public/releases/artifacts/stable/1.3.1/`, returned HTTP 404. This establishes absence at that location, not that the asset is unavailable everywhere.
- `ctx upgrade --dry-run --format json` rejected the unmanaged installation and directed it back to the hosted installer.

No CUDA inference failure has been observed: model loading is blocked before successful inference.

### Narrowed cause and loader contract

The observed failure is a runtime-provisioning failure before inference: the Core executable and local model files are present, but the required native runtime is absent. The upstream release-publication reason for that absence has not been established.

For CUDA, the source shows that supplying an arbitrary ONNX Runtime library path is not sufficient:

- `verified_accelerator_runtime_candidates` searches runtime roots for `onnxruntime/1.27.0/linux-x64-cuda12/lib/libonnxruntime.so`. Unlike the general CPU candidate search, it does not consume the direct `CTX_ONNXRUNTIME_DYLIB` or `ORT_DYLIB_PATH` selections.
- `validate_runtime_candidate` requires `ctx-runtime-install.json` with the expected version/platform, `manager = "ctx-hosted-installer"`, and `metadata_trust = "signed-release-metadata"`.
- It also verifies the exact file allowlist, sizes, and hashes, including the bundled CUDA/cuDNN dependencies.

These checks are in [verified_runtime.rs](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.3.1/crates/ctx-semantic-model/src/model_runtime/onnx/verified_runtime.rs). The distinction from general runtime-path lookup is visible in [onnx.rs](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v1.3.1/crates/ctx-semantic-model/src/model_runtime/onnx.rs).

Consequently, CUDA recovery needs a supported way to provision the complete expected runtime bundle and manifest. The generic missing-library advice about setting a direct dynamic-library path does not explain this CUDA-specific requirement. This is a provisioning/documentation gap in addition to the high-level status hiding `model_load_failed`; it is not evidence of a CUDA kernel or GPU failure.

### Expected behavior

- Surface the missing-runtime/model-load error in human-facing semantic status instead of only reporting preparing.
- Document a supported way to install the CUDA runtime and its required layout for direct-release installations, or clearly state if this requires a hosted installation.
- If automatic runtime acquisition is intended, make the necessary runtime artifacts discoverable and report why acquisition cannot proceed.

This is related to #947, but the missing-runtime reporting and direct-install provisioning path are separate from the installer's rejected internal command.

title: test(release): bind native smoke to current analytics outbox

## What changed

title: Clean up failed rebuild candidates and report observed disk pressure
body:
When a rebuild fails while writing its manifest, wait for the original index writer to finish and remove only that unpublished candidate while retaining the writer lock. Preserve the original failure and leave the candidate intact if completion or directory ownership cannot be established. Generations already made visible remain available after a durability error.

title: Report Semantic startup failures and document runtime installation
body:
Fixes #948. Release metadata and older-install verification remain tracked in #953 and #928.

## Summary

Surface persisted Semantic startup failures instead of reporting that the runtime is still preparing. The shared daemon report now preserves the failure reason and error detail, and status, doctor, and Semantic status project those facts consistently. Keyword-search readiness and the existing Semantic projection inventory remain intact.

title: Stable v1.3.1 metadata omits semantic runtime and model entries
body:
While investigating #948, I checked the stable release metadata on September 8, 2026:

https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v1/releases/stable/ctx-release-metadata.env

It reported version `1.3.1`, published September 3, and contained no `CTX_RELEASE_SEMANTIC_*` or `CTX_RELEASE_ONNXRUNTIME_*` entries.

The CUDA sidecar URL checked under that metadata’s artifact base returned HTTP 404. This establishes absence at that location, not that the artifact is unavailable everywhere.

The hosted installer delegates semantic provisioning to `ctx upgrade`. The repository’s semantic metadata parser returns no semantic catalog when those fields are absent, so this appears to leave that provisioning path without runtime assets to select.

The repository includes CPU/CUDA sidecar build scripts and gated Buildkite steps. I haven’t established whether those steps ran for this release or why the metadata omits the assets.

Could you clarify:
- Should stable v1.3.1 advertise these assets, or is another endpoint intended?
- If provisioning is unavailable for this release, can the installer report that explicitly?

Related: #948 tracks the misleading status and direct-install recovery experience. #952 proposes local archive installation. #947’s managed-pair installer failure was reported fixed separately.

title: Restore macOS background freshness and preserve supported history sources
body:
## Problem and behavior

A macOS history writer that was already open and dirty before watcher registration could append records without a native notification, leaving search stale until the writer closed. Keep native notifications and add bounded metadata-only polling every five seconds on macOS. Compare full modification timestamps, length, and file kind; do not descend known symlinks. Both event streams use existing coalescing and route admission.

This change also fixes source-completeness failures found during recovery:

- Preserve valid Codex prompt neighbors when one retained record exceeds its bound, recording the rejection through the current structured rejection API. Advance the parser revision (v5 was used by the local repair; v6 includes upstream structured rejection reporting).
- Admit same-thread paginated history boundaries without weakening explicit parent/fork conflict checks.
- Preserve distinct reverted Codex rollouts while coalescing raw/compressed copies of the same rollout. Canonical original rollout identities stay unchanged; reverted source identities are corrected.
- Accept Goose schema 9 with required-column validation, retaining schema 15 support and rejecting unknown schemas.
- Extend incompatible-generation recovery coverage to admission-pending requests and preserve successors. Current upstream recovery already handles this state, so its implementation is retained.
- Canonicalize test roots on macOS and resolve provider fixtures through Bazel runfiles.

## Validation

Against current main (`1e199c7e95960f48af4d5dbb02f2d259a5aea26c`):

```sh
scripts/bazelw test //crates/ctx-history-provider-codex:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-refresh:unit_tests //crates/ctx-daemon-runtime:unit_tests //crates/ctx-history-providers-sqlite-selected:unit_tests --test_output=errors
scripts/bazelw test //crates/ctx-history-capture-composition-qualification:provider_lifecycle_tests --test_arg=codex --test_output=errors
```

The Codex lifecycle integration suite passed. The four unit suites passed: 58 Codex, 202 refresh, 50 daemon-runtime, and 62 selected SQLite tests (372 total).

The stable-base local repair previously passed release-mode Bazel construction and live full-import, background-freshness (`--refresh off`), and daemon stop/restart checks. That installed binary is still the stable-base repair; this PR integrates the fixes with current main. Live data and transcripts are not included.

Prior broader stable-base validation recorded four Lingma fixture-discovery failures and three semantic tests deferred by host energy-saving policy. This is not a claim that all repository suites passed. Semantic indexing was disabled in live validation.

## Release boundary

The installed repair remains unmanaged. Restoring official managed upgrades and native login startup requires an upstream signed release containing these fixes, followed by the documented installation-wide lifecycle handoff and hosted installation. No installer marker is forged or ownership policy bypassed.

title: Workspace clippy and tests fail because companion contract tests use unavailable CARGO_BIN_EXE_ctx
body:
## Problem

- The current upstream tip `1e199c7e` cannot pass the documented workspace gates because `crates/ctx-cli/src/companion/contract_tests.rs` uses `env!("CARGO_BIN_EXE_ctx")` in unit tests, but Cargo does not define that integration-test executable variable for this compilation path.

- This blocks both `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo test --workspace` before the tests can run.

## Reproduction

- From a clean checkout of `1e199c7e`, run `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo test --workspace`.

- Both commands fail while compiling `crates/ctx-cli/src/companion/contract_tests.rs` with `error: environment variable CARGO_BIN_EXE_ctx not defined at compile time`.

- The two failing call sites are the subprocess checks in `paid_blame_wrapper_records_after_companion_exit_and_remains_controlled` and `blame_usage_root_preserves_non_utf8_native_paths`.

## Impact

- The failure prevents the workspace lint and test gates from providing any signal for the current upstream line. It also blocks downstream forks using `git overlay sync` from safely rebuilding and installing the current default branch.

## Suggested fix

- Move the subprocess checks to a test target where Cargo provides `CARGO_BIN_EXE_ctx`, or use a test-supported executable discovery mechanism that works for this package's unit-test compilation. Preserve the existing assertions and run both workspace gates after the change.

## Validation

- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` passes at `1e199c7e`. The clippy and workspace test commands both exit `101` on the missing compile-time environment variable before test execution.

title: fix(cursor): time unavailable on every message
body:
Every Cursor message rendered "time unavailable" because the importer read a nonexistent top-level timestamp field. In reality, the turn time is only in the user message's generated timestamp envelope. The fix is to parse that envelope and carry it across the assistant and tool records that follow, until the next turn.

The parser revision is rotated so sessions imported before this change are rescanned rather than replayed from their existing certificates, and the superseded revision is moved into the migration test's prior slot.

Transcripts written before Cursor began injecting the envelope stay undated and keep their existing identities.

title: ctx import hangs forever on macOS, daemon stuck in FSEvents stop/join
body:
## What happened

`ctx import --all` stopped working on our Mac. It never returned, and `ctx search` had quietly gone stale: nothing indexed after Sep 3, while sessions from Sep 9 existed on disk.

ctx 1.3.1 (mise install), macOS 27.0, notify 9.0.0-rc.4.

```
$ ctx import --all
# never returns

$ ctx status
Daemon         running
Refresh        partial (automatic retry partially paused)
Issue          The same internal refresh failure happened twice.

$ ctx index --format json | jq '.refresh.progress.phase, .daemon.status'
"admission_pending"
"running"
```

## What we found

We had Claude Code investigate. The daemon process was alive for 3.5 days but its heartbeat was 2.5 days old:

```
$ jq '.heartbeat_at_ms' ~/.ctx/daemon/status.json ; date +%s000
1788766862929
1788989331000        # 62 hours later
```

`~/.ctx/daemon/wakeup.json` showed 97 forced rearms and 1756 registration attempts.

`sample <daemon pid>` showed the main thread blocked in a join, and two FSEvents run loop threads both idle:

```
Thread main
  ... FsEventWatcher::stop
  _pthread_join
  __ulock_wait

Thread "notify-rs fsevents loop"      (two of these alive)
  CFRunLoopRun
  __CFRunLoopServiceMachPort
  mach_msg2_trap
```

Meanwhile the `ctx-daemon-query` thread was still serving the socket, so every import and refresh request was accepted and parked in `admission_pending`.

Killing the daemon fixed it:

```
$ kill -TERM <daemon pid>
$ ctx import --all
# fresh daemon starts, completes, sessions 2768 -> 2855
```

## Agent's read of the cause

Our agent pointed at the rearm path in `crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/watch.rs`. `reconcile_paths` replaces the watcher and calls `replacement.watch(path)` once per root (18 roots here). notify's fsevent backend implements `watch()` as `stop(); append_path(); run()`, so each call stops, joins and respawns the run loop thread. `run()` hands the runloop back before entering `CFRunLoopRun`, and `stop()` only sets a flag and calls `CFRunLoopStop`. If `stop()` lands in that gap, the stop is lost and `join()` never returns. A rearm is forced on every rename or folder create under a watched root, so with 18 roots per rearm there were many chances to hit it.

We could not reproduce it on demand. It is a race that surfaced after a few days of Claude Code and Codex use.

Related: #954 changes the same file but still registers roots one by one, so it does not look like the same problem.



See also #958 for the CLI never noticing the stale heartbeat.

title: CLI keeps queueing behind a hung daemon whose heartbeat is days old
body:
## What happened

While debugging a hung `ctx import` (see #957) we noticed the CLI never treated the daemon as unhealthy, even though its heartbeat was 62 hours old.

```
$ jq '{status, pid, heartbeat_at_ms}' ~/.ctx/daemon/status.json
{ "status": "running", "pid": 76178, "heartbeat_at_ms": 1788766862929 }   # 62 h old

$ ctx status
Daemon         running

$ ctx doctor
[2] History refresh is partial
  The component is not ready.

$ ctx import --all
# hangs, ctx index shows request_state "admission_pending"
```

Nothing in `ctx status` or `ctx doctor` mentioned the stale heartbeat. Killing the pid and rerunning import recovered everything.

## Agent's read of the cause

Our agent found that `autostart_request.rs` treats the daemon as healthy when `daemon_lock_is_stale()` is false, which only checks that the pid exists. The heartbeat age bound (`DAEMON_SETUP_HANDOFF_MAX_HEARTBEAT_AGE_MS`, 30 s) is only consulted in `readiness_receipt.rs` while waiting for a freshly launched daemon. An already-running pid is never checked for a fresh heartbeat.

title: fix(macos): prevent lost watcher stops in 1.4.2
body:
## Fix

Fixes #957.

The macOS notify backend can lose a stop sent after its worker reads the stop flag but before it enters CFRunLoopRun. The following join can then wait indefinitely during watcher re-registration.

Repeat stop and wakeup until the owned worker finishes, yielding one millisecond between attempts. This runs only during shutdown and retains the existing join. It adds no idle timer and does not treat a stale heartbeat as permission to kill a responsive daemon. A callback blocked for an unrelated reason remains outside this fix.

Bazel and the official macOS Cargo release factory apply the same patch to the checksum-pinned notify archive. The factory uses a task-local Cargo paths override with an unchanged manifest and dependency graph. Release inventory checks the actual selected source and includes the local-patch notice. Plain Cargo/source-install builds do not automatically apply this factory override.

Prepare version 1.4.2 across package and plugin metadata. Correct one stale Go SDK negative fixture to use an unsupported contract instead of the now-supported v2 contract. No runtime SDK validation or developer-tool dependency versions change.

## Verification

- Native macOS comparison forced the stop/run-entry race through notify's real stop method: the unmodified baseline failed as expected; separately compiled patched source passed the same case, busy-runloop stop and watcher-drop tests.
- Native repeated-stop primitive passed 100 repetitions.
- Actual Bazel and Cargo-prepared patched source digests match.
- Full CI passed all 451 build targets and all 212 test targets; both dependency-boundary checks additionally passed fresh uncached runs.
- Repository policy and whitespace checks passed.

These are source and native dependency checks, not a claim that signed-release qualification or publication is complete.
