title: A per-source spool overflow is route-fatal, so one OpenCode scan over the 256 MiB bound aborts the whole refresh attempt
body:
## Summary

An OpenCode logical scan whose encoded retained records exceed the 256 MiB spool bound cannot complete, and the resulting `ResourceUnavailable` is route-fatal: it aborts the whole refresh attempt, so that attempt published no updates for healthy peer providers either.

```text
run capture-owned source-backed refresh: source-backed scan failed for opencode:
ResourceUnavailable: logical-snapshot Core-record spool encoded-byte bound exceeded:
maximum 268435456, observed 268436253
```

797 bytes over the bound.

## Mechanism

`LOGICAL_SNAPSHOT_SPOOL_MAX_ENCODED_BYTES` is a compile-time `256 * 1024 * 1024` at `crates/ctx-history-capture-composition/src/source_backed/family/document/spool.rs:18`, unchanged at `v1.5.0`.

`DeferredCoreRecords::push` checks the encoded-byte bound *before* writing, so the over-limit record is rejected and previously staged bytes are not truncated (the neighbouring test is named `..._rejects_n_plus_one_before_writing` and asserts exactly that retention; the zero-length assertion in the other test uses an oversized *first* record, so that file was already empty). When the error unwinds the scan, the disk-backed temporary spool is dropped and its staged records are never published.

The disk-backed spool has no rollover and no cross-refresh checkpoint, so an overflowing attempt cannot bank partial progress for the next one.

The route-fatal part looks deliberate, which is why this is a question rather than a bug report. `SourceBackedRouteErrorKind::ResourceUnavailable` maps to no source failure class (`crates/ctx-history-capture-runtime/src/source_backed/driver.rs:72`), and `route_attempts.rs:740` therefore returns a `SourceBackedCoordinatorError::RouteScan` rather than retaining the source and publishing certified peers. The doc comment above `is_logical_source_failure` states the intent:

> Source drift, schema ambiguity, aggregate resource failure, and internal failures remain route-fatal.

So the spool bound is classified as an aggregate resource failure and inherits that policy.

## What reproduces, and what does not

I saw this once, on the recovery attempt after the store had been left in `core refresh failed` by an unrelated problem. That attempt performed a full logical scan, whose encoded retained records exceeded the bound. The next `ctx import` exited 0 (`+57` sessions, `+9,898` searchable events) and `Refresh` returned to `ready`.

Later imports against the same 1.05 GiB database succeeded, so database size alone is not a reproducer, and I have not found a deliberate trigger for the oversized scan. This report therefore rests on the constant, the reject-before-write path, the dropped temporary spool, and the route-fatal classification, not on a repeatable recipe.

This differs from the per-row case fixed by #1024: the failing bound is the per-logical-source spool rather than one oversized row, and its error aborts the whole refresh attempt rather than the one source.

## The question

Is an aggregate resource failure on a per-source spool bound the right thing to treat as route-fatal? A per-source byte ceiling is a property of that source's scan, so retaining it and publishing certified peers seems closer to the treatment the per-row case now gets, but the policy comment suggests that was a considered choice and I may be missing what makes the aggregate case different.

If it should stay route-fatal, two smaller things would have helped: rolling the spool into bounded chunks or checkpointing durable partial progress across refreshes, so a scan that cannot fit one pass is not permanently stuck; and surfacing the exact source path in `ctx doctor`. The raw error names the provider and the numeric bound but not which source it was.

## Environment

```text
ctx 1.5.0 (managed install, upgraded 1.4.12 -> 1.5.0)
Linux x86_64, data root on ext4
source: OpenCode session database, 1.05 GiB, actively written during the failure
```

title: fix: stop low-headroom refresh retry loops
body:
When a generation republish first writes a record and discovers that disk headroom is too low, the shared capture boundary currently converts the typed index error into an internal refresh failure. The daemon then enters its internal-failure confirmation loop, while human status output hides the required and available capacity and can separately describe a live daemon as unhealthy because its scheduler heartbeat is old.

This change:

- routes lifecycle write errors through the existing typed refresh classification so low-headroom failures remain `resource_unavailable`
- keeps resource exhaustion out of internal-failure confirmation retries and shows its capacity detail in status, daemon status, doctor, and terminal refresh output
- treats scheduler heartbeat age as diagnostic metadata instead of downgrading a daemon whose live ownership is confirmed

Addresses the low-headroom retry and misleading status behavior reported in #1030.

title: Proposal: Multi-user Shared CTX Index Service
body:
## Summary

note: the suggestion and motivation are the key parts here, to solve real pain points, not all ACs, design decisions, etc. that is more for the implementer/owner.

Add an optional brokered CTX service that allows multiple operating-system
users and harnesses on one machine to share a single CTX-owned index without
sharing a writable private data directory directly.

The service should own the CTX data root, serialize refresh/publication work,
allow concurrent read operations, and enforce explicit per-user access policy.

## Motivation

Users may have several operating-system accounts on one machine—for example,
personal and work accounts—or may run harnesses under separate service users.
Each account currently tends toward its own `~/.ctx` root and therefore its own
derived Core/Tantivy and semantic indexes.

That is a safe isolation boundary, but it duplicates potentially large derived
indexes when the users intentionally want one shared searchable corpus. A
shared origin archive can avoid duplicating the source backup, but it does not
avoid duplicating CTX's derived index.

The desired topology is:

```text
user A harnesses ─┐
user B harnesses ─┼── authenticated CTX service ── one owned index
user C harnesses ─┘
```

## Pain points

### A shared directory is not sufficient

CTX data roots are intentionally owner-private. On Unix, the root and files
are verified against the current user and restrictive permissions. A directory
owned by one account and group-readable/writable by another is expected to
fail CTX's private-root checks.

Changing the directory mode would weaken the current security model and would
not address the ownership of configuration, semantic indexes, attribution
state, daemon state, and usage state.

### Existing locking is not the complete service boundary

The Core/Tantivy generation layer already has useful concurrency primitives:

- readers can hold shared generation leases;
- competing writers are excluded;
- a writer waits briefly for handoff and then reports a lock failure.

Those primitives protect index publication, but they do not provide:

- OS-user authentication;
- conversation visibility policy;
- service discovery;
- cross-user request routing;
- source ownership or tenant isolation;
- lifecycle management for one shared daemon.

The feature should build on the existing locks rather than introduce an
uncoordinated second lock protocol.

### The current daemon is current-user oriented

Automatic indexing is associated with a current-user supervisor, and the
current MCP server communicates over local stdio. Neither is a general
multi-user service endpoint.

### Privacy becomes an explicit product decision

If multiple accounts share one index, the default behavior cannot assume that
all users may see every conversation. The service needs an explicit policy:

- one shared corpus visible to all authorized users;
- per-user source visibility within one physical index;
- administrator-only import with user-scoped search;
- or a strict single-tenant mode that is merely operated by a service account.

## Proposed solution

Introduce an optional CTX service mode. The service owns one data root and is
the only component allowed to perform writes there. Client processes use a
versioned authenticated protocol for search, retrieval, status, and import.

### Service responsibilities

- own and validate the private CTX data root;
- run automatic provider refresh and semantic indexing;
- serialize import and publication jobs;
- expose concurrent read operations against immutable generations;
- queue or reject overlapping writes with clear status;
- retain the existing atomic generation publication behavior;
- expose health, readiness, and job status;
- maintain archive/export integration from the portable-archive proposal.

### Client responsibilities

Client-side harness integrations should be thin. They should:

- authenticate to the local service using OS-native credentials;
- submit search, show, list, status, and import requests;
- receive bounded structured responses;
- never open the service-owned index directly;
- never modify the service-owned data root.

### Transport

The first implementation should prefer a local OS-protected transport:

- Unix domain socket on Unix-like systems;
- named pipe or equivalent protected local endpoint on Windows.

Network exposure should be a separate, explicit feature. It should not be
enabled merely because the local service exists.

### Authorization model

The service should make visibility explicit in source configuration. A source
could carry an owner or access-group policy, for example:

```toml
[sources.roots.work-codex]
provider = "codex"
path = "/srv/ctx-sources/work-codex"
visibility = "work"

[sources.roots.personal-claude]
provider = "claude"
path = "/srv/ctx-sources/personal-claude"
visibility = "personal"
```

The exact configuration vocabulary can be designed later, but source names
and groups must not be mistaken for access control without an explicit service
policy layer.

### Concurrency model

The service should use the existing CTX concurrency design:

```text
many readers ───────────────┐
                            ├── immutable published generation
one queued writer at a time ┘
```

Import and refresh requests should be admitted through one service-level job
queue. Readers should continue using the previous verified generation while a
new candidate is built. A failed writer must leave the last verified
generation active.

## Suggested CLI and protocol surface

Possible lifecycle commands:

```bash
ctx service install
ctx service start
ctx service status
ctx service stop
ctx service run
```

Possible client selection:

```bash
ctx --service search "failed migration"
ctx --service import --all
ctx --service status --format json
```

The exact names are open for discussion. The important distinction is that a
client explicitly selects a service endpoint rather than silently assuming
that a shared filesystem is safe.

The protocol should include:

- protocol and schema version;
- authenticated caller identity;
- request ID and idempotency key for mutations;
- bounded response sizes;
- source and visibility filters;
- import job status and progress;
- structured authorization and conflict errors;
- generation identity in read responses.

## Security requirements

- The service-owned root remains private to the service account.
- Client access is authenticated through the operating system by default.
- Search and retrieval enforce source visibility before reading content.
- Import authorization is separate from search authorization.
- Logs and errors must not leak transcript content across policy boundaries.
- Network listeners, if added later, require explicit opt-in and transport
  authentication.
- Service upgrades must preserve atomic generation and recovery guarantees.
- The service must not weaken existing symlink, ownership, or private-file
  checks merely to support sharing.

## Non-goals

- Making the CTX data directory group-writable.
- Asking independent CTX processes under different users to coordinate through
  an ad hoc shared lock file.
- Automatically merging private and work histories without an access policy.
- Replacing the portable archive/backup format.
- Exposing the service to a network by default.

## Acceptance criteria

- Two different OS users can use one service-owned CTX index without direct
  access to its private data root.
- Multiple readers can search and retrieve concurrently.
- Import and refresh writes are serialized and cannot corrupt the active
  generation.
- A failed or interrupted write leaves the previous verified generation
  usable.
- Access policy prevents an unauthorized user from searching or retrieving a
  source.
- The service exposes machine-readable health and job status.
- A client can reconnect after service restart without losing completed work.
- Existing single-user `~/.ctx` operation remains unchanged.
- The service can consume portable archives from the companion archive
  proposal.

## Suggested implementation phases

1. Extract or formalize a service protocol around the existing local daemon and
   query paths.
2. Add a service-owned data-root lifecycle and local authenticated transport.
3. Add queued import/refresh jobs and service health/status reporting.
4. Add source visibility and per-user authorization.
5. Integrate portable archive import/export.
6. Consider optional network transport only after local multi-user behavior is
   stable.

## Open questions

- Should the first version be single-tenant, with all authorized users seeing
  the same corpus, or multi-tenant from the start?
- Which existing daemon/query IPC pieces can be reused safely as the service
  protocol?
- Should service-owned indexes be allowed to ingest provider files belonging to
  users who cannot read the service account's source directories directly?
- Should the service expose MCP, a CTX-native protocol, or both?
- What is the desired behavior when two users request overlapping imports for
  the same source?

title: Proposal: Portable Conversation Archives and CTX History Export/Import
body:
## Summary

Add a first-class, portable archive format and CLI workflow for moving indexed
conversation history between machines, operating-system accounts, and
harnesses.

The archive should preserve the origin and identity of each conversation,
support incremental updates, work well with compression and encryption, and be
re-importable into a fresh CTX data root without requiring the original
harness installation.

## Motivation

CTX currently treats provider-owned histories as the acquisition authority and
Core/Tantivy as derived local storage. That is a good indexing architecture,
but it leaves migration and backup workflows incomplete.

Users increasingly run several coding-agent harnesses across multiple
machines and accounts. They need to be able to:

- retain conversations after cleaning up harness-specific JSONL, JSON, or
  SQLite files;
- move history between machines without losing provenance;
- merge histories from several machines into one searchable corpus;
- keep a compact, encrypted, versioned backup;
- restore into a new CTX data root and rebuild the index deterministically;
- perform incremental exports without rewriting the entire corpus.

Today, `ctx show` and `ctx list` can produce JSON/JSONL output, and CTX can
import `ctx-history-jsonl-v2`, but there is no corresponding first-class
`ctx export` operation. Query output is also not guaranteed to be a complete,
round-trippable archive.

## Pain points

### No supported CTX export path

There is no command that exports all retained, policy-selected conversation
records into the public CTX import format. Users must either preserve every
provider's native files or write a custom transformation around `show` and
`list` output.

### Derived indexes are not sufficient as the only backup

The local Core/Tantivy index can continue serving records after a provider
source disappears, but it is derived storage. It may be rebuilt, invalidated,
or become unreadable after a schema or policy transition. It also intentionally
does not retain every provider payload class.

### Provenance can be lost during merging

Provider session IDs can repeat across machines or exporters. A migration
format must preserve a stable provider/source route, machine or account
origin, and the provider-native session identity so that two unrelated
conversations are not merged accidentally.

### Large raw histories are expensive to transfer

Users need compressed archives and incremental snapshots. A workflow that
rewrites and transfers a multi-gigabyte uncompressed JSONL file for every
update is impractical.

### Native formats are not portable across all harnesses

Preserving native provider files gives the best fidelity but remains tied to a
specific harness and importer. A portable normalized representation is needed
for harnesses that do not have a native CTX adapter on the destination.

## Proposed solution

Introduce a versioned CTX archive package with two related payload types:

1. **Native source payloads** for lossless recovery. These are the original
   provider files or directory trees, stored as compressed, checksummed archive
   members.
2. **Normalized CTX payloads** using `ctx-history-jsonl-v2`, for portable
   cross-harness import and reindexing.

The native payload is the fidelity-preserving backup. The normalized payload is
the interoperable exchange format. An archive may contain either one or both.

### Suggested archive structure

```text
ctx-archive/
  manifest.json
  sources/
    codex-machine-a-account-1/
      source.json
      native.jsonl.zst
      normalized.jsonl.zst
    claude-machine-b-account-2/
      source.json
      native.sqlite.zst
      normalized.jsonl.zst
  checksums.sha256
```

The exact container can be decided during implementation. The important
properties are:

- explicit archive schema version;
- per-source checksums;
- compression independent of the logical record format;
- optional encryption handled by the archive workflow;
- deterministic manifests;
- independently transferable source chunks.

### Stable source identity

Each source should have a durable identity such as:

```text
provider_key: codex
source_id:    machine-a-account-1
```

The identity must remain stable when the physical path changes. The archive
should record, where available:

- provider and source identity;
- machine/account origin label;
- original provider path;
- source format and schema;
- export time and covered time range;
- cursor or high-water mark;
- producer and CTX versions;
- content and archive checksums.

The archive must not use a CTX-generated session ID as the primary portable
identity. It should preserve provider/source/session identity and allow the
destination CTX instance to derive its own local IDs.

### Incremental archive workflow

Exports should support append-only or chunked operation:

```text
2026-09-01.jsonl.zst
2026-09-15.jsonl.zst
2026-09-29.jsonl.zst
manifest.json
```

New conversations should create new chunks rather than rewriting the whole
archive. An explicit compaction command may later merge old chunks. Compaction
must preserve source identities, checksums, and record semantics.

### Suggested CLI surface

Possible commands include:

```bash
ctx export --all --archive ./ctx-archive
ctx export --source codex-machine-a-account-1 --since 2026-09-01 \
  --archive ./ctx-archive
ctx archive verify ./ctx-archive
ctx archive compact ./ctx-archive
ctx import --archive ./ctx-archive
```

The existing explicit import form should remain available:

```bash
ctx import --input-format ctx-history-jsonl-v2 --path ./history.jsonl
```

An archive import should stage or decompress the relevant source payloads,
validate the manifest and checksums, then use the existing CTX import and Core
publication pipeline. Archive files should remain available as durable source
inputs when future incremental refresh is desired.

## Design requirements

- **Round-trip identity:** exporting and importing must preserve source,
  provider-session, event, and lineage identity as far as the source format
  permits.
- **Idempotence:** importing the same archive twice must not duplicate records.
- **Incremental operation:** new chunks can be added without rewriting old
  chunks.
- **Integrity:** manifests and payloads are checksummed and verified before
  publication.
- **Versioning:** incompatible archive schema changes fail clearly and do not
  silently reinterpret records.
- **Privacy:** archives are treated as sensitive local history and should
  support encryption or integrate cleanly with external encryption tools.
- **Policy fidelity:** the archive must clearly distinguish lossless native
  payloads from policy-selected normalized CTX records.
- **Atomic restore:** a failed import must leave the previously published CTX
  generation usable.
- **Path independence:** moving an archive must not change its logical source
  identity.

## Non-goals

- Replacing provider-native storage for active harnesses.
- Making compressed files directly readable by every native provider adapter.
- Guaranteeing preservation of provider payloads that CTX intentionally excludes
  from normalized Core records.
- Making one archive a live multi-user search service; that is a separate
  proposal.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user can export all supported local history into a versioned archive.
- The archive can be compressed and transferred to another machine/account.
- A fresh CTX data root can import the archive and recover searchable sessions
  with stable provenance.
- Two archives from different machines can be merged without colliding when
  their source identities differ.
- Re-importing an unchanged archive is a no-op.
- Incremental export adds only new or changed source chunks.
- Corrupt, incomplete, or incompatible archives fail before replacing the
  active generation.
- Documentation explains the fidelity difference between native and normalized
  archive payloads.

## Open questions

- Should the first implementation export native payloads, normalized payloads,
  or both?
- Should archives use a CTX-owned container format or a directory convention
  built from standard compressed files?
- Should encryption be built into CTX or delegated to filesystem/archive tools?
- Should an archive import register a durable source automatically, or require
  an explicit source manifest?
- Should export include repository/Git attribution inputs, or only conversation
  history?

title: Allow history-only imports without Blame materialization
body:
## Problem

In ctx 1.6.1, every import synchronously materializes the native Blame index after Core history has already been published. There is no CLI flag or configuration switch to skip this work when the user only wants history search.

On a large existing history corpus, Blame materialization can take longer than the Core import itself. The phase also has no visible progress, so the command appears stuck after history is already searchable.

## Reproduction

1. Use manual indexing mode with semantic search disabled.
2. Start from a data root without an attribution index.
3. Run ctx import --all.
4. Observe that Core history becomes ready, but the command continues materializing search/attribution before it returns.

## Observed

With approximately 18 GiB of processed history and 12.7k sessions:

- a clean Core rebuild took about 31 minutes;
- Blame materialization then ran for at least another 29 minutes before the test was stopped;
- a second import reproduced the same post-publication phase;
- the attribution directory grew steadily while CPU time increased, confirming active work rather than a deadlock;
- status did not expose useful materialization progress and could block while the attribution writer lock was held.

The implementation matches the observation: the import path unconditionally calls complete_attribution after Core publication.

This differs from #872/#887, which addressed generation certification and post-publication lexical rereads. The work here is native Blame materialization introduced with the public Blame feature.

## Expected

Provide a supported history-only import mode that publishes Core history and returns without building or updating Blame. For example:

    ctx import --all --no-blame

Normal imports that do materialize Blame should expose the phase and progress through import and status output.

The opt-out should preserve existing behavior by default and should not affect Core publication, history search, semantic configuration, or daemon ownership.

title: fix(history): isolate logical spool overflow

Regression coverage exercises both cold partial publication and warm last-good carry-forward. Shared scratch exhaustion and arithmetic failures remain fatal.

title: Fix Devin history failing to index when a session has repeated subagent-lineage rejections
body:
Devin history stops indexing entirely once any Devin session has two or more rejected subagent lineages. Every refresh of the Devin route fails with a misleading internal error and is retried indefinitely:

> generation-owned state envelope is malformed or non-canonical

The existing index stays searchable, but no Devin records are ever published and `ctx status` doesn’t list Devin under “Agent histories.”

The trigger is the persistent `sidekick` subagent of the [Fusion model pairing feature](https://docs.devin.ai/cli/fusion). Lineage rejections expose two separate bugs:

1. Duplicate diagnostics fail the whole route. `record_repeated_devin_rejection` recorded one identical warning per rejection. The route-result check requires warnings to be unique, so `provider_route_results` failed. The publication step then reported that failure under the unrelated “generation state envelope” error.
2. Compacted sidekick transcripts were rejected as separate lineages. When the sidekick compacts, Devin forks a new chain off the shared system-prompt node. The new summary node’s `summarized_from` points into the old chain, but to a node _before_ the previous handoff’s tip. The planner only extended a same-agent lineage if the new walk reached that exact previous tip. So every handoff after a compaction, plus the durable `subagent_heads` entry, was rejected and its nodes left out of the index.

The fixes are to keep only one warning per repeated rejection, and extend same-agent lineages across compaction.

Follow-up to #1017

title: Blame indexing aborts the whole pass when one segment exceeds a hard bound, and deletes the partial index
body:
## Summary

On ctx 1.6.3 (managed install, macOS arm64), Blame indexing does not finish against a large retained history. After `ctx index mode manual`, `ctx import --all` runs for about 34 minutes, reaches 2381 of 9715 sources, then fails. The partial attribution segments are deleted. Core search stays ready.

The same error happened on 1.5.0 on this machine when automatic refresh was already off (about 34 minutes, roughly 33 segments). 1.6.3 adds Blame progress and `[blame] enabled = false`, but the catch-up still aborts the whole pass on this bound.

```text
Core history remains available; attribution completion failed.
segment materializer exceeded a hard bound
```

The error does not name the bound or the source that exceeded it.

## Steps

1. Corpus at the time: about 10,975 sessions, 9,715 sources, 1,539,720 events. Lexical search was ready.
2. `ctx upgrade check` reported 1.6.3 up to date on the stable channel.
3. `ctx index mode manual`, so a newer Core publication would not replace the generation under the pass.
4. `ctx import --all`, with Blame left at the default (enabled).
5. Progress reached `Indexing Blame: 2381/9715 sources; 368609 changes applied`. The attribution progress file showed `elapsed_millis` 2019531.
6. The process then exited 1 with the two lines above.
7. Afterwards, `search/attribution/` contained 0 `attribution-segment-*` files. `ctx status` reports attribution `currentness=not_materialized` and `file_blame=false`. A search against the existing generation still returns hits (10,975 sessions, lexical ready).

## Why this is not the auto-refresh reset

Before that import, with indexing mode `auto`, an in-progress Blame pass on 1.6.3 was cleared to 0 twice in the same minute the source total changed:

- 2361/9686 applied 365020, then 0/9709
- 2820/9709 applied 441224, then 0/9714

The second drop matches a Core generation file written at that minute whose source count is 9714. Segment files from the previous pass were gone. The daemon process was the same one. That matches the documented behavior that Core publication schedules attribution catch-up, and a new pass starts its counters at 0.

The manual-mode import above did not reset. It still died on `segment materializer exceeded a hard bound`. Stopping publication is not enough for this history to finish.

## Expected

One source or record that does not fit in a segment should not discard segments already written, and the message should name the bound and the source. History that did fit should remain queryable. `ctx import --all` is the documented completion path, including when Core is already current.

## Local workaround

`[blame] enabled = false`, then `ctx index mode auto`. History search keeps updating. The daemon does not start another Blame pass. There is still no committed Blame index to query.

title: Unify ctx history, graph, and Sift for 2.0
body:
ctx 2.0 brings agent-history search and Blame, the local code graph, and Sift tool-output compaction into one executable. Search and Blame remain the default setup; graph indexing and Sift hooks require explicit commands. The graph and Sift implementations are owned by ctx crates, with the old separate-product command paths removed. The README introduces the four capabilities and keeps the benchmark and migration context.

title: Accept ctx 2.0 hosted release publications

The ctx 2.0 runtime handoff stopped on a valid signed `v2.0.0` publication because the hosted release loader accepted only `v1.x`. Use the existing canonical release-version parser so the shared loader accepts current stable versions while retaining the frozen-bridge minimum and signed-identity checks.

body:
The current ctx.rs installer serves 1.6.3, whose historical factory handoff is unavailable on the release host. The installer needs to be updated before exposing 2.0 because the 1.6.3 script cannot download the larger 2.0 executable.

Add a distinct current-feed verification mode that checks the signed stable and versioned metadata, exact annotated tag, complete release asset checksums and hosted asset identities without claiming a fresh factory construction. The normal future-release contract remains unchanged. The installer deployment gate accepts this evidence and keeps its real candidate and live-install checks.

title: Fix 2.0.1 upgrade reconciliation for core-only installs
body:
Upgrading a managed core-only installation can replace the executable but leave integration ownership reconciliation pending when the older install has no companion directories. Reconciliation now creates the missing directories through the existing owner-safe layout check before publishing the integration record.

The regression exercises that exact layout and checks the executable and published record. The affected managed-pair and upgrade-engine suites pass (214 tests). This commit also updates the workspace and bundled plugin versions to 2.0.1.

title: Fix redundant integrity hashing after unchanged refresh
body:
Repeated refreshes that discarded an unchanged hard-linked index candidate could invalidate the active generation's integrity certification. The next open then rehashed retained index files, consuming CPU and cached reads even though the generation was unchanged.

Keep the authenticated candidate proof through cleanup and preserve the active certification across the link change. If that proof or the cache update fails, the existing full verification remains the fallback. A same-size, restored-mtime mutation still rejects the generation.

On the 2.0 base, the new regression fails before the fix (19,654 artifact bytes hashed versus 11,748 expected) and passes after it. The index, generation, format, query, and writer integration suites pass. Full CI on current main: scripts/check.sh --mode=ci passed (254/254 targets; 252 named cases, 0 failures).

Addresses one confirmed cause of #1030. The issue should remain open until the reporter's broader OpenCode/Blame symptoms are checked on a fixed build.

title: Document ctx 2.0.2 release
body:

title: Repair daily telemetry materialization as receipts grow
body:
The daily telemetry rollup had stopped advancing as receipt volume grew. It sent all nine days through one database request; a single recent day now contains roughly two million relevant receipts.

This keeps one fixed UTC anchor but materializes each day in a separate, idempotent request. Migration 0052 gives only that function 64 MiB of sort memory, and staging runs at 04:17 UTC so its serialized scan no longer starts alongside production at 03:17. A failed day leaves earlier completed days committed and can be retried or explicitly backfilled.

Validation: `//services/telemetry-worker:maintenance_test`, `:maintenance_postgres_test`, and `:package_test` pass. The PostgreSQL test exercises the migration, delayed receipts, failed-day recovery, and exact daily SQL.

title: Make Sift the sole output CLI and unify serde_json
body:
## What changes

`ctx sift` is the single output-filter entry point. Remove the old top-level `output`, `run`, `compact`, `restore`, and `recall` routes; update help, skills, and integration examples to use the Sift route. Existing exact `ctx output hook` installations are recognized as outdated and can be upgraded or removed without disturbing unrelated hooks. Wrapper detection recognizes `ctx sift` invocations without re-filtering child commands or standalone Sift lookalikes.

Consolidate Cargo and Bazel on the same crates.io `serde_json` 1.0.151 release, with the raw-value feature retained.

## Validation

- GPT-6 Sol code review completed; fixed both reported compatibility gaps.
- Cargo: 426 library tests across Sift, codec, and agent integrations; 28 unified CLI integration tests.
- Bazel: unified CLI, slash-command, agent-integration, presentation, and semantic dependency-boundary targets passed.
- Push guards: LOC, Cargo/Bazel ownership, and public-disclosure scan passed.

title: Preserve Blame facts when large imports reach size bounds
body:
Large Blame imports could lose otherwise valid attribution when a publication or prepared page crossed a size bound. This keeps publication within bounded pages, splits a page only when its aggregate preparation is too large, and preserves the other events in their original order. An individually oversized event remains indexed but has its facts omitted with a per-event marker, so the current graph reports Partial while retained Blame facts remain queryable. Replacing or deleting that event clears the marker.

The split path retries an owned page without cloning every ordinary Core record, restores repository preparation state before retry, and stages children through the existing publication transaction. Failure on a later page still aborts the candidate. Errors identify the source and event without exposing private details through the public protocol.

Validation:
- `ctx-attribution` library: 245/245 tests pass with default parallelism; 244/244 passed serially before the final omission test.
- `ctx-attribution-derivation`: 54/54 library tests pass; the eight direct-session lifecycle tests pass after the final change.
- Strict Clippy for changed crates, repository policy, docs checks, and formatting pass.
- Independent GPT-6 Sol review found no remaining blocker after the real omission/reopen/tombstone test.

Complexity: ordinary pages retain the existing bounded path and do not retry. Oversized pages split in halves, with at most 256 input events per page; a synthetic 256-event ordinary page took 0.30 s in both base and candidate runs, with peak RSS 27.5 MiB versus 27.0 MiB (one run each). Reporter-corpus confirmation is still pending.

Addresses #1046.

title: One file appended during capture keeps the whole provider at its previous index (`provider source changed during bounded capture`)
body:
## Summary

On a host with several agent sessions writing at once, `ctx import` (and `ctx search --refresh wait`) often keeps the previous index for a whole provider because one file changed during capture. The newest content, which is usually what an on-demand refresh is for, then does not land. Retrying immediately tends to fail the same way, because the actively written session is still being written.

`ctx doctor` after the most recent scheduled import:

```text
[1] History refresh is partial
  cursor: invalid provider transcript path "<home>/.cursor/projects": provider source changed while its authority handle was retained; claude: provider source changed during bounded capture
```

## Environment

ctx 2.0.2 managed install, macOS 15.7 arm64, manual indexing mode, about 9 concurrent agent sessions (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok, Antigravity), about 11.9k sessions / 16 GB of history.

## Observations

- Full imports in the foreground: 4 of 8 ended with a provider kept at its previous index for this reason.
- `ctx import --provider claude` five times in a row: the first 2 succeeded, the next 3 all failed with `provider source changed during bounded capture`.
- `ctx search --refresh wait` took 32-198 s per call on the same host, so retrying is expensive.
- The scheduled import also logs, intermittently: `start or recover daemon before source-backed refresh: ctx finite Core worker did not become ready: timed out waiting for live daemon lifecycle readiness`.

## Expected

One actively appended JSONL session should not hold back every other session of the same provider. Possible directions: capture up to the last complete line of an append-only file and take the rest next time; or fail only the changed session and publish the rest of the provider.

Related closed issues with similar symptoms on earlier versions: #283, #631, #662.

title: Each `ctx search` peaks at ~2.3 GB memory regardless of query or filters
body:
## Summary

Every `ctx search` call peaks at about 2.3 GB memory footprint for 2-4 seconds, whatever the query and filters. On a 16 GB machine with several agents that each search history, concurrent searches stack up to several GB.

## Environment

ctx 2.0.2 managed install, macOS 15.7 arm64, 16 GB RAM, manual indexing mode (daemon disabled), about 11.9k sessions / 16 GB of history.

## Measurements (`/usr/bin/time -l`, "peak memory footprint")

| Command | Peak footprint | Wall |
|---|---|---|
| `ctx search "<query>" --refresh off` | ~2.3-2.45 GB | 2-4 s |
| same with `--backend lexical`, `--since 1h`, or `--provider claude` | same ~2.3 GB | similar |
| `ctx show session <id> --mode lite` | ~0.5 GB | - |
| `ctx status` | ~0.23 GB | - |

Changing the query text or narrowing with `--since` / `--provider` did not change the peak, so it looks like a fixed cost per process (for example loading or mapping a whole index structure) rather than work proportional to the result set.

## Ask

- Is ~2.3 GB per search expected for a corpus of this size?
- Could narrow searches (a short `--since`, a single provider) avoid loading the full structure, or could repeated searches share one resident process instead of each paying the peak?

title: Reduce search memory and keep active transcript refresh moving
body:
Active Claude and Cursor transcripts can grow during refresh without blocking every other session in the provider. Capture authenticates the admitted prefix, leaves incomplete trailing records for the next refresh, and still rejects rewritten or replaced files and copies that could change session selection.

Search uses read-only mappings of already-opened index files instead of copying whole term dictionaries into heap buffers. Compact result formatting releases its active query reader before opening the pinned previous generation. Reference resolution and generation lifetime protections are preserved.

Refresh uses binary lookup for retained sources and reuses authenticated manifests when no permission repair is needed. This removes repeated work associated with #1030; the reported sustained CPU symptom still needs field confirmation, so that issue remains open.

Validation: `scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` passed all 254 targets, including strict Clippy. Independent GPT-6 Astra reviews covered capture integrity and mapped-reader lifetime. Focused capture qualification passed 58 tests. On an isolated 8,193-session Linux corpus, median peak compact-search RSS was 164 MiB versus 201 MiB for the published 2.0.2 binary, with identical results. A separate vocabulary-controlled comparison reduced rare-query RSS from 51 to 33 MiB and absent-query RSS from 48 to 26 MiB on the larger unique-vocabulary case; some small repeated-vocabulary cases increased. These measurements do not reproduce the reporter's full macOS corpus.

Fixes #1068.
Fixes #1069.
Refs #1030.

title: fix(source-io): keep retained file identity stable across macOS reboots
body:
macOS assigns `st_dev` when a volume is mounted, so the same APFS volume can report a different device number after a reboot. The retained JSONL and ordinary-file identities (`retained_file_identity` in `ctx-history-source-io`) hash `st_dev` into the stable token. After a reboot every retained source therefore looks like a different file object. The capture fast path (`observation != base.observation()` in `ctx-history-jsonl/src/family/route/capture.rs`) misses, the reader classifies the leaf as `Replace` because `same_stable_file` is false, and every source is re-projected in full.

What I observed on a large macOS history after a reboot:

- Certificates published before the reboot carried the previous boot's device number for the Data volume. After the reboot that number belonged to a different volume.
- With temporary tracing in the retain loop, almost every Pi leaf failed the fast path with only `stable_identity` differing. Length, mtime and the change token were equal.
- Daemon refreshes took 11–27 minutes each and reported thousands of processed sessions per run while only a handful of files had changed. Hours after the reboot, the published generation still carried the old token for every source.

On macOS this change binds the identity to the volume UUID instead of `st_dev`. The UUID is read with `fstatfs` on the open file, then `getattrlist(ATTR_VOL_UUID)` on its mount point, and the mount root's fsid must match the file's filesystem. The UUID is stable across boots and still distinguishes different volumes mounted at the same path, which an inode-only token would not. A volume that does not report a UUID keeps `st_dev`. Any other lookup failure is returned as an error, so a transient error cannot switch a token between the two forms. Other Unix platforms keep their exact token bytes. On macOS the token-byte tests now require the UUID form.

The lookup adds one `fstatfs` and one `getattrlist` per identity observation. An ordinary-file observation takes two identity observations.

Inode reuse at the same path on the same volume behaves as it does today within one boot; this change only stops a reboot from resetting every token.

Upgrading changes the macOS token once, so each retained source is re-projected one more time. On a copy of the same data root in `source-refresh-only` mode, the first refresh with this build rebuilt everything in about 3.5 minutes. The following refreshes took 19–36 seconds, with no Pi leaf failing the fast path. On a smaller copy, every published certificate carried the volume UUID form.

Tests (macOS arm64):

- `ctx-history-source-io`: 70/71. The failure, `inventory_rejects_non_utf8_symlink_and_nonregular_components`, also fails on unmodified `main` because APFS rejects non-UTF-8 names with EILSEQ.
- `ctx-history-jsonl` 112/112, `ctx-history-providers-jsonl-shared` 62/62, `ctx-history-provider-codex` 104/104, `ctx-history-provider-claude-cursor` 54/54.
- These four were run with `TMPDIR` pointing at a non-symlinked directory. Under the default macOS temp dir, 9 `ctx-history-jsonl` tests fail with "0 retained root authorities" on both `main` and this branch.

Not changed here, same `st_dev` pattern:

- `ctx-history-source-sqlite` `NativeFileIdentity`
- `ctx-history-provider-gemini` `GeminiFileObservation`

Related to #1030.

title: Prepare ctx 2.1.0 with scalable Blame and reliable setup
body:
Large histories could fail Blame at 16,384 sources, and incremental refresh could demand another full index worth of free space. Installation could then return success despite a failed history refresh, while uninstall/reinstall left automatic indexing disabled.

Stream source inventories through disk-backed reconciliation and read prior event proofs only for changed or deleted sources. Account for actual candidate writes and clone obligations, preserve the prior readable generation on storage failures, and retain bounded retries with the previous failure visible. Make setup and installer results reflect what completed, preserve indexing preferences through legacy and current uninstall, and ignore only updater errors superseded by a verified new installation.

Prepare one 2.1.0 release. The existing legacy upgrade bridge remains unchanged.

- Independent code review and focused regression tests for source identity, pagination, replacement/deletion, rollback, cancellation, disk-full recovery, and retained readers.

- Populated-index work counters show unchanged event payloads are not decoded or spilled during a one-source update.
- Installer tests with PowerShell enabled: 390 passed; native Windows-specific cases were not run.

title: Support relocating the managed data root to another filesystem
body:
CTX currently keeps managed state under `~/.ctx`. Please provide a supported way to move the entire managed data root to another filesystem while retaining normal CLI and daemon behavior.

`CTX_DATA_ROOT` is not a complete solution for a managed installation: the [managed root used by the installed lifecycle](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/crates/ctx-history-platform/src/paths.rs#L13-L19) remains tied to `~/.ctx`. Replacing `~/.ctx` with a symlink is [rejected by installation identity validation](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/main/crates/ctx-cli/src/identity.rs#L79-L95).

Could CTX support one configurable managed root used consistently by the CLI, daemon, supervisor, and index components? A safely validated symlink could be another approach. This is not a request to remove the existing safety checks.

The solution should preserve installation identity, ownership and permission checks, protection against path substitution, and separation of provider source data from CTX-managed data. Please also document a safe migration procedure.

title: Reduce history refresh CPU and fix SQLite WAL replay
body:
Codex watcher events for ordinary non-transcript files could trigger repeated history refreshes. This change filters those events where the file identity proves they are irrelevant, retains transcript and ambiguous-event handling, and recognizes densely populated Codex session directories.

It also removes a redundant Codex validation pass, adds a bounded in-memory index for Blame source lookups, and reuses prepared statements during OpenCode scans. SQLite replay now detects committed edits and deletions after rollback and WAL frame reuse; old physical replay checkpoints are recertified once.

Addresses #1030. Changed OpenCode databases still require a full scan; this does not claim to resolve every busy-host CPU report.

Validation: all 255 normal CI targets passed, including focused provider edit/delete/WAL replay and relocation regressions. Independent code review is clear. An isolated watcher check retained every transcript update while avoiding refreshes from irrelevant file activity; final signed-release CPU comparisons will follow before publication.

title: Show readable sizes and actionable disk-space shortfalls
body:
Disk-space errors print raw byte counts and leave users to calculate how much space to free. Share the existing byte formatter across resource diagnostics, stats, and compaction output; when required and available space are known, also show the upward-rounded amount to free. The reported example now reads `free at least 121.5 MiB; required 8.1 GiB; available 8.0 GiB`.

Keep exact numeric fields and admission decisions unchanged. Unknown requirements report observed availability, and size-limit errors do not suggest freeing disk. No new external dependency.

Fixes #1082.

Validation: `scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` passed (build, Clippy, all 255 test targets). Independent code review found no remaining blockers; 11 focused cases passed across stats, compaction, and shortage/capture/restart regressions.

title: Fix graph YAML streams and local document error handling
body:
Valid YAML streams containing multiple documents made `ctx graph` abort, and `--json` still emitted an unstructured error. Read local documents through one immutable-byte extraction path and let the existing YAML parser iterate the stream. Fields and references retain their document number, limits apply across the file, and a malformed later document cannot publish partial facts.

Directory indexing now records known local syntax/encoding failures as file diagnostics, removes that file's stale facts, and continues with other files. Diagnostics survive unchanged scans; edits, forced updates, and parser revisions retry extraction. Explicit imports preserve previous captures on failure. Resource limits, converter/provider failures, and storage errors remain fatal and preserve the previous graph. Both CLI entry paths share human/JSON error rendering. No new dependency or custom parser is introduced.

Validation:

- 89 focused tests covering YAML streams, aliases and limits, document provenance through reference rebinding, stale-fact replacement and recovery, capture preservation, parser revision changes, and both CLI error paths.
- 11 independent CLI acceptance checks passed on the final rebuilt binary, including ordinary DOCX import and graph preservation when generated Markdown cannot be parsed.
- `scripts/check.sh --mode=ci`: strict build/Clippy and all 255 default-CI test targets passed on the integrated commit.
- Independent GPT-6 Astra review approved the implementation and integration with current main.

Fixes #1083

title: Don't demand as much free space as the opencode sqlite file to process it
body: The OpenCode database can run into tens of gigabytes even though, as we've discussed here before, not all of it is stuff you need to index.

title: Reduce history refresh CPU and explain daemon activity
body:
Large history refreshes repeatedly searched source inventories and rebuilt search records whose contents had not changed. This patch uses sorted source lookups and retains exactly matching indexed records. Linux source reads also avoid repeated ancestor probes while preserving replacement, symlink, and mount checks. Older message edits and deletions still pass through complete source validation.

`ctx status` now shows the recorded history stage and trigger. `ctx status --sample 5` adds a short, read-only CPU and activity report, with JSON available through `--format json`. It reports aggregate counts and known status codes, excludes paths and transcript content, and leaves stale or missing evidence unknown. Blame and semantic progress are explicitly advisory rather than attributed to daemon CPU.

Validation: all 256 normal CI targets pass. Independent implementation and integration reviews are clear. Exact-history, WAL lifecycle, restart, mixed-provider watching, and diagnostic privacy/read-only checks pass. The five-repeat comparison passes all 350 import checks and the performance/scaling limits; both watcher orders pass too. A matched diagnostics control shows no measured idle CPU increase, no material import slowdown, and 3.8 ms of CPU for a ten-second report. These prelanding performance comparisons use different build pipelines; exact signed-release qualification will run before publication.

Prepares version 2.1.4, including the disk-space diagnostics and graph YAML/document fixes already on main. Linux performance measurements do not establish resolution of the separate macOS report in #1030.

Override it to 7.29.1 and regenerate both pnpm lockfiles to address [Dependabot alert 224](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/security/dependabot/224) and the [matching docs-site alert 215](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/security/dependabot/215). title: Use CTX_DATA_ROOT for the complete managed data root
body:
`CTX_DATA_ROOT` now selects the complete managed root, including `config.toml`, daemon state, and default runtime assets. Native supervision and detached workers preserve that selection. An unset or empty value uses `~/.ctx`; `--data-root` remains a command-specific history override.

The migration guide covers stopping writers, copying the complete root, setting the environment, and restarting. Windows private status-file replacement also supports long selected paths, preserving existing write-through, retry, and ACL behavior.

An upstream indexing optimization can refresh an optional certification cache after committing a generation. The affected fault-injection test now recognizes that exact optional write and checks that its failure leaves the generation usable, while retaining every required publication-stage failure assertion.

Validation:

- Integrated CI: all 256 targets pass; implementation and subsequent fixes independently reviewed.
- Windows x64: 72 native assertions cover actual scheduled-task startup, supervised restart, long-root copy/reselection, environment capture, search identity preservation, command override, and default fallback. The private-JSON regression suite passes 5/5.
- macOS ARM64: native launchd startup/restart and copy between distinct APFS filesystems preserve config, installation identity, and search results. Registration from the copied root, command override, default fallback, and cleanup pass.
- Linux cross-filesystem migration preserves config, identities, runtime files, and search results; focused lifecycle/upgrade and installer checks pass.

Native runs used diagnostic binaries and synthetic fixtures, rather than release qualification. The Windows copy used one volume. Its product harness passed, but the outer lab wrapper reported a temporary-directory removal failure; product task/process cleanup and VM shutdown were verified separately. macOS cleanup and restoration passed.

Fixes #1084.

title: Add optional hosted history and portable backups
body:
Back up retained agent history or share selected sessions through a ctx server. The feature is an opt-in beta: ordinary local use does not start a server, connect to one, or upload history.

- Portable archive export, verification and restore; server checkpoints and a documented encrypted-backup workflow with restic.
- Collection-scoped read, publish and manage permissions, single-use enrollment, additional devices, credential rotation and revocation.
- Explicit sharing selection, resumable upload queues, remote search/retrieval and read-only MCP tools.
- A short README introduction and setup guide.

The server is a single process. It uses filesystem storage, SQLite and the existing search index; live storage encryption belongs to the operator. SSO, SCIM and multi-node operation are outside this beta.

Validation: `scripts/check.sh --mode ci` passes all 264 targets on the final integrated tree, including build, Clippy and repository audits. The full hosted lifecycle E2E passes on the identical final binary, including encrypted backup and fresh restore. Independent security and integration reviews are complete.

Related to #1035 and #1036. Archives preserve retained normalized history; they are not native agent-session backups.

title: release: prepare ctx 2.2.0
body:
Prepare ctx 2.2.0 with opt-in hosted history beta, portable archive export/restore, and the managed data-root fix already on main. Align workspace, plugin and marketplace versions, regenerate the build locks, and add release notes.

Validation: normal integrated CI on the release branch; external Cargo dependency records are unchanged. Signed release artifacts are built separately from the landed source.

title: 2.0.x managed installs can't upgrade: installer rerun fails with "did not return typed lifecycle proof"; ctx upgrade reports latest 1.6.5
body:
## Summary

A 2.0.2 managed install cannot reach 2.1.x. `ctx upgrade` says it is up to date with "latest 1.6.5". Rerunning the hosted installer, which the 2.0.5 release notes suggest for "existing 2.x installations that miss the transition", fails every time with:

```
Installing ctx 2.1.4...
error: managed ctx upgrade did not return typed lifecycle proof; rerun this installer to finish any retained attempt
```

Rerunning, as the message suggests, gives the same error. Nothing is changed: the binary sha256 stays the same and no transaction files are left behind.

## Environment

ctx 2.0.2 managed install (hosted installer), macOS 15.7 arm64, manual indexing mode (daemon disabled). Installer run as `curl -fsSL https://ctx.rs/install | sh -s -- --no-skill --no-setup --no-modify-path`.

## What happens

`run_managed_core_upgrade` hands the upgrade to the installed 2.0.2 binary with `CTX_RELEASE_METADATA_URL` / `CTX_RELEASE_METADATA_SIGNATURE_URL` pointing at the downloaded v3 metadata. I printed the receipt the installer validates:

```json
{
  "applied": false,
  "artifact_url": "https://cli.ctx.rs/storage/v1/object/public/releases/artifacts/stable/1.6.5/ctx-macos-arm64",
  "channel": "stable",
  "current_version": "2.0.2",
  "latest_version": "1.6.5",
  "metadata_url": "https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v2/releases/stable/ctx-release-metadata.env",
  "status": "up_to_date",
  "update_available": false
}
```

The receipt shows 2.0.2 ignored the override. It still read the v2 feed, which now serves the 1.6.5 bridge, so `validate_managed_upgrade_result` rejects the receipt.

## Likely cause

In 2.0.2 the metadata URL override is only compiled into qualification builds: [`metadata_url()` @ v2.0.2](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.0.2/crates/ctx-upgrade-engine/src/upgrade/metadata.rs#L84-L104) reads `CTX_RELEASE_METADATA_URL` under `#[cfg(ctx_release_qualification)]`, and otherwise hard-codes `functions/v2` for `stable`. Release binaries therefore can't be redirected to the new feed.

Current feeds:

| Feed | `CTX_RELEASE_VERSION` |
|---|---|
| `functions/v1/releases/stable` | 1.3.2 |
| `functions/v2/releases/stable` | 1.6.5 |
| `functions/v3/releases/stable` | 2.1.4 |

So a 2.0.x install on the stable channel always sees 1.6.5 (older than itself) and never reaches v3, whether through `ctx upgrade`, automatic upgrades, or the installer. Setting `CTX_UPGRADE_FUNCTIONS_BASE=https://cli.ctx.rs/functions/v3` (with or without `CTX_ALLOW_CUSTOM_RELEASE_BASE_URL=1`) does not change this either.

## Expected

Either rerunning the installer upgrades a 2.0.x managed install to the current release, or the release notes say what 2.0.0–2.0.4 installs should do.

## Possible fixes

- Have the installer apply the new candidate itself (the candidate-apply / hosted-transaction path) when the installed version is below the first release that honors the v3 feed, instead of delegating to the installed binary.
- Or have the v2 feed serve the current 2.x release to 2.x clients, while keeping the 1.6.5 bridge for 1.x.
- Add a 2.0.x starting point to the upgrade walk tests.

Context: I'd like to pick up the fixes for #1068 and #1069 (released in 2.0.4), but this install is stuck on 2.0.2.
