## Related work

This extends retrieval ergonomics around [ctxrs/ctx#1035](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/1035), not the already-delivered shared service. Archive provenance already shipped in [ctxrs/ctx#1134](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/pull/1134). The maintainer should decide the implementation and whether an existing abstraction can supply these outcomes.

title: Lexical search stops after 65,536 candidate events, so multi-word queries on large histories miss their best matches
body:
## Summary

Lexical search scores at most 65,536 candidate events per query (`LEXICAL_WORK_BUDGET_V1.maximum_candidate_docs`, `crates/ctx-history-index-query/src/contract/lexical.rs:144-162` at v2.3.0). The executor walks the union of the query terms' postings in segment and doc order. When the budget runs out it stops (`break 'segments` in `execution/search/executor.rs`) and ranks only the candidates it has seen so far.

On a large history, a multi-word query with common words easily matches more than 65,536 events. Whether the best match makes the top 10 then depends on where it sits in scan order, not on its score. ctx does report it: the JSON has `truncation.lexical.exhaustion = {counter: "candidate_docs", limit: 65536, used: 65536}`, and the text output warns "Search reached a bounded candidate or work limit" and suggests adding a filter. But the user can't raise the budget, and when you don't yet know which session to filter to, you need a query without filters.

## Repro (synthetic)

ctx 2.3.0, built from the v2.3.0 tag with `cargo build --release -p ctx`, on macOS arm64. Runs used a scratch `HOME`, `CTX_ANALYTICS_ENABLED=false`, `CTX_UPGRADE_AUTO=off`, semantic search off, and network access denied.

- **Corpus:** one `ctx-history-jsonl-v2` file with 19,500 sessions of 50 events each (975,000 events). Each event has 30 tokens drawn from a Zipf(1.07) vocabulary of 50,000 words.
- **Size:** just under the 1,000,000-record bound for one custom import file.
- **Planted targets:** 40 sessions spread evenly through the file. Each holds one short event made of three common words (vocabulary ranks 20–60), each repeated three times. The query for a target is those three words, so the target should be the top hit.
- **Candidate pool:** for these queries, the union of matching events is 155,742–289,588 (median 205,976).
- **Command:** `ctx search "<3 words>" --backend lexical --events --limit 10 --format json --refresh off`

| build | recall@1 | recall@10 | queries that hit a work cap | `query_seconds` median (max) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| v2.3.0 as released | 0.325 | 0.325 | 40 / 40 | 5.0 ms (5.8) |
| caps raised 16× | 1.000 | 1.000 | 0 / 40 | 11.0 ms (14.5) |

Both rows are the same on a second run. The raised build changes only two constants:

```diff
-    maximum_candidate_docs: 65_536,
-    maximum_body_posting_advances: 2_097_152,
+    maximum_candidate_docs: 1_048_576,
+    maximum_body_posting_advances: 33_554_432,
```

With the released caps, the 13 targets found are the ones that sit early in scan order: almost all are in the last third of the file. Recall (0.325) is close to the share of the candidate pool the budget covers (65,536 / about 206,000 ≈ 0.32). Raising both caps restores every target and adds about 6 ms per query.

## Suggested fix

Any of these would help. The first two are small:

1. **Make the budget configurable.** For example, `search.lexical.max_candidate_docs` and `max_body_posting_advances` in config, or an environment variable, with today's values as the default.
2. **Make it adaptive.** Scale the candidate budget with the index's document count, or with a time budget, instead of a fixed count. 65,536 is a large share of a small index and a small share of a multi-million-event one.
3. **Bound top-k work by score, not by doc order.** Tantivy's block-max WAND (`TopDocs` over a BM25 `BooleanQuery`) skips candidates that can't enter the top k. That keeps the work bounded without making results depend on scan order.

<details><summary>Corpus generator (Python)</summary>

```python
# usage: python3 gen.py <out.jsonl> <events> <targets.json>
import bisect, json, random, sys
out, n_events, targets_path = sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]), sys.argv[3]
rng = random.Random(7)
V = 50_000
words = ["w" + format(i, "x") for i in range(V)]
cum, s = [], 0.0
for r in range(V):
    s += 1.0 / (r + 1) ** 1.07
    cum.append(s)
draw = lambda: words[bisect.bisect_left(cum, rng.random() * s)]
PER, N_T = 50, 40
n_sessions = n_events // PER
target_at = {int((i + 0.5) * n_sessions / N_T): i for i in range(N_T)}
targets, src = [], "synthetic"
with open(out, "w") as f:
    w = lambda o: f.write(json.dumps(o, separators=(",", ":")) + "\n")
    w({"record_type": "manifest", "schema_version": "ctx-history-jsonl-v2"})
    w({"record_type": "source", "source_id": src, "provider_key": "synthetic-agent",
       "source_format": "synthetic-jsonl", "raw_source_path": "/tmp/synthetic.jsonl"})
    for si in range(n_sessions):
        sid, day = f"s{si:06d}", 1 + si * 27 // n_sessions
        w({"record_type": "session", "source_id": src, "provider_session_id": sid, "cwd": "/workspace/app",
           "started_at": f"2026-01-{day:02d}T00:00:00Z", "agent_scope": "primary",
           "role_hint": "developer", "status": "completed"})
        tgt = si in target_at
        if tgt:
            q = rng.sample(words[20:60], 3)
            targets.append({"session": sid, "query": " ".join(q)})
        for ei in range(PER):
            text = " ".join(q * 3) if tgt and ei == 25 else " ".join(draw() for _ in range(30))
            w({"record_type": "event", "source_id": src, "provider_session_id": sid, "event_index": ei,
               "event_type": "message", "role": "user" if ei % 2 == 0 else "assistant",
               "occurred_at": f"2026-01-{day:02d}T{ei // 60:02d}:{ei % 60:02d}:00Z", "payload": {"text": text}})
json.dump(targets, open(targets_path, "w"))
```

Run it with `python3 gen.py corpus.jsonl 975000 targets.json`, then `ctx import --input-format ctx-history-jsonl-v2 --path corpus.jsonl`. For each target, run the search command above and check whether `provider_session_id` of a top-10 result equals the target's session.

</details>

Prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); each repro was run on the stated version and is included above.

title: Feature request: opt-in usage-aware project archiving and inactive-history retention
body:
## Problem

CTX 2.3.0's local usage report keeps daily aggregates by operation, outcome, result counts, and bytes for about 400 days. It does not retain conversation or event identities or per-conversation access timestamps. That retention applies to usage aggregates, not indexed history. `ctx archive export` can preview and export selected workspace and time ranges, and `ctx archive verify` and `restore` can preserve and recover a snapshot, but this remains a manual workflow and does not remove a project from the active index.

## Impact

As histories and local index data grow across projects, an operator cannot identify which conversations were recently returned to agents, determine which project histories appear inactive, or reclaim the corresponding active-index storage without manually assembling and checking archive selections. Logging full queries or content would create unnecessary privacy risk.

## Suggested improvement

- Offer an opt-in, local-only "last surfaced by CTX" signal for a conversation when a supported CLI or MCP operation returns its content, including search results and `show` output. This records delivery by CTX, not proof that an agent consumed the content; label it accordingly. Do not retain prompts, query text, content, file paths, or machine identity.
- Provide a read-only project/workspace activity report with last source update, last surfaced timestamp, approximate active-index storage, and coverage state. Distinguish never observed from no tracking data, and reuse explicit project mapping rather than guessing from the current checkout.
- Let an operator preview projects or conversations beyond a configurable inactivity period, export an archive using the existing scoped selection, verify it, and then explicitly remove the selected records from the active index. Keep archived records restorable, and prevent an archived scope from being silently re-added by automatic refresh until it is explicitly restored or re-enabled.
- Keep native provider histories and source files untouched. Do not switch global indexing to manual, delete archives, or purge history automatically. Preview and export must be read-only until the operator explicitly confirms the active-index change.

## Privacy and safety

Usage marks should remain in the owner-private local data root, be opt-in, and use only the minimum session identity and timestamps needed for the report. The existing aggregate `ctx stats` behavior should remain content-free and should not become a per-conversation access log by default. CTX can observe returned content, not whether the agent actually read or relied on it.

## Related work

Coordinate project mapping with [ctxrs/ctx#1149](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/1149), reuse the project/time archive selection shipped in [ctxrs/ctx#1138](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/pull/1138), and keep repeated snapshot-transfer work in [ctxrs/ctx#1148](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/issues/1148). This request is for local inactivity review and reversible reduction of the active index, not another context-view or incremental-transfer proposal.

title: Two search generations are copied instead of hard-linked
body:
ctx 2.3.0, macOS (Apple silicon), APFS. Data root on the internal volume.

`ctx docs show storage` says:

> Generation candidates hard-link unchanged base segments when the filesystem
> supports it.

On this install they are copied instead. After a publication (reproduced twice:
once with `ctx import --all --incremental`, once with `ctx doctor --repair`),
the active and previous generations contain the same segments under the same
names and sizes, but every file is a distinct inode with link count 1:

    $ ls -i generation-A/02c7e979ed20490e820d961e8c99eb4c.store \
             generation-B/02c7e979ed20490e820d961e8c99eb4c.store
    335206715 generation-A/02c7e979ed20490e820d961e8c99eb4c.store
    335219263 generation-B/02c7e979ed20490e820d961e8c99eb4c.store

    $ stat -f "%l links" generation-B/02c7e979ed20490e820d961e8c99eb4c.store
    1 links

    # files present in both generations, by name: 228
    # bytes those files occupy twice:            9 GB
    # shared inodes across the two generations:   0

Hard links do work in that exact directory, so this is not a filesystem
limitation:

    $ cd ~/.ctx/search/lexical && echo probe > .hl && ln .hl .hl2
    $ stat -f "%l links %i inode" .hl .hl2
    2 links 335175734 inode
    2 links 335175734 inode

Impact: `~/.ctx` is 20 GB — 9.3 GB active + 9.3 GB previous + 0.9 GB
attribution — where the shared segments should cost nothing extra. The
generation sizes themselves look normal (store 5.25 GB, term 2.52 GB,
pos 1.18 GB, idx 0.52 GB for 4,402 sessions / 547k searchable events).

To reproduce:

1. `ctx import --all --incremental` (or any command that publishes a new
   generation).
2. Read `search/lexical/active-generation.json` for `active.directory` and
   `previous.directory`.
3. Compare `ls -i` for the file names present in both directories.

Expected: unchanged base segments are hard-linked, so their inodes match and
the parent directory's `du` stays close to one generation.

Actual: every segment is a fresh copy.

title: Add Prime Agent history support for 2.4.0
body:
Adds Prime Agent as a distinct history provider, including automatic discovery of CLI sessions, RLM child sessions, and T3 stores. Version 3 transcripts retain conversation and custom messages, Python tool calls/results, session relationships, and declared file/diff evidence for ordinary history and Blame. Human output displays “Prime Agent”; machine output uses `prime_agent`.

Discovery follows Prime's environment/settings precedence and bounded native layouts. Imports preserve valid records around malformed or oversized rows, authenticate session headers across rewrites, and isolate unreadable files in registered sources. The shared explicit-directory preflight limitation is documented with a named-source workaround. Python payloads do not claim exact file production or MCP server identity.

Prepares version 2.4.0, updates provider contracts/docs/fixtures and plugin manifests, and upgrades Markdown/Zstandard dependencies flagged by the release advisory scan. The existing exact-version paste maintenance exception is time-limited through November 8, 2026.

Validation: normal CI passes all 269 Bazel targets, and independent code re-review passes with no remaining blocking findings. Debug and optimized Linux builds each pass 115 real-session assertions across seven sessions and three stores; scratch Blame passes 30 assertions and cites Prime evidence without inventing a producer. All five cross-compiled diagnostic artifacts pass compatibility and artifact checks. Official signing, release review, and final-artifact qualification follow the documented release process after merge.

title: fix(opencode): enforce payload bounds during snapshot acquisition
body:
## Problem

OpenCode copied oversized SQLite cells before hydration could reject them.

## Fix

Check payload lengths in SQL and retain row metadata for typed rejection. Bounded copies preserve safe lookup prefixes without payload-dependent constraints. Canonical joins and ordering keep results stable across optional indexes; the parser revision forces old receipts to rescan. Generic selected copies preserve native schema and values.

Fixes #1128

Thanks to kvnloo for the report and the analysis in #1129.

## Tests

Owning suites and strict Clippy pass: 80 SQLite-source and 118 provider tests, with 3 existing diagnostics ignored. Regressions cover both migrated-overlap cases, automatic UNIQUE indexes, and 72 randomized full/bounded comparisons. All 269 default CI targets pass.

For a 128 MiB TEXT cell, peak SQLite allocation falls from 403,608,408 to 234,256 bytes; peak RSS from 401,948 to 9,520 KiB.

title: Fix primary Claude and Pi commit attribution
body:
## Problem
Primary Claude Code and Pi sessions lose commit attribution despite carrying a real commit command and its exact result.

## Fix
Require native ownership for both the command and result. Preserve Claude sidechain markers and Pi parent claims. Keep child sessions, forks, copied evidence and unknown-origin imports unattributed, and reject failed or incomplete results. Older lossy projections require reimport.

## Tests
Synthetic import-to-blame tests use real temporary Git commits, including mixed primary/sidechain files, Pi nested and parallel calls, Codex code mode, and oversized failed results. Migration tests, owning suites, affected tests and strict Clippy pass.

Fixes #1142

title: Report active lexical storage sizes in status
body:
## Problem

Status reports processed source bytes without explaining the active lexical generation's storage. Refs #1147.

## Fix

Report docstore/Core, terms, postings, positions, fast fields, other, and total bytes in human and JSON status. Read the bounded publication-time inventory without scanning index contents. Document logical-byte accounting and unavailable measurements. The shared schema requires all seven counters in `0..2^53-1` and defines `size_unavailable`.

## Tests

All 133 affected targets passed on the final serial run after JVM timing and test-daemon failures in the first run. Owning tests, strict Clippy, docs, formatting, and policy checks passed. Coverage includes accounting, human rendering, malformed storage, and CLI-to-SDK normalization. The schema regression fails before the fix. Swift was unavailable locally.

On a synthetic 300,000-document, 1.31 GB index, JSON status took 365 ms median and 518 ms p95 across 30 fresh-process runs after five warmups (Linux x86-64, fastbuild, shared host load).

title: Fix lexical top-k retrieval with global block bounds
body:
## Problem

Broad lexical queries stopped in posting order before reaching stronger later hits, especially in output-heavy histories or segments with deleted rows.

## Fix

Skip native posting blocks using coverage, global BM25 bounds for each class weight, and exact identity ties. Exclude deleted rows from rank bounds and search candidate charges. Inspections and cursor movements stay metered, with unchanged ceilings and JSON/text exhaustion reporting.

Fixes #1152.

## Tests

9,600 independent BM25 comparisons, late-winner and production-budget regressions, malformed tombstones, citations and determinism. Owning CI and all 123 affected targets pass; one JVM deadline test passed unchanged on retry. At 800k tool outputs, three/four-word queries find the best hit with complete work in 35.9/49.2 ms median; at 3M messages, 127.4/170.6 ms. The benchmark reproduces these runs.

title: fix(index): prefer hard links for unchanged generation segments
body:
## Problem

Generation cloning preferred reflinks, and macOS hard-link attempts always returned `EOPNOTSUPP`. Unchanged segments could therefore retain separate inodes despite filesystem support for hard links.

## Fix

Prefer directory-relative hard links for certified immutable segments on Linux and macOS. Both native unsupported errors (`ENOTSUP` and `EOPNOTSUPP`) allow reflink or verified-copy fallback; unrelated errors remain fatal. Mutable control files stay independent. Document the fallback order and reflink accounting in `du`.

Fixes #1154.

## Tests

The publication regression fails on the original base on XFS and passes with hard-link preference. Direct classifier tests cover unsupported and fatal errors; a native Darwin probe fails with the old classifier and passes with this fix. Owning suites, strict Clippy, and the affected tier pass after rebasing onto main.

Native APFS file-operation probes passed. The full macOS suite was not run because the test machine lacked disk space.

title: fix: isolate Pi sidecars and retain tool activity
body:
## Problem

A single non-session or unreadable JSONL file could block Pi imports. Nested tool calls also lost their invocation activity.

## Fix

Report invalid or inaccessible files individually, retain prior history, and import healthy peers. Keep torn headers pending and preserve existing size limits and symlink restrictions. Parse nested and top-level calls and results.

The activity result `structured_content` field is absent; Core retains the native envelope. Producer-authority changes remain in #1157, which will rebase afterward.

## Tests

155 owning test cases and 15 edge probes passed. All 269 affected targets have passing results; one CLI cancellation failure passed on an unchanged rerun. Synthetic fixtures cover sidecars, permissions, symlinks, header limits, recovery, tool activity, and commit evidence.

Fixes #1143
Fixes #1145

title: Fix Codex code-mode exec attribution
body:
## Problem

Codex code-mode `exec` calls retained JavaScript arguments but produced no command evidence. Their array-valued outputs also lacked captured result text, leaving commits unreachable from blame.

## Fix

Capture `input_text` items and recognize a single literal `tools.exec_command` call followed by unchanged result output. Support printed stdout and printed exec-result objects. Ambiguous scripts retain searchable text without command authority. Advance the Codex parser revision so existing sessions are reprocessed.

Fixes #1144.

## Tests

Synthetic regressions cover real disposable Git commits reaching blame, full-OID output, duplicate fields, dynamic and multiple calls, failed results, patch evidence, and publication replay/append. The initial regressions fail on the base. Five owning Bazel suites pass with strict Clippy, and all 117 affected targets pass locally. Two lifecycle tests passed on an unchanged rerun.

title: Keep large live Codex journals incremental
body:
## Problem

Small appends to large live Codex journals repeatedly replay history and publish full generations.

## Fix

Resume authenticated suffixes, use exact generation-owned membership, and coalesce small appends within two seconds. Keep compatible schema-22 snapshots readable for search and blame, refresh attribution automatically after upgrade, and report search availability and progress.

## Tests

Append/restart regressions, main-produced schema-22 search and blame fixtures, owning CI checks and the affected suite. The isolated 320 MB upgrade preserves search and blame before, during and after automatic publication.

Fixes #1146

title: docs: finalize ctx 2.4.0 release notes
body:
Replace the Unreleased and previous 2.4.0 changelog sections with the reviewed 2.4.0 release notes, dated November 4, 2026.

Validated the exact notes text, release metadata, release-note parser, and affected documentation tests. The change contains no code edits.

title: Reduce attribution and CLI contract crate sizes
body:
## Problem

Attribution and CLI contract tests exceed the 21,000-line crate limits.

## Fix

Reuse the model's diagnostic-candidate validation and move native-blame tests into the existing CLI qualification crate. No behavior change; limits and assertions are unchanged.

## Tests

Crate-size preflight, repository policy, owning tests, and `bash scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` pass. All 13 native-blame tests still run with unchanged results. One existing semantic-wait assertion failed initially and passed on rerun without changes.

title: Report automatic Blame upgrade rebuilds as retryable
body:
## Problem

After upgrading from 2.3.0, Blame recommends a full import while automatic maintenance is already rebuilding its incompatible projection.

## Fix

Report retryable rebuilding for admitted work on a responsive persistent daemon, with progress and `ctx status` guidance. Show worker failures and preserve manual or unavailable-maintenance repair advice. Keep status polling from prolonging finite Core workers, and update the docs and release note.

## Tests

The published-2.3.0 fixture covers queued, suspended, failed, restarted and recovered Blame and status. The failure regression fails on the previous head. Import cancellation, owning suites, crate-size preflight and full CI passed.

title: Replace paste with a compatible upstream tokenizer dependency
body:
The release dependency closure still includes `paste 1.0.15` (RUSTSEC-2024-0436) through `tokenizers 0.22.2`, used by fastembed 5.17.2 and directly by the macOS semantic model. The November 4 review found no compatible published replacement: tokenizers 0.23.2 still requires paste, including through fastembed 7.5.0.

Follow a supported upstream migration to tokenizers 1.0 with coordinated embedding and Core ML changes, or a compatible maintained pastey-based upstream. Do not create a local fork or vendor tokenizers. Re-review before the renewed exception expires on February 5, 2027, or sooner if a compatible upstream becomes available.

Acceptance:

- Remove paste from the release dependency closure and remove its advisory exception.
- Verify numerical embedding compatibility on a sample and preserve existing indexes; explicitly document any unavoidable re-embedding.
- Preserve the Core ML / ONNX runtime handoff.
- Update Cargo and Bazel locks consistently and pass advisory, semantic, and full CI checks.

title: Renew paste advisory exception through 2027-02-05

## Problem

The paste advisory exception expires November 8, blocking release scans afterward.

## Fix

Renew it through February 5, 2027 after reviewing fresh OSV/RustSec data, checksum-verified locked sources, and current upstream releases. The advisory remains unmaintained-only, with no compatible upstream replacement. Track the migration in #1167.

Governed release advisory preflight, advisory gate/input tests, repository policy checks, and old/new expiry boundary checks passed.

title: Fix telemetry deployment tooling for pinned pnpm and idle staging
body:
## Problem

Unpinned pnpm rejected frozen installs, and the Queue gate rejected valid Cloudflare responses and normally idle staging queues.

## Fix

Pin telemetry and docs-site to pnpm 10.34.9 without changing lockfiles. Accept REST errors that are absent, null or empty; reject malformed or error-bearing responses.

For staging publication and ongoing checks only, allow three explicitly empty GraphQL datasets when both REST metric envelopes succeed with numeric zero backlog, bytes and oldest age, and topology passes. Sampled idle staging still requires valid zero concurrency. Missing or errored data fails closed; production and rollback requirements stay unchanged.

## Tests

Telemetry tests, reviewer compatibility/adversarial suites, and affected Bazel targets pass. All 124 production/rollback comparisons match base. Read-only live staging passes. No deployment performed.

title: Report active Blame catch-up as retryable
body:
## Problem

When Blame lagged newer history, negative queries told agents to run a full import even while the daemon was already catching up.

## Fix

Apply the existing admitted, responsive maintenance check to stale diagnostics. Blame and status return retryable `rebuilding` with `check_status` during catch-up. Failed or unavailable maintenance retains repair advice, and successful `stale_committed` results stay unchanged. Update the recovery docs and changelog.

## Tests

The catch-up regression fails on the base. Owning Bazel suites and `bash scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` pass locally, including active catch-up, suspension, worker failure, recovery, and retained commit results.

title: Reclaim abandoned candidates before retrying index rebuilds
body:
## Problem

Interrupted search index rebuilds leave abandoned candidate directories until a later publication succeeds, so repeated retries accumulate disk use.

## Fix

Reclaim inactive directories before rebuilding when the publication pointer is understood. The existing writer lock and retention leases protect active and previous generations, live readers, and a writer's in-progress candidate. Unknown pointer formats remain untouched during staging.

## Tests

The repeated-rebuild regressions fail on the base and pass with the fix. All five owning suites and `bash scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` pass under the build governor.

title: Preserve per-file isolation for explicit Pi imports
body:
## Problem

Explicit Pi folder imports stopped during inventory when a neighboring file was unreadable, before the provider could import healthy sessions and report the problem file.

## Fix

Let directory accounting defer permission-denied regular files to provider refresh. Preserve counts and fatal root/enumeration errors, omit incomplete change tokens, and keep symlinks unfollowed. The shared change also fixes Claude, Codex and Prime explicit-path imports.

Cline SDK requires both present session catalogs to be readable before certifying membership. An unreadable catalog reports failure and preserves prior sessions; index-only and database-only roots remain supported when the other catalog is absent.

## Tests

Added Pi regressions for unreadable sidecars, non-session JSONL, symlinks, retention, retries and fatal directory failures. Cline SDK regressions cover both disjoint-catalog directions, repeated failures, repair, append and single-catalog roots. Owning suites pass (548 cases), and full local CI passes (269 targets). One semantic-readiness test failed once and passed on the unchanged full retry. The two unreadable-file Pi regressions fail on the base, and both Cline SDK regressions fail without the catalog fix.

title: Speed up class checks in broad lexical searches
body:
## Problem

Broad multi-word searches repeatedly checked event classes for each body posting, adding millions of lookups on dense histories.

Fixes #1152. Follow-up to #1159.

## Fix

Recognize exact segment-wide classes and merge sorted membership lists for mixed blocks. Preserve class precedence, per-class bounds, scoring order, identity ties and all work ceilings. Add regressions and an Unreleased changelog entry.

## Tests

Owning suites and full CI pass (269 targets), including 9,600 independent BM25 comparisons and the late-winner regressions. The new homogeneous-work regression fails on the base. Results are byte-identical when both executions complete, but queries that previously exhausted their budget may now complete because removed work no longer consumes units.

Warm synthetic latency, five warmups and thirty samples per query, on the same immutable corpora:

| Corpus | Words | Before median / p95 ms | After median / p95 ms | Median reduction |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 800,000 messages | 3 | 27.1 / 29.3 | 16.8 / 20.8 | 37.8% |
| 800,000 messages | 4 | 36.7 / 36.9 | 25.8 / 39.1 | 29.7% |
| 800,000 tool outputs | 3 | 42.7 / 61.3 | 15.7 / 16.8 | 63.3% |
| 800,000 tool outputs | 4 | 39.7 / 56.5 | 22.6 / 36.1 | 43.0% |
| 3,000,000 messages | 3 | 100.2 / 103.8 | 56.3 / 56.7 | 43.8% |
| 3,000,000 messages | 4 | 132.4 / 134.1 | 73.5 / 75.2 | 44.5% |
| 3,000,000 tool outputs | 3 | 109.8 / 158.1 | 56.0 / 57.3 | 49.0% |
| 3,000,000 tool outputs | 4 | 138.4 / 176.2 | 73.3 / 73.6 | 47.0% |


Shared-host observations. 800,000 message / 4 words: p95 rose from 36.9 to 39.1 ms (6.0%). All medians improved; these timings are not isolated performance qualification.

title: Fix daemon teardown and serial sift test harness failures
body:
## Problem
Daemon test cleanup could mistake the brief interval between lock release and process exit for a leaked process. The sift runner fixture missed its startup marker when serial libtest printed its progress prefix on the same line, leaving cancellation tests waiting for EOF.

## Fix
Keep the daemon identity checks, wait up to the existing five-second deadline for a released process to exit, and verify the lock has not changed before removing artifacts. Accept only the bare runner marker or its exact serial libtest prefix, reject unrelated prefixes, and exercise cancellation with both one and two child test threads. Add controlled teardown regressions for delayed exit, timeout, lock replacement, and identity mismatches. All changes are test-only.

## Tests
- Current head, after merging main at `483fad33`: all 223 sift tests passed with each of `RUST_TEST_THREADS=1` and `2`; 10/10 uncached serial cancellation runs passed. Strict Clippy, rustfmt, and repository policy passed.
- All 52 affected targets passed under the governor, including 16 native-blame tests.
- Earlier head `faa8bd20`: 50/50 daemon teardown runs, 50/50 cancellation runs at each thread setting, and all 269 full-CI targets passed.

title: Publish daemon lock metadata atomically
body:
## Problem

`ctx status` could briefly report a stale daemon lock while the daemon was starting or updating it, including replacement of a killed owner. Concurrent readers could also fail on empty or partial lock JSON.

## Fix

Publish complete JSON atomically while retaining the existing separate guard, owner identity, and `released: true` handshake. Reclaim abandoned publication temporaries under the exclusive guard, preserving other files and the guard inode.

The updated CLI reports an unverified identity while a held guard has absent or incomplete metadata, or metadata naming a confirmed-dead predecessor. Live-PID identity mismatches remain rejected, and truly abandoned locks remain stale. The metadata format and upgrade protocol remain compatible with 2.4.0; older CLIs retain their existing first-publication reporting limitation.

## Tests

Regressions cover concurrent reads, first publication, killed publishers and restart, guard exclusion, release, older writers, and genuinely stale locks. The killed-owner regression fails with the previous status code. A real replacement paused before publication returns nonrecoverable unverified status through both CLI status commands; free-guard stale and live-PID mismatch controls still pass.

All ten owning targets and `bash scripts/check.sh --mode=ci` (269 targets) passed locally under the governor. Native macOS and Windows execution was not run.

title: release: prepare ctx 2.4.1
body:
Prepare ctx 2.4.1 by updating the workspace, lockfile and plugin versions and replacing Unreleased with the reviewed release notes. Existing dependency versions stay unchanged.

Validation: docs and plugin-version checks, release source audit tests, repository policy checks, Cargo metadata and lock consistency, and frozen Bazel repository resolution passed. The changelog matches the reviewed entry exactly.

title: Windows: Devin import fails because a missing sessions.db-journal surfaces as SystemIo, not NotFound
body:
# What happened?

Devin import fails on Windows. Devin's `sessions.db` is in WAL mode, so `sessions.db-journal` never exists, but the `open_optional` probe treats the missing file as a hard error:

```text
SQLite source snapshot is unavailable: opening a SQLite source family member relative to
retained authority for "C:\\Users\\<user>\\AppData\\Roaming\\devin\\cli\\sessions.db-journal"
failed: system I/O error during provider source target open: ... (os error 2)
```

Claude Code and Cursor import fine. After the failure repeats, `ctx status` shows `Refresh paused`.

Cause (reading `33ba4645`):
- On Windows, a failed `NtOpenFile` becomes `SourceIoError::SystemIo` (`root_handle/windows.rs:579-591`, `diagnostics.rs:58-65`). On Unix it becomes `SourceIoError::Io` (`unix.rs:489`).
- `map_provider_source_error` (`sqlite_source/family.rs:758-780`) maps only `Io` to `SqliteSourceAccessError::Io`. `SystemIo` falls into `SnapshotUnavailable`, which loses the `NotFound` kind.
- `open_optional` (`family.rs:369-383`) returns `None` only for `Io` with `NotFound`.

# What did you expect?

A missing `-journal` should count as absent on Windows, as it does on Unix, so Devin history gets indexed. One possible fix, not built or tested:

```rust
SourceIoError::SystemIo { source, .. } if source.kind() == std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => {
    SqliteSourceAccessError::Io { operation, path: path.to_path_buf(), source }
}
```

# Reproduction steps

1. On Windows, install ctx with `irm https://ctx.rs/install.ps1 | iex`, with Devin CLI local history present (`%APPDATA%\devin\cli\sessions.db` with `-wal` and `-shm`, no `-journal`).
2. Run `ctx import --provider devin`, or `ctx setup --wait`.
3. It fails with the error above every time. A placeholder `-journal` file doesn't help, because ctx rejects one on purpose (`UnsupportedSidecarIdentity`).

# Environment

- Windows 11 Enterprise, build 26100, PowerShell 5.1
- ctx 2.4.1, hosted install
- Devin CLI, local history in WAL mode

title: 2.4.1 import --all cannot upgrade a 2.3.0 index: retired route was not carried
body:
## What happened

ctx 2.4.1 reports an existing index as awaiting a generation upgrade (`lexical.status=awaiting_upgrade`, `history_epoch.reason=generation_upgrade_required`, `generation_matches=false`). The binary and install marker are already 2.4.1. The previous managed version was 2.3.0.

`ctx import --all --incremental --no-blame --format json --progress none` then fails before publishing a new generation:

```
Error: publish provider inputs through the Core refresh engine

Caused by:
    daemon-owned source-backed refresh failed (code=source_refresh_failed, class=internal, retryable=true, retry_advice=Some("retry_request")): run capture-owned source-backed refresh: source route plan is incomplete or internally inconsistent: retired route <64-hex> was not carried when the active route began
```

The same failure happens on a clone of `search/` plus `config.toml` (indexing mode manual, upgrade auto off), so it is not limited to one live lock. A single-provider incremental import on that clone failed separately with `code=source_changed`. `ctx status` on the clone still showed `awaiting_upgrade`. `ctx doctor` lists history and the search index as awaiting upgrade and does not repair this route plan.

## Expected

`ctx import --all` (or `ctx doctor --repair`) should carry or drop the retired route and publish a 2.4.1 generation in place, without deleting the data root.

## Workaround

A new empty data root plus `ctx import --all` (not an in-place upgrade of the 2.3.0 generation).

title: Feature request: `ctx sessions` to list sessions by workspace, provider and time window
body:
## Problem

ctx 2.4.1 can list events (`ctx list events`) and show one session (`ctx show`), but it has no way to list sessions. Questions like "which sessions touched this repository in the last two days?" or "what was the last Codex session in this workspace?" need `ctx list events` pages folded by session ID on the client side. That reads every event in the window just to recover a few dozen session rows.

Agents ask this question constantly when they pick up earlier work: they want the sessions first, then `ctx show` or `ctx search --session` on the one that matters.

## Proposal

Add `ctx sessions`, which reads the active generation and returns one row per session, newest activity first:

```
ctx sessions [--since 2h|30d|RFC3339|DATE] [--provider P] [--workspace SUBSTRING]
             [--no-subagents] [--limit N] [--format text|json]
```

Each row has:

- `ctx_session_id`, `provider`, `provider_key`, `source_id`, `provider_session_id`
- `parent_ctx_session_id`, `root_ctx_session_id`
- `cwd`, `project`, `branch`
- `started_at`, `last_activity_at`, `events`

The JSON wraps them as `{"schema_version": 1, "payload_type": "session_list", "generation_id": ..., "truncated": bool, "sessions": [...]}`.

- `--workspace` uses the same case-insensitive cwd/workspace/project substring match as `ctx list events --workspace`.
- `--no-subagents` drops sessions that have a parent (Claude task/workflow agents, Codex subagents), so the list shows what a person started.
- `--since` also takes relative windows (`2h`, `30d`), which is how agents usually ask.
- Every value comes from the session summary the index already stores, so the command stays a bounded index read with no transcript access.

A follow-up could add the commits each session produced, since Blame already derives session-to-commit attribution.

## Notes

We have been running this in a downstream build for a month, with `ctx_history_index::SessionListFilters` plus an `execute_sessions` read-application entry next to `list` and `show`. The implementation can be shared if that helps, but the CLI and JSON shape above are what matters.

fix(hermes): index tool-call rows stored with empty content
body:
## Problem

Hermes stores `content = ''` for assistant rows that only carry tool calls. `hermes_native_event` treated `''` as present text, so it skipped the existing fallback body and produced a Core record with an empty normalized body. Core rejects that record (`CoreRecord(InvalidContentPolicyState)`), and import reports the row under `Skipped records`. These rows hold the tool-call arguments and reasoning, so the commands an agent ran were missing from search.

On two real installs, every skipped Hermes record was one of these rows: 30,271 across 8 profiles on one machine and 3,481 on another, matching the per-route rejection counts exactly.

## Change

- Treat empty text like absent content, so these rows get the existing fallback body (`tool: <name>` or `Hermes <role>`). The raw empty `content` stays in the structured body.
- Bump the Hermes parser revision and update the two route-control test fixtures that carry it.
- Add a regression test for an assistant tool-call row and a tool row with empty content.

## Validation

- The new test failed before the fix with `CoreRecord(InvalidContentPolicyState)` and passes after.
- Passing: `cargo test -p ctx-history-provider-hermes` (24), `-p ctx-history-capture-composition --features test-support --lib hermes` (8), `-p ctx-history-refresh --lib startup_observation` (5), `-p ctx-daemon-service --lib hermes` (1). The daemon test fails if its fixture keeps the old revision.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` and `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-provider-hermes --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.
- End to end with a snapshot of a real Hermes profile DB containing 296 such rows, a fresh data root reports 296 skipped records with `main` and 0 with this branch.
- Not run: the Bazel suite.

## Open question

An index built before this fix keeps those rows skipped. In my tests, neither the parser revision bump, a later DB change, nor `--reset-cursor` made `ctx import --provider hermes` revisit them; only a fresh data root did. Is there an intended way for a refresh to re-admit previously rejected records, or should this change bump a different revision?

title: fix(history): keep history when providers delete transcripts
body:
Provider cleanup could make a saved ctx event ID stop working on the next refresh. Keep that history, including across index rebuilds, even after the original transcripts are gone.

Since deleting a provider file no longer deletes ctx's copy, add explicit per-session erasure. Erasure discards queued uploads and blocks future indexing and sharing of that ctx session ID within this data root.

title: fix(source-io): qualify ZFS source roots on Linux
body:
Provider history on ZFS cannot be imported on Linux: `fstatfs` reports `ZFS_SUPER_MAGIC`, every source root fails `linux_filesystem_is_qualified`, and `ctx sources` lists providers as `unsupported`. #981 suggested qualifying ZFS but did not test it, and #982/#985 qualified only tmpfs and eCryptfs. OpenZFS meets what the allowlist protects (kernel-local, nanosecond ctime/mtime, per-dataset mount IDs), so this adds it. The eCryptfs backing check shares the allowlist and now accepts ZFS too.

Tested on Linux 7.2 / OpenZFS 2.4.4 with an encrypted ZFS home and temporary directory.

Follows up on #981.

title: Manual selective history pruning without resetting the whole search store
body:
## Problem

Daily agent use over months or years accumulates retained conversations and tool outputs. Operators need a deliberate way to retire history they no longer need in the active index, especially after moving a project to another account. Adding disk capacity or filtering search results does not bound stored history, and exporting an archive alone leaves the indexed copy in place.

In the installed 2.4.1 documentation, `ctx sources remove` withdraws a named root's future refresh ownership but preserves its indexed history. Purging that retained history is documented as removing the root, resetting local search storage and rebuilding. That is a broad operation when the desired change is to retire a small, reviewed subset while preserving unrelated indexed conversations.

## Motivation and impact

The concern is sustainable local storage, not automatic judgments about which conversations an agent finds useful. A complete growing history needs space for the active index, publication and recovery, plus any archives. A manual selective operation would let an operator archive and retire old or migrated material before disk headroom becomes critical, without rebuilding all unrelated history. This is not a claim that ctx lacks internal garbage collection or that every old generation is retained indefinitely.

## Suggested scope

Please consider a manual preview-and-confirm operation for removing an explicitly selected subset of retained history from the local index. The smallest useful version could accept exact source identities, initially restricted to an already-deregistered named root; exact conversation selection could be added where its ownership and refresh semantics are safe.

- Preview the exact selected identities and event counts before mutation. If selectors are available, an explicit last-conversation-update cutoff and existing workspace metadata filter would help identify old project candidates; allow their intersection rather than requiring automatic project classification.
- Treat workspace matching as metadata, not exclusive project ownership. Keep whole-conversation semantics, identify uncertain or mixed scope where known, and require the operator to review the final selection. Missing timestamps must not silently qualify as old.
- Preserve unrelated indexed history and provider-native files. Make any destructive operation explicit; keep archive export/verification as a separate supported preparation step rather than introducing an archive planner or incremental transfer system.
- Define refresh behavior before allowing pruning. Reject a selection that remains actively discoverable unless there is a supported explicit way to keep it retired; do not let the next refresh silently undo the operation or change global indexing policy.
- Report logical removal separately from physical space reclamation. Respect readers and recovery retention, and explain when storage can be reclaimed rather than promising that removed event counts translate directly to freed bytes.

Age and workspace filters are conveniences, not prerequisites for the minimal exact-source operation, but definitely relevant for a tool like this and having so many projects and conversations. I have already more than 40GiB of indexes having conversations along more than 50 projects, all from the same harness (provider). Disk saturation is a real problem, and ctx should provide ways to prune/clean old conversations and/or per project, otherwise we keep fiding the disk and we have no ways to solve the situation, just keep getting it worse every day.
If only deregistered roots can be handled safely at first, that would still improve project migration and cold-history workflows.

## Deliberately excluded

No last-access or "less used" tracking, automatic eviction, inactivity scoring, unified project views, incremental archives, or deletion of native conversations. The operator chooses what to retire and when. A missing or ambiguous selection should fail closed, not expand to all history.

## Relationship to the earlier request

I recognize that #1153 was declined with a preference for keeping the index complete and leaving archiving manual. I am not requesting its usage tracking, automatic inactivity policy or project activity reporting again. This narrower request is for an explicitly destructive manual storage-maintenance operation replacing the documented whole-store reset/rebuild when only a selected retired source is unwanted. If selective retirement itself is outside that product boundary, clarification of that limitation would be useful rather than implying the earlier proposal has been accepted.

## Evidence and validation

The request is based on the installed 2.4.1 command and storage documentation, not a confirmed reconciliation bug. Small isolated native fixtures successfully removed indexed events after provider history was moved outside discovery, while a live migration removal remained unresolved and was rolled back. Those results do not establish a general deletion defect or a reliable index-only pruning workflow.

A minimal acceptance case would retain two independently selected sources, deregister one, preview and explicitly prune only that source, verify the other source is unchanged, and run another refresh to check that the retired source does not return. A verified archive should remain restorable through the existing archive workflow. Physical reclamation should be measured independently after applicable reader and recovery lifetimes.

title: fix(codex): retain sub-agent lifecycle notices
body:
## Summary

Retain Codex `item_completed` / `SubAgentActivity` lifecycle records as source-backed notices rather than rejecting the known variant. These are provider notices, not inferred conversation or parent/child relationships.

- Validate the known lifecycle kinds and closed payload shape; reject malformed selectors, duplicate fields, and unknown payload additions.
- Preserve the original structured metadata and turn-qualified completed-item identity.
- Bump the Codex capture revision so previously rejected records can be reparsed.
- Add synthetic regression fixtures for lifecycle kinds, malformed/future variants, distinct identities across turns, append/no-op/cold replay, and raw/zstd equivalence.

This is deliberately scoped: `EnteredReviewMode`, `ExitedReviewMode`, and `Extension` remain explicitly unsupported. It does not silently accept opaque extension payloads or change raw conversation authority.

## Validation

On the repository-pinned Rust 1.97.1:
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-provider-codex --locked`: 127 passed.
- `cargo test -p ctx-history-capture-composition-qualification --test provider_lifecycle paginated_item_completed --locked`: 3 passed.
- `cargo clippy -p ctx-history-provider-codex --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings`: passed.
- Formatting for both touched packages, provider-support matrix validation, LOC guardrail, and staged diff checks: passed.

Full local `provider_lifecycle` suite: **105 passed, 5 failed** on macOS. An unchanged-base comparison at `33ba4645b620fd89d138c6db1fabf33096a0ee16` reproduced the same 105 passes and identical five failures:
- `compound_root_ownership::released_compound_roots_filter_exactly_and_preserve_automatic_peers_and_bytes`
- `compound_root_ownership::released_shared_route_build_is_independent_of_root_order`
- `openclaw_v19::native_openclaw_v19_discovery_import_repeat_and_readonly`
- `released_root_equivalence::matching_released_roots_reproduce_automatic_authority_and_record_bytes`
- `released_root_equivalence::moved_released_roots_survive_restart_and_second_move_without_rotating_bytes`

The failures concern Lingma/OpenClaw SQLite route availability, not the Codex change. No tests were skipped or relaxed. Full repository/Bazel CI has not been run locally. Fixtures contain synthetic identifiers and no private session content.

title: Antigravity: no provider-local root override; automatic brain root can exceed the 32,768-directory inventory bound
body:
**Type:** capability request / capacity limit. This is not a parsing bug.

**Version:** ctx 2.4.1 (tag `v2.4.1`, `33ba4645b620fd89d138c6db1fabf33096a0ee16`), Linux.

### What happens

The Antigravity automatic root (`$HOME/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain`) can grow past the JSONL membership inventory bound (32,768 directories) even when only a small part of it holds transcripts. The route then fails with `JSONL membership directory count exceeds the provider inventory bound`.

On a real machine the brain tree has 37,870 directories. Only about 500 transcript selector candidates (`transcript_full.jsonl` / `transcript.jsonl`) exist, and they need about 1,501 parent and ancestor directories.

There is no supported way to point Antigravity alone at a narrower root:

- **No provider-specific environment variable.** `crates/ctx-history-source-discovery/src/provider_sources/resolvers/platform.rs:482-499` always resolves `context.home()/.gemini/{antigravity-cli,antigravity-ide}/brain`. Gemini has `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`, Grok has `GROK_HOME`, and so on, but Antigravity has no equivalent.
- **A named root is appended, not used as a replacement.** `ctx sources add <name> --provider antigravity --root <dir>` adds the root, but `provider_sources/discovery.rs:305-330` still keeps the automatic root, so `import --all` still walks it.
- **`[sources] automatic = false` is global.** See `crates/ctx-app-config/src/lib.rs:311-313,505-506`. Using it to drop one provider means registering roots for every other provider by hand.
- **Changing `HOME` moves every HOME-based provider at once.**

The inventory walk (`crates/ctx-history-jsonl/src/family/route/membership.rs:295-311,372-380`) counts every directory it enters. It recurses whether or not that subtree can contain a selected file.

### Minimal reproduction (sketch)

1. Use an isolated `HOME` and `--data-root`.
2. Put one valid synthetic `transcript.jsonl` under `$HOME/.gemini/antigravity-cli/brain/<session>/…`.
3. Add 32,768 empty directories elsewhere under `brain/`.
4. Run `ctx import --all --incremental --format json`. The Antigravity route fails on the inventory bound.
5. Run `ctx sources add view --provider antigravity --root <narrow-copy>`, then `ctx sources --provider antigravity --format json`. Both roots are listed. With global `automatic = false`, only the named root is left.

We have confirmed the configuration behaviour in steps 4–5 at small scale. We have not run the full 32,768-directory import in isolation; it was observed on real data.

### Request

Any one of these would fix it:

- a provider-local root override for Antigravity, similar to `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` or `GROK_HOME`;
- a per-provider `automatic` switch, so a named root can stand in for the automatic one;
- pruning of subtrees that cannot contain selector files, if that is compatible with the membership-safety design.

It would also help to know whether the bound is meant to apply to unrelated directories.

Related, and already fixed in 2.4.1: #1145, #1068, #664.

title: GEMINI_CLI_HOME missing from DAEMON_CHILD_ENV_ALLOWLIST: finite worker / autostarted daemon imports $HOME/.gemini instead of the custom root
body:
**Type:** bug. `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` is dropped when the daemon launches a finite worker or an autostarted detached daemon.

**Version:** ctx 2.4.1 (tag `v2.4.1`, `33ba4645b620fd89d138c6db1fabf33096a0ee16`), Linux.

### What happens

With `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` set in the client environment, `ctx sources --provider gemini` resolves the custom root correctly. But `ctx import --all` imports from `$HOME/.gemini` instead. On a large real `~/.gemini` tree, this then fails with `JSONL membership directory count exceeds the provider inventory bound`.

### Cause (source)

- `crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle/launch.rs:50-65,80-157` copies the parent environment into the child through `DAEMON_CHILD_ENV_ALLOWLIST`. The list has `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, `CODEX_HOME`, `GROK_HOME` and `PI_CODING_AGENT_SESSION_DIR`, but not `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`.
- `crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/launch.rs:66-74` runs the child with `env_clear().envs(launch.environment)`, so any key missing from the list is lost.
- The Gemini resolver (`crates/ctx-history-source-discovery/src/provider_sources/resolvers/simple.rs:442-460`) reads `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`. When it is unset, it falls back to `HOME`.
- For comparison, `DISCOVERY_ENV_ALLOWLIST` in `crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/supervisor/environment.rs` does include `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`. Only the child-launch list is missing it.

### Minimal reproduction

No large directory tree is needed. The bug shows up as the wrong root being selected.

1. Use an isolated `HOME=H` and `--data-root D`, with `indexing.mode = manual`. Add one valid Gemini chat file under `H/.gemini/tmp/workspace/chats/` (sessionId A), and another under `V/.gemini/tmp/workspace/chats/` (sessionId B).
2. `GEMINI_CLI_HOME=V ctx --data-root D sources --provider gemini --format json` lists `V/.gemini`. This is correct.
3. Run `GEMINI_CLI_HOME=V CODEX_HOME=... ctx --data-root D import --all --incremental --format json`. The finite worker's `/proc/<pid>/environ` contains `CODEX_HOME` but not `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`. The index contains only sessionId **A**, from the native root. Codex follows its custom root.
4. Control: start `ctx --data-root D daemon run --force` in the foreground with `GEMINI_CLI_HOME=V`, then run the same import with `--no-daemon`. The index now contains sessionId **B**.

We ran steps 1–4 in isolation with the authentic resume capture fixture from `tests/fixtures/provider-history/gemini/`. The result was the same with all five provider variables set: the child kept four of them and dropped only `GEMINI_CLI_HOME`.

### Suggested fix

Add `GEMINI_CLI_HOME` to `DAEMON_CHILD_ENV_ALLOWLIST`. A regression test could assert on the environment of the spawned child together with the imported session, rather than only on `sources` output. It may also help to derive the child list from the discovery list, so the two cannot drift apart.

Related, but a different problem: #1188. Antigravity has no root override at all, and adding this key does not fix that.

title: A finite `ctx import` killed by its caller's timeout leaves its auto-started daemon rebuilding for an hour in manual mode
body:
## What happened

With indexing mode `manual`, a finite `ctx import --provider claude --quiet` was wrapped in `timeout 220` (a scheduled-job budget). The CLI was killed at 220 s, but the daemon it started kept running for 53 minutes, until I stopped it by hand:

```
ctx --data-root <root> daemon run --start-mode auto --trigger-command import
```

During that time:
- `ctx index --format json` still reported `indexing.mode = "manual"`;
- the daemon's `VmHWM` was 4.08 GB (it ran inside a 4 GiB cgroup cap) and it had pushed 7.3 GB into swap;
- `refresh.physical_attempt_state` was `running`, with about 23 of 26 GB processed, so the daemon carried on with the whole generation rebuild that the import had triggered (`lexical.reason = generation_upgrade_required`).

Once I stopped the daemon's cgroup, `ctx index` reported `daemon.status = "stale_lock"`.

So a caller that bounds a finite import by time still gets an unbounded background job, in manual mode, with nothing tying the daemon's lifetime to the request that started it. On a shared host that job was the biggest memory user, and the caller had no way to see it.

## Environment

- ctx 2.4.1, official Linux x86_64 binary; the index was created by 2.3.0 and is awaiting a generation upgrade (this may be the same index state as #1178)
- Linux 7.3 (Arch-based), systemd user session, no ctx-managed supervisor unit active
- About 26 GB of certified source, about 23.8k sessions, Blame on
- The import ran under `systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=4G -- flock … timeout 220 nice -n 15 ctx … import --provider claude --quiet`

## Reproduction notes

On a fresh scratch `--data-root` with one to forty Claude Code session files, the same timed-out import never starts a daemon: the import runs in-process and the root reports `daemon.status = "disabled"`. The daemon only appeared on the existing index whose refresh is daemon-owned, here a generation upgrade. I have not built a small repro of that state.

## Expected

One of the following:
- a daemon started only to serve a finite import (`--trigger-command import`, mode manual) stops when its requesting CLI goes away, or after the import's refresh attempt ends, rather than continuing a full rebuild nobody is waiting for; or
- `ctx import` documents that the work outlives the CLI and gives a bound, such as `--max-runtime` or a cancel-on-disconnect flag, so schedulers can keep the job inside their budget; and
- `ctx status` / `ctx index` show a detached refresh that is still running, plus how to cancel it.

Related: #1124 (a search silently starting a persistent indexer), #1097 and #1107 (finite scheduled maintenance), #1178 (2.3.0 to 2.4.1 generation upgrade).

title: Pi importer reports OMP's `changes.jsonl` edit journal as an unreadable source
body:
## Summary

Since OMP 18.20.1, each OMP session writes an edit journal, `changes.jsonl`, to its artifacts directory next to the session file ([source](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/commit/selective/journal.ts)). The journal has no session header. Its records are `{"type":"call"|"change"|"commit",…}`.

The Pi importer reads every `*.jsonl` under an OMP root, so it reports each journal as `unreadable` and `ctx import` exits 1. The session transcripts still import. Since #1161 each failure is isolated to its own file. But OMP writes a journal on every shell call or file edit, so the failure count grows with each new session and a healthy OMP tree never imports cleanly.

## Environment

```text
ctx 2.4.1
OMP 18.20.3
```

## Reproduction

```bash
REPRO="$(cd "$(mktemp -d)" && pwd -P)"
export HOME="$REPRO/home"; mkdir -p "$HOME"
S="$REPRO/sessions/-tmp-proj"
ID=2026-11-16T00-00-00-000Z_01a01e7d-c7ed-7000-a578-c944045672fe
mkdir -p "$S/$ID"
cat > "$S/$ID.jsonl" <<'JSONL'
{"type":"title","v":1,"title":"Minimal reproduction","source":"auto","updatedAt":"2026-11-16T00:00:00.000Z","pad":""}
{"type":"session","version":3,"id":"01a01e7d-c7ed-7000-a578-c944045672fe","timestamp":"2026-11-16T00:00:00.000Z","cwd":"/tmp/proj"}
{"type":"message","id":"11111111","parentId":null,"timestamp":"2026-11-16T00:00:01.000Z","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Hello from the reproduction fixture."}],"timestamp":1794787201000}}
{"type":"message","id":"22222222","parentId":"11111111","timestamp":"2026-11-16T00:00:02.000Z","message":{"role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Hello back."}],"timestamp":1794787202000}}
JSONL
echo '{"type":"call","agent":"Main","tool":"bash","start":1794787203000,"label":"echo hi","end":1794787203100}' > "$S/$ID/changes.jsonl"
ctx --data-root "$REPRO/ctx" sources add omp --provider pi --root "$REPRO/sessions"
ctx --data-root "$REPRO/ctx" import --provider pi; echo "exit=$?"
```

## Actual result

```text
! History import completed with source failures
Sessions           1
Searchable events  2
Source 1  $REPRO/sessions/-tmp-proj/<ID>/changes.jsonl (pi, unreadable): Pi source has no valid session header within the bounded identity probe
✗ 1 import source failed; first failure: Pi source has no valid session header within the bounded identity probe
exit=1
```

If you delete `changes.jsonl`, the same import exits 0.

## Expected result

The importer skips OMP's `changes.jsonl` inside a session's artifacts directory without reporting a failure, and the import exits 0.

Related: #1145, #1161

title: Lexical generation upgrade has no memory bound: on a 26 GB corpus it fills a 4 GiB cgroup, stalls ~70% of the time, and keeps two 58 GB generations
body:
### What happened

After upgrading to ctx 2.4.1, `status` reports `lexical.reason = generation_upgrade_required` and every refresh starts a full rebuild of the lexical generation. On a 26 GB history corpus (Claude, Codex, Hermes and pi sources, `sources.automatic = false`, semantic off), that rebuild cannot finish inside a memory budget a workstation can spare:

| | measured |
|---|---|
| corpus (source bytes) | ~26 GB |
| one lexical generation on disk | 58 GB (active) + 58 GB (previous) + a third in progress |
| rebuild progress under a 4 GiB cgroup (`MemoryMax=4G`, `MemoryHigh=3.5G`, `MemorySwapMax=1G`) | 14 GB of new generation in 43 min, then stopped by us |
| cgroup `memory.pressure` during the rebuild | `full avg10=68.87 avg60=74.22 avg300=71.15` (stalled ~70% of the time) |
| daemon RSS | at the cap the whole run (VmHWM 4.08 GB earlier, plus swap) |

So the rebuild is memory-bound with no way to tell ctx to use less: it fills any cap it is given and then thrashes, and the host-wide memory pressure it causes (`some avg60=54`) is what we have to stop it for.

### What I looked for

- No documented setting for indexing memory. The binary reads `CTX_CORE_PREPARATION_WORKERS` and `RAYON_NUM_THREADS`, but neither is documented as bounding memory, and the tantivy writer heap is not exposed.
- `ctx status` / `progress` do not report expected peak memory or remaining work for a generation upgrade, so a caller cannot admit it safely.

### Asks

1. A documented knob that bounds rebuild memory (writer heap and worker count), and a statement of how peak RSS scales with corpus size, so a capped rebuild finishes slowly instead of thrashing.
2. Keep at most one previous generation, or say how to drop it: during an upgrade the store holds two full generations plus the one being built (~2.2x the corpus each).
3. Report the upgrade's estimated total and its done-so-far in `status`, so a supervisor can decide to run it now or later.

ctx 2.4.1, Linux x86_64, data root on btrfs HDD, daemon disabled (`daemon_mode = source-refresh-only`), rebuild started by `ctx import --all`.

title: `ctx import` exits with 'daemon source refresh queue is full (8/8)' while the daemon keeps running the rebuild it was handed
body:
### What happened

A supervised `ctx import --all` (ctx 2.4.1) exited with:

```
Error: publish provider inputs through the Core refresh engine

Caused by:
    daemon source refresh queue is full (8/8 active or pending requests); retry after a refresh finishes
```

while the daemon it handed the work to kept running a full lexical rebuild (`generation_upgrade_required`) for about 45 more minutes. Our supervisor had to treat the importer's exit as "import failed" even though the rebuild was progressing; from then on the only live signal was the daemon's own status.

About ten long-lived `ctx mcp serve` processes (one per agent session) were connected to the same data root at the time.

### Expected

One of:

- the import waits for, or attaches to, the in-flight refresh and exits when it finishes (with its result), or
- the error names the in-flight request id so a caller can poll it, and exits with a distinct code for "accepted elsewhere, still running" versus "failed".

### Related

#1190: the same import/daemon hand-off, when the import is killed by a timeout, leaves the daemon rebuilding in manual mode.

title: Preserve daemon state during external ctx replacement
body:
## Problem

Replacing an unmanaged ctx executable requires installation-wide quiescence. The existing removal handoff persists manual indexing for every registered root. A package update needs to quiesce the same roots while preserving their indexing choices.

## Change

Add a Unix pipe protocol for owner-writable unmanaged installs. The installed or staged executable acquires the existing installation lock and daemon handoff. The installer receives a ready receipt, atomically publishes its verified candidate, and sends commit. If stdin closes, the handoff resumes the original or staged executable according to the observed command path.

Retain the previous registration namespace across publication. Settle publication before restarting so the installation fence cannot block secondary roots. The existing native restart path remains responsible for readiness.

## Verification

- Linux Bazel on `f6f8bf14b`: all 199 `//crates/ctx-upgrade-engine:unit_tests` and both `//crates/ctx-daemon-cli:unmanaged_daemon_tests` passed with `--config=test --config=dev-linux`.
- The executable contract covers two running roots and a retained manual root, concurrent refusal, in-place replacement, symlink changes, and disconnect before and after publication.
- Formatting and git whitespace checks passed.

title: Use the shared scratch budget for large Zstd rollouts
body:
Codex rollouts could exceed the 256 MiB per-leaf cap while their compressed snapshot and decoded spool fit within the existing 1 GiB route budget. The catalog and reader now admit a leaf against that shared budget. Worker admission uses the largest bounded spool in the batch to keep the sum of concurrent spools within the route budget. Decompression still enforces the expansion ratio, the frame window and the certified compressed prefix.

The regression constructs a synthetic multi-frame Zstd stream that decodes past 256 MiB. It fails on current main at the combined per-leaf scratch limit and passes with this change. Small inputs still qualify for four workers, and a large input selects one.

Verified with Rust 1.97.1 and `cargo test --locked -p ctx-history-jsonl -p ctx-history-provider-codex --features ctx-history-jsonl/test-support,ctx-history-provider-codex/test-support --lib`. All 267 tests passed.

title: macOS: a default-mode `ctx search` boots out a healthy launchd daemon, then times out ("daemon did not become ready") while the replacement is still starting
body:
## Summary

On macOS, a default-mode `ctx search` (refresh `background`) booted out a live, 25-hour-old launchd daemon, reinstalled the LaunchAgent, and then gave up after about 120 seconds with `ctx daemon did not become ready`, while the replacement daemon was still starting. The replacement served again about 2.5 minutes after the bootout. Nothing was wrong with the old daemon beforehand: it was making network and fsevents calls up to the bootout, and an external health check had passed it 2 minutes 40 seconds earlier.

So a read-only search caused the outage it then reported.

## Environment

- ctx 2.3.0, hosted installer, managed data root `~/.ctx`, indexing mode `auto`, semantic enabled, `[upgrade] auto = "off"`
- macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon, 14 CPUs, launchd GUI domain, label `rs.ctx.daemon`
- The search was run by a coding agent (Claude Code) through `zsh`. Several agent harnesses on this machine call ctx concurrently.
- Heavy host load. `uptime` 15 minutes after the incident: `load averages: 77.96 51.64 35.20`.

## What happened

The client was `ctx search --limit 8 -- "<query>"`, no `--refresh` flag. It started at 20:30:18.620Z and exited at 20:32:18.021Z (119.4 s) with:

```text
✗ start or recover daemon before source-backed refresh
  ctx daemon did not become ready. Run `ctx status --format json`, then `ctx daemon run` for details: timed out waiting for live daemon lifecycle readiness
```

`log show` for launchd/launchctl over that window (local time, UTC−8):

```text
12:30:21.79–21.85  launchctl print ×3
12:30:22.032  [gui/501/rs.ctx.daemon [37687]:] booting out service: caller = launchctl[14191]<-ctx[13124]<-zsh[13113]<-claude[25168]<-…
              signaled service: Terminated: 15
12:30:23.131  [37687] exited due to exit(1), ran for 89847468ms
12:30:23.190  launchctl bootstrap  → spawned pid 14581
12:30:23.208  launchctl kickstart  → [14581] signaled service for aborting trampoline: Killed: 9
              Service only ran for 0 seconds. Pushing respawn out by 10 seconds.
12:30:33.214  xpcproxy spawned with pid 16149
```

Afterwards `launchctl print gui/501/rs.ctx.daemon` showed `runs = 2` and `last terminating signal = Terminated: 15`. In `~/.ctx/daemon/`, the client had written a new supervisor environment snapshot (`captured_at_ms` = 12:30:21) and `status.json` for pid 16149 (`started_at_ms` = 12:30:33, `start_mode: manual`). pid 16149 was serving by 12:32:47, 29 seconds after the client gave up.

No other agent session ran a ctx lifecycle command in that window. I extracted tool calls from every Claude Code transcript modified that day (11:00–12:33 local) and every OMP transcript (11:30–12:36 local). This search was the only ctx or launchctl call.

## What the code appears to do (v2.3.0)

The launchd sequence above (`print`, `bootout`, `bootstrap`, `kickstart -k`) is exactly [`install_launch_agent`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/supervisor/platform.rs#L390-L425) plus [`start_launch_agent`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/supervisor/platform.rs#L515-L523). In [`ensure_native_supervisor_with`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/supervisor/mod.rs#L75-L160), that path runs whenever `backend.verify_registration(...)` fails. The live-owner check only runs on the branch where registration verified. When registration fails, the code goes straight to `prepare_mutation` and `install`, and never asks whether the current owner is healthy.

On macOS, [`verify_launch_agent_registration`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-runtime/src/supervisor/platform.rs#L455-L477) fails if any of these is true:

1. `verify_supervisor_environment(spec)` fails. The spec is built from the calling process's environment.
2. The plist on disk is not byte-identical to the plist rendered from the caller's spec.
3. `launchctl print` exits non-zero.

All three depend on the caller or on launchctl latency, not on whether the daemon is healthy. This is the class of problem in #1002 (locale variables), which was fixed for `LANG`. I confirmed that a `LANG`-only difference no longer sets `restart_required` in 2.3.0. I could not determine which of the three checks failed here, because the client writes no log of its decision and the daemon's stdout and stderr go to `/dev/null`.

There is a second, separate recovery path in [`lifecycle.rs`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs#L591-L606). After a `DaemonHandoffTimeout` with an existing owner, [`recover_unusable_daemon_owner`](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs#L255-L327) terminates an identity-verified owner if one lifecycle-endpoint probe bounded by [`DAEMON_HEALTH_TIMEOUT` = 500 ms](https://github.com/ctxrs/ctx/blob/v2.3.0/crates/ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs#L60) returns `Unavailable`. The bootout sequence above matches the supervisor reinstall, not this path. Still, on this host the daemon has missed 10-second status and socket-accept deadlines 15 times in a week (external health-check log). A single 500 ms probe is not a reliable liveness signal under that load.

## Problems

1. **A retrieval command replaces a healthy daemon.** A failed registration or environment comparison triggers `bootout` of the live owner without checking whether that owner is healthy. The daemon had a fresh heartbeat and was doing work.
2. **`bootstrap` followed immediately by `kickstart -k` kills the process `bootstrap` just spawned.** That cost a 10-second launchd respawn throttle: `Service only ran for 0 seconds. Pushing respawn out by 10 seconds.`
3. **The client gives up before a cold start can finish.** The search exited after 119 s. The replacement was serving after about 134 s from spawn. The client reported a failure that resolved on its own half a minute later. (I did not find a 120 s constant. The constants I found are the 5 s resettable handoff stall timeout and the 500 ms health probe, so the 119 s is the measured wall time.)
4. **The error hint points users at `ctx daemon run`.** After a supervised daemon fails to become ready, a foreground `ctx daemon run` competes with the launchd-managed replacement. For a supervised install, `ctx status --format json` and waiting seem like the right advice.

## Expected

- A search (or any retrieval command) does not boot out a live owner whose identity verifies and whose heartbeat is fresh. If the registration differs from what this caller would write, report `stale_registration` and leave the reinstall to `ctx index mode auto` or the next supervisor-owned maintenance.
- If a reinstall is required, don't `kickstart -k` the job that `bootstrap` has just started.
- When the client starts or replaces the daemon itself, its readiness wait covers a cold start on the current index, or it returns a non-error "starting" result (as #791 asked for `ctx setup`).
- The client records why it chose recovery, e.g. a line in `ctx status` or a `~/.ctx/daemon/` receipt, so the next report like this can name the failed check.

## 2.4.x

I don't think 2.4.0 or 2.4.1 changes this. `git log v2.3.0..v2.4.1` touches none of `ctx-daemon-application/src/lifecycle.rs`, `ctx-daemon-application/src/supervisor.rs`, `ctx-daemon-runtime/src/supervisor/`, `ctx-daemon-runtime/src/handoff/` or `source_backed_refresh_coordinator/`. #1175 (atomic lock metadata, in 2.4.1) changes how a status reader sees a lock while it is being published. It does not change the registration-verification reinstall path. I have not reproduced this on 2.4.1.

## Related

- #1002: supervisor verdict flipping with the caller's `LANG` caused needless restarts (closed). Same class, different variable.
- #791: same error text from `ctx setup` when startup exceeded the 5 s handoff (closed).
- #1097: finite refresh waits time out during productive work (closed, Linux).
- #999: a live daemon was misreported as `stale_lock` (closed, Linux).
- #1190: a finite import's auto-started daemon outlives its caller (open). Adjacent: a client-driven lifecycle decision outlives the client.

title: docs: align Codex Zstd scratch budget notes with shared 1 GiB limit
body: Follow-up to #1195. Updates docs/limitations.md and docs/provider-import-policy.md to match the shared 1 GiB scratch budget limit updated in docs/providers.md and docs/provider-support-matrix.json.

title: fix(hermes): escalate incremental refresh when parser revision changes
body: Follow-up to #1183. Ensures hermes_incremental_requires_exhaustive and may_increment check parser_revision against HERMES_SOURCE_PARSER_REVISION so incremental refreshes escalate to exhaustive re-capture after a parser revision bump, with a regression test.

title: test(history): update Codex Zstd leaf limit tests for 1 GiB scratch budget
body: Updates downstream Codex Zstd leaf limit tests in `ctx-history-capture-composition-qualification` and `ctx-history-refresh-execution` to match the 1 GiB shared scratch budget introduced in #1195.

title: fix(cli,observability): health optional sub-paths and local usage store recovery
body:
Combines two fixes:
- Do not mark configured roots partial for absent optional sub-paths in history health checks.
- Recover the local usage store from stale SHM and replayable WAL on write.

title: refactor(upgrade): move external replacement pipe and protocol check out of ctx-cli
body: Follow-up refactor to #1194 moving external replacement pipe and protocol check out of `ctx-cli` into `ctx-cli-presentation` and `ctx-upgrade-engine`.

title: test(terminal): allowlist external replacement stdout protocol in raw output policy
body: Follow-up to #1194 and #1201: register `crates/ctx-upgrade-engine/src/upgrade/command/external.rs` in `raw_output_policy` as a framed JSON pipe stdout boundary.

title: fix(terminal): exit cleanly on BrokenPipe across CLI stdout/stderr paths
body: Handle `BrokenPipe` cleanly across CLI stdout/stderr output paths in `ctx-terminal` and `ctx-cli`, with regression coverage in `offline_default`.

title: Allow flat manifest deltas to carry added sources
body:
Extend `ctx-manifest-flat-delta-v1` with optional canonical `added`, `route_additions`, and `generation_state` fields and raise the flat-delta ceiling to 1024 touched sources (8 MiB) so steady-state refreshes that discover new sessions persist small flat deltas instead of rewriting corpus-sized full manifests.

Preserves strict backward compatibility with existing flat deltas, enforces full canonical sorting, disjointness, exact source descriptor preservation, 1:1 route-addition bijection, and full-manifest fallback on removals or structural changes.
